data.brief: Google's open protocol for agent intercommunication (agent cards carrying name/description/capabilities, plus extensions such as A2UI); at OpenGov repurposed as the internal spec for agent routes — the rigorous contract both front end and back end consume and produce
data.name: A2A (agent-to-agent) protocol

data.brief: Google's open spec for declarative generative UI: the agent streams UI-as-data component blocks alongside conversation blocks; clients render them natively and fall back safely on unknown types
data.name: A2UI

data.brief: The #1 OWASP vulnerability class (~$30B industry): logic-based access breaks (not code bugs) where two very large systems check the same thing differently and a seam lets a low-privileged user reach privileged actions — requires reasoning across the system, not pattern-matching
data.name: Access-control logic vulnerabilities

data.brief: Prompted instructions fail because they live in the agent's memory and get compacted away or argued around — an alignment director's "confirm before deleting" did not stop 200 deletions. Two layers outside the agent instead: deterministic access control over what it can reach (a hiring agent reads email only; a support agent creates drafts but cannot send), which cannot be forgotten, plus natural-language policies over behavior within that reach ("never delete more than ten emails without my permission," "never email outside this domain"). Together: gates sized to blast radius, as branches, code owners and preview deployments are for code, so the agent can "go berserk" on safe paths and never touch the unsafe ones
data.name: Access plus policy governance

data.brief: At the bottom of every real decision a human signs, and accountability cannot be delegated to software. Evidence offered is an airline whose website chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy and which then argued at tribunal that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions — "the corporate version of my dog ate my homework"; the tribunal disagreed and the airline paid. Product requirement: a real human approval gate that is logged — who reviewed what, what changed, when they signed — and that log is the audit trail. "If your architecture doesn't have an accountable human at the end of it, you have not built a product, you have built an excuse generator."
data.name: Accountable human signature

data.brief: Live AI voice tutor that runs a full multi-step lesson start-to-finish reliably by keeping the LLM out of the control loop
data.name: Ace

data.brief: Open JSON-RPC protocol from Zed standardizing agent↔client communication, LSP/MCP-style: initialize/authenticate/session/prompt lifecycle; streamed session updates (agent message chunks, tool-call → tool-call-update status); diff content type (agent sends old/new text, client renders the diff); client-advertised capabilities the agent can call back into (buffer-aware file-system proxy, managed terminals). Transport is stdio today; remote transport in progress (JetBrains)
data.name: Agent Client Protocol (ACP)

data.brief: Classic ML technique repurposed for LLM agents: instead of reviewing every output, select the cases the system is most likely to get wrong and spend human attention there; for LLMs the reliable selection strategy is disagreement across repeated runs/models (query-by-committee), not self-reported confidence
data.name: Active learning (for agent QC)

data.brief: Open-source, event-sourced graph runtime for auditable agents (BabyAGI 4). A single immutable typed event log — recording both what the agent does AND every change to the agent — is the ground truth; agent state is a graph projected from it. Behaviors subscribe to graph changes (subscriptions can be graph queries, e.g. claim-contradicts-claim) and emit events; LLMs never talk to each other, only through shared state; views = graph queries as context management; policies gate what may change autonomously vs via proposed patch vs human-in-the-loop; packs bundle object schemas, tools, behaviors, and pack policies into modular harnesses (core/tool/secret/memory/identity/communication/chat), loadable across repos. Replay, rollback, and forks come natively. Explicitly "not a harness — a runtime": common harnesses (e.g. ReAct) can be rebuilt on top.
data.name: ActiveGraph

data.brief: Why the weight-sync link can shrink by three orders of magnitude. Two ingredients. The floor: the optimizer keeps high-precision master weights, but the rollout engine serves a low-precision *view*, and a BF16 value only changes if the update crosses the nearest rounding boundary — roughly half a ULP, about θ/256, ≈0.0039 for weights near 1. The push: an Adam step is the learning rate times a normalized direction (the raw gradient is divided by running gradient statistics), so the per-weight push is bounded on the order of the learning rate — at RL post-training rates, ~3e-6. The push is more than a thousand times smaller than the floor, so the served value does not move. Crucially this is *not* a claim that the master weights are frozen: "it is saying the value that the rollout engine would serve does not change." Small weights move; large weights absorb their updates
data.name: Adam absorption

data.brief: The synthesis: web-data infrastructure "is not a build-once business, it's an adapt-forever business" — targets, layouts, detection, market, and client needs all change constantly, so "innovation is the ability to keep adapting fast enough that changing requirements become new infrastructure." The value proposition: "you build the intelligence, we take the messy maintenance underneath." The closing thesis — "the next generation of AI will not be powered by better models; it will be powered by better infrastructure around it" that connects models to reality
data.name: Adapt-forever infrastructure

data.brief: On-device agent that dynamically tunes accessibility "dials" (input tolerance, step granularity) to the player's live context — grounded in WCAG 2.2's four pillars and following WCAG 3.0's shift from binary pass/fail to graded bronze/silver/gold; senses friction (eye-gaze vision models, shaky taps, keyboard focus traps), flags violations, and rewrites the layout live (resizes targets, injects exit routes) — adapting the game to the human
data.name: Adaptive accessibility agent

data.brief: Deployment monitoring beyond fixed CI/CD checks: on each release event (a GitHub tag in Slack), the agent reads the actual changes, works out which telemetry would evaluate those changes, and builds a customized check plan for that specific release — e.g. checkout replaces the currency service → watch checkout latency and error rates *and* the Kafka pipeline as the causal chain. Nothing hard-coded: the agent chooses its own re-check cadence and watch window ("maybe I'll come back in 3 days"), and the same mechanism covers change systems that bypass CI/CD entirely — feature flags, infra changes — which today get no monitoring beyond "trusting that an alert might fire"
data.name: Change-aware deployment verification

data.brief: Chandegra's proposed successor discipline to fixed-harness ("factory"/Taylorist) AI engineering: instead of pre-engineering roles, tools, and sequencing ahead of runtime, the engineer designs *constraints* — enable vs govern, reward coherence toward a goal vs cost excursions outside a container, tune the coupling rate — and lets the harness emerge, stabilize, adapt, and dissolve mid-runtime from agent interactions: "the harness becomes the ongoing output rather than the input".
data.description: Grounded in complexity science (emergence, attractors, self-organization, specialization from local interaction, conventions without a governor); distinguishes *horizontal intelligence* (group coordination — his claimed higher-leverage axis) from *vertical intelligence* (making individual agents smarter, e.g. Hermes-style skill learning); named failure modes: drift without genuine selection pressure, monoculture (agents trained on the same data lack diversity), legibility collapse, no predictability ahead of runtime
data.name: Adaptive engineering

data.brief: Evals as the operating system: benchmarks before any product, staged rollout (alpha clinicians who understand the stakes → beta → A/B at scale → continual monitoring), and judges that encode clinician judgement so the non-clinician majority can hill-climb. In contextual decision support the generator–verifier gap is small — a verifier good enough to grade the answer would be the generator — so no single judge suffices: a clinical-quality judge, a boundary/adversarial judge, a clinical-safety judge and product judges for tone and style each capture a piece. The quality judge is grounded in human references built for variability: two independent physicians write rubric elements for a real case, a third adjudicates them into one rubric, a fourth QAs it, and the LLM judge semantically matches responses to the elements while the team iterates on architecture, models and ranking
data.name: Expert-calibrated judges with adjudicated rubrics

data.brief: TypeScript-like language for building agents (agencylang.com; ~6 months old, built by Bhargava as personal research): every function is automatically a tool (JSON schema from the signature, docstring as description); interrupts are first-class pausable/resumable execution — raise one inside a for-loop/tool-call/sub-agent, serialize the run, resume a week later at that exact point; partial function application locks tool arguments away from the LLM; sub-agents are plain functions; built-in prompt optimizers (mark variables `optimize`, give a goal, measure against a baseline); stdlib includes read/write/search tools where every mutating or sensitive action throws an interrupt by default
data.name: Agency (agent language)

data.brief: DevRel's history: 1980s software evangelism (one-way) → 2010s developer advocacy (a feedback loop with developers as kingmakers, DX as GTM) → 2026, when developers "no longer work alone" and their job changes, so the advocate's must too. Other users appear: engineers as orchestrators of agent fleets expected to have AI fluency, and non-engineers who can now use dev tools through agents. The agent itself is a user (reads docs differently, calls the API, has its own frustrations recovering from errors) *and* a recommender, driving the bottom-up adoption DevRel exists to encourage — via ChatGPT/Claude Q&A or by installing the library directly into a workflow
data.name: The agent advocate

data.brief: The talk's method claim: the 1990s design-patterns movement has re-run for agents — "we now have patterns for agents, but there's also anti-patterns," and the anti-patterns are the pedagogy, often the key to the exam questions. The walked set: consume responses without checking stop_reason; the overloaded generalist agent ("you hire a carpenter and the guy shows up with plumbing tools, carpenter tools, electrical tools — 'I can do anything'; maybe you want a professional carpenter" — specialize to one job, one or two tools); subtask context spilling into the main thread; unbounded context growth; sharing the generator's reasoning with critic agents (groupthink); interactive modes inside CI pipelines. ⚠ merge-check vs el-pattern-anti-pattern-catalog — see review note 5
data.name: Agent anti-patterns (design-patterns redux)

data.brief: Each rung was "arguably the leading approach for that moment": models — train your own → fine-tune → frontier API → open-weight self-hosted → bring-your-own-key → adaptive model selection; agents — single-shot LLM call → chain-of-thought → graph-based agent (Kus's own talk a year ago) → planning agent that figures out what to do → dedicated sub-agents → generic recursive agent with skills → agent with a code sandbox ("agents are great programmers; let them live in their own computer") → bring your own harness; retrieval — BM25/keyword → RAG embeddings/ANN ("mimics randomness as you keep going") → graphs ("difficult to get working well, probably not the best") → hybrid lexical+semantic with rank fusion → agentic search. Today's pick: adaptive models, a recursive skilled agent, agentic search over hybrid — "and it's going to change again"
data.name: The approach ladder

data.brief: Adaptive, dynamic evaluation of an agent *by* an agent: instead of scoring one output against a fixed rubric with fixed scores, a long-running evaluator agent reads incoming traces, roams whole trajectories, and discovers failure classes nobody enumerated in advance — looping on the same tool call repeatedly, an inefficient trajectory, not recognising a task is done, dropped context — then acts on them (opens a PR with a fix). Motivated by trajectory variance: when every user interaction produces a different path and a freshly generated UI, there is no stable rubric to score against. Explicitly positioned as a *third tier* added to deterministic evals and LLM-as-judge, not a replacement for either.
data.name: Agent as a judge

data.brief: Companies move "from buying software to onboarding actors that read context, make decisions and call real tools." Not that agents become people — they occupy an operational slot the enterprise already understands: someone who can be registered, provisioned, authorized, monitored, investigated and revoked. So the question changes from *can it do the task* to who owns it, what can it touch, on whose behalf, how do you stop it, how do you explain what it did. Needs a runtime identity card: actor, owner, subject acted for, delegator, exact capabilities, governing policy, revocation speed. OAuth token exchange gives the actor/subject/delegation shape, but there is no agent-identity standard yet. Management is "human employee management moved down a layer — the only difference is speed, scale and ambiguity." "If you're not a little scared to run your agent, it probably isn't autonomous enough"
data.name: The agent as a managed worker

data.brief: Three roles that "building for agents" must disambiguate. Product: companies launch agents as the product, so usage pricing is needed because the agent can run up a token bill. Buyer: the agent procures its own Stripe instance and backend services (Stripe Projects) — make services discoverable to agents on the open web, B2C (agentic commerce) and B2B. User: agents operating platforms end-to-end — HubSpot lowering seat prices and adding a credits model because an agent can operate the whole system and seat-based access stops making sense; five of five companies at a demo day were sales-led agents operating SAP or invoicing platforms; "all the value accrues to one user, which is an agent"
data.name: Agent as product, buyer, and user

data.brief: When the thing that runs software can also modify it, development and distribution stop being separate phases: correct changes are produced where the software runs (server, client, live user session) instead of frozen at build time — dissolving the build→freeze→ship pipeline and the one-version-for-everyone assumption it encoded
data.name: Agent as the runtime

data.brief: The stance the whole talk rests on: "you can't rely on the agent itself to guard what it's doing — you can't put the guard inside the agent." Opus refuses delete users table "over and over," but security "can't just be wishful thinking that Opus will always obey"; support-connected agents are prompt-injectable from outside, so any string could push the model into a bad state. Alignment is good but not a security boundary — the boundary has to be elsewhere. As models get smarter the problem shrinks but "we're always going to have to have backstop security mechanisms"
data.name: The agent is untrusted software

data.brief: Open protocol making the agent a first-class principal: each agent gets its own cryptographic identity (private key) permanently bound to a user and a "host," so it can sign/mint its own tokens and every action is attributable, auditable, and independently revocable; solves discovery + authorization + identity + traceability; ships as three layers — an agent plugin (server-side: verify agent, issue grants, enforce constraints), an SDK (mints keys, assigns agent identity, exposes an MCP), and a directory
data.name: Agent Auth protocol

data.brief: A "phone book for agents": a well-known agent-configuration endpoint (OIDC .well-known analog) where an agent discovers a service's capabilities; in the interim (before services adopt), built by translating a service's OpenAPI spec into fine-grained capabilities and matching user intent → capability(ies) → tool call; a directory (not a data-carrying proxy — "a proxy uses data, not scalable"), with logs cut down per provider
data.name: Agent capability directory

data.brief: Giving agents a "save button": a durable runtime *below* the harness/framework layer that snapshots full execution state at each step — code, variables, artifacts, environment (Docker image/sandbox) — connecting OTel-style observability spans to the actual execution.
data.description: Enables replay-from-checkpoint with modifications (swap model, mock a tool, degrade intentionally), diffing outcomes against the grounded baseline, and cohort-scale what-if analysis on production runs: checkpoint → replay → diff → decide
data.name: Agent checkpoint-and-replay

data.brief: Retrying agents cause cascading failures: put circuit breakers in front of unhealthy downstreams, exponential backoff, and hard budgets — max turns, max parallel calls, max spend — so fan-out and cost are bounded. The default of granting every privilege ("read/write on the whole table") must become scoped credentials with separate read and write permissions and tool allowlists — "a harmless model becomes dangerous when it can perform unsafe operations." Human approval must not be blanket: bind it to action, timestamp, actor, expiration and parameters — approving a $30 refund must not authorize a $300 one
data.name: Circuit breakers, budgets and parameter-bound approvals

data.brief: Four bidirectional layers: the agent layer (instructions down, observations up) chooses a policy; a policy provider serves policies trained the traditional way (collect data, simulate, train a VLA model); a backend runs the policy (simulation or real hardware); the physical robot acts. Strands runs on the edge and the cloud — policies and VLAs trained on the cloud with AgentCore, inference called on the edge for speed, the agent choosing which — so the robot collects data continuously and executes fast at runtime. Until VLA models are as large and general as LLMs and need no per-robot training, the agent on top of existing policies is the stepping stone to "not training robots anymore"
data.name: The agent decides what, the policy decides how

data.brief: Thesis (extending a François Chollet tweet): agents are a form of machine learning and agent performance is a blackbox artifact managed via empirical evaluation, not read-the-code reasoning. Explicit mapping: training data→environments; test/validation set→evals (also environments); weights→skills/prompts/tools/model choice; loss function→environment rewards; backprop/optimizer→context-optimization algorithms (GEPA) or a coding agent in a loop; gradient step→a pull request; overfitting→reward hacking
data.name: Agent development as machine learning

data.brief: Uber's cloud dev environments for million-line monorepos, agentified: pre-provisioned Kubernetes balloon pods with all repositories snapshotted and the search index built, so an agent starts in seconds; isolated, globally available, any number. Roles blur, so a mega devpod holds all repos for autonomous cross-repo agents; non-engineers get any harness in seconds
data.name: Agent devpods

data.brief: Meurer's July-2024 coinage: a subdiscipline of AI engineering carrying FDE-grade customer accountability but constituted as its own domain (she joined Sierra's "deployment team" and disliked the name). Her 2026 revision: agent engineering was not a peer discipline but a flavour of forward deployed engineering, heavily focused on outcomes — and harness engineering has since appeared as a further subdiscipline underneath it.
data.name: Agent engineering

data.brief: The runtime pillar: as agents walk the semantic-layer graph they record where they were, what they tried, their context, the outcome — rolled into a score that biases future data-source selection ("DMV lookup worked, prefer it in this context next time"). Trust established bottom-up from what actually worked, complementing top-down human curation; enables self-learning and cross-agent learning.
data.name: Agent execution traces

data.brief: Quick start for DevRel: point a coding agent at your docs, read the transcript, and write up the agent's experience; for GTM, build the GEO prompt set and track mentions versus recommendations. Credibility differs by audience: humans "know what Claude's slop is and nobody likes it," while "Claude loves its own slop" — agent-facing content can be structured and em-dashed. The curb-cut argument: built for wheelchairs, used by everyone with wheels — serve the agent and the human path clears too
data.name: The agent experience report

data.brief: Six flag types matched to the six behavior surfaces agents have that CRUD apps don't: prompt variant, tool access, model routing, memory policy (retention/scope/write/user-visibility), autonomy level (suggest / auto-approve / auto-execute), and kill switch. Lives in a middleware layer between user and agent loop, on existing flag backends (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, homegrown) — no new flag infrastructure needed; sub-agents must route through the same middleware
data.name: Agent feature-flag taxonomy

data.brief: Tooling designed for agent consumers rather than for humans, contrasted explicitly with decades of IDE tooling built for people. Three demonstrated shapes: describe-a-symbol replacing ripgrep — `describe calculate` returns docstrings, the actual source, and every place it's used, for local and external libraries, collapsing several tool calls (and a web search) into one; every function immediately runnable as a CLI command with its parameters attached, so an agent can execute rather than infer; and standalone bundled binaries for any target (Windows, Mac, Linux, WASM) so agents never handle deployment.
data.description: Rationale from the speaker's own training: "the code is always the source of truth. The docs may lie, the readme will definitely lie, but the code cannot lie".
data.name: Agent-first tooling

data.brief: Apify's way to accept any payment protocol without forking its API: agi.apify.com is a single markdown page, ugly for humans, telling an agent how to buy a prepaid Apify token with x402 or MPP and then use the ordinary API or MCP server for jobs. It can change any time — agents re-read it — unlike a backward-compatible API with tens of thousands of dependent customers; no skill file required, ten minutes to first payment. The ecosystem is so early Apify wrote its own local wallet tool with a QR code to fund it
data.name: The agent general interface (AGI)

data.brief: Blocking contract checks placed at the handoffs of an agent pipeline: a pre-save output contract (required shape before saving), a voice/domain contract (output matches the rules the system was designed around), a verification contract (any claim must trace to a source — "trust me is not a verifier"), a deduplication check (genuinely new vs. recycling), plus an audit trail recording which gate failed, which contract was violated, and why. A gate that only logs warnings is a suggestion; a gate must block the artifact from moving forward.
data.name: Agent handoff gates

data.brief: Deterministic interception points on agent tool calls / session events; fire scans and policy checks without consuming context tokens
data.name: Agent lifecycle hooks

data.brief: Designing agent runs to be safely retryable in messy realities (double-fired webhooks, crashed sessions): log every side-effecting action to memory, resume half-done runs by checking what the system wrote down and completing only what's missing, and run periodic lint passes over agent state; the agent-specific trap — a retried model may reword the request enough to look like a new task — means idempotency must be enforced by the system, not the model
data.name: Agent idempotency

data.brief: The infrastructure role the talk argues must exist: someone to "negotiate with the anti-bot providers of the world and say: we are the platform for trusted agents, and we can broker access for your agents as you use the web." Model-agnostic infrastructure plus brokered identity plus observability as the platform requirements for production browsing
data.name: Agent identity brokering

data.brief: Classic infrastructure (databases, identity, multi-cloud storage) has a half-life of 3–5 years — "MySQL is still pretty good" — and switching is avoided because migrations always break something. AI infrastructure's half-life "is measured in months": a few months after adopting the best possible thing there is a significant chance you must replace it. It hurts engineers (what they just built is obsolete), startups (the first AI wave is being disrupted by the second), buyers ("good luck with a three-year deal") and VCs
data.name: The half-life of agent infrastructure

data.brief: Pre-wired off-toggle, agent-wide and per-tool, with three defining properties: flips in seconds (no deploy), in-flight requests respect it at the next decision point, and the wiring exists from design phase — turning runaway-agent incidents from hot-patch firefights into a 30-second mitigation
data.name: Agent kill switch

data.brief: The other half of the problem: "we have to improve the web itself… be evangelists that you want agents coming to your website." Three fronts: accessibility — best-in-class agents consume the accessibility tree and ARIA tags, not raw DOM; Chrome shipped WebMCP, letting sites publish in-page MCP servers agents can call without pre-installation ("submit the registration form" as a blessed, context-efficient tool call); llms.txt / skills.md / agents.md published alongside sites. Authentication — passwords, service accounts, and WorkOS's auth.md (agent-first signup/login discovery); "agents are going to be using your software whether you like it or not — best to let them use it securely." Trust — CAPTCHAs don't work against agents; good agents need distinguishing from bad bots (Web Bot Auth), and "there needs to be a Verisign moment for web agents — who is the certificate issuer? Nobody's done that yet"
data.name: The agent-legible web

data.brief: Plan (retrieves from data sources) → act (calls APIs, tools, databases) → observe (partial results drive the next action) → persist (may store incorrect data) → decide (may choose a wrong action or start a retry storm). Because each step crosses a boundary, persist every step — actions taken, context retrieved — so a failed run can recognize where it failed and take a reversible/undo action, and define an explicit transaction per step with its compensation for irreversible or unsafe operations (a wrong email to a customer needs a defined corrective email)
data.name: Every step of the agent loop crosses a boundary

data.brief: Long-lived agent cycles: persistent context + delegation + triggers (Steinberger's formula) — a schedule or event wakes a manager agent, which discovers the task, plans/writes its own prompts, delegates to worker agents, self-verifies, retries, and only surfaces a reviewable artifact (PR + issue + diff + video/VNC build) to the human; Volkov's gloss: "fancy cron jobs" that grade their own work against the goal
data.name: Agent loops (manager-agent pattern)

data.brief: Post-open-source: a new issue triggers an agent that researches the codebase and repo context, asks clarifying questions when the report is vague, drafts an initial spec, implements, and provides a review gate — every contributed PR goes through multiple agent-managed review iterations and "we don't ping any human reviewers until an agent has approved." Thousands of PRs reduce to the high-signal ones for humans; the agents improve as more PRs and code examples arrive (self-improvement loops as part of the SDLC)
data.name: Agent-managed open-source repository

data.brief: Six-stage model of an engineer's relationship with agents: 0 no AI → 1 autocomplete → 2 chatting, no PRs → 3 delegating + reviewing → 4 multiple agents in parallel → 5 delegating complete tasks with shippable results, no hand-holding. Jones reorganized her earlier model after Steve Yegge's "Gas Town" article
data.name: Agent-relationship maturity model

data.brief: Rebuilding search for LLM agents instead of people: agents can read thousands of very long snippets, where the human product is ten blue links with short snippets — so the retrieval product's shape, not just its API, changes. Generalized in the talk into a program: every layer built for humans (the internet, browsers, search, GPUs) can be rethought and rebuilt as infrastructure for superintelligence, and there is a startup in each layer.
data.name: Agent-native web search

data.brief: Multi-agent fleet structured as a corporate hierarchy — CEO / VP / manager / worker as real entity types (not metaphor), each an agent with its own scoped context and its own approval boundary. Context flows down in slices ("each layer only gets the slice it needs"), results flow back up; the human reviews only what reaches the top. Includes a review gateway: any layer's plan blocks until approved, then a hook fires execution automatically.
data.name: Agent org hierarchy

data.brief: Schema-defined structured outputs (decision, score, reason) written to a queryable agent-memory layer instead of free-form session text; makes one agent/step's output another's input without a human in the loop, makes memory queryable ("every house rated 4+ with commute ≤ 15 min"), and defining the shape forces clarity about what you're asking the agent to produce
data.name: Agent output contracts

data.brief: What enterprises and financial institutions require before agents may pay: is the counterparty sanctioned or tied to terrorist activity, who is the identity behind a bare wallet address, will the agent hallucinate, overspend or break policy — because a chief legal or policy officer signs off and fines reach billions. "Governance simply hasn't caught up." Demo: good claw and bad claw both pay 0.1 cent per scrape until wallet screening is enabled; then the sanctioned wallet's transactions are rejected as block-listed. Both buyer and seller sides need it
data.name: The compliance layer for agent payments

data.brief: In roughly a year every payments incumbent shipped an agent protocol — L402, Mastercard Agent Pay (and Agent Pay for Machines), x402, KYAPay (Skyfire/Visa), AP2 (Google), ACP (OpenAI/Stripe), Tab (Visa), UCP (Google/Shopify), ACTP and AMP (Alipay), MPP (Stripe/Tempo), UnionPay, OKX — "a heated battleground" hard to track. The crypto-rail argument: cards, PayPal and ACH cannot do microtransactions; without agent identity, buyer disputes must be impossible, so payments are one-way; a decentralized public standard prevents a card-network duopoly from extracting fees. Sellers hedge by implementing the two largest (x402, MPP)
data.name: The agent-payment protocol sprawl

data.brief: The utility belt, packaged as a framework-neutral pipeline from .mdx: a hand-written llms.txt — roughly 40 good lines written to get the answer across beats 1,000 generated lines; an llms-full index with a description per page, because agents fetch, they do not browse; markdown twins of every page (a .md suffix, a header advertising the alternate, content negotiation on the Accept header, and ?mode=agent for agents that cannot set headers), since HTML is expensive and support varies by agent; and WebMCP tools (search docs, get pages, ask docs) so an agent can ask the site instead of scraping it. Applies to marketing sites and blogs, not just docs; agent-readiness harnesses (Cloudflare's, Aura AI) score the result and keep moving
data.name: The agent-readable docs pipeline

data.brief: A property of a codebase measured by how many deterministic validation loops it contains — linters, type checkers, security scans, end-to-end tests: things that pass or fail with no judgment. Density of these loops sets how long agents can run on how complex a task without human intervention; the quality of a long-running harness's output is directly proportional to how far its work can be validated. Explicitly analogized to post-training: models need dense reward, and these verification signals are that reward over long-horizon goal-directed work. Consequence for deployments: the investment is "less solving the problem, more preparing the environment for verification of the problem".
data.name: Agent readiness

data.brief: Code mode plus persistent state: variables survive across REPL tool calls, so the agent builds on prior work; observed effects vs plain code mode: shorter scripts, reasoning interleaved between steps, better answers faster; new capabilities ship as runtime methods plus a TypeScript type-definitions file in the prompt rather than new tool schemas
data.name: Agent REPL (persistent code mode)

data.brief: The inner-loop failure mode: when an agent receives a low-quality review comment it "fixes" it, gets re-reviewed, and has to fix backwards — oscillating on a bad comment. So for agent consumers the accuracy bar must go *up*, not down, even though agents are "more than happy to fix 100 nits" that would frustrate a human. Agents in the loop get the same rules and review as humans; the interface and the accuracy threshold are tuned per audience
data.name: Agent review cavitation

data.brief: StarlightSearch's runtime memory layer that lets agents improve from execution experience without retraining, fine-tuning, or manual prompt engineering: it consumes traces, absorbs eval/outcome verdicts (including human-submitted failure reports via a dashboard), and converts both into retrieval guidance for future runs; contrasts with compile-time optimizers (DSPy — lessons baked into the prompt) by improving while executing; once enough memories accumulate, validated reasoning is baked into skills
data.name: Agent RX (agent runtime experience)

data.brief: Authorization model for non-deterministic agent actors: agent has its own identity permanently bound to the principal it acts for, least-privileged by default, with fine-grained scopes at attribute/context/principal level (which senders, which recipients, which hours), time-boxed credentials, and just-in-time elevation — explicitly beyond today's coarse OAuth scopes
data.name: Agent-scoped authorization

data.brief: Append-only event history — every user input, model output, tool call/result, permission prompt, and failure; every state transition — treated as the agent's identity (the Skyrim save file: the character is data, not the PlayStation). Everything else is a projection of the log: the model's context, the UI, debugging/traceability, auditing, compaction.
data.description: Executors become disposable: a worker claims a session, reconstructs state from the log, advances one step, writes back, and disappears. The log records the agent's *view* of the world, not the world itself
data.name: Agent session log (log-as-agent)

data.brief: Shareable natural-language capability packages for agents (SKILL.md + files); higher default privilege than code packages, NL payloads evade code scanners, can persist via agent memory
data.name: Agent skills

data.brief: Nightly offline consolidation pass for an agent system: replay the day, lock in useful facts, hunt contradictions, decay stale junk, distill the day's work into reusable skills, and emit a morning "dream report" for the operator. The system measurably "gets smarter overnight" without any training run.
data.name: Agent sleep cycle

data.brief: What an executable procedure needs that a legacy SOP lacks: preconditions, decisions, identifiers, back-end calls, validation, recovery, and evidence of successful execution. "Experts own the what, agents own the how; an exception becomes a guardrail." Most of the effort is translation and negotiation between expert and engineer to align on common sense
data.name: Agent SOP

data.brief: Since agents "can run away with spend," the failure impact of billing is growing: controls customers can offer their customers — an agent with a wallet it alone can spend from; credits, commits, sales-led discounts and offers beyond pay-as-you-go; prepaid-credit auto-recharge (dominant since OpenAI launched it via Metronome); coding-agent vendors (Cognition, Cursor, OpenAI, Anthropic) adopting CSP-style prepaid/postpaid commitments in the enterprise
data.name: Agent wallets and spend controls

data.brief: A workflow expressed as explicit states with harness-owned transitions; each step hands the model a single-step "neural contract" (do one thing, return it) and the model never decides which step it is on
data.name: Agent state machine

data.brief: Capability tiering of agent harnesses as a trust/procurement criterion: important work needs at least "tier 2" — a powerful reasoning model plus subagents, plan mode, full MCP support, and file editing. AI crowbarred into a pre-existing subscription price point can't afford intelligent reasoning models under its margin — "you can't fix stupid; friends don't let friends use really bad harnesses."
data.name: Agent tiers

data.brief: Boundary's loop for designing the language itself: agents run continuously writing BAML programs from scratch; the full agent transcripts (tool calls, errors, retries) are then inspected — by humans and, more importantly, by other agents — for what worked and what didn't, including efficiency defects invisible to a test suite ("what took three tool calls when it should have only taken one"). Humans triage which findings are real, which are hallucinations and which "don't have taste"; agents then author the fixes.
data.description: The final step is the point: candidate language features and skills are A/B tested on tool calls consumed, errors produced and correct outcomes, so "you can start building data-driven systems without ever writing a single line of code".
data.name: Agent-trace-driven language design

data.brief: The talk's central practice: point agents at other agents' traces at scale to answer questions no dashboard can. Worked examples given — find interactions where users got upset or delighted; determine whether "the agent gets really dumb after the first compaction, after the second, or never"; and test counterfactuals across models ("I ran GPT 5.5 for this and heard GLM is really good — what happens if I run GLM 5.2 and how do I compare them?"). The argument for traces over metrics is that "the trace level captures the actual behaviour that users see," at a granularity aggregate metrics erase
data.name: Agent trace mining

data.brief: The agent-development lifecycle (spec → build → eval → ship → monitor → diagnose → optimize) staffed by agents instead of humans: evaluator agents build/run eval suites, diagnostics agents do root-cause analysis over traces, optimizer agents generate targeted mutations and re-test; the human designs the loops and their eval/termination gates rather than performing them
data.name: Agentic AI engineer

data.brief: The end state Feng extrapolates to: stop scoping training to one task and treat the model as a single deployment interacting across many settings and many users, where the task is improving itself on everything. The model performs reflection/introspection per interaction type — "for this sort of interaction, here's how I self-evaluate" — and those interactions are turned automatically into weight updates. Restates the environment question as: what if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?
data.description: Motivation is explicitly the failure mode of the alternative: fixing one task or one flagged failure mode at a time is whack-a-mole, requiring new data or a new environment every time something new pops up.
data.name: Agentic citizen (self-improving deployment)

data.brief: The acronyms sorted by job: MCP — how the agent discovers and calls merchant capabilities (product search, product details, loyalty); A2A — how a customer agent and a merchant agent, or domain agents (payments, loyalty), talk; ACP (OpenAI) and UCP (Google) — the commerce primitives: carts and line items, checkout sessions with states (not ready for payment → ready → completed), cancellation; AP2 (Google, extending UCP) — the scoped payment mandate for autonomy: who authorized the agent, what it may buy, the maximum amount, a revocation URL, proof of user consent, single use. Stable today: MCP, A2A, UCP/ACP. Still forming: real AP2 usage, ACP↔UCP convergence ("do we always need two specs?"), identity standards, multi-agent checkout delegation
data.name: The agentic-commerce protocol stack

data.brief: An agent loop built to the control-theory template instead of while true: a set point (desired end state of the codebase with respect to one property), a sensor that measures current state (deterministic — ast-grep, ESLint rules, Packwerk — or non-deterministic — an agent plus a skill and natural-language rules — or a pipeline mixing both), the measured error (the violation list), a controller that turns that error into a control signal about one incremental change, and an actuator that applies it, all while the system takes disturbances (teammates shipping). Because the components are agents, the lines blur in practice: a hybrid sensor+controller or a merged controller+actuator are both normal. The controller is the load-bearing part — without a well-tuned one the loop makes too large a change or the wrong change, repeatedly. Precedents named as existing control loops: thermostats, Kubernetes autoscaling, infrastructure-as-code, Postgres autovacuum, React's virtual DOM.
data.name: Agentic control loop

data.brief: Emerging infrastructure layer for autonomous agents — scheduling, memory coordination, policy enforcement, evaluation, monitoring, workload routing — analogous to what Kubernetes was for containers and service meshes for microservices; "an operating system for autonomous AI" (paraphrase)
data.name: Agentic control plane

data.brief: The framing insight: from an infrastructure standpoint an agentic video editor is the same shape as an agentic app builder — prompt (here media+prompt) → a remote sandbox spins up → an agent with tools and skills works → a result (there an app preview; here a rendered video). The difference: the artifact is a video composition instead of a codebase. Positions media agents inside the established coding-agent infrastructure pattern
data.name: Agentic video editor ≈ agentic app builder

data.brief: The unit of both agent evals and RL training data: an instruction (what the agent should do), a sandbox (a virtual computer where it tries), and a verifier (programmatic tests, rubrics, or a judge agent that decides whether it did it, emitting a reward). Specified as a file-directory layout that has "become relatively standard in a lot of the environment space", so environments pass between hands and interoperate
data.name: Agentic environment (instruction + sandbox + verifier)

data.brief: A perceive→predict→decide→act loop where LLM agents reason over game state via in-context learning and local tool calls (no reward to grind), adapting dynamically to new situations — contrasted with RL, which changes model weights and must be tuned per game; demoed as agentic Space Invaders and a backtracking constraint-satisfaction mini-crossword agent
data.name: Agentic game loop

data.brief: The second retrieval tool: instead of only hybrid search, let the agent browse the knowledge base via sandboxed read-only bash commands over a raw/generated/wiki folder tree (the wiki built by Claude Code from the raw files, per the Karpathy LLM-wiki idea), with limits (8s command timeout, 40k-char output cap, 20-command ceiling, read-only). Honest finding: it was used ~90% of turns but produced no recall improvement and was 50% slower — hybrid search alone was enough for their real (complex) student questions. A negative result kept as a result
data.name: Agent-browses-knowledge-base retrieval

data.brief: Emergent, non-eval use of a rollout engine ("prod rollouts"): fan a ton of agents out over distributed sandboxes in parallel, each producing a structured artifact, then aggregate the results intelligently with a second (usually stronger) agent pass. Observed uses: scanning many trajectories to detect reward hacking, processing receipts for reimbursements, semantic search over an Obsidian vault, asking a question across many PRs. Cost split is explicit — cheap/fast model for map, high-intelligence model for reduce. Harbor's builders did not design for this, saw people doing it anyway, and shipped a feature (Harbor Exec) for it
data.name: Agentic map-reduce

data.brief: The layers that "have crystallized" for running agentic flows reliably: runtime (stateful, persistent sessions, isolation, a different lifecycle than an API service — cloud providers have each shipped an agent runtime), memory (ingest → extract → consolidate → retrieve; short-term → long-term → episodic), context management, cross-cutting operations (tracing, evals, guardrails/authz, cost), orchestration. Graded: runtime solved, memory maturing, MCP de facto, OTel pushed but unproven for agentic calls, testing hard but workable, orchestration "don't over-engineer," cost and replay/debugging unsolved. "If you can't build a well-structured monolith, why try microservices" → "if you can't build a single agentic loop, why build a multi-agent system"
data.name: The agentic reference architecture

data.brief: Retrieval as a reflective loop rather than single-shot search: the system inspects the dataset, decides whether the stated information need is satisfied, and iterates before returning; in Microsoft's evals it consistently beats individual simple methods on difficult cases (evidence recall, answer completeness), at a latency/quality trade-off
data.name: Agentic retrieval

data.brief: Sites that read the browsing user's intent and personalize pages in real time to drive engagement or conversion. Not whole-site generation — marketers "have very strict brand guidelines, you don't want hallucinations" — but per-block personalization (hero, product cards, blog feeds, navigation, calls to action, comparisons), with the whole site as a RAG corpus so every generation is grounded. Modes: instant persona adaptation, query-generated result pages, "for you" recommendation pages built from accumulated signals (pre-generatable and pre-fetchable, with cost implications per generation). Marketers define the strategy in natural language and close the loop with analytics
data.name: Agentic sites

data.brief: Capability ladder analogized to self-driving autonomy levels. Agent over LLM: loop, tool calls, memory, retries, context engineering, state. Harness over agent: durability + "doggedness" — persisted/resumable streams, planning mode, parallel sub-agents, TUI affordances + slash commands, skills, dynamic agent creation, background bash, autocompaction, thread persistence, queue/steer/interrupt, session-long tool approval. Then local → always-on cloud harness (Slack/mobile channels, cloud sandboxes, PR output). Claw over harness: initiative + learning
data.name: Agentic spectrum (LLM → agent → harness → claw)

data.brief: The lineage the talk is built on. Messages API (with Claude 3): tokens in, tokens out. Claude Agent SDK: packages the Claude Code harness with a built-in agentic loop, file-system access, tools and sandboxing — but leaves credentials, hosting and scaling to be hand-rolled. Claude managed agents: the loop, the sandbox, credentials, session management, observability and hosting all operated by Anthropic, leaving the developer "your product, your task, your context, and your domain knowledge." The driver named is task complexity climbing from questions → delegated tasks → "agents own entire outcomes"
data.name: The three agentic surfaces

data.brief: The six-step loop most teams converge on for LLM-driven security work: threat model + sandbox as per-codebase setup, then a discovery → verification → triage → patch loop. Maps to an ML pipeline: recall (discovery), precision (verification), ranking (triage), closing the loop (patching)
data.name: Agentic vulnerability pipeline

data.brief: Symbolica's RLM agent harness; scored ~30% on ARC-AGI-3 within hours of the benchmark's release while frontier models sat at 2–3%
data.name: Agentica

data.brief: The closing prediction of *how* the web actually gets agentified: not by rebuilding 30 years of human-built infrastructure in "two, five, ten years" (a "fantasy") but by extrapolating current trends — accuracies rising, benchmarks falling, latencies and costs dropping — until "we just pile on another layer of mess on top of the mess that the web is": hundreds of browsers clicking buttons like humans behind a task endpoint, returning structured results for under a penny in sometimes <100ms. "At some point you will say: yeah, that's an API. Why do I care?"
data.name: Agentification by accretion

data.brief: What the flashlight showed internally: entitlements need a new paradigm — large enterprises are full of over- and under-entitled people, and the model breaks when agents need to act fast, on many things, with judgment. "Agents inherit your foundations; when processes or people go rogue, agents will 100× that problem." Companion lessons: cross-platform integration moved up the stack (AI is only as good as what it reaches); centralized, consumable knowledge for "thinner agents and a smarter substrate"; possibly a separate ecosystem for experimentation when the legacy gap is too vast
data.name: Agents inherit your entitlements

data.brief: A developer library's growth curve inflected the day assistants started recommending it: the onboarding form's top answer to "how did you hear about us" became Claude, ChatGPT/Codex and Gemini. Where the founders once installed software on your laptop ("a Collison install") a prompt now does; a developer asks an agent for a capability and accepts "we should install this library." Developer-experience primitives — docs, onboarding, error messages — are now agent primitives, and the same DX-first product that beat marketer-oriented competitors is what agents pick
data.name: Agents install your library now

data.brief: Cross-agent instruction-file convention: OpenAI deliberately picked a vendor-neutral name instead of a Codex-proprietary format so other agents could adopt the same file; part of the open-layers strategy
data.name: AGENTS.md

data.brief: Kramer's name for the current frontier just past bare agents, anchored on the played Nadella clip: multi-model harnesses ("you want the harness to define the models, the data and the tools, so you have a loop across those three") with tool access, progressive disclosure of tools for token efficiency, and rich context feeding; software copilots embedded in every piece of software; organization-level harnesses. The through-line from last year's loops/tool-calls/context-engineering to this year's emerging ideas
data.name: Agents plus

data.brief: Before agents, "you were the context layer": trawling data sources and discussions, building tribal knowledge, accumulating battle scars from incidents. Agents inherit all those challenges plus one: they reset every task — an expert engineer onboarding for the first time, rediscovering the codebase, how you build, test and deploy, on every task. The human layer hasn't gone away — accountability stops with whoever hits merge
data.name: Agents reset their knowledge every task

data.brief: Everyone has seen the demo; walk into a 200-person property-management firm and nothing has changed — "totally normal, what we should expect" for a general-purpose technology. Electricity was demoed at Pearl Street in the 1880s; a Ford electrified moving assembly line is 1924: rip out the motors, bring in new equipment, train everyone. "AI diffusion is perhaps the single most important problem for the next 20 years"
data.name: AI diffusion is a generation-long problem

data.brief: In finance and pharma the expert does the work and the AI assists: it proposes five candidate trade theses or drug candidates and saves hours, but which will work in the market or the clinic is still the expert's call, "and it will stay this way for a really long time" — models pattern-match past statistics, they do not model causation, and there is no verifiable reward outside math and code. The "AGI line" is when a model can make a drug; until then vertical AI is decision support with the human deciding
data.name: AI-in-the-loop, not human-in-the-loop

data.brief: The talk's one transferable point: "the last 6 months with AI have pushed these projects forward — it's super easy now to build whatever cool thing you're passionate about; time is typically not the big time-suck it once was." The charge to the audience: pick a passion project and build it, because AI has removed the friction. A hobbyist-side echo of the democratization-of-building thread
data.name: AI collapses the cost of building

data.brief: The proposed post-agents category: software built from the ground up with LLM inference at the core of every interaction at every moment — not a model bolted onto conventional software. Positioned by analogy: AI-native software is to today's agents what the modern internet (web apps, native mobile) is to the hand-written web pages of 1995 — and, per the talk's method, it will be *discovered by building*: "we now actually have the ability to build the memex, and Jarvis from Iron Man, and Knowledge Navigator, for real, completely working — and by building those things we'll figure out what we want to build next"
data.name: AI-native software

data.brief: The failure mode of AI-accelerated research: "you look at a deep research report that's 20 pages long and you say 'wow, this looks good' — and then those features don't actually exist in the product, and you've set yourself back." Named in the talk as the reason acceleration (evaluation work "90% faster now") must keep the old quality bar: hidden assumptions surface late (an open-source library's feature that was actually in beta). ⚠ merge-check vs el-automation-bias (same psychology, artifact-trust flavor) and name-collision check vs el-benchmark-psychosis (different claim — that one is misreading benchmark numbers; this is trusting fluent research output)
data.name: AI psychosis (unverified-artifact trust)

data.brief: Open workshop repo by Decoding AI + Towards AI: a set of Claude Code / Codex skills (packaged as a Claude Code plugin) that runs personal deep research over your second brain (Obsidian, Readwise, NotebookLM, GitHub repos, YouTube transcripts, web links/documents) and materializes the results as a three-layer file system — immutable raw/ sources, an index.yaml reference catalog (per-source link, origin, title, authors, date, summary), and an LLM-maintained wiki/ of derivatives (concepts, entities, comparisons, notes, open questions). No vector DB, no knowledge-graph infra — plain markdown + references. Wikis are scoped per project (article, video, book, course, codebase), and the wiki keeps evolving from the questions you ask, not just from ingestion
data.name: AI Research OS

data.brief: The semantic-accuracy half: humans re-identify the same review issues over and over, so codify recurring review comments into a registry that then auto-flags them — "every recurring comment is now a guardrail you don't have to review again." Framed as learning on top of the base LLM from the review experience humans provide; compounds with every merged PR. Homework offered: "mine your last 1,000 review comments and build a registry for the repeatable ones." Follows a J-curve (upfront pain before payoff)
data.name: The AI slop registry

data.brief: Repeatable end-to-end design lifecycle for AI systems: (1) product requirements — quantified solution-agnostic business problem, business/performance constraints, AI's role (critical vs complementary, reactive vs proactive, autonomy ceiling), SMART success metrics; (2) system design — data strategy, retrieval choices, architecture from a pattern menu (RAG, agents, control-flow agentic systems, LLM-as-router, human-in-the-loop, fine-tuning), UX + feedback capture; (3) evaluation before ship + monitoring after; (4) optimization for cost, latency, reliability — with every downstream decision traceable to a constraint gathered upfront
data.name: Four-phase AI system design framework

data.brief: User-research-derived framework grouping the main challenges users have with AI features into five categories, each with concrete interface patterns: trust (citations, plan approval, AI-content labeling), clarity (streaming, think-out-loud, change highlighting), control (emergency stop, undo/version history, granular revert), transparency (granular revocable permissions, cost/time estimates, agent-driving indicators), meaningful benefit (suggested prompts, next-step actions, workflow integrations)
data.name: Five pillars of AI UX (trust, clarity, control, transparency, meaningful benefit)

data.brief: Not more dashboards or chatbots: an identity for every actor, short-lived capability tokens for actions, policy gates that cannot be talked out of, receipts for everything, and clear revocation. MCP and A2A are important rails (agent-to-tool, agent-to-agent) but insufficient — the enterprise still needs the system that decides who can move where, under whose authority, with what audit. "The oldest enterprise IT playbook pointed at a new kind of worker." Market signals: Microsoft Agent 365, Okta onboarding agents into its identity layer, AWS AgentCore identity
data.name: An IT department for the AI workforce

data.brief: Weco's earlier machine-learning-engineering agent (~2024), independently evaluated by OpenAI in the MLE-bench paper as the top auto-research/MLE agent of its time; predecessor of Aiden
data.name: AIDE (Weco)

data.brief: Weco's experimental multi-agent, self-improving auto-research agent: reads public information (papers, other participants' PRs), runs its own experiments, and submits a PR only once findings pass a quality gate — i.e. an auto-researcher that publishes into a human community rather than hill-climbing privately
data.name: Aiden (Weco)

data.brief: Proposed successor role to product engineering: engineers spend less time on the product and more on making the AI able to work on the product — perception tools (screenshots, token-compressed UI snapshots, log extraction), codebase legibility, knowledge bases; deliverable as CLI, skill, or MCP. Rule of thumb: "put the mask on the AI before your own" — make the AI self-served before feature work; the up-front slowdown pays off once agents are multiplied or run overnight
data.name: AIX engineering (AI experience engineering)

data.brief: Large DARPA program run at DEF CON last year; the speaker designed its scoring algorithm. Cited as evidence that expert curation cannot guarantee a known bug set: 18 of the bugs found in it were unintended ones the organizers had not planted. Companion data point in the same argument: DARPA's earlier Cyber Grand Challenge — ~$60M, the first demonstration of fully autonomous cyber — had unknown vulnerabilities in 50% of its hand-curated challenges, and those were actually exploited.
data.name: DARPA AIxCC (AI Cyber Challenge)

data.brief: Kiduna's recipe for an agent ("ally"): inform — load its knowledge into a vector store; instruct — the system prompt, its character and stance; empower — connect enterprise and social accounts (Slack, Telegram, X); enact — abilities and automations for long-running goals; align — a purpose so it works for you the same way in every context. Any LLM behind it
data.name: Inform, instruct, empower, enact, align

data.brief: Alpha = the gap between what you can do and what current models can do; decay = the clock on that gap. Half-life of a capability edge ≈ one model release (speed and recall already decayed; verification is moving into harnesses; taste decays slower but still resets); half-life of a signature — credibility, expertise, the name behind shipped work — is much longer
data.name: Alpha and decay (career math)

data.brief: Google DeepMind. Gemini-powered evolutionary coding agent. Beat Strassen. Production deployments.
data.description: DeepMind's Gemini-powered evolutionary coding agent. Beat Strassen's 1969 matrix multiplication (first improvement in 56 years). In production: 23% Gemini kernel speedup, data center scheduling, chip design. UK automated lab opening 2026.
data.name: AlphaEvolve

data.brief: Morgan Stanley's open-source agentic harness for automated quant research. Input is a path to a dataset (or an API spec) plus a natural-language description of what to predict; output is a suite of trained, containerized ML models. Three phases: research (~3-4 hours: builds and works a to-do list, sets up its Python environment, loads data, runs statistical tests, reads arXiv and technical blogs via web search, taking markdown notes per item that later agents query), eval building, and mass experimentation. Deliberately not built on any off-the-shelf agent framework — all custom code, itself largely written by Claude, for maximum freedom to tweak; functional tool calling keeps it provider-agnostic across OpenAI, Anthropic and open-source models. Three main tools: full shell access, web search, and a Slurm abstraction where the agent declares hardware and submits a job. 1.0 released ~April 2026 with a ~40-page tech report and all code on GitHub.
data.name: AlphaLab

data.brief: Ramp's first FDE principle, against the belief that an FDE's job is to say yes to the customer: you want to find a way to say yes, but you have to deliver good software and build the right thing. Practically it is a context-gathering interrogation before any build — what is actually driving the urgency (an end-of-quarter sales rep chasing quota is not the customer), who will use this, have all workarounds been exhausted, is there a manual stopgap, does the customer have technical resources to hit the API instead — and, most important, does anyone else in the pipeline or customer base benefit. Validate even the most basic assumptions ("horses with rockets strapped to their legs" is what saying yes without scoping builds).
data.name: Always be scoping

data.brief: Agentic checkouts with a financial harness: a wallet the agent spends from, a marketplace of paid MCP tools reached through one skill file, a transaction log of every authorized payment, compliance screening of counterparties (TRM integration; a toggle that blocks sanctioned wallets), and merchant checkout via Shopify UCP. Incubated inside Edge & Node from its micropayments and x402 work
data.name: Ampersend

data.brief: Response to sparse reward while models are weak: grading only the end scientific outcome yields almost no signal, so break the analysis DAG into manageable component steps, take the data to the state it would be in right before a scientist or theoretician does the interpretive work, and define ground truth at that node. Verifiability is bought by choosing where to cut.
data.name: Analysis-DAG decomposition

data.brief: Fleet of real AI-run businesses: retail space on Union Street SF (Claude), a Stockholm cafe (Gemini, then GPT), AI radio stations free to broadcast anything, and the original vending machines; models operate autonomously and Andon observes. Capability treadmill: vending machines didn't work 18 months ago, worked at 6 months, now too easy — upgraded to a cafe
data.name: Andon Labs real-world deployments

data.brief: Open-source Chrome extension (first of two harness pieces): select/mark elements on any screen and describe a change; captures the exact location, style, and feedback into a complete structured summary handed to the coding agent — removing the write-a-long-description back-and-forth
data.name: Perception-agent annotation tool

data.brief: Hosted service for long-running agents. Public beta Apr 2026.
data.description: Hosted service for long-running agents (hours/days, not single-turn). Public beta Apr 2026.
data.name: Anthropic Managed Agents

data.brief: Cai's term for the bespoke system that translates a specific business's messy context into evals (and RL environments) — the piece labs need for real-world seed data and enterprises need to own rather than rent intelligence. Named as one of the three missing layers of the coming enterprise abstraction stack, and now the name of his company.
data.name: Antikythera mechanism

data.brief: RAG benchmark (agent is given files and asked questions about them), used as the operational ability antipattern: in some tasks the file contents and the rubric's expected answer contradict each other, so an agent that faithfully follows the ground truth scores negative; and much of the data is visibly synthetic — placeholder values, dates and places that don't exist — which both pushes the model toward eval awareness and takes the task out of distribution from real-world data. Name from captions ("Apex").
data.name: APEX (RAG benchmark)

data.brief: "The key component of a platform": agents, sub-agents, environments/compute and artifacts are all exposed via API so people build on top rather than inside the vendor's UI or opinion. Result: non-engineering teammates (developer relations, social) built Slack bots on the SDK — agents that pick up tweets and Reddit posts, run sentiment analysis, infer intent and propose responses — plus competitive-research and product-Q&A agents
data.name: An API for every primitive

data.brief: "The log is the system's memory. Nothing is lost and everything is observed": one append-only events table, events causally linked (which event triggered which), everything queryable — built because a voice note vanished and a brief posted twice (no queue, no attempt counting). Debugging headaches start "even with three agents"
data.name: The append-only event log

data.brief: Seven steps that were identical at a hedge fund and a pharma startup and, per peers, in legal and proptech: (1) formulate a narrow problem — one market, one sector, one parameter; build more agents rather than one that does everything; (2) identify data, especially proprietary data nobody sells, curated from your own unstructured history; (3) model the problem as the expert would, step by step, in the prompt; (4) observability; (5) iterate — the step where projects die; (6) hire the user; (7) ship to paying users once it beats the general models on the expert's judgement. Steps 1–4 fit on one screen and take a good engineer minutes; they are commodity, not moat
data.name: The applied-vertical-AI recipe

data.brief: Diff-based file-editing tool that all models from GPT-5 onward were trained on — used both to edit and to create files, with a general shell tool for everything else. The training-shaped-the-harness consequence is explicit: the model "naturally" reaches for Ripgrep because that is what it saw in training, so the Codex harness ships Ripgrep for users who lack it; on Windows the model was trained to emit PowerShell natively
data.name: Apply patch tool

data.brief: Codex capture that sends not just a screenshot image but the app's entire accessibility tree (channel IDs, user IDs, field IDs), so a task that used to need OCR + multi-hop tool discovery collapses to a single one-hop tool call; Liu's most-cited feature and primary context-ingestion path
data.name: Appshots

data.brief: Three principles of an agent-first company: it must be API-first — good programmatic interfaces (MCP, CLI, whatever) over every internal and external data source, or agents have no access; not everything is a chatbot — dynamic UI is possible, but crystallized, consistent GUIs for repeated use cases and arbitrarily flexible chat agents are both needed; and buy-vs-build is a false dichotomy — the highest-order bit is whether a system is arbitrarily customizable, which self-built code is by definition and purchased SaaS can be if it exposes MCP and can be made to work on your behalf (Salesforce, kept as a good database with good sales choices, used daily by every agent)
data.name: Arbitrarily customizable beats buy-vs-build

data.brief: Grounded in an SRE agent with read and write tools (roll back, page). Single prompt (~3 years ago): eval the final answer — accuracy, factuality, hallucination, stale knowledge — against a golden dataset. Chain/RAG: parser, retrieval, context, synthesis — several failure points, still a fixed path. ReAct loop (late 2023–early 2024): flexible self-orchestration, but models mis-called tools, mis-orchestrated, collapsed on long context — "fell short of the promise." Workflow graphs / state machines (late 2024–early 2025): teams took orchestration control, models operated at the node level — reliable in distribution, brittle outside it, growing special-case branches; evals now per node, branch consistency, node contracts, retry loops. ReAct again (mid/late 2025): reliable tool calling, planning, long horizons, self-correction — high trajectory variance, so the unit of eval becomes a distribution (pass@k, pass^k). Product systems (now): the loop plus memory (in- and cross-session), code sandboxes, MCP/skill directories — new surfaces the old evals only partially cover
data.name: Architecture generations and the evals each needs

data.brief: A visualized internal (plus some external) dependency graph with semantic boundaries and individual packages, and CLI tools that assert invariants over it inside CI. When an agent adds a leaky dependency or a package that violates a boundary, CI or a git-commit diff shows exactly where it broke — so architectural drift is caught mechanically rather than in code review. Reported outcome: architecture unchanged for three to four months while the codebase kept moving.
data.name: Architecture invariants in CI

data.brief: A deliberately tiny, model-agnostic architecture.md instead of CLAUDE.md — "pick something every model can just understand" — containing only what will not change for months or years (in Boundary's case, the layers of the compiler), plus one procedural rule: work deeper in the compiler requires talking to at least one other person, which intentionally slows that work down. Adopted as the alternative to standardizing on tools: "the hard part about hiring great engineers is you sadly can't tell them what to do", so the invariant lives in the repo rather than in a policy.
data.name: architecture.md (invariant-only agent guidance)

data.brief: Arize's in-UI assistant agent, first shipped ~2 years ago ("our first version frankly sucked"); long memory, dynamically generated UI per interaction, search across very large trace volumes. Doubles as the company's own failure-mode laboratory — its dogfooded failures (forgetting context, not knowing when a task is done, looping on the same tool call) are the stated origin of both Signal and agent-as-a-judge.
data.name: Alex (Arize in-product agent)

data.brief: Open-source LLM observability and evaluation framework from Arize (phoenix.arize.com); used here to run capability evals (small-vs-frontier model comparisons over a golden dataset) and CI/CD-style regression evals
data.name: Arize Phoenix

data.brief: Long-running background agent that turns production telemetry into a code fix: triggered on a schedule or on an error event, it pulls traces/logs/eval values through observability skills, lands the evidence as files in the repo next to the code, and opens a GitHub issue or PR. Fully open-box configuration — you pick the coding harness (Claude Code), the sandbox (Arize sandboxes, Anthropic managed agents, Daytona), the skills, and the driving prompt ("don't be aggressive", "look for security issues"); findings can be converted into an evaluator or added to a dataset. Ships in the AX SaaS platform (also VPC-deployable).
data.name: Arize Signal

data.brief: Users rarely arrive with well-formed intent and the right keywords; they have a fuzzy feeling or a vibe, especially when shopping. Agents built as wrappers on the search bar assume the opposite and fail. The agent's job becomes hand-holding: understand and proactively elicit preferences, show possibilities, then converge on recommendations within the user's constraints — "design the product to accept vibes"
data.name: The articulation gap

data.brief: Today "your developer holds the judgement of what's bad and what's good — not your software, not your AI tools." Moving that judgement into tools means codifying experience — accepted and rejected changes, discussions, incidents — in the right form and the right place for both agents and humans. If you ship AI code faster than humans can review, "you are in the problem, not ahead of it"; the 10× velocity comes only after the governance infrastructure exists
data.name: From artificial intelligence to artificial wisdom

data.brief: The mechanism: reframe the game-dev entity-component-system / data-oriented design as tags describing intent — "everything is an asset, everything renders, everything has physics; you add tags to describe intent." Systems query for assets by tag ("move everything tagged vehicle+player+drivable"). Recyclable across games (tag a building vehicle+drivable and it's a Mario-Kart obstacle). The LLM assistant applies/removes tags via tool calls; tags and systems are built into the engine, no scripting layer by design
data.name: Asset-tag system (ATS)

data.brief: The talk's explanatory frame for why AI looks simultaneously superhuman and useless. Tasks where AI excels are not merely tasks that happen to have a human in the loop — their goal is to please the human in the loop (chat, coding agents, unsolved math). Tasks where AI fails are ones whose goal is to remove the human: ideally running in a server nobody looks at until it becomes boring legacy software. These "way way way easier" tasks — customer service decisions, back-office work — still require humans, and the divide, not the difficulty, is what predicts which is which.
data.name: The assistance / automation divide

data.brief: Neither Gemini nor ChatGPT calls a merchant's search catalog; merchants push a product feed the assistant indexes ahead of time — for ranking, sponsored products and retail media, and because M merchants × N products cannot be queried live. UCP, ACP and Meta each define a feed that is "similar but different"; feeds must conform to the spec or the assistant rejects them, and they sync continuously so inventory is not stale. The catalog, not the storefront, is what the assistant sees
data.name: Product feeds for assistants

data.brief: Language-agnostic structural code search and lint used as a deterministic loop sensor: a rule matches the unmigrated code pattern, granular include/exclude paths scope it, extra rules layer on over time for other patterns to remove, and it works across a multilingual monorepo. Explicitly chosen over an agent, ripgrep or TypeScript-native tooling because it is out of band from tsconfig and ESLint — the config an agent will happily disable with an inline comment. Raw output is ~50 keys per violation, filtered to ~4 and sorted deterministically before it reaches the controller.
data.name: ast-grep

data.brief: Same-size actions have different blast radius by direction. Some verbs fail out loud (unskip a test → CI goes red; page a human → a nuisance) and some fail silently (skip a test → a real bug walks into production under green checks). Give agents the loud-failing verbs; keep a human on the silent ones. In Anthropic's CI the agent may re-enable quarantined tests (cheaply reversible) but skipping is a break-glass verb needing a human and an audit row — written by the proxy, "the agent never holds the pen on its own provenance"
data.name: Asymmetric verbs

data.brief: For code the async rung is solved: wrap the coding agent in a sandbox, let it run, get a PR; engineers already parallelize ("job seven finishes before job three"). Services work is serial (an inbox, one email at a time). Open questions: represent knowledge work as code so coding agents can do it now; parallelize traditionally serial work; find form factors per industry — the code launcher won't work for architecture or property management
data.name: Asynchronous agents for serial work

data.brief: Full-text search delivered by a separate mongot process wrapping Apache Lucene alongside the MongoDB server (core MongoDB provides no full-text engine); transparent to the caller — the same unified query API, with a $search stage in an aggregation pipeline naming the Lucene index. Adopted at the Hub to replace regex matching over the token array, which "doesn't scale well" and produced the latency problems that appeared as the dataset grew.
data.name: MongoDB Atlas Search (Lucene-backed full-text)

data.brief: Who arranges the components the orchestrator picked? Borrowed from atomic design: a hierarchy of page layout → slots (header, main) → sub-slots → eligible component categories, with templates for what the optimal layout is in a given situation. Because the orchestrator works bottom-up, the mapping is flipped — components map to sub-slots, sub-slots to slots, slots to templates — and the UX agent is "harnessed" with this codified UX knowledge so placement is steerable rather than random
data.name: Atomic design as layout grammar for agents

data.brief: Group-chat memory strategy: instead of storing the whole transcript and compacting it once it becomes overhead, extract atomic, high-value facts as the conversation accumulates (a plan, a date, an added constraint) and store those. Requires purpose-built auto-raters, on five axes: did we extract high-value atomic facts; are they the relevant ones for this conversation; are they hierarchically related; is their temporal weighting right; and is retrieval returning the right set — ideally intelligent, graph-organized retrieval rather than crawling everything.
data.name: Atomic-fact memory

data.brief: Kepler tenet 1. The model is never allowed to write or manipulate a number — it writes a reference to the number and hands off to a system built for numbers (a database). Every produced figure runs through a deterministic check against the provenance ledger; anything that can't be independently verified is stripped out and never reaches the user, and the cycle repeats at least twice. Explicitly not a multi-model cross-check ("these are not probabilistic systems evaluating each other's work") — the atomicity is database atomicity: extract, persist, confirm the process occurred. The ledger resolves a number to one of three origins: extraction from a filing, a derivative calculation, or the firm's internal documents.
data.name: Atomic provenance

data.brief: Human attention is the scarce resource, so mark what was generated by AI versus written by a human so readers know how much time to spend and how much slop to expect. Team convention: every PR description opens with a hand-written paragraph, then the AI description; same in Slack and email.
