Cautionary tale: sending a senior skeptic an AI-generated analysis without marking it — "I did not expect somebody I respect this much to send me something this sloppy" — fixed by labeling intent: this is mine, this is the AI's, here is the feedback I need
data.name: Attention-aware communication

data.brief: LLMs are trained on what people say, not what people do, so stated attitudes are easier to predict than actions. Evidence: across replicated social-science studies an LLM matched expert forecasters overall, but the two study families separate cleanly — surveys (natively language, measuring attitudes) are predicted well, field experiments (behaviors, which must be transcribed into text before they can enter training data) noticeably worse. Practical rule given to clients: build questions that triangulate to behavior from attitudes — to learn about gym attendance, ask about attitudes toward working out and test whether that proxies.
data.name: Attitude/behavior gap

data.brief: The marketing dream of personalizing for each individual, now operational: users bucketed into intent groups (exploring / buying / informing — marketers decide the groups), pages assembled per query ("a coffee machine for camping" → rewritten copy, camping-suitable products, tips). Beyond the browser: a voice query to an assistant rendering a fully personalized page on a Google TV — "no phone, no computer, just my voice." "Is the web still the future? Nobody knows — but we can do this with generative sites"
data.name: Audience of one

data.brief: Replaces the standard RL prompt "find and exploit the vulnerability" with "find all vulnerabilities". The model submits multiple proofs of vulnerability; a deterministic grader uniquifies them by stack backtrace (the same technique OS crash reporters use to dedupe); the known-vulnerability set is renormalized when the model proves a bug the authors did not know about; the score is precision (found ÷ submitted) against recall (known-found ÷ total known), which simultaneously rewards discovery of unknown bugs and penalizes proof-of-vulnerability spam. Consequences: open-world grading on real open-source targets instead of artificially perfect single-bug environments; no easiest-bug reward hacking; a clean learning trajectory; and the model is never told how many bugs exist — or that any exist at all.
data.name: The audit task

data.brief: Answer to approval fatigue and to the "IT and security really hates that you turn on full access" problem. When a sandboxed action escalates, the harness spins up a read-only auto-review subagent that cannot itself spawn subagents, and hands it the user authorization, a risk taxonomy, judging criteria, and the transcript plus the pending tool calls. It returns a judgment on authorization strength, blast radius, and disposition — auto-approving the unpredictable-but-benign while holding the line on data exfiltration. Applies symmetrically to file-system and network actions ("curling Google to see if the internet works is fine, but maybe not uploading a file"). Context-sensitivity is the point: deleting a .git folder is fine if asked for and catastrophic if not
data.name: Auto review (auto-approval subagent)

data.brief: Adaption Labs' system for automating the training of models. Distinguishing claim: it co-optimizes the entire loop from data to alignment and self-evolves per domain and data type, rather than treating data as something the agent merely decides whether to generate — "we did not get the returns until we controlled for data quality; we co-optimized the data exactly as we would the model." Reported to outperform research staff, attributed to the search space being broader than any individual's experience across model types, sizes, and dense-versus-MoE architectures, and to its willingness to change many hyperparameters at once "that humans are much more wary about changing." Win rates cluster just above 60% because a budget-stopping rule exited at 60; with that removed, performance continues climbing. Beta uptake most acute in medical, sciences, legal and code — domains where models fall short and last-mile customization is acute
data.name: Auto Scientist

data.brief: Graziano's eval-gated agent-optimization loop, Karpathy's autoresearch applied to agents instead of ML models: a coding agent (Claude Code) rewrites a target agent — system prompt, tools, tool logic — one hypothesis per git branch, runs the eval suite, continues from improvements and rolls back regressions, keeping a cross-run memory file and per-hypothesis reports.md; the human steers via a markdown job spec and hypothesis review
data.name: AutoAgent

data.brief: Enterprise tool-calling benchmark used as the ambition antipattern: verifiers are hard-coded string matches, e.g. one arbitrary phone-number format among many acceptable ones, and the prompt never says which. Result: Haiku and Fable both score 20% — Haiku by making mistakes, Fable by getting it right 80% of the time and formatting differently. A task that cannot separate those two models measures nothing, and a hard-coded string match cannot be the instrument that tells us when AI is ready to remake an industry. Name from captions.
data.name: AutomationBench

data.brief: Human tendency to defer to an automated/AI signal instead of exercising independent judgment — the reviewer becomes a rubber stamp. The failure mode human-in-the-loop systems must be designed against; Wharton's "cognitive surrender" (adopting AI output as one's own with minimal scrutiny) is the same phenomenon
data.name: Automation bias

data.brief: Internal MCP server giving AI tools access to Automattic's decades of documented knowledge, decisions, and data; used daily for research and planning by non-engineers — the context layer that grounds org-wide vibe-coding in real institutional knowledge
data.name: Automattic internal knowledge MCP server

data.brief: Factory's internal autonomy instrumentation: the ratio of actions taken by AI systems to actions taken by humans before an interruption. Factory reports ~15-20% "autonomy" with an autonomy ratio in the upper 80s for its own codebase; some customer codebases score higher because they operate under more constrained conditions; its internal legal-workflow droid is ~100% autonomously maintained while its own terminal harness is not — visual defects like flickering have no verifier. The 15-20% vs upper-80% figures are as-spoken and internally ambiguous.
data.name: Autonomy ratio

data.brief: Karpathy. 70.5k stars. Single GPU, single file, 5-min cycles. MIT.
data.description: Karpathy's autonomous research loop. 70.5k stars. One editable file, one scalar metric, 5-min time budget. Human writes `program.md`; agent runs ~100 experiments overnight. MIT.
data.name: autoresearch

data.brief: The goal: an avatar "indistinguishable from a human on a video call" — not just photorealism but the long tail (emotions, object interactions, micro-expressions, an internal state). LemonSlice's bet: most AI-human interaction will have a visual layer, because humans are biologically wired to understand best with a visual component. They plan to define and publish their own avatar-Turing-test with real people ("we won't pass it this year, but we'll track it")
data.name: The avatar Turing test

data.brief: Nakajima's March-2023 autonomous-agent experiment that went viral ("people thought it was going to work; it didn't work at all"); nine lower-fanfare iterations over three-plus years, usually themed on self-improvement — "build the simplest thing that can build itself." ActiveGraph is the fourth major generation.
data.name: BabyAGI

data.brief: Always-on agents for the production work that has no owner and no page: watching deploys out to health, morning incident digests, chasing the returned P99 drift nobody alerts on, capacity reports against quarterly goals, recurring health checks "not waiting for a customer to complain first". Trigger model: schedules, weekly ceremonies (Thursday on-call handover), event streams (CI/CD deployments, Slack messages), or direct message ("go do some work"). Runtime model: always running, in the cloud ("if you close your laptop, it's okay"), inside a sandbox with a filesystem underneath so the agent self-organizes its work; a task system plus imported skills plus integrations tell it what to do; a shared learning loop reflects on each task and carries lessons across tasks
data.name: Background agents (ops long tail)

data.brief: A diagnostic list, offered as things that *indicate* the setup is wrong rather than that the model is bad. Babysitting agents at all is the first tell. "The model is being really dumb today" — the model did not change; the harness may have, and a setup that cannot absorb small harness changes is not set up well. Silently burning context and money — blowing through 500k, 750k or a million tokens and hitting auto-compact on tasks that do not warrant it. Long sessions needing constant intervention. A constant slop factory. And asking how other companies ship so fast when model labs release on a six-to-eight-week cadence — "clearly they have something which we don't"
data.name: Symptoms of a bad agent setup

data.brief: Boundary's programming language, positioned as a from-first-principles substrate for a world where humans write no code. Demonstrated properties: inferred, exhaustively-checked error types; zero-cost per-file execution tracing; every function auto-exposed as a CLI command and bundleable into a standalone cross-platform/WASM binary; and callability from any host language (Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java, "anything new that comes up") with type-safe sync and async bindings and lambdas, closures and generics passed across the language boundary. No function coloring. Gloss from the talk: "basically a made-up language".
data.name: BAML (Boundary)

data.brief: The talk's thesis. The old base model was a compressed reflection of the whole human internet, accumulated by next-token prediction over web text, and it defined how good your model could get — it was the bulk of the compute budget and the core of the process, with post-training merely surfacing that knowledge into a chat template and RL "a cherry on top shaping the flavour of interactions". After o1 (2024) and R1 (January 2025) the base model's job changed: it now supplies the atomic skills that RL composes, plus reasoning and agentic behaviour priors.
data.description: Supporting result cited: a base model needs exposure to the atomic skills it will have to compose during RL, and given a sufficiently difficult environment the model extrapolates from there. Generalizing clause the speaker is careful to add: today those priors are reasoning and agentic behaviour because that is how the models get used — if a new interaction paradigm took off, the base model's job would be to build a prior for that instead.
data.name: Base model as an RL prior

data.brief: Academic benchmark (ETH Zurich / UC Berkeley) measuring security of LLM-written code; finds even the best models introduce vulnerabilities ~20-40% of the time
data.name: BaxBench

data.brief: First-generation AI products "put the model too much in a box" — constrained tools and degrees of freedom made it hard to be unreasonable ("I can write code but can't really run it"). Cowork giving every knowledge worker a VM that can run bash looks excessive until the model remediates its own PDF-parsing failure with a script. Teach users and product teams to ask for more; a non-technical colleague asking for changes was told "why don't you ask Claude?" Personal extreme: porting a couple-hundred-thousand-line Python codebase to TypeScript over a weekend via a dynamic workflow that ported, verified, cross-read and churned until Monday
data.name: Be unreasonable

data.brief: Yegge's task tracker for long-running agent loops; queue work, agents claim it (Gas Town = "a beads machine"); planned donation to the Agentic Foundation
data.name: Beads

data.brief: AWS managed service "dedicated only to agents in production": serverless runtime (any framework inside), Gateway with built-in semantic tool routing (register tools once, it selects per request), short/long-term memory, policy service enforcing code-level rules structurally, steering rules stored in DynamoDB (live-updated without redeploy), CloudWatch observability
data.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

data.brief: AWS's service letting agents discover, authorize and execute payments "with a few lines of code": bring wallets from Coinbase or Stripe (preview); payment connectors, x402 first and protocol-agnostic by design; instant settlement; payment sessions that cap the amount and expire in minutes or days; built-in observability with a full trace; wallet secrets stored in a KMS-secured token wallet so the agent never holds private keys; integrated with AgentCore Gateway (which also MCPifies internal APIs) for Coinbase's discovery service of 10,000+ x402 endpoints. When a tool call returns 402 the service completes the transaction and returns control to the agent
data.name: Bedrock AgentCore Payments

data.brief: Always-on wrist microphone that records everything and builds a personal agent over a stateful, persistent-memory runtime; captured data is user-extractable into other systems/agents; backend is provider-blind (Amazon cannot read it)
data.name: Bee wearable + personal agent

data.brief: Deliberately jargon-free decomposition arrived at after hitting "a wall of keywords" (graders, long horizon, verifiers, rubrics): a benchmark is a prompt/instruction fed to models and agents which produce solutions, verified and graded by verifiers and rubrics, all wrapped in a harness that isolates the run from external factors, emitting trajectories, scores and metadata used to rank models. Its analytic value is the implied conjunction: the equation only yields a meaningful ranking if every stage is sound, so a single weak stage (usually the prompt or the verifier) silently invalidates the score.
data.name: Benchmark anatomy (the five-stage reduction)

data.brief: "Benchmark is software. It's code. It's files. You need to treat it as such" — including its own CI pipeline: pinned dependencies, correct base image, no missing fixtures, an oracle run that must pass (or, absent an oracle, verifying that the verifiers correctly fail), several real agent runs to confirm the task is solvable *and* hard, difficulty tagging (simple/medium/hard by success frequency), and an explicit approval step before the task joins the suite. Exists because benchmark construction fails in four recurring ways: agents reward-hack the simulation once they detect it, over-broad verifiers pass everything, incorrect verifiers fail everything, and unstable agents produce high-variance results.
data.name: Benchmark as software (benchmark CI)

data.brief: Worked arithmetic for why benchmarks are built badly: 1,000 tasks x 60 expert-hours per task, at a software engineer costing $500k/year, is roughly $15M to build an agentic coding benchmark — plus roughly a third of tasks washed away every year by model progress, roughly $5M/year to replace. Out of budget for most projects, so builders reach for the workarounds (heavy AI assistance, cheap labor) that produce every antipattern downstream. The causal root of the talk.
data.name: Benchmark build economics (the cost wall)

data.brief: Human eval is the actual target ("AI exists to serve humans"), but it's expensive, so benchmarks distill human preference into something scalable and hope the distillation stays faithful. Past some point, hill-climbing the benchmark leaves human eval flat — and can be pushed further until human eval declines. Illustration: for the prompt "what time is it?", a response no human evaluator would ever choose sits at the top of the LMArena leaderboard. If you're benchmaxxing, you simply stop caring about the divergence.
data.name: Benchmark/human-eval divergence

data.brief: A single benchmark number under a single scaffold is one sample from a distribution nobody measured — a noisy sample treated as a measurement. Two mechanisms named: contrived benchmarks only ever test a single isolated in-distribution question and so cannot test whether a model sustains correct reasoning across a long dependent episode; and cross-harness or cross-infrastructure differencing is the primary cause of benchmark divergence, producing false-positive and false-negative rates that headline stats hide.
data.name: Benchmark psychosis

data.brief: Vendor framework for authoring tasks: (1) human instructions — authored and reviewed by humans, expressing desired behaviors, objectives and hard constraints rather than implementation detail; (2) holistic graders — behavioral tests for broad surface plus precision where it matters (security, business logic get the full unit/integration/e2e stack; the rest doesn't need 100% coverage), mirroring how engineers actually test; (3) production grade — economically valuable tasks, judged by whether an engineer can say "if the LLM fixes this, I trust it to fix that"; (4) contamination-free by design — novel tasks only plus private hold-out sets, since today's benchmarks are drawn from public repos;
data.description: (5) informative leaderboards — the benchmark must tell a story and support a decision, surfacing the run data instead of only who won.
data.name: Five principles for benchmark tasks (G2i)

data.brief: Labs training too hard on benchmarks in ways that diverge from what people actually care about; restated at the end as "the exploitation of misalignments between benchmarks and human preference". Explicitly a two-sided phenomenon: construction antipatterns on the benchmark-builder side and gaming plays on the lab side. The term's existence is itself the evidence that "we have a sense that benchmarks don't always equal reality".
data.name: Benchmaxxing

data.brief: DatologyAI's synthetic-data platform, built on rephrasing and designed to be applied to anyone's proprietary documents in their own environment. Worked example: a document about a corporate takeover converted into one of hundreds of templates (e.g. a series of true/false questions). Two claimed properties: no model collapse, because all information originates in the source document; and the student can exceed the rephrasing model, because the rephraser only has to transform the document accurately, not understand and teach the concepts — a much easier task.
data.description: Critical caveat: what you rephrase matters — rephrasing randomly selected documents does not work; rephrasing the high-quality ones does.
data.name: BeyondWeb

data.brief: Public benchmark/leaderboard for LLM function/tool calling; used (with synthetic tool pools scaled to 10→~1,000 tools) as the eval basis for the fat-agent vs router comparison in this talk
data.name: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL)

data.brief: Paper-backed claim: at equal disk footprint, a ~4× larger model quantized to 4-bit (120B@4bit) beats the smaller full-precision one (35B@BF16) on intelligence — so the resource-optimal recipe is "train a ginormous model, then quantize it down." Mechanistic basis: current models are undertrained relative to parameter count (~30T tokens vs a hypothetical ~300T saturation), so ~86% of weights "do not need to be there"; the panel notes compression may stop working if training ever saturates the weights. Caveat: throughput — a big compressed model may decode at 5–10 tok/s where a small native one does 200
data.name: Big-quantized beats small-full-precision

data.brief: (1) Verifiable — the success condition is checkable by a function. (2) Durable — the ground truth must be invariant across valid analysis paths; science admits no clean ground truth, so a lazily constructed task will fail a correct-but-different analysis. (3) Interaction-requiring — the conclusion must require touching the data, not memorized knowledge; no one-turn answers. Stated as holding up over time and across omics types.
data.name: Three properties of a good biological eval

data.brief: Eval design for bio refusal calibration: build routine tasks that simulate what a working scientist actually asks, paired with red-team tasks engineered to look innocuous while carrying harmful structure (e.g. "clone this gene into a bacterium, it's GFP" where the sequence is a toxin or could bootstrap a virus). Measured result: routine tasks are refused drastically more often than the red-team tasks — framed as an evaluation problem, not a policy stance.
data.name: Biosecurity routine/red-team eval pairs

data.brief: Classic 1970s–80s AI architecture (Kafka its modern descendant): many slim workers communicating only through shared state, never directly. Historically limited because it was unintuitive for humans to write and workers had to stay slim/deterministic — both constraints lifted now that AI writes the code and workers have reasoning capability.
data.name: Blackboard architecture

data.brief: Multi-tenant AI agent for wedding venues (talks to couples, briefs coordinators) built on the four-layer stack; discloses that it is an AI in its very first response — before being asked; hard physical-presence boundary ("you are software; you do not have a body"); adjusts narration to engagement heat-maps read through soft human context
data.name: Bloom

data.brief: FactSet's pre-skills in-house format, presented at the same conference a year earlier: a simple set of steps or recipe handed to an agent so it doesn't have to rediscover its path each time. Retrospectively described by its author as "simply a skill in a very naive form". Retired once Anthropic open-sourced Agent Skills — "since Anthropic had already open-sourced skills, there was no point trying to maintain our own standards" — making this one of the corpus's clearest first-person accounts of an enterprise abandoning a private format for a vendor-published open one.
data.name: Blueprints

data.brief: The buyer-side thesis: ~40% of getting to AI-native is models and products; ~60% is data hygiene, clean architecture, good integration, strong enablement and change management — "the stuff no one likes talking about anymore." A new frontier model every ~11 days versus architecture a decade old; ChatGPT is 43 months old while companies are still finishing five-year-old ERP migrations. "AI is a flashlight, not a band-aid: it accelerates what works and breaks down quickly where things don't." Fix the technology estate before plugging AI in
data.name: The boring 60%

data.brief: Don't offload the thinking: at the start truly understand the problem and decide what to work on; let the machine rip in the middle; at the end raise the bar ("we're not shipping shitty code"). If you're still needed in the middle, spend time on the middle until a three-hour run is always good. "Implementation is only getting cheaper and judgement is not"
data.name: Brain at the ends

data.brief: The load-bearing architectural decision. The first implementation put the agent loop and tool execution in one container, which meant the model could not begin reasoning until the container finished setting up, and one component failing took the whole agent down. Separating them yields three benefits: sandboxes spin up just in time and only when needed; a dead sandbox can be replaced while the loop continues; and — the measured payoff — the model reasons immediately while container setup runs in parallel, or is skipped entirely when the task needs no container
data.name: Decoupling the brain from the hands

data.brief: Machinecraft's forkable "company brain" architecture, shipped as an empty nervous system (forkmybrain.org): ~39 single-job specialist agents (orchestrator, sales, pricing, machine specs, fact-checking, corrections-guarding) that hold moderated "meetings"; layered engineered memory (working memory / pinned facts / episode stories / relationship warmth) behind a salience gate, with corrections always beating conflicting facts; a nightly sleep cycle; and a values "soul file" (Jain family-business principles compiled to engineering rules: cross-check before speaking, cite document + date, never speak in absolutes). Built on off-the-shelf models from three providers — no fine-tuning — over vector + relationship-graph + CRM databases, with ~213 tools exposed over one protocol. Golden rule: agents draft, humans send.
data.name: Brain OS

data.brief: The framing of what current models lack. Models have superhuman breadth across public knowledge but not the "almost subconscious intuition" that comes from prolonged practice in one area. Three concrete failure classes: no knowledge of anything after the training cutoff; poor long-tail skill acquisition where public examples are thin (AMD kernels given as the example — "there are not that many good kernels written on AMD GPUs that are public"); and no knowledge of *you* — your emails, your writing style, your company's partnerships — "unless you happen to be famous enough to appear in the pre-training data"
data.name: Breadth versus depth

data.brief: Training directly inside the customer's real production setup instead of a replica: "if the agent learns the exact environment distribution, why don't we just use the real environment?" Architecture: all orchestration loops and logic stay on the customer's side, run however they already run them; the vendor keeps only the model completion endpoint plus a way to record the requests and responses going in and out of the model. Eliminates environment fidelity risk by construction and lets a vendor "meet customers where they're at" — including harnesses they cannot read the source of. Cost: non-replayability and off-policy data, described by the speaker as two names for one problem.
data.name: Bring your own harness (BYOH training)

data.brief: Fixed-corpus variant of OpenAI's BrowseComp deep-search benchmark: complex browsing questions answered over a fixed 100k-document corpus instead of the open web, which makes Oracle-vs-tools comparisons possible; Oracle ceiling ~93% for frontier models per the talk
data.name: BrowseComp Plus

data.brief: What working browser agents share. Multimodal: model-mix per page difficulty, and code alongside clicking — "the most reliable browser agents in production are often writing code alongside using the browser," e.g. intercepting network requests and replaying them by script (Claude Code emitting a script beats Claude-in-Chrome for repeatable tasks — context-efficient). Harness-engineered: memory and skills so nothing is discovered twice — Browse.sh publishes per-website skills an agent reads before visiting; token-optimized context, not whole-page dumps. Reliable infrastructure: environments that render identically every run — "if your infra renders mobile one time and desktop the next, you get inconsistent results"; the Mac-mini-under-the-desk OpenClaw setup named as the anti-pattern ("I've yet to see a SOC 2 compliant Mac mini setup at scale")
data.name: Multimodal, harness-engineered, reliable infra

data.brief: The vendor answer: prompt in, and the platform stands up "the harness, the runtime, the sandbox, the code execution, the fetch, the search tools, and the models." Sessions feed observability (screen recordings, logs, network activity) back into the agent — "every agent you run should get better every single time" — with an optimization pass that reviews completed runs. Pitched as a subagent for larger agentic systems: "you should be focusing your time on solving customer problems, not rebuilding best-in-class browser agents"
data.name: Browserbase agents

data.brief: Invert the traditional playbook: rather than hiring salespeople, RevOps and sales engineers and automating the bottlenecks later, start with what the 2026 toolset can automate — inbound capture and response, outbound research, sequencing and dialing, security questionnaires — find what is broken, and add humans only there. Launch self-serve first and learn what buyers cannot get before building the expensive tier and hiring to sell it: OpenAI did it backwards ("the Porsche before the Prius") and the self-serve tier cannibalized the enterprise one within a quarter
data.name: Build the machine before the team

data.brief: Block's internal orchestrator, built by engineers/AI champions to coordinate fleets of parallel agents; consumes the company world model to plan work spanning multiple codebases; any employee can invoke it from Slack to fix bugs or ship features — no GitHub account needed
data.name: Builder Bot

data.brief: Intuit's training substrate. From the general ledger, P&L, cash-flow statements and invoices across QuickBooks, TurboTax, Credit Karma and Mailchimp, build business states (detailed point-in-time summaries of a business), derive actions from the ledger itself (a marketing campaign was funded, payroll was paid, hiring costs rose), and attach outcomes over multiple horizons (profit, revenue, cash flow, or combinations). The result is millions of state-action-outcome vectors — the raw material for learning which actions lead to which outcomes for businesses in comparable situations.
data.name: Business trajectories (state-action-outcome)

data.brief: Per-buyer connected record rolling every signal into persona ↔ account ↔ deal: individual touchpoints link to their account, accounts surface the buying committee, deal-level state records what sales/marketing already did — the structure that makes account prioritization and alert throttling possible at all
data.name: Buyer context graph

data.brief: The best startups arrive with security architecture that works, a responsive support engineer, an admin API from the beginning, a 90-day plan that deploys into the buyer's cloud, and let the buyer write the success criteria. The worst bring salesmanship, no diagrams, no deployment control or audit logs, no ETAs. Weekly pilot check-ins on non-production data surface the difference fast
data.name: Buyer-written success criteria

data.brief: The core insight: every nefarious and every good action an agent takes "comes in the form of some network communication — some bytes over the wire," whether via MCP or a spawned subprocess. ACLs, read-only credentials, and MCP-tool scoping all help "up to a point" but break down because access composes into holes (reach one system, tunnel to another — e.g. through an EKS endpoint into a VPC Postgres to DROP TABLE) and because "as soon as OpenClaw spawns psql you've broken through the MCP boundary." So the guard must understand the actual bytes, at the protocol level, not just HTTP
data.name: Byte-level egress control

data.brief: Load the whole document collection into a large context window and persist the model's KV cache (captions: "KB matrix" = KV matrix), so questions are answered from cached context with no per-query retrieval; corpus refresh = reload + re-cache, cheap relative to graph recomputation. Limits: the context window is finite, and overfilling it degrades answer quality
data.name: Cache-augmented generation (CAG)

data.brief: The load-bearing economic insight: providers cache already-sent tokens (KV cache), and cached tokens are far cheaper — up to ~50× on DeepSeek, ~90% cost saving typically — and faster (already computed). But any transformation of the context (summarize/compact) creates a new context the provider can't cache, so you pay full price for the transformed tokens. Consequence: for compaction to be worthwhile you must compress by more than the cache multiplier (>50×) without losing quality — usually impossible — so "summarization is potentially a trap." The most serious harnesses (Claude Code, Codex) use caching plus very specific, non-summarizing compaction
data.name: Caching makes summarization a trap

data.brief: "The more we used the model, the more rigid everything became." Model lock-in: fine-tuning was supposed to make them model-agnostic (just pass the data to a new model) — instead, training-data formats differ between versions and radically between providers, so switching was too costly and the model was frozen for consistency. Architecture lock-in: built on late-2024 workflow orthodoxy and unable to adopt newer architectures because all effort went to keeping it running
data.name: The calcification tax

data.brief: TypeSafe's proposed third branch. Each post-training family has one North Star — RLHF optimizes human preference, RLVR optimizes pure correctness — and this one optimizes calibrated decision-making, framed as "mainlining the intelligence of pre-trained models into being actually useful for software". Stated to be neither RLHF nor RLVR, with a different API shape from both, and reasoned about from scratch on the analogy that "no one thought about instruction following before we made instruction following happen": a genuinely new post-training branch "looks totally alien, and then in hindsight becomes super obvious".
data.description: Also carries his ordering of the stack — "data matters more than compute, and doing the right task matters way more than data" — offered as a correction to the bitter lesson, which he says holds in games but not in reality.
data.name: Calibrated decision-making as a post-training objective

data.brief: The verification primitive that gates an agent-authored performance fix: two instances, one running the old code and one the candidate optimization, receiving the same traffic for ~10 minutes, producing a comparison report of CPU reduction, latency change and error rate. The agent reads the report and decides whether the change is worth a human's attention — a rise in error rate is a "red signal" that it broke business logic while optimizing. Mental model as stated: "profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, an engineer makes the decision." Explicitly not an AI problem — observability, canary and verification logic are standard pre-AI infrastructure that the agent only needs to know how to invoke and read.
data.name: Canary as the agent's ground truth

data.brief: Latent model capability exceeding what current prompts/harnesses extract — "models get smarter in spiky ways": a chat model cannot list the Pokémon whose names end in "-aw", but the same model with a code-execution tool fetches every name and filters (Croconaw, Drednaw). Models are "grown, not designed", so the harness encodes our *understanding* of the model; "unhobbling" = mapping and unlocking the overhang, and each frontier release (Fable) ships with a largely unmapped one
data.name: Capability overhang

data.brief: Two-class taxonomy for agent skills: capability skills teach a model what it can't yet do consistently — temporary by design, retired as models improve (evals tell you when); preference skills encode company/team-specific workflows, style, and references — durable, never absorbed by foundation models, and protected by evals against regression on agent updates
data.name: Capability vs preference skills

data.brief: JavaScript RPC system (Cap'n Proto lineage, ⚠ captioned "captain web") used as the single communication channel of the confinement architecture: a session over postMessage from the sandboxed iframe, forwarded to the gadget's Durable Object server code
data.name: Cap'n Web RPC

data.brief: The measurement discipline that makes outcomes usable: you cannot run the same business twice, so take two groups of similar businesses with the same propensity to take an action, where one group took it and one didn't, and compare. Worked example: businesses that raised prices gained $4,200/day in profit, those that didn't gained $2,800/day — the naive read is a $1,400 impact, but the price-raisers were already more successful (which is why they could raise prices), so the corrected impact is nearer $1,150.
data.name: CATE / conditional average treatment effect

data.brief: The framing device for the capacity mismatch. The cathedral — one region, fast interconnect, many GPUs wired together — is the right shape for a trainer and the hardest thing to get. The bazaar — different providers, regions, prices and availability — is where most usable compute actually lives. RL's default loop demands the cathedral for the whole system, so it inherits the scarcest resource's constraints: "RL wants all four of these at the same time — enough GPU, same region, fast fabric, and available now. Any of these is manageable, but all four is pretty hard." Underneath sits the asymmetry that training capacity is not elastic the way inference capacity is: "you cannot assume you can grow the trainer cluster halfway through a run just because rollout wants more nodes"
data.name: Cathedral vs bazaar compute

data.brief: The three technical moves that make a video model real-time and interactive: (1) causal attention mask — past-only, since the future doesn't exist yet at inference (no future audio); (2) step distillation — 30 denoising steps → 1, noise-to-video in a single step; (3) a novel solution to error accumulation — the compounding-drift problem where past-only generation feeds its own errors forward, which is fatal for the 8–16-hour continuous streams they run. Cost brought to ~voice-model parity
data.name: Causal, one-step, low-error real-time video

data.brief: Anthropic's certification for agentic engineering, released March (⚠ 2026 presumed; verify official name/date — captions say "Claude Certified Architect"/"Claude Certified Exam"). Scenario-based, timed, proctored; offered to companies in the Anthropic ecosystem, and individuals can pay $99 to sit it once every 6 months. Multiple-choice, but grounded in realistic constraints. Five weighted domains: agentic architecture 27%; Claude Code configuration & workflow 20%; prompt engineering / structured output (JSON everywhere); tool design & MCP integration; context management & reliability. Six production scenarios — customer-support resolution agent, code generation with Claude, multi-agent research system, developer productivity, Claude Code for CI, structured data extraction — of which each sitting randomly draws four and centers all questions on them
data.name: Claude Certified Architect (CCA) exam

data.brief: The premise on one slide: "a CDP browser is just like a meatbag with a mouse — as far as Google and Cloudflare can tell." An agent driving Chrome through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (the F12 panel's own protocol) sends clicks and keystrokes down the exact same internal path a human's do. Delivered as a CLI, not an MCP server, on three grounds from an Arize AI study: capability is a wash (~83% task success either way), but the CLI wins on reuse (a sequence is programmed once, run 1,000× with no model in the loop; MCP hits the model every turn), speed (7 turns / <1 min vs MCP's 71 round trips / 8 min for the same task), and cost (Anthropic-reported up to 75× cheaper in tokens). CDP is large — 57 domains, hundreds of methods — but only a small subset is needed, grouped as digital senses
data.name: Driving Chrome via CDP from a CLI

data.brief: AWS's open-source authorization policy language has its functional specification in Lean and its production implementation in Rust; properties such as "for any satisfied forbid policy the request is always denied" are proven on the model, and ~100 million differential random tests run nightly to check the Rust code matches the Lean spec on the same inputs — "no version ships until this is satisfied." The pattern for verifying code you don't rewrite in Lean
data.name: Cedar: spec in Lean, production in Rust, nightly differential testing

data.brief: Pre-vetted vulnerability-free base images, continuously updated — "your inputs" side of the supply chain
data.name: Chainguard Images

data.brief: Three-part anatomy of an interface: **channel** = the physical transport (keyboard, microphone, screen, punch card, prompt box); **expression** = the range/richness of meaning the channel is permitted to carry; **protocol** = the rules and shape of the exchange. Diagnosis of AI today: channels unchanged for decades (the QWERTY patent is ~1860s), expression exploded with natural language, but the protocol — prompting — is still batch: encode a complete request, submit, wait, read, repair, resubmit; inherited punch card → loom lineage
data.name: Channel / expression / protocol

data.brief: Listening for orders every few seconds of a live visit with a large model "would break the bank," so a series of cheaper, faster gates detects the right events in the conversation and only then hands off to heavier models that match the spoken order against orders approved by the system and relevant to the visit, queuing them for the clinician to sign in the EHR. Latency and cost handled by deciding when intelligence runs, not by running less of it
data.name: Cheap gates trigger heavy models

data.brief: TNG's automated chess-video pipeline: nightly Lichess game download → background analysis → tool-using agent that explores the game in depth (legal-move tool to bar illegal reasoning; an interactive board it can play/take back/branch on; chess-engine evaluation on demand; a checks-captures-threats saliency tool; human-move models; web search for historical context) → intermediate explanation format → rendered video with ElevenLabs V3 narration (audio tags for excitement). The agent itself decides which squares to highlight, which arrows to draw, and what counts as a brilliant move; videos upload automatically every night.
data.name: TNG chess explainer agent

data.brief: For long-horizon science tasks where a terminal verifiable reward is "somewhat uninformative": treat the set of valid analysis paths as a tree, find nodes that are invariant across paths, and build rubrics at those choke points using knowledge of how the task works. Observed to be associated with the verifiable outcomes but only loosely correlated numerically — explicitly not yet trusted for RL or benchmarking.
data.name: Choke-point rubrics

data.brief: Proof-of-concept record/replay framework for agents built by the speakers: a `boundary` annotation wraps any node (tool call, LLM call, RAG retrieval) and records its input/output pair plus frozen run state (model version, code/build version, sampling params) as a trace; replay mode stubs every node except the one under test, turning any recorded production failure into a rerunnable, zero-model-call test case with assertions
data.name: Chronicle

data.brief: RAG without a chunker, embedding model, or vector database: parse the document into a layout-aware structured object (Docling's Pydantic document), then use its markdown outline + per-section summaries as the *entire* retrieval index; an agentic loop (~5 iterations in the demo) picks candidate sections relevant to the question, pulls full section text from the structured document, judges sufficiency, and iterates; demonstrated on Docling's own 8-page paper (20 sections) and scaled to IBM's 2025 annual report (418 sections)
data.name: Chunkless RAG (outline-as-index agentic retrieval)

data.brief: Running agent loops on the CI system you already have (GitHub Actions, GitLab, CircleCI) rather than new infrastructure: it already holds code access, secrets, and dispatch plus scheduling primitives. One workflow run equals one loop iteration (sense, control, actuate, open PR), scheduled daily so the team walks in to one small, low-risk PR. We don't need a new cluster for this.
data.name: CI as the loop runtime

data.brief: Three layers: agent wallets that let an agent hold and spend money autonomously within guardrails the wallet enforces (max per call, per session, per day); merchant SDKs that wrap endpoints and resources in a paywall "with a few lines of code"; and USDC plus nanopayments to settle at the speed agents operate, sub-second. Set up "in a couple of clicks" at agents.circle.com; demonstrated with Claude Code paying for data, email and a phone call on a single research task
data.name: The Circle agent stack

data.brief: Why existing benchmarks cannot simply be chained. Headroom — the task must actually require online adaptation; if a model could improve by offline training on that data, it does not measure continual learning, which rules out most benchmarks for frontier models trained on "almost everything on the internet." Shared structure — instances must have shared latent structure to exploit, whereas traditional benchmark instances are *designed to be independent*, which is the fundamental reason chaining AIME problems into a sequence cannot work. A learning mechanism — the environment must return signal (scalar reward, error messages, textual feedback) that makes improvement realistically possible
data.name: Three criteria for a continual-learning benchmark

data.brief: The closing argument, framed as a sunk-cost critique. Today's stack — pre-training, mid-training, RL against teacher models, finishing with multi-tier on-policy distillation — produces a frozen checkpoint, and continual-learning research then tries to bolt learning onto models "never designed to be continual learners to begin with." If it were a first-order requirement, the architecture might look nothing like this: "in the purest sense, continual learning might just be one phase of training, and everything after that is deployment" — one learning phase, then a model updating its weights in the environment indefinitely
data.name: Continual learning as a first-order design requirement

data.brief: From scheduling through treatment, documentation (even an X-ray), submission, the 999 syntax acknowledgment, status checks and the 835 payment, a claim is dozens of small steps, each with its own compliance and each a chance for an error that propagates. Too-strict guardrails reject correct work; pure agentic reasoning across 50 multimodal steps is slow, expensive and error-prone; hard-coding everything bloats into a system that needs a huge team. The design task is the balance — and the cost discipline: a routine step run a thousand times a day cannot use the most expensive model. Reducing an image to conclusions early is a false economy when a later step needed the context
data.name: The claims journey as fifty constrained steps

data.brief: The scalable-filtering method: use a large vision-language model to make a filtering decision (is this an AI image? does it have watermarks/borders?), then distill that decision into a cheap SigLip-sized classifier you can run over a billion+ images affordably — the same approach cited for text (essential-web-data's LLM-taxonomy distilled to a ~500M model). Plus SAE-based unsupervised tagging: a sparse autoencoder on a vision model yields off-the-shelf feature tags (horse, blurry, watermark) to oversample/filter on. Krea ended with ~30–40 custom in-house classifiers/heuristics
data.name: Big-VLM-to-small-classifier distillation

data.brief: Permission layer replacing manual prompts: a Sonnet classifier judges every tool/bash call against conversation context and the user's own dynamic instructions ("don't push"), and adjudicates sandbox escapes (e.g. network requests); internal-only since January 2026, hardened via commissioned red teams and thousands of evals before public rollout; the layer that makes Claude Tag's exposure to whole-channel input viable
data.name: Claude Code auto mode

data.brief: Anthropic's terminal coding agent; launched February 2025 as a bullet point on the Sonnet 3.7 launch, now the center of an agentic product family (Claude Tag, Cowork, workflows, remote control, sub-agents); built and maintained using itself
data.name: Claude Code

data.brief: Anthropic's enterprise AI plugins for legal, finance, HR, cybersecurity. Catalyst for $830B SaaS selloff.
data.description: Anthropic's enterprise AI plugins covering legal, finance, HR, cybersecurity, and COBOL modernization. Sequential launches in Feb 2026 directly catalyzed the $830B SaaS selloff.
data.name: Claude Cowork

data.brief: Claude Code capability (released weeks before the talk; Anthropic's "A Harness for Every Task" post shows six workflow patterns) that lets the agent generate and run recursive, model-chosen workflows — the change that made RLM co-author Omar Khattab publicly declare Claude Code "finally an RLM"
data.name: Claude Code dynamic workflows

data.brief: Anthropic frontier model released around this conference; described as a step change: one-shots many product features, enables ~80% system-prompt reduction, does long-horizon multimodal work (autonomous video editing incl. dynamic cropping, transcript sync, HTML-slide substitution). Captions have the speaker start to say "mythos" then self-correct to "fable", suggesting Mythos was the preview name (flagged, not merged with el-claude-mythos-preview)
data.name: Claude Fable

data.brief: Anthropic's small/fast model; carries Ace's per-turn work once the reasoning is scaffolded out
data.name: Claude Haiku 4.5

data.brief: Emergent cybersecurity capabilities. Zero-day exploitation. Not generally available — Project Glasswing only.
data.description: 100% on Cybench. Autonomously writes zero-day exploits for Firefox, FreeBSD, VMs, phone lock screens. Capabilities emerged from general reasoning improvements, not cybersecurity training. Not generally available — Glasswing only.
data.name: Claude Mythos Preview

data.brief: Anthropic frontier model; the "heavy" baseline Ace deliberately avoids for the live loop
data.name: Claude Opus 4.7

data.brief: Claude living in team collaboration tools (launched publicly in Slack the week before this talk): multiplayer by default (whole channel steers one session), proactive rather than reactive (standing instructions like "monitor bug reports in this channel, put up a PR, tag the last-touching engineer"), with channel-scoped team memory (markdown file per channel); positioned internally as "the evolution of Claude Code"
data.name: Claude Tag

data.brief: Deno's MIT-licensed proxy that sits in front of agents. Operates below HTTP — parses every byte of each protocol (Postgres wire protocol included), with a plug-in system for unknown protocols. Holds credentials like Agent Vault and injects them so the agent never sees secret values. A dashboard shows every "action" (more general than an HTTP request) per device/agent — allowed, denied, or pending approval — with analytics. Treats the agent software as a black box requiring no modification. Runs over Tailscale/WireGuard; Claw Patrol acts as a Tailscale exit node and reuses Tailscale identity for dashboard auth
data.name: Claw Patrol

data.brief: Follow-up on GitHub issues as a fully autonomous agent: Claude Agent SDK; bash as the tool, driving the Hugging Face CLI; one skill (the HF CLI skill) — "that's all it needs"; deployed on Modal's batch processing, one container per GitHub issue, fast starts; posts results to Slack. Model: initially Claude, now GLM 5.2 via Hugging Face inference providers (cheaper; beats Opus 4.8 on some Cursor benches). Invoked as a Cursor skill (process unread) that has Composer 2.5 fan out the agents — "the loop people are talking about"
data.name: The CLI + skill + sandbox agent

data.brief: The product node (company ≠ artifact): open-source coding agent, any-API/bring-your-own-key, CLI + VS Code + JetBrains; origin of custom rules and plan mode (claimed firsts); positioned in-talk as the neutral harness for feeling out how far open-weights models have come, and now as the vehicle for an open-weights subscription
data.name: Cline (open-source coding agent)

data.brief: Speech recognition rebuilt for noisy phone lines and clinical vocabulary: a decoder-only audio LLM whose encoder is Whisper v3 large-turbo fine-tuned on millions of clinical conversations, a conformer projector that compresses audio into tokens while preserving prosody (pauses, stress — "the how, not just the what"), and two extra inputs — the conversation so far and the domain knowledge of the task (the patient's medication list, the form being filled, the policy) — so a drug name is chosen from a finite list. Contextual biasing is trained in with millions of synthetic patients' addresses and numbers ("1100 Geary Boulevard" stops being phonetic garbage); single-word answers get a second scoring pass because "a" → "no" or "five" → "fine" is catastrophic. Medical word-error rate down more than 50% vs off-the-shelf; P99 latency 3× faster
data.name: The context-conditioned clinical audio LLM

data.brief: Hand prompt-engineering is brittle, subjective, unreproducible and slow (formatting changes alone have swung benchmarks by 76 points; reordering few-shot examples flips near-random to state-of-the-art). Ufonia uses GEPA: define the metric, run the data, have a strong model reflect on the failures and rewrite the prompt, iterate on a Pareto frontier until the budget is spent — an optimized prompt in 30–60 minutes with an audit trail, turning prompting into a data-science problem. The metric is not flat accuracy but a cost matrix set with clinicians: a caught red flag is good, a missed one catastrophic, an over-called one mildly annoying — so optimize for sensitivity; a different clinical priority is a recompile
data.name: Prompt optimization against a clinical cost matrix

data.brief: Response logic grounded in the two validated standards of care — Gottman's patterns and EFT's attachment layer under every argument — so the coach reflects patterns, names dynamics rather than feelings, and asks the question underneath the question. Before any sensitive reply it screens in the background for what clinicians catch in 90 seconds (escalating control, fear-based language, risk to self or others) and, when found, stops coaching and follows protocols written from 30 years of practice — knowing when not to coach is as important as knowing how. Disclosures are treated as privileged, the bar being "would I be comfortable if this were my own marriage"; the value is immediacy, an informed intervention six seconds before the text, for couples who otherwise wait six years
data.name: The clinically grounded coach (Maxine)

data.brief: The pipeline that puts an accountable licensed expert, not the engineering team, in charge of correct. Every conversation is traced; a flagged edge-case moment goes into the clinician's annotation queue with a small rubric — expected result, expected observation (which becomes the eval's assertion), turn index (which lets the conversation be replayed up to the point where the guardrail should have fired), category metadata, and a note that tells the engineer how to categorize the scenario. An annotation-extraction script triages the flagged traces into a report for discussion and normalizes the same annotations into the eval schema as typed evals. Once committed, a clinician's judgment is living in CI: every prompt change, model change and guardrail change is scored against what the clinician taught the system.
data.name: Clinician-annotated typed evals

data.brief: The eval math that rules out synthetic-only testing: at 10,000 calls a day a 1% error rate is 100 wrong appointment types, and catching a 1% error with 99% confidence needs ~450 tests (1,900 to see it ten times). So 7,000 trained clinicians on the platform continuously evaluate — ~800,000 clinical conversations so far — and outputs are graded on the scale used for humans (correct, no harm, minor harm, severe harm, death): 99.89% no-harm for the fifth product generation vs ~81% for humans on the same rubric, because AI does not get tired and has thirty specialists at its side. Empathy had no good benchmark, so the company built and published one (HEART) — safe is not enough if patients will not open up
data.name: Clinician-graded safety at scale

data.brief: Domain experts, not engineers, decide what good data looks like — so the whole generation pipeline (journey, documents, enrichment, evals) is a set of skills running on a generic internal agent harness, and clinicians can steer generation at any step (often to reproduce a case they saw in production) or add a new document type for a new customer by writing a skill file, with no engineering change. Skills as the interface between AI engineers and domain experts, seen across Anterior's internal and production workflows
data.name: The clinician-owned, skills-based pipeline

data.brief: A production loop that re-tunes the agents themselves with no human in the loop: sample production data on a cadence → send it to human labelers under the same guidelines used for the golden set → diff agent output against labels → route mismatches to a diagnoser that localizes the failing component → a prompt-optimizer agent (a *reflect* sub-agent that denoises the mismatches and extracts systemic issues, feeding a *synthesize* sub-agent that rewrites the target agent's config) → re-benchmark against the golden dataset → on pass, register the new agent version in an agent store that the next production run picks up. Entirely config-driven, with guardrail observability and one-step rollback around the loop.
data.name: Closed-loop agent auto-tuning

data.brief: An internal agentic workspace running on Cloudflare: each seller gets their own compute and a persistent environment (Workers plus Durable Objects as storage), curated expert-level skills, MCP connections and an AI gateway, and uses it for forecast briefs, QBR decks, purchase decks for onboarding customers, account planning, renewal preparation and general data questions — the expert's approach delivered at the moment of the customer conversation. Next: artifacts embedded into meetings, meeting notes ingested, and the harder write paths — quoting, approvals, CRM updates — built as checked workflows
data.name: Cloudflare OS, the seller's agentic workspace

data.brief: Serverless application-hosting platform (2017–), millions of developers, trillions of requests/day; Gadgets is built entirely on it — the talk's aside is that "you can actually build complex apps on Workers," containerless and databaseless, with dynamic workers as the sandbox substrate
data.name: Cloudflare Workers

data.brief: Terminal multiplexer built for parallel AI-agent work: manager-style operation via notifications (clear notifications instead of watching sessions), a Claude Code Teams integration that auto-spawns terminals to watch agent sessions, and SSH support for driving agents on remote machines (e.g. OpenClaw on Mac minis via Tailscale). Captions oscillate between "tmux" and "Cmux" — verify before public-facing use
data.name: cmux

data.brief: An LLM pipeline that builds a record layer by layer the way the real world does: patient invariants (sex, birth date, blood group) → an ordered patient journey of events and provider encounters (documentation only exists at encounters) → a document plan per encounter conditioned on the preceding history → parallel fan-out of the actual documents → a refinement loop where evals (cross-document consistency, label round-trip) feed corrections back. Layering keeps every prompt token-efficient and scales to long journeys; everything stays in text/markdown because state-of-the-art PDF parsers make rendering pointless
data.name: Coarse-to-fine medical-record generation

data.brief: Probabilistic systems generate; they are unreliable for what can never be wrong, so must-not-fail behaviour lives in a code layer that runs first on every turn and makes the irreversible decisions — the model never gets a vote on high-stakes calls. Three residents: emergency escalation (self-harm, suicidal ideation, acute emergencies route to 911/988 before the model sees the turn), intent routing (a clinical question must never quietly reach the tech-support agent, so high-stakes paths are deterministic even if the model helps classify), identity verification (authentication is a security boundary; prompts are not). A model is not a guardrail and a model with a system prompt is not a guardrail: the labs' published authority hierarchy makes every layer above "user" one prompt injection from override
data.name: Code above the model

data.brief: Pixel-perfect is half the story: enterprises want their battle-tested, accessible, internationalized components used. Code Connect links design components to codebase components, so the server sends a pointer ("use Button component") instead of a Tailwind blob — higher-fidelity output and far less context. When a component isn't linked, the server prompts the user (mimicking elicitation) and has the agent scan the codebase for matches (mimicking sampling), then bulk-creates the links
data.name: Code Connect pointers

data.brief: Replace many tool schemas with one code-execution tool: the agent writes code that composes tool functions in a single call instead of chaining sequential tool calls; industry-visible (shipped in the Anthropic API, promoted by Cloudflare)
data.name: Code mode

data.brief: The scaling technique: apply the code-mode idea familiar from MCP to trace analysis — write classifiers as code, run them in a sandbox, and run them at production scale rather than feeding traces through a model. Paired with the complementary lesson on anomaly detection: "agents are very, very bad at anomaly detection — don't ask your agent to find anomalies, ask it to investigate anomalies you've already found," with as much as possible pulled out deterministically (keyword frequency is the example) so there is something tractable for an agent to investigate
data.name: Code mode over traces

data.brief: AlphaZero-style self-play applied to code: with human training data mined out, frontier code models create their own challenges, judge answer validity, and to some extent judge architecture — hundreds of millions of hours of verifiable self-play as the route to superhuman coding; works because code is uniquely verifiable (compile, run, test)
data.name: Coding self-play

data.brief: Benchmark harnesses/models on *your own repo*: select pull requests that represent great engineering work (agent-, human- or hybrid-authored), run the candidate agents, and read quality-vs-cost and quality-vs-time curves for your codebase — because public benches don't transfer ("SWE-bench is all in Python, we're Ruby on Rails"). Their curves: Anthropic agents consistently better but not faster and far more expensive; Codex fast, good and cheaper; open models improving but slow. Feeds the roadmap claim: per-task auto-routing grounded in your own data, since no third party can know what routes best for your codebase. ⚠ merge-check vs el-private-benchmark — see review note 4
data.name: Per-codebase agent benchmarking

data.brief: The engineering problem statement of clinical safety: the words are not the message. The worked example — I packed a box today, just to feel what it would be like to be gone — is a real scenario contributed by a clinician from patient experience, and it reads as risk to a clinician while defeating every naive detector: regex lists of self-harm words and phrases, safety rules buried in verbose prompt instructions, and broad third-party moderation APIs. The signal is the implication, the context, and the position in the conversation, not any one word.
data.name: Coded risk disclosure (the sentence underneath the sentence)

data.brief: Hundreds of SDLC-representative tasks run by agents with and without Sourcegraph's code-navigation MCP tool, producing thousands of traces that show where the tool helps and where it breaks. Example: the model's training-data bias expected a read_line parameter where the tool offered start_line; the description didn't say otherwise, the call failed, the error explained why, the agent recovered — but burned a whole turn. Fix the description. Organizations will evaluate tools by tokens consumed and speed, not only success — "measure how these users are using it"
data.name: CodeScaleBench

data.brief: OpenAI's agentic coding system spanning CLI, IDE extension, the Codex app, iOS, and Codex Cloud; deliberately built as open layers — open-source harness, open-source app server (the same path OpenAI's own products use), open plugins (browser use, computer use, role-specific), models defaulted but not hardcoded — so anyone can fork or rebuild any layer while keeping the agent loop
data.name: OpenAI Codex

data.brief: The UI↔harness protocol (the Responses API being harness↔inference). Powers the first-party Codex app, so third parties building on it inherit full Codex functionality; community clients include Theo's T3 code and Remote X, and the speaker used it to embed Codex inside Claude Code as a plugin and inside Doom. Framed explicitly as open-ecosystem surface area: "if you're building your own UI… you can actually build on top of the Codex harness"
data.name: Codex app server protocol

data.brief: Codex's computer-use + Chrome extension that controls any application in the background without taking over the screen; "locked use" lets you trigger it from your phone while the laptop is closed; used for tasks the CLI can't do (fill a form, edit iMovie, DocuSign + fax)
data.name: Codex computer use

data.brief: slash goal defines a verification step and loops until it passes; ultra-goal externalizes the goal + plan to an editable goal.md (plus a work-log/state.md) so scope can change mid-run; with a good verifier, large autonomous migrations become tractable
data.name: Codex goal / ultra-goal

data.brief: "Loop"/"keep an eye on this every 30 min" automations that schedule a message back into the same thread (not a new one each time), waking a thread over time to take real-world actions
data.name: Codex heartbeat automations

data.brief: Pinned, self-managing threads that behave like teammates: pin + rename to a project ID, delegate to sub-agents, create new threads, write to memory; threads can list/rename/message each other, composing into manager-threads directing IC-threads — an org of agents
data.name: Codex pinned threads

data.brief: All file-system and network interaction routes through a per-platform sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox OpenAI had to build itself (shipped in the same repository; a companion article covers the rejected Windows alternatives). The layer that makes auto-approval decidable rather than advisory
data.name: Codex sandbox layer

data.brief: Skills = a few files + scripts; plugins = a library of skills; skills self-improve (allowed to edit their own file when they learn); installable from an in-app registry (Slack/Gmail/Teams/Notion/Linear/Obsidian) plus external registries (skillset.sh, Vercel skills); team-shared plugins are the "AI champion" force-multiplier (reward = how often teammates use your plugin, not tokens burned)
data.name: Codex skills & plugins

data.brief: Graph-backed agent-memory product: builds a knowledge-graph memory (Neo4j backend) from the same source files agents otherwise keep as markdown, storing embeddings on graph nodes so vector and graph search compose.
data.name: Cognee memory engine

data.brief: Erosion of a team's understanding and memory of how its own system works as delegation to agents grows; for code, the gap between how much code exists in the repo and how much any human on the team genuinely understands. Related failure modes named in the talk: cognitive surrender (adopting AI's answer before forming your own) and orchestration tax (parallel agent loops multiplying routing/merge/verify decisions while human bandwidth does not parallelize)
data.name: Cognitive debt

data.brief: Fuzzy intent → goal in four stages. Discovery: assemble a working state (session history, user context, hard constraints from the query, soft constraints inferred from reference images with confidence scores, real-time variables like inventory) and find the intent gap. Collaborative strategy: enumerate the unknowns, compare possible moves, and ask about the single variable with maximal information gain — the one that would change the conversation's direction — without over-asking. Research: bridge each constraint to the product ontology in real time, elicit it in the right format, do the comparisons and trade-offs in the background. Adaptive response: choose the presentation that makes the answer easy to find and act on
data.name: The collaborative shopping loop

data.brief: Models predict the most likely next outcome and assume the most likely is the ideal. For math and code that holds — the average answer to "what is 2+2" is also the right and optimal one. For writing and design it fails: "a lot of greatness and creativity happens at the ends of the distribution... when you actively break from rules and from patterns." The pervasive feeling of slop is exactly this collapse plus repetition. Also afflicts the data side: preference data pooled from raters whose identities and reasons aren't modelled re-collapses to the mean, because genuine disagreement cancels instead of registering.
data.name: Collapse to the mean (the mechanism of slop)

data.brief: Months after a successful launch users come back frustrated — "I can't do this in the product" — because the habit became the baseline and they have seen other AI products. The expected journey: talk to your data (no more dashboards or analyst queues) → automate my workflows (MCP integrations; monitoring inbox and Slack, drafting and sending, automating outreach — the user becomes an orchestrator) → team empowerment (team skills, custom dashboards, apps, automations, alerts, no IT backlog) → hyper-personalization with living customer context. Stop at stage one and you are disrupted within months, because switching is now easy; "every time people are happy, be paranoid"
data.name: The collapsing wow factor

data.brief: Armed-forces doctrine applied to prompting: tell agents why you want something, not micromanaged steps — they perform markedly better (as do humans). Requires active counter-pressure: models trained on human material micromanage themselves, so pull them back to the why.
data.name: Commander's intent prompting

data.brief: An agent is a brain (the model), hands (commerce tools: request payment method, complete checkout), an instruction loop, and a system prompt that is its persona and its ethics policy in English — the same tools serve a helpful honest assistant or a deceptive pushy salesman. The checklist for anyone shipping a shopping agent: always disclose the user is talking to an AI; disclose fees up front; honor "stop" or "cancel" at any point; keep the total at or below the user's maximum; never use urgency language or dark patterns; log every agent decision for auditability. The demo's snarky, pressuring agent was one wrong persona prompt away from the trustworthy one
data.name: The commerce-agent guardrail checklist

data.brief: The job: watch arXiv/GitHub for trending work, find the repo, read the README, check whether weights/datasets are on the Hub with proper cards and metadata, open a GitHub issue ("could you release this checkpoint on Hugging Face?") or a PR adding cards, follow up. Hundreds of papers a day made it unscalable by hand. Stage one (2024): a deterministic workflow mirroring his own steps — LLM API calls inside a predefined pipeline, no framework, deployed as a nightly cron on GitHub Actions ("free cron jobs"), traced in Langfuse. Hundreds of issues per night
data.name: The community-science outreach agent

data.brief: The survey of ways to shrink context: trivial no-LLM tools (truncate outliers keeping head+tail, sliding window / trim to last-N turns, always-clear specific tool outputs) and LLM-based ones (selective retention — the model decides what to keep/discard; summarization; delta summarization — Claude Code's running-summary update, useful with sub-agents; full summary-and-reset at the limit). Plus offload: save to files/memory (the Karpathy LLM-wiki idea) or RAG. The two that worked best in their experiments: selective retention and summarization — but see the caching caveat
data.name: The compaction toolkit

data.brief: The library plus the librarian: a curated organizational memory (every email, meeting, decision + reasoning, customer conversation, postmortem) with an arbitration layer deciding which "three books" get loaded into an agent's ~1M-token context per task; retrieval is the primitive ("this is just RAG" the way Postgres is just B-trees) — curation, enrichment, hot-vs-cold promotion, and contradiction arbitration are the product
data.name: Company brain

data.brief: Emulated's unit of training data: a software-engineering company put into containerized environments, not a repository. Contents named: organizational context — projects, incidents, tickets, postmortems, customer conversations, "and often times those aren't necessarily up to date", so the agent must reason about stale documentation; scale-only failures — network failures between distributed nodes, data corruption, clock skew, flapping nodes, lagging learners, stale deprecated nodes; and operational judgment — orchestrating across distributed clusters, kicking off rolling deployments that may conflict or fail, migrating from old to new hardware while the service serves live traffic, and reasoning about blast radius in real time.
data.description: Worked example: an ETCD consensus cluster, where the old-style environment operates only on "that little blue square entitled ETCD source code in the bottom right" and everything that surrounds it is where the model capability gap lives. Horizon is lengthened by running multiple deployments rather than one.
data.name: Company-in-a-sandbox environment

data.brief: Machine-readable map of Block's entire 25,000-repo codebase — every service and what depends on what — that orchestrators and delegated agents pull context from as needed; enables agents to explore different parts of the system in parallel and reassemble cross-codebase plans
data.name: Company world model

data.brief: Multi-step runs succeed on the first steps and fail later, often across systems — update the internal ticket, email the customer, fail to update the CRM. The whole transaction must be reversible, so define the compensation operation for each failure point (an apology or correction email, an undo), the saga pattern applied to agents
data.name: Compensating transactions across system boundaries

data.brief: Repeatable successful step-sequences are aggregated and merged into bigger reusable tools — proven scenarios become snippets other agents can call — and rolled out to hundreds of countries in one go. "An AI-native operation is a system that learns from what works and folds it back into code as new composite tools." Tools are tuned via function calling with distilled responses; MCP deliberately not used ("bloated")
data.name: Composite tools from proven scenarios

data.brief: Extract your thinking and taste into a system that compounds, so the next feature is easier to build than the last — flipping the usual accrual of complexity. The loop: brainstorm → plan → work → review → polish → compound → repeat, a "human–AI sandwich" with the brain on at both ends (deciding what and why; raising the bar on taste) and a middle that must run without you, overnight, in parallel. Rule: 50% of time on the feature, 50% teaching the system what it got wrong. "One engineer with a compounding system beats full teams that use AI without one"
data.name: Compound engineering

data.brief: Open-source plugin for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and ~10 other harnesses, used by hundreds of thousands daily. /ce ideate — structure open tickets/issues/Slack/Intercom into scored ideas (against OKRs, a /ce strategy doc, past experiments) as a shareable HTML page; /ce doc-review — sharp questions on a PRD, answers compounded; /ce brainstorm — the brain-on command that pulls compound knowledge and personas and asks just enough questions; /lfg — the overnight loop: plan, work, review, test, dogfood, fix, open a PR with before/after video; /ce polish — raise the bar on the result, not QA; /ce compound — extract the learning so it never repeats. Grew into "compound product" for PMs, designers and knowledge workers
data.name: The compound-engineering plugin

data.brief: ARK's browser-agent perception layer: renders the entire web page as ~1.8k tokens of markdown (vs ~20k tokens of raw DOM, or ~1.1k tokens for a screenshot that shows only one viewport snippet), paired with a screenshot and explicit state-diff feedback — what appeared, what's gone, that a blocking element was removed, that an attempted click didn't land — so a cheap model can see the whole page, diagnose failures, and plan long action sequences
data.name: Compressed markdown page representation

data.brief: Verification channel where a computer-use agent drives the *submitted application* through its real UI like a human — logging in, creating channels, posting messages, reacting with emotes — scored against a rubric; validates that a user can complete the product's intended workflow rather than that an API contract holds. SWE-Marathon claims first benchmark use for full-stack tasks, which is why product-clone tasks were previously absent from long-horizon benchmarks (unit tests pass while the product is unusable)
data.name: Computer-use-agent verifier

data.brief: TEE-based encrypted-in-use compute; Bee replicates device-held keys only to attested confidential-compute nodes and runs its own inference inside the perimeter because unencrypted data may never leave it
data.name: Confidential computing

data.brief: Isolated cloud environment per project with an explicit allowlist of reachable destinations; any out-of-list access attempt pauses and prompts ("tried to access something — do you want to give it access?"), grantable per ticket or per project. Coupled with least-privilege credentials (agents get only what they need — not whatever tokens live on a developer's laptop) and anti-exfiltration (code/secrets/content can't be pushed somewhere they shouldn't be). Also what lets non-technical teammates trigger real work: no local dev environment required
data.name: Configurable network-egress sandbox

data.brief: Harness principle for coding agents in domains without verifiable answers: let the agent write code freely (expression), but force all critical side effects through a typed SDK of well-scoped edit primitives (editable vs. derived fields, typed output objects) and have the harness own deterministic final execution — lint → conflict-detect → run → validate output artifacts → generate a structured review artifact. The process becomes valid, traceable, replayable, and reviewable by non-coders; failures are rejected and sent back to the agent
data.name: Constrain the effects, not the expression

data.brief: What a coding agent shows you "is kind of a lie" — compaction, quirks, hidden thinking traces mean you don't know what the model saw. So every prompt part (system prompt, each skill description, tool descriptions, user message) is stored by hash and a prompt is a list of hashes; the answer is stored the same way. Like git or Nix. Gives exact provenance of context, diffs between runs (which components changed), replay (rebuild the request, resend to a different model — how he re-evaluated open-source models when cost ramped), easier compaction ("you manipulate a graph, not strings") and indirectly KV-cache management. "Probably the main advantage at scale is auditability"
data.name: Content-addressed prompts

data.brief: Treating technical content (docs, changelogs, product emails, tours, video) as a declarative pipeline generated from the codebase as source of truth — "content shifting left to code"; depends on structured code, design tokens, clean tagged PRs, and accurate internal docs/skills
data.name: Content engineering
