One agent builds the evaluation — writing all the code — and hands it to two critic agents with different mandates: one high-level, hunting conceptual errors and forward leakage of information; one programmatic, writing unit and integration tests against it. Findings return to the builder and the loop does not terminate until every critic is satisfied. Rationale stated: "LLMs aren't malicious, but they make very silly mistakes".
data.name: Builder/critic eval construction

data.brief: TDD's equivalent for agent building: an eval suite (metrics/criteria + datasets) is the termination condition that decides "good enough" for every build and gates every deploy; the complete suite cannot be pre-written by domain experts — it is a product of discovery, continuously extended with criteria and edge-case data minted from production failures and user feedback
data.name: Eval-driven development (EDD)

data.brief: Everyone accepts the diagram — harvest production data to keep evals reflective of the real world — and the best teams run it religiously; in practice many teams' evals are static, so even without architectural change they stagnate. Through a generational shift you need both: production harvesting for the failures you defined ("what good looks like") and something to shine a light on new failure types you didn't anticipate
data.name: The eval flywheel, and why teams skip it

data.brief: Moving evaluation out of a post-hoc batch benchmark and into the generation path, as early as the artifact allows: check the two start frames of consecutive shots for character drift *before* spending a generation; check each ~6-second clip *before* assembling long-form video. Correction cost rises with pipeline stage, so the earliest catchable frame is the cheapest one; requires a judge fast enough to sit inline.
data.name: Eval inside the generation loop

data.brief: "Don't change because of a trend or a new paper." Define change: same inputs, expected outputs, graded on cost, speed, quality and capability — what the customer cares about. If the new approach beats the eval sets, strongly consider switching; if not, don't bother (or finish exploring). The CEO-forwarded-a-paper reflex is explicitly named as the thing this rule blocks
data.name: Eval sets as the switching arbiter

data.brief: The methodological claim. Eval discourse is "still stuck in the chatbot era" — build a 1,000-row dataset and check the string contains the right answer — which worked when "you knew the answer to most questions your users would ask." It fails now because "the prompt is actually the whole thing: it's all the code, it's your whole harness," and curated eval sets "break as soon as you have a new model or you switch harnesses" (switching to Claude Code CLI is given as an example that invalidates 80% of tool-calling evals). The prescription is that evals should look like unit and end-to-end tests kept in code and run locally, citing Sentry's Vitest-evals package and OpenAI's "macro evals" as the same idea under different names. The trade-off is stated bluntly: "you want more safety but you don't want theater" — nobody actually delays a model upgrade two weeks to update evals
data.name: Evals as tests, not datasets

data.brief: Evals are "not just an engineering harness" — a team sport that injects domain knowledge into AI quality. Strategy & operations set priorities and the quality bar; product translates requirements into rubrics and workflows; operations run annotation; engineering provides APIs, telemetry, datasets and judges. Teams differ in who owns the judge prompt (S&O, PM, or engineering) and the platform lets that org design evolve
data.name: Evals as a cross-functional sport

data.brief: Evals are hard: non-determinism makes it tricky to pin the change that moved an output, offline datasets may not represent production, and data drifts. The three primitives give privacy-preserving evals as a byproduct: the ledger lets you replay any point in time and tweak a prompt, model or code to see the exact impact; human–agent equivalency means the human's and the agent's performance on the same task *is* the eval; object storage lets evals run on production data inside the customer's environment without the sensitive data ever leaving. "Eval emerges as a first-class property of the system rather than something bolted on"
data.name: Evals as an emergent property

data.brief: Every step-function model release (tool use, long context, sandboxed code, memory) unlocks capability the previous system — built around the old limitations — cannot tap without re-architecture, so teams are re-platforming, not iterating. Each re-architecture opens new surface area for failure, so evals must be made congruent with the new architecture; kept static they give partial coverage and miss the ways the new system is fragile. "Evals are the durable asset that describes how your system is supposed to work" across generational shifts
data.name: Architecture follows models; evals follow architecture

data.brief: Cron covers *when* (one point in time); events cover *because this happened*. Each agent declares what it accepts and what it returns as typed events (voice note → voice note processed; the daily-brief agent subscribes to that plus the cron output; a Slack poster subscribes to slack.message.post). "Frameworks will sell you graphs. You do not need graphs. All you need is events — no edges to maintain; agents subscribe; anyone can edit; drop a file and the topology emerges — whatever the log says happened"
data.name: Event-driven agent topology

data.brief: Using the event backbone as the agent's context supply: domain/integration events from every bounded context (transaction, accounts, device, payment) are propagated by CDC or by message-broker publication into a worker process, massaged in a projection layer, and landed in a materialized view the speaker calls a semantic layer — denormalized counts and averages, device trust scores and location/IP history, KYC status and account age, recent payments and chargebacks. Agent tools read the projection, never the source contexts, so agents need no privileged cross-context access and inherit the domain's own asynchronous boundaries.
data.name: Event-sourced agent context

data.brief: Storage methodology where a user command appends an immutable business fact to an append-only event store instead of mutating state; domain events (transaction created) and integration events from other bounded contexts (payment approved, transaction rejected) accumulate as the system of record. Because the store is write-optimized, reads are served by separately projected read models (timelines, customer view, risk/fraud-indicator view) kept in sync by CDC — in NoSQL terms a change feed — rather than by querying the log.
data.name: Event sourcing

data.brief: The doctor–patient conversation is the root and the administrative machinery — the note, billing, clinical-trial matching, decision support, orders — is built around it; automate from the root and the machinery follows. The agent's context is the full EHR (prior labs and notes), the live conversation (where the patient's current state is "debugged"), and the world's medical literature and guidelines; from that it prepares pre-visit topics, writes the note and visit summary, pends orders spoken in the room, answers trial-eligibility and criteria questions, and preps tomorrow's charts
data.name: Everything in healthcare is downstream of the conversation

data.brief: Practitioner taxonomy separating anomaly (one-off incident — the commute that took an extra hour once) from drift (the baseline itself shifted over a year), then categorizing drift: structural (node/step added or removed), scale/volume (service saturating under load), covariate (traffic mix changed — 60/40 local/foreign becomes inverted while the system itself is fine), and behavioral (same request, different behavior). Each category maps to a different response: rebaseline, scale out / go async, segment baselines, or roll back.
data.name: Execution-drift taxonomy

data.brief: Messaging is where GTM engineering is hardest: cold-email reply rates decline every year (≈0.5–1% across ~20M emails per Smartlead; LinkedIn three to four times cold email; cold calling about the same), so one contact in a hundred replies and every agent misstep costs revenue. Human problems come with it: send as the rep (a real address, the company domain's reputation at stake) or from agent-owned domains with replies routed back; coordinate channels (stop the sequence and pull the contact from campaigns when a meeting is booked); rep mode links rep inboxes to the sequencer for a portion of accounts and multi-domain sending covers the rest. The hardest open problem is the human–agent handoff — a rep not knowing the agent already acted
data.name: Execution is the hard part

data.brief: With engineers authoring less and a short path to a percentage of code landing with automatic approval, the question becomes whether to remove the human from review. The catch: the human feedback that flowed back into uReview is what made review high quality, so removing it invites quality degradation and slop. The industry is coalescing instead on moving human responsibility up a layer — the agent writes and increasingly reviews at the implementation level (performance, API compatibility); the engineer's outer loop becomes architecture, domain expertise and product thinking
data.name: Expanding, not killing, the outer loop

data.brief: Nakajima's hypothesis: long-running agents need not just a predictive world model (the priors) but an experiential one — an immutable event log of lived experience that projects current state and feeds back into the priors via replays/dreaming/sleep (hippocampus analogy). The agent's identity — beliefs, knowledge, behaviors — derives from its own log, not from its reasoning capability.
data.name: Experiential world model

data.brief: Two measurable quality controls for subjective annotation. Specificity: the precision of an expert's language when asked to say why something is good or bad predicts how rich and high-signal the data point is, so specificity is scored rather than assumed. Code-linking: models struggle to connect a rendered visual to the source that produced it, so tying each critique to the exact code component it refers to (rather than accepting a free paragraph about a landing page) yields "data that is way less noisy and way more clear".
data.name: Grounded expert commentary

data.brief: Litt's agent skill (published free at the talk, HTML and Notion variants) that turns a code change into a personalized explainer doc: background/system context first, intuition before details ("the goal of this commit is…"), interactive figures where tasteful, literate code diffs in narrated order — ending in a 5-question spaced-repetition-style quiz that gates whether you understood; used daily by Litt and coworkers at Notion
data.name: ExplainDiff (code-explainer skill)

data.brief: Two-axis curriculum design for teaching machines to hack, taken directly from how elite human hackers are trained. Axis 1, target difficulty: toy programs → CTF/synthetic problems → hardened real-world targets. Axis 2, exploitation difficulty: locate the bug → prove it by triggering a crash → arbitrary read/write in memory → full arbitrary code execution. Instantiated for the V8 experiment as 16 bucketed capabilities, which is what supplies partial-credit signal on a target so hard that pass/fail yields almost nothing. "Hacking is really a ladder" — a task ladder plus a good oracle is exactly what makes cybersecurity fit RL.
data.name: Exploitation capability ladder

data.brief: Public benchmark at exploitbench.ai: 41 V8 vulnerabilities, each hand-verified as genuinely exploitable (verification done by the current Chrome security lead), packaged as Docker images pullable from GitHub with an MCP interface — "you can just point Claude at the MCP interface and see if it can hack it". All environments, data and model transcripts published except the Mythos transcripts (NDA plus a weaponization concern).
data.name: ExploitBench

data.brief: The delegation shift as models reached the Mythos/Fable snapshots: from "break the idea into steps in my head and iterate" to "describe the goal, let it work, discuss trade-offs and questions along the way, then figure out where it landed." The model is "way smarter than me" — "explain it to me like I'm a little dumber than you are." Former CTOs are joining Anthropic as ICs because the building is that interesting
data.name: Express the end state

data.brief: Orbis's extension for all-documents-relevant, fast-churn corpora: shard documents across multiple parallel CAG context buckets — deliberately NOT organized by domain (balanced counts, fewest buckets needed) — and put a smarter supervisor model on top that interrogates each bucket, progressively builds its internal understanding, directs follow-up questions to specific buckets, and synthesizes the final answer; because all caches load in parallel, knowledge-building is significantly faster than GraphRAG construction while staying more accurate than plain vector RAG; KV-cache cost is contained by optimizing how long each cache lives
data.name: Extended CAG (parallel cache buckets + supervisor)

data.brief: Facts and estimates must live in visibly separate boxes, because fluent generation melts them into one smooth sentence — "the company will likely receive approval next quarter" reads like a fact and is a guess wearing fact-shaped clothing. A committee's entire job is to argue with the guesses while trusting the facts, which it cannot do if it can't find the seam; the only remaining options are to approve or reject the whole document. Observed failure: "approval expected" drifting to "approval received" across three drafts, nobody lying, until nobody remembered it began as a guess — and the approval didn't arrive. Fix is cheap: a label, a tag, a colour — anything that survives being copy-pasted into someone else's slides three weeks later.
data.name: Fact/guess separation

data.brief: Factory's long-running harness for hard, validatable knowledge work: an extremely bounded task with an explicit definition of "complete", after which inference is pushed like a lever until the task is done, with human involvement only at the planning stage. Presented as the end-game of the agent era (pre-software-factory): if a problem can be framed as the set of verification systems that must validate it, it is solvable with AI today. Cited runs: fully autonomous migrations of 30-50M+ line codebases, deep-learning work in biomed/healthcare, equity-research modelling at financial institutions.
data.name: Missions

data.brief: A triage bench clusters failures and hands back something actionable; heat maps turn thousands of traces into priorities so experts and engineers look at the same problems. Every cell is a group of tracked scenarios; turning one cell green-to-red-to-green is "one to two months of the whole team's effort." "The agent failed" is where investigation starts, not ends — each failure maps to a specific fix: wrong workflow → classifier eval; wrong write → write gate; wrong assumption → review
data.name: Failure heat-map triage

data.brief: Tier-2 topology: one inbound event is fanned out to specialist agents in parallel — a risk-analyzer (fraud-history tool, device-trust tool, migrated business rules) and a behaviour-analyzer (transaction-pattern plugins) — after which a third agent reads both agents' responses and issues the verdict, which is published back to the message broker as an event. Coined because the alternative was tried and failed: collapsing the verdict into a metric or an if condition "goes back to the same criteria as the rule engine" and reproduced its false positives.
data.name: Fan-out agent consensus with a verdict agent

data.brief: Oxylabs' search product built for agents: compact JSON under ~2,000 tokens per response, under ~700 ms average, high success rate at a predictable low price, access to many search engines. Replaces a predefined retailer list plus browser-driven search pages; small responses let the discovery stage run on a cheap model fast
data.name: Agent search API

data.brief: Dual-timescale context construction: a slow engine mines weeks of activity into a durable, reinforcement-updated user profile ("knows you"); a fast engine recomputes live signals over a short recent window ("knows your day"); merged into one served view. Deliberate analog of complementary learning systems (hippocampus/neocortex) in neuroscience and lambda architecture (speed/batch layers) in data infrastructure.
data.name: Fast/slow context engines

data.brief: Widely used MCP framework; already carries server-side MCP Tasks support (and some client pieces) and is what both demo processes run on. Davis's stated plan: land a full client-side tasks implementation in FastMCP within a month or two, "so you can use the same framework you're using probably for your MCP servers today"
data.name: FastMCP

data.brief: Apple's 0.5B-parameter vision-language model, shown running fast on an Android device with hardware acceleration. Cited as the exemplar of the off-the-shelf fixed-task tier — ASR, vision and embedding models that are stock features needing no fine-tuning — and as the cheapest way to add a first level of visual awareness to an edge or IoT device.
data.name: FastVLM

data.brief: Varick's in-house "Codex for our FDEs", built because forward deployed engineers were uploading ~150 pages of client documentation to Claude, waiting ~2 minutes and getting verbose, incorrect analysis. Three stages, the third still unbuilt: (1) engagement agent — the FDE's assistant, ingesting Granola meeting notes, documentation and PowerPoint decks, answering the questions FDEs actually ask all day ("who is responsible for this process?", "the Sarah in this email and the Sarah in this Slack message — are these the same person?"); (2) workflow agent — the same agent embedded inside the platform while the FDE builds a workflow, flagging missed edge cases and process ownership so the built workflow actually shadows the real process, running alongside whichever coding agent the engineer uses; (3) autonomous agent (in development) — receives client change requests by email, queries the existing model of the company, and ships the workflow change without the FDE, reserving human time for on-site interviews and process discovery.
data.name: FD agent (forward-deployed-engineering agent)

data.brief: The talk's thesis and its explicit inversion of the go-to-market framing: "this is not a role, this is a product strategy" — an FDE is judged by their ability to be an extension of the product team, to identify areas of opportunity inside a customer and to generalize product solutions out of them, not by contract size or customer satisfaction. Attributed to Palantir's CTO (the person who named the discipline) in a statement made days before the talk. Corollaries stated: the field work is an input to a generalizable product rather than the deliverable being sold; making customers successful is a solutions architect's job, not an FDE's; and running FDE as a go-to-market extension is a luxury affordable only to a company with twenty years and unlimited money.
data.name: FDE as product strategy

data.brief: Exa's go-to-market is AEs and SDRs — who have learned to use the AI tools well through training but are not vibe-coding the interfaces — plus a forward-deployed-engineering org of 8–9 people in a 115-person company that supports and runs deals and also builds and maintains the AI systems that smooth everything for the AEs. Solutions and sales engineers used to support revenue; because of AI the technical person can now also build the tooling — two jobs became one, at least until the team grows
data.name: The FDE org that runs deals and builds the sales system

data.brief: Ramp's internal agent on the #fde-requests channel, where account managers, solutions and sales reps post any prospect/customer blocker large enough to escalate; the underlying Notion workflow holds the detail. The problem it attacks is variance — some submitters write a thorough customer-sourced request, others write one line ("we need this SAP integration") — which previously forced FDEs to read, interpret, check what already exists in the product, and run manual back-and-forth. The V1, built with Notion agents, only read the request and asked a couple of questions; the current version runs several rounds of questioning with the submitter until it judges the request ready to become a spec (with a penguin persona to make it approachable). Results reported after a couple of weeks: reply latency from hours or days down to seconds, reps engaging with the agent directly, and roughly 20% of scoping time saved.
data.name: FDE request intake agent

data.brief: The org split that hypergrowth forced: the original generalist "agent software engineer" — who configured the agent brain beside the customer, built back-end integrations and upstreamed platform work — divides into two lanes. Agent builders are product experts with intuition for the models underneath, working in the UI wherever possible and flagging what must go off-UI; agent software engineers are the front line for customer product asks, responsible for getting them into the platform. Staffed on top with vertical expert pools — the people who ran financial-services customers A, B and C get staffed on D — so domain lingo, credibility and success criteria compound instead of being relearned per logo.
data.name: FDE role specialization (agent builder / agent software engineer)

data.brief: Meurer's taxonomy of forward deployed engineering as five cumulative eras rather than a single job: 2008 platform stability / DevOps ("hints of panic" — the onboarding project was deploying the software on an EC2 instance; the 2 a.m. "someone unplugged the instance again" email), 2012 data integration (integrating a customer's data out of 20 places and modelling it into Palantir's ontology — "data integration software without integrated data is a movie theatre playing nothing"), 2016 custom solutions (Slate dashboards mapping page components to data sources), 2020 customer enablement (platform era: training thousands of customer engineers to do FDE work themselves), 2024+ all of the above plus agent building. Jobs-to-be-done accumulated over time instead of rotating out, which is why the title now means everything and nothing; proposed as an interview question — "what vintage of FDE are you?"
data.name: FDE vintage

data.brief: The framing device for adoption as a human problem. Plot each developer on two axes — fear (is this coming for my job, or is it a handy tool?) and utilization (how much are they actually using it?) — and trace the arc: at first fear high and utilization low; then early adopters get outsized leverage and others try harder ("it looks like I'm still needed if I figure out how to use this thing"); then mandates and token-maxxing raise utilization without confidence; then slop and sev-2s lower fear but leave confidence flat. The goal is to move everyone toward low fear and high utilization, and the explicit instruction is that "fear is real, human emotions are real, we should recognize it"
data.name: The fear × utilization map

data.brief: Why vibe coding cannot produce 4–5×: a back-and-forth conversation keeps the human in the loop, waiting 30–60 seconds per turn, unable to run agents in parallel or "clone yourself." Feeding means giving the agent what to do *and how to self-validate*, so it self-corrects and only comes back when it meets a quality bar — compiles, passes tests, is testable, has coverage — and then putting that bar into the steering file so it happens every time without prompting. The mechanism behind hours-long runs and parallelism
data.name: Feed agents, don't babysit them

data.brief: Prototype an LLM feature with a feedback button and text box; during the day collect a handful of runs (system prompt, inputs, feedback) as JSON dumps in Downloads — 5 to 30 is enough, more with colleagues. At 5 p.m.: turn the JSONs into an eval set (SQLite or Markdown), interactively agree scoring functions, build a harness that runs the call against the evals and hill-climbs until scores rise — "just tell it not to overfit," and it mostly doesn't — then save the flow as a reusable skill. Shipped to employees the quality holds; used for the internal code reviewer too
data.name: Feedback JSON → eval set → overnight hill-climb

data.brief: Sends context between design and production code both ways so AI tools need no dedicated integration. Local first (Electron desktop app → IPC bridge → node process → SSE server; enterprises liked that data stayed local) as the fastest path to product-market fit; then remote (streamable HTTP + OAuth); GA October 2025; read tools for Dev Mode data (components, spacing, variables), FigJam, Make, then write capabilities. Resources expose help articles and usage guidance so the agent doesn't burn inference discovering how to use the server
data.name: The Figma MCP server

data.brief: Agent state moved out of the context window onto disk: every entity gets a workspace (mission, current status, handoff folder with the actual work product); shared context all agents must honor lives in a shared dir; machine-bound state under machines/. Enables "reset, don't compact" — wipe the context entirely and let the agent re-read its own handoff/history files to resume — plus crash recovery, one-command fleet reboot, and cross-machine migration via git.
data.name: Filesystem as agent state

data.brief: Before fine-tuning, cross off your reasons: accuracy (the rebuild beat the fine-tuned model); cost at volume (looked at the wrong costs — per-message up, total down); latency (marginal gains on small models, no practical difference); narrow structured task ("our textbook case still became tech debt"); vendor control (not as simple as plugging data in). Legitimate remaining reasons: privacy/data control, or an offline requirement — with caution. "Fine-tune only when you literally cannot call a frontier model, and even then your decision still has to beat the tax"
data.name: The fine-tune decision list

data.brief: The fix cycle: gather examples of a failure, synthesize more via an LLM if too few, validate manually, label into six intent bins, validate again, fine-tune (~1 hour — "surprisingly the shortest part"), evaluate — and find the fix caused regressions elsewhere. About a week per cycle, so issues were triaged by frequency and severity ("is there a band-aid so we don't retrain?") — "we ranked our own bugs by how much customer pain we could tolerate." Failure exhibits: the *confused confirmer* (customer says "sounds good" to tomorrow's appointment; model calls now) and the *overeager puppy* ("good morning" → "I'm giving you a call")
data.name: Fine-tune whack-a-mole

data.brief: AWS's microVM monitor; gives an agent + its own Docker daemon a private kernel, solving the Docker-socket-escape problem that userland sandboxes (landlock, bubblewrap, seccomp, gVisor-style) can't compose around
data.name: Firecracker

data.brief: Interviews across the pilots found habits, not a sprint. (1) Invest in agent context — everything transferred by Slack, onboarding, mentors, code review and stand-ups gets written down; every agent mistake asks "what is missing from my skills/steering files?" — and, as models improve (Sonnet 3.7's quirks needed many do-nots; Opus 4.5 did not), "do I still need this, or is it bloating context?" (2) Slow down to speed up. (3) Feed agents, don't babysit them. (4) Make intent explicit — behaviour-driven development and specs; iterate with the model on a document, not on code spread across a code base. (5) Shift testing left — linters, unit/integration/performance/security tests, and locally-run deterministic mock services so the agent's feedback loop is fast and entirely on the laptop; "good hygiene we should have done all along, but now the ROI is finally high enough"
data.name: The five frontier habits

data.brief: One flat JSON record covering every agent in an end-to-end run, rather than nested per-agent traces. Chosen for legibility: non-technical and technical staff alike can open a single case to diagnose it and roll the same field up in aggregate. Framed as the prerequisite step — "if you don't start with logging you have nothing to optimize for, let alone set up a self-learning loop".
data.name: Flat end-to-end orchestration log

data.brief: NVIDIA technology (⚠ name from captions): a main model is distilled into smaller footprints inside one model artifact, and the system switches which footprint does the decoding per task — activating "a class of model or a section of weights depending on the complexity at hand." Paired claims: with access to the training recipe you can literally determine whether a question is in-distribution, and distillation-gap studies across teachers tell you where the small footprints are weak — both "work very well for open models"
data.name: Flex Run (NVIDIA elastic model footprints)

data.brief: The organizing fix: the messiness of the real world must be *modeled into the simulation during training* so the model falls into the traps, learns from them, and recovers — "not just producing a generation rewarded by a reward model, but the environment and training setup reflecting all the edge cases." Requires upgrading three components: the simulator, the pilot (model), and the cockpit (harness)
data.name: Flight school, not exams

data.brief: The talk's organizing distinction. The ceiling is the best, most surprising emergent thing your agent can do — "things people would just not expect that it could do." The floor is the worst: recommending a competitor, deleting data, or "accidentally sending an AI slop email to a customer because it technically had access to your email." The argument is that the floor is what breaks user trust, and that most publicly visible AI harms — sycophancy being the named example — "are more on the floor side rather than the capability side." Formalized as a customer-segmentation question: are you a benchmark-maxxer or a floor-raiser?
data.name: The floor versus the ceiling

data.brief: Generative modeling that matches the data *distribution* from Gaussian noise rather than compressing to a latent vector; empirically better on single-cell data
data.name: Flow matching (for single-cell)

data.brief: The burnout risk of frontier development: engineers staying up late chasing the perfect prompt that will run an agent for hours overnight so a change is ready in the morning; cognitive load from running multiple agents in parallel and constantly switching terminal tabs; and reviewing AI output being harder than writing it for many — senior engineers have spent careers reviewing others' code, early-career engineers do not have that muscle yet, so review feels like more load than authoring
data.name: Flowmaxxing and the hidden load

data.brief: The speaker's name for the failure mode: a generic, fluent, confident answer about money, learned from what people wrote about money on the internet — blogs, books, advice columns — rather than from what actually happened when businesses acted. His claim is that almost every money-related answer from a frontier model is one. Measured shape from the Intuit study: across ~100,000 business situations, 40% of frontier-model advice reduced in essence to "acquire a new customer" and a further 14% to "increase revenue from your product" — over half of all advice collapsing into two generic moves, regardless of the business's actual constraints.
data.name: The fluent bluff

data.brief: Vendor function embedding senior engineers ("magical unicorns": deeply technical + high EQ) inside customer organizations to co-design and co-build strategic AI deployments in the customer's codebase — distinct from professional services and staff augmentation; fit is a 2×2 of customer digital maturity × product customizability, with FDE value concentrated in the middle band (accelerate the mature, embedded transformation for the less mature); doubles as the tightest product-feedback loop the vendor has
data.name: Forward deployed engineering (FDE)

data.brief: A digital clone of the CEO built in a week with Opus 4.5: a writing voice distilled from 760 emails, a decision-making framework derived from hundreds of past decisions found in Slack and email and turned into evals that calibrate the agent to decide as he would, and read/write access to every system he can reach. Anyone in the company asks it for a draft answer or decision as a Slack message or email; for everyone but the founder it can only draft, and it does not receive all his MCPs and tools — a deliberate guardrail
data.name: The founder clone (JeffBot)

data.brief: Go-to-market motion where the founder's personal brand and founder-led sales are the primary distribution channel: undelegatable authenticity, quirks as "genius zone", trust built by a real human behind the product; AI amplifies the founder's signal (text, video) but cannot replace it
data.name: Founder-led GTM / personal brand as moat

data.brief: Foundry component materializing the "learned knowledge" loop: generates a task-adherence eval from an agent's traces and instructions if none exists, establishes a baseline, then hill-climbs candidate configurations (instructions/tools/skills) GEPA-style and applies the winner by swapping externalized config
data.name: Foundry agent optimizer

data.brief: DatologyAI's pipeline model. Clean: heuristic filters (Gopher-style, dropping 10-character or all-whitespace documents) plus rigorous benchmark decontamination at a low n-gram threshold against all downstream benchmarks — table stakes because "benchmaxing has become a real problem and makes it very difficult to interpret model results". Curate: quality classifiers, topic taxonomy and balancing, redundancy reduction (dropping points that are semantically near-identical even when not byte-identical), up/down-sampling by quality and relevance, and task-distribution matching to the intended outputs.
data.description: Create: synthetic generation to grow a now-high-quality but too-small set. Compose: mixing sources and sequencing them across training stages — "table stakes that any large model is trained for at least three phases of data" — up to continuous curricula.
data.name: The four C's (clean, curate, create, compose)

data.brief: From Julie Zhuo's poll of technical leaders: internal tools and codebase gardening; artifacts to celebrate people; and, most important, vision — playing with new model families to feel what's possible and building products that show it. Never critical-path work: you will be dragged into fires and recruiting
data.name: What leaders should (and shouldn't) build

data.brief: The instrumentation inherited from the text and image eras: CLIP-style scoring for "does this single frame match the prompt that generated it", LPIPS-style perceptual distance for drift between adjacent frames. Composable and cheap, and jointly still blind to everything that only exists across time — story, pacing, character continuity, audio sync.
data.name: Frame-level video metrics (CLIP score, LPIPS)

data.brief: Protocol for agents to discover, transact with, and receive verifiable receipts from external data/service providers across organizational boundaries. Homogeneous nodes playing requester/provider/marketplace roles; keypair identity per node; every step signed into a tamper-evident chain (descriptor → offer → quote → deal → invoice → receipt); marketplace only for discovery/indexing, then peer-direct execution; two-part payments (base payment + success fee). Integrates with existing payment rails, agent harnesses, execution environments, and transports — same interface, not same stack.
data.name: Froglet

data.brief: Load-bearing constraint invoked twice: AI assistance cannot author frontier-grade benchmark tasks, and LLM-as-judge cannot grade domains where the models themselves lack taste. Both require injecting external human expertise — and it has to be good expertise; "if you try to use cheap labor, you're going to get what you pay for". The economic justification for expensive human workforces in benchmark construction and evaluation.
data.name: You can't push the frontier from within the frontier

data.brief: Cognition's maintainability-oriented benchmark: multi-PR tasks; penalizes model-written tests that don't fail on pre-patch code; judge model scores adherence to code-quality rules
data.name: Frontier Code (Cognition)

data.brief: The early-adopter phase after inline completion, chat and vibe coding, defined by three behaviours: hands-off coding (frontier developers write maybe 1–2% of the code they produce; the rest is agents), infrequent interaction (aiming for the assistant to run up to hours without intervention), and minimal idle time (multiple agents in parallel churning through a backlog). Anecdotally the earlier phases felt 10–20% more productive; Amazon pilots of this phase show a median 4.5× and sometimes >10×
data.name: Frontier development

data.brief: How Amazon built evidence. Pathfinder (Bedrock's new inference data plane: estimated 30 people / 18 months; six people built it in 76 days with Kiro — but two distinguished engineers and distributed-systems/LLM experts, "unachievable for a lot of teams"). Structured sprint (Prime Video: six engineers, 10 days, project estimate 90 weeks → 24 by commit history — but no on-call, few meetings, and a senior engineer had spent three weeks pre-writing small well-scoped tasks). Structured pilot (Amazon Stores: 50 normal-distribution teams on existing code bases, watched most of a year, metric = deployment velocity to production, not commits). Scale-out (2026: the next 2,000 teams instead of 50). Each rung answers the previous rung's confound
data.name: The pathfinder → sprint → pilot → scale-out ladder

data.brief: Gemma variant carrying extra pre-training on function-calling patterns, used as the fine-tuning base when the target task is free text in, structured call out. Distinguished in the talk from general-purpose Gemma at the same parameter count; the open mobile actions dataset exists so the demo can be reproduced by fine-tuning Function Gemma from scratch.
data.name: Function Gemma

data.brief: Gadgets' distribution mechanism: export a useful gadget's code without its data as a blueprint; others instantiate fresh gadgets from it (document editor, kanban board, slide builder). Distribution becomes template-instantiation of per-user code rather than deployment of one multi-tenant service — and the blueprint author's "roadmap" ends at v1, because each user's agent forks features locally
data.name: Blueprints (code-without-data sharing)

data.brief: Vibe-coding platform with an office-suite model: like Google Docs, but the unit is a *gadget* — an app with its own code — and a user accumulates hundreds of them, instantiating one per shareable thing (one slide deck = one instance of the slides gadget). Shown from Varda's own use: a one-shot collaborative whiteboard, a Spanish-email filter, a GitHub PR-sorter, a slide builder. Sharing is a platform feature (a Docs-style share dialog), not app code — "the platform can implement the sharing model and the access control such that the gadget itself can't possibly get that wrong." Every gadget automatically integrates with agents, which can both use it and rewrite it. Entire stack (minus the LLM) runs on Cloudflare Workers: no containers (dynamic workers), no database (Durable Objects)
data.name: Gadgets (Cloudflare personal-app platform)

data.brief: The metric that makes learning measurable rather than inferred. Every system is run through the benchmark twice: once normally, allowed to maintain state across instances (updating a policy, its notes, or just growing context), and once as a stateless baseline reset between every instance. Gain is the difference. It answers "how much did my prior experience on the first four tasks actually improve performance on the fifth," isolating learning from base-model strength — the confound that cumulative reward alone cannot separate, where a stronger model that learns nothing outscores a weaker one that learns well
data.name: Gain (stateful minus stateless)

data.brief: Meta's science LLM, released two weeks before ChatGPT in November 2022 and withdrawn after public backlash — shipped as a bare base-model demo, so it hallucinated and complied with adversarial prompts (a research paper on Dyson spheres; a report on the benefits of eating crushed glass). The technical record the talk wants remembered: at 30B parameters it beat PaLM (540B) on chain-of-thought (36% vs 19%) and beat GPT-3.5 on mathematics (68% vs 49%), state of the art in scientific domains with far less compute.
data.description: It was the first LLM to crack data efficiency — a 105B-token curated corpus against Chinchilla's trillion, contrarian in an era where "everyone was like, we just need more tokens" — and the first major LLM to crack multi-epoch training, at a time when the consensus was never to exceed one epoch.
data.name: Galactica

data.brief: An LLM gateway — routing, auth, fallback, rate limits, governance between apps and providers — has at its heart a fight between availability, latency, guardrails and cost. In a degradation you cannot maximize all four; pick per use case. If you use a gateway, choose the trade-off; if you build one, expose those levers to callers
data.name: The gateway's four-way fight

data.brief: Tan's MIT-open-source company-brain / personal-AI retrieval layer ("Postgres for agents"); works with any harness, pairs with OpenClaw + Hermes agent; his personal instance: ~220,000 pages written mostly by his agents from 20 years of email, meetings, and notes
data.name: G Brain

data.brief: Google's recently released frontier model (caption garble — see notes); per TNG the best chess model observed so far — reasoning traces show genuinely better positional understanding, suspected chess-specific post-training. Powers the chess explainer agent.
data.name: Gemini 3.1 Pro

data.brief: Google's open model family as the on-device workhorse, with the talk's measured numbers. The ~2B E2B variant reasons on par with a much larger Gemma from ~12 months earlier; quantized to a mix of 2-, 4- and 8-bit with per-layer embeddings it reaches ~2.9 bits per weight, 841 MB of weights for a text-only model, ~2 GB active RAM once runtime and KV cache are added, hence the ~4 GB DRAM rule of thumb for shipping this grade of model on a device. Vision tokenization: a medium-resolution image is about 500 tokens, high-resolution about 1,120 tokens. Tiny variants start around 270M.
data.name: Gemma (open model family)

data.brief: The synthesis stage: over the enriched corpus, an agent generates a browsable wiki per focus area, structured as people, concepts, organizations and sources, with entries and backlinks to the raw notes. Demonstrated on two corpora (an AI-news wiki and a religious-texts study wiki) and pitched for workplace use — a people section built from meeting notes, with backlinks to every related meeting, useful for customer-success and client work. The point of the structure is that entity extraction turns a pile of notes into something with an index
data.name: Agent-generated wiki

data.brief: Named forward direction: rather than querying personas independently, simulate a population of them interacting — dynamics between personas rather than isolated responses — as the path to turning static human research data into "a living, queryable asset". Thin: named and framed in the closing minute, with "we didn't get time for this"; coined because it is the field's stated next step and connects the persona cluster to the corpus's simulation material.
data.name: Generative agent-based modeling

data.brief: SEO for agents and chatbots: design prompts around what the ICP actually does. In a pilot, comparison-shopping prompts recommended the product ~65% of the time; a pain prompt ("we keep breaking downstream services when we change shared libraries because we can't see all the consumers") got zero mentions — the agent suggested a wiki page. Re-run on Sonnet 4.6, the model pitched the retired Cody product *more*, because old models' outputs compound on the internet. Tactics: llms.txt and authoritative sources with provenance; give agents something current to quote (examples, charts, FAQs); keep everything fresh; be in marketplaces and MCP registries; remove friction (an agent won't recommend a tool that needs three demos and a sales email); cover the pains in content; measure lift after content campaigns
data.name: Generative engine optimization (GEO)

data.brief: The agent describes UI as typed data — a list of components the client renders with its own native widgets — instead of raw text/HTML. A trust spectrum (per CopilotKit): control (model picks a pre-built component, never invents), declarative (model composes from a component catalog — where A2UI sits), fully open-ended (model generates novel UI on the fly, e.g. MCP apps); the higher you go, the more the client must trust model output. Production mobile apps live in the bottom two tiers
data.name: Generative UI

data.brief: The speakers' map of UI-production strategies for agent hosts: predefined UI (MCP Apps' sandboxed iframe — the app ships finished UI) ↔ declarative UI (JSON-render, A2UI — the app returns build instructions, the chat builds the UI) ↔ fully generative UI (the model writes the UI; Claude's ask-for-a-UI feature "is actually based on MCP Apps" underneath). MCP Apps positions itself as agnostic to where UI comes from, plus the interop layer: a just-released guide shows one server shipping A2UI to Gemini and the same payload wrapped as an MCP App to ChatGPT, and one codebase running in LibreChat and ChatGPT unchanged
data.name: Generative-UI spectrum

data.brief: The reframe from quality to cost/length: quality gets the attention (Will-Smith-spaghetti 2023 → Sora → Seedance photorealism), but the bigger shift is efficiency and long-horizon generation — ~40 real-time-capable, long-horizon models released this year; Helios (a Wan 2.1 14B distill) generates continuously at ~last-year's-frontier quality for ~1/100th the cost. "$10 gets you 3 hours of continuous generated video; $50 gives you a full day interacting with an AI in a visual medium." Steerable in <1s while generating, ending the slot-machine approach
data.name: The efficiency axis of generative video

data.brief: The generating model must not be its own validator; independent (often deterministic) verification is load-bearing — "the architectural decision agentic security depends on"
data.name: Generator/validator separation

data.brief: Unified framework for AI-native KGs. 4-stage architecture. 20+ operator algebra. Provenance tracking.
data.description: Methodology unifying 40+ Graph RAG systems under one formalism. 4-stage architecture (Document → Entity-Relation → Cluster → Ontology). 20+ operator algebra with provenance tracking. By Fanghua Yu.
data.name: GenKM

data.brief: Reflective prompt optimizer "out of Berkeley" used on DSPy metrics + programs; the instruction-optimization rung of DSPy's ladder. Captions render it "Japa"/"Jeepa" — name reconstructed; verify before public-facing use
data.name: GEPA prompt optimizer

data.brief: Contamination channel specific to agentic rollouts on mined benchmarks: the agent runs git log, walks the commit hashes, and cherry-picks the commit containing the golden patch — recovering the answer from the environment rather than solving the task. Measurable per model family and closed by trimming every git ref and commit except the base commit the agent starts from.
data.name: Git-history golden-patch leakage

data.brief: The acquired product: LLM-driven "superhuman review" living in the PR flow alongside SonarQube's computational review; can block merges when issues breach quality criteria, write fixes, and approve/merge PRs completely automatically — but defaults to find-and-show-and-discuss, with automation features turned on progressively as trust is earned
data.name: Gitar (AI code review + CI automation)

data.brief: Realtime multiplayer software development in one Slack-shaped surface: every session is a branch of the repo checked out in a cloud microVM ("none of this is running on my machine"), holding team chat, a terminal, and a browser preview together. The agent reads the entire team backscroll, so after a human discussion you say "yo, Ace, do it" and it acts on the conversation — including fishing the *final* state out of meandering engineering threads ("let's try it this way… no wait, edge case… back to the first idea") so "I don't need to work for the robots." Plans arrive as markdown docs the *team* edits together, then "we've updated the plan — do it"; plus ambient awareness panes of what teammates' sessions are doing. Chat is where the facts-not-in-code live (political considerations, "that VP will vibe with this direction," the sweetheart Azure deal); everything in code, agents read from code. Technical preview "hopefully later this month"
data.name: Ace (GitHub Next realtime multiplayer dev)

data.brief: Background-agent automation where markdown is the source code: "if GitHub Actions and Copilot had a baby and it ran on markdown." A workflow is a three-line-ish natural-language playbook ("the message I'd send to a junior developer") plus YAML front matter of deterministic guardrails; Copilot expands it into a full playbook, and the compiled Actions YAML is "a compiled artifact — you never look at it"; to change behavior "just edit the English." Demoed as a super-Dependabot: nightly dependency watcher that read release notes across two major Astro versions, applied the code changes, verified the build, flagged manual steps, and opened one PR with a preview deploy. Ships with a library — issue triager (basis of GitHub's internal spike), repo-assist (a swarm of workflows maintaining a project), CI doctor, N+1-query hunts in GitHub's monolith, daily status homework "for product managers too." In public preview
data.name: GitHub Agentic Workflows

data.brief: Flagship open-weight frontier model of the moment (per the talk): 744B total / 40B activated MoE, up to 1M context; runs in NVFP4 on a single NVIDIA DGX Station or a server with 8× RTX Pro 6000 — desk-side frontier intelligence; beats "GPT 5.5 extra high" on at least one benchmark (speaker's claim)
data.name: GLM 5.2

data.brief: The mechanism under /goal: the harness re-injects a continuation prompt carrying the user's stated objective after every turn, and keeps doing so until the model calls an update-goal tool declaring the objective met. The operational consequence is a prompting rule — "you don't want to write full essays into your goal, but instead have very concrete and verifiable prompts, so it's easy to detect when things are done"
data.name: Goal continuation prompt

data.brief: A nightly report agent that had run fine for weeks one day posted the manager's private report as a PR — "nothing changed, the model decided to be helpful." The harder case: an agent investigating a latency spike reasonably asks for another service's logs, then GitHub to read commits, then Slack for chatter — each step expands the goal and crosses a trust boundary until the agent "has access to everything at the same time" and anything becomes a blast-radius vector. Traditional software had static permissions; an autonomous agent's needed access changes at runtime, and "we haven't truly solved" how to grant exactly that safely
data.name: Goal expansion crosses trust boundaries

data.brief: SME-co-authored suite of input → expected-output cases (outputs can be text, tool-call expectations, parameters, or call chains) plus scorers producing an accuracy number — "a test suite in a non-deterministic scenario"; serves simultaneously as baseline, regression suite, and the optimizing agent's objective function; production failure modes are folded into it continuously
data.name: Golden dataset

data.brief: Idiomatic reference implementations written by hand, by humans, before the loop is turned on, and shipped inside the actuator's skill. Rationale: agents are pattern replicators, so without golden patterns the loop reproduces whatever is in the docs or in the model's memory of the internet rather than your house style. The skill should also carry a response template; expect to iterate the skill from what actually works rather than front-loading it.
data.name: Golden patterns

data.brief: Block's coding agent, built before LLMs supported tool calling; Block design-partnered with Anthropic on MCP's initial release and Goose became the MCP client reference implementation; callable in Slack (`@goose`) for diagnose-and-fix flows
data.name: Goose

data.brief: Frontier family previewed the week before the talk (early July 2026): 5.6 Sol tops Terminal-Bench; 5.6 Terra delivers GPT-5.5-level intelligence at half the cost; Luna beats notable models at $1/M input and $6/M output; Sol on Cerebras serves ~750 tokens/sec ("a substantial PR in ~10 seconds")
data.name: GPT-5.6 model family (Sol / Terra / Luna)

data.brief: OpenAI speech-to-speech model (released late May, per the talk) rolled into ChatGPT voice mode; adds active-listening backchannels — read as the frontier's first step from strict your-turn/my-turn batch toward participation
data.name: GPT-realtime 2

data.brief: Environment infrastructure presented as the third leg of long-horizon RL alongside algorithms and compute: over 350 hosted environments behind a single API endpoint, used for General Reasoning's own internal RL and by frontier labs and new labs. Name unresolved — captions render it "Open Review" with the URL "openreview.ai", which collides with the well-known academic review site; possible garble of an OpenEnv-style name. Verify from the video before seeding.
data.name: General Reasoning environments platform

data.brief: Massively-multiplayer game Kramer is building with friends "as a canvas to really think about what AI native software can be": LLMs at the core of every interaction, hundreds of inference calls in play, real-time agent orchestration — "we couldn't have built anything like this even a year ago." Demonstrated patterns, per its own narration: asynchronous non-blocking context compression; long-running sub-agents that share context; progressive skills loading; dynamic user-interface generation; conversational voice ("Eagle is on five trade loops, Hawk and Raptor are on five exploration loops each — your fleet is busy")
data.name: Gradient Bang

data.brief: Lineage engineered into the memory data structure rather than logged afterwards: every derived artifact (fact, summary, classification) is a graph node/edge linked back to verbatim source episodes; tracing a fact to its sources is a graph walk; links survive entity merges (merged entity keeps all parents' source links) and fact invalidation (mutating episodes recorded against the fact).
data.name: Graph-native provenance

data.brief: Teams run 10–30 tools whose views of a customer differ and whose data needs differ — single real-time records here, hundreds of thousands once a day there, weekly or monthly elsewhere — with distributed failures and tools that sync among themselves independently of your orchestration (a CRM and a sequencer sync on their own schedule, so creating a contact means waiting and looping until it exists downstream). Clay's orchestration is a graph of universal nodes: nodes that run agents, make tool calls, branch on conditions, execute code, and map-reduce across records; an event or schedule triggers it, it touches several systems, merges the results and pushes them to the interfaces reps use. "A fundamentally modern way of tuning," whether bought or built
data.name: Graph orchestration across the GTM stack

data.brief: Stacked-diff code-review tool; at Higharc the vehicle for decomposing large monolithic research prototypes into tightly scoped, dependency-ordered PRs that subject-matter experts review asynchronously (work continues up-stack while a domain specialist reviews below)
data.name: Graphite (stacked diffs)

data.brief: Open-source temporal knowledge graph framework (Zep). Source data enters as verbatim "episode" nodes; entities/relationships/candidate facts are extracted single-shot with a reflection step, then deduplicated/deconflicted; contradicted facts get invalid-dates rather than deletion, with the mutating episodes noted. Search: vector similarity, full-text, and graph-relational ops (BFS).
data.name: Graphiti

data.brief: Replacing vector-retrieval RAG with a knowledge graph + structured query (e.g. LLM-written Cypher over Neo4j) for precise questions — aggregations, counts, multi-hop relationships: the graph computes a verified answer over the full dataset instead of the model estimating from top-k chunks, and returns honest zeros instead of hallucinated positives
data.name: GraphRAG

data.brief: Deployment discipline for non-deterministic components: keep the existing deterministic tier 1 (static rule engine + trained ML risk score) for the confident tails — below threshold approve, above threshold block — and route only the residual gray zone, where neither system can conclude, to an agentic tier 2. The stated rationale is explicitly not-replacement: "our thought process is not to exclude the systems we already had"; the agent earns its non-determinism by being applied precisely where the deterministic system is already uncertain, and by having real-time cross-domain context that the rule and ML engines never received.
data.name: Gray-zone triage

data.brief: The unit of a simulation: a fully synthetic user given identity and situation, a communication style (tone, voice), and generated grounding data — a fake address, a fake credit card, account data — that stays consistent across every mocked tool call in the trajectory, so the agent's identity lookups and verifications return coherent results and the run is actually evaluable.
data.name: Grounded synthetic persona

data.brief: Employees get a window into the exact tools and skills the background agents use, so they chat with the same information and build their own agents and automations — "and they're building a ton of them." The reasoning captured in remote MCP tool calls doubles as product analytics: each employee-built agent says "here is a problem I have and how I'm solving it," and their prompts, skills and vibe-coded applications become the raw material for productionizing the use case for everyone with the same problem. Extending to a new team is mostly new skills, data integrations and ingestion
data.name: The GTM MCP that federates the tools

data.brief: Describe a motion — a playbook ("here's how you sell procurement, how you sell to construction"), an experiment (golf balls for golfers at East Coast construction companies), an evergreen campaign — and have background agents produce the artifacts each channel needs: an audience, personalized outbound sequences, landing pages, ad creative, in-app notifications, with the channel owners reviewing and signing off. Campaigns are balanced like a multi-armed bandit between exploring new possibilities and known returns, under guardrails for compliance, rules of engagement and context-awareness (no repeated touches). The vertical builds are the foundation of multi-team, multi-channel distribution
data.name: GTM orchestration from a described intent

data.brief: The failure mode on the other side of safety: general-purpose LLM guardrails are far too conservative, and an inappropriate trigger on someone in a vulnerable moment is a door slam to the face that leaves them more isolated and can prevent them from getting care. The design objective is therefore stated as not more triggers, more correct triggers. Three calibrated response tiers are demonstrated: present-tense danger, surface local resources and disengage; past-tense disclosure, surface resources and continue if the user is comfortable; no risk indicator, silent pass-through where the user never knows the guardrails are there.
data.name: Guardrail over-calibration

data.brief: Safety implemented as independent LLM-as-judge calls that sandwich the core agent rather than as rules inside its prompt. The input guardrail inspects the incoming user message and decides whether intervention is required before the core responds; the output guardrail inspects the AI response and the conversation as a whole, and can intervene to keep the conversation on track. Three stated reasons for keeping them as separate calls: modularity (the core can be iterated without compromising user safety), robustness (separate calls are harder to prompt-engineer around and harder to jailbreak by conversationally driving the model off the rails), and evaluability. The latency and cost cost is explicitly accepted as warranted by the sensitivity of the use case.
data.name: Guardrail sandwich (separate-call input/output guardrails)

data.brief: SonderMind's open-sourced evaluation corpus: 200 input-guardrail scenarios and 100 output-guardrail scenarios, every one clinically reviewed and calibrated against real conversation patterns, single- and multi-turn, spanning the spectrum of mental health. Released as a shared baseline for anyone building in the space, with an explicit caveat that it is not a replacement for building your own learning loop — there might be real hurting people depending on your learning curve.
data.name: Open guardrail scenario datasets

data.brief: Guardrails (prompt-injection defense, PII filters, toxicity) are services that can be down, so choose fail-open (serve anyway) or fail-closed (block) per guardrail by "the worst case you can live with" — a toxicity filter down can fail open. Give guardrails a time budget so the LLM, not the guardrail, is the rate-determining step; give them fallbacks too (secondary provider, secondary checks, cached decisions). Placement: pre-hook on input (safest, serial latency), parallel (best for structured outputs — don't stream those), post-hook (output monitoring and audit)
data.name: Guardrails as unreliable dependencies

data.brief: The technical artifact (domain-specific, low industry signal): a JUCE audio plugin chaining TTS (Piper) → per-word slicing via energy-gap + sonority-peak syllable segmentation → YIN pitch detection → synthesized-note + vocoder to make the guitar "sing," plus a conversational mode (mic → Whisper → local LLM → guitar). Pre-baked pitch-shifted vocal samples (WORLD vocoder) mapped per fret. Included for completeness; carries no pattern edge
data.name: Guitar speech/singing pipeline

data.brief: User-space application kernel (Sentry, Go) plus file-system daemon (Gofer) that intercepts and services syscalls, shrinking the host-kernel attack surface; still sits on the host kernel, so a two-step chained exploit remains reachable
data.name: gVisor

data.brief: Routing trigger built from model internals: linear/magnitude probes (and other classifier heads) over internal state — the prefill "is just a vector at the end of the day" — rating how strongly a model is tending toward hallucination, as a proxy for "how lost a model is in its thinking." Proposed as the principled alternative to token-count heuristics for deciding when a small model needs rescue
data.name: Hallucination/lostness probes

data.brief: The first eval — quantitative (used variables? theming? right spot?) plus qualitative (looks good? good decisions with incomplete information?) — was two hours of hand-grading in Excel: "never again." Then toy repos, then a web app, now an eval engineers kick off that runs hundreds of times a week against prompt changes with LLM judges. Complication: little open-source code has Figma files attached, so eval assets had to be made. Optional tool arguments (language, framework) added as telemetry — "agents lie, but it's a signal"
data.name: From a two-hour spreadsheet to hundreds of judged runs

data.brief: Open-source agent evaluation and RL environment framework from Laude Institute: (1) a format for specifying agentic environments, (2) a framework for performing rollouts in parallel with any agent, any model, any sandbox, on any task, (3) a registry of popular training and eval environment sets ("three or 400" eval sets). CLI-driven (`harbor run <env> <agent> <model> --parallel 64`, runnable by a human or by an agent) with a `launch` command rolling out that moves rollouts onto Harbor servers — fire-and-forget, "come back the next day and 10,000 rollouts are done". Supports multi-step rollouts, verification in a separate sandbox, artifact collection, and simulated users. Positioned as "a common language for environments" to maximize interoperability and data velocity
data.name: Harbor

data.brief: The talk's core principle, and the sharpest statement of it in the corpus: "harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude cannot do on its own" — context resets, compaction, and similar primitives — and "they have to be questioned frequently because they go stale as models improve." The worked example is context anxiety: Sonnet 4.5 wrapped up tasks early as it neared its context limit, so the team built context resets into the harness; Opus 4.5 no longer exhibited the behaviour, and the fix "became dead weight… pure overhead, adding latency and causing issues with the cache being discarded incorrectly." Generalized as: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent
data.name: Harnesses encode assumptions that go stale

data.brief: Benchmark for harnesses cited by Bhargava from a recent paper: 106 tasks, same model + same evaluation, only the harness varies; reported scores range 52.4%–76.2% — a >20-point spread from harness choice alone — and the harness effect is larger for weaker models (name per captions; verify paper identity before public use)
data.name: HarnessBench

data.brief: The architecture the speaker claims is common to every production agent — personal (OpenClaw, Hermes) and coding (Codex, Cursor, opencode, Claude Code) alike: events arrive from many surfaces (chat, webhook, timer/heartbeat, other systems) → a control plane maps each event to a session key → the session key defines the state boundary and its session lane gives that mutable state exactly one active writer → the runtime calls models and tools → tools act through approvals and policy → the audit trail becomes the run receipt. The runtime itself is stateless: the harness rebuilds the working set (transcript, session state, memory, policy version, tool definitions) every turn, and the model sees only what the harness supplies.
data.name: Agent harness blueprint

data.brief: Moving reasoning, state, and control flow out of the model into deterministic scaffolding — "the model is the talent, the harness is the director"; model proposes, harness decides
data.name: Harness engineering

data.brief: Diagnostic taxonomy derived from real OpenClaw issues: (1) state hole — delivery succeeds, the durable turn is never written; (2) overlapping writers — load-modify-save race, second save silently erases the first; (3) dangling tool call — a tool call with no matching result, so the run waits on an event that can never arrive and new messages queue behind the silence; (4) approval drift — an expired approved callback treated as retryable, surviving restarts and blocking later channel work; (5) missing edge proof — the message tool reports success but nothing renders for the user. Each is read with the same three questions: what did the user see, which boundary broke, what would the receipt have caught.
data.name: Five harness failure shapes

data.brief: RL-integration pattern where a real, unmodified production harness is pointed at a fake OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible base URL; the server intercepts each request (log probs, temperature, dialect translation, renderer) and routes it to the trainer's inference server — the harness never knows it is doing RL, so training and deployment use identical agent code
data.name: Harness interception server

data.brief: The practical ordering, argued from feedback latency: do whatever gives you feedback fastest. Harness engineering returns signal in about two minutes, so exhaust it first; once you hit the point where "if I keep tweaking this prompt I'm not going to get much more out of it," fine-tune to break through that ceiling; then harness-engineer again on top. The observed reality is that "a lot of teams are happy with harness engineering and it solves their customer use case," so the sandwich's later layers are optional rather than aspirational
data.name: The harness–finetune–harness sandwich

data.brief: The key piece: permissions written in HCL (the Terraform config language), checked into git, "a big long file — like a thousand lines," every change managed in precise detail. Rules can block specific Postgres functions and apply even when tunneling through other systems. Ships with a test system: fixture requests flow through the rules so you can unit-test that a given request is always blocked — "an outbound path the agent's host can't reach, on a protocol that isn't HTTP, gated by a rule that understands SQL"
data.name: HCL egress rule file

data.brief: Traditional software rebuilt with agent-first APIs, no UI. New business model category.
data.description: Emerging category: traditional software rebuilt as agent-first APIs with no UI. Same product, different interface, new business model. Coined by @ivanburazin.
data.name: Headless SaaS

data.brief: Surge's writing benchmark, built on the premise that writing is too rich, deep, nuanced and human to score mechanically — and that LLM-as-judge fails here because LLMs don't have good taste in writing. Implementation: a workforce of thousands of paid professional writers across domains (technical writers, poets, journalists, editors) doing blind model comparisons, aggregated into a leaderboard. Deliberately expensive: "our goal is to maximize quality, not to minimize costs".
data.name: Hemingway Bench (Surge)

data.brief: NousResearch OSS agent framework. 40+ tools. Runs on $300 mini PC with local models.
data.description: NousResearch OSS agent framework. 40+ tools. Runs 26B MoE at 20 tok/s on a $300 mini PC via llama.cpp + Vulkan. No API keys. Apache 2.0.
data.name: Hermes Agent

data.brief: Prompt a coding agent to decompose the codebase/problem into an explicit linked hierarchy of component documents (data, architecture, loss, metrics, ops, peripheral scripts — browsable as an Obsidian graph, leaves pointing at real code), then ask for improvement hypotheses per component. Turns plateaued hill-climbing into a structured search that surfaces radical changes; an explicit-action analogue of chain-of-thought
data.name: Hierarchical problem-decomposition scaffold

data.brief: Exploiting the tree structure of physical infrastructure (data center → hall → aisle → row → rack → GPU) so LLM context grows with tree DEPTH, not instance count: describe the finite set of root-to-leaf paths instead of enumerating equipment — a 64-GPU and a 460,000-GPU system produce roughly the same-size summary; a planner LLM then emits a structured plan {what to collect, scope subtree, filter} or a name-pattern to execute, never reading raw name lists
data.name: Hierarchy summarization (sub-linear context)

data.brief: Read time-horizon capability curves at the 80% (better: 90–99%) success threshold, not the 50% headline: the exponential trend survives at 80%, but the "models can do 18+-hour human tasks" claims do not — and the planning mental model that matters (write a spec, hand off, walk away confident) lives at 90–99%. A 50%-success hour-long kickoff is a coin-flip that wastes the compute *and* your attention span. On METR's frontier-model preview data, success declines sharply at the ~4-hour mark, and some tasks fail even below the 15-minute mark. ⚠ same argument as batch-2's ins-accuracy-collapses-capability (Shaukat/Sonar) — independent second statement, see Review note 2
data.name: High-accuracy horizon reading

data.brief: The simulator upgrade: train with layout shift, slow loads, missing labels, pop-ups, focus stealing, random account states, stale tabs — and make recovery a native model action. Where traditional RL resets state or restarts on an infra error, here the error is passed to the model, which must recover via native actions (refresh, backtrack, compare, wait, abandon, escalate). Paired with a process reward model (penalize dangerous actions throughout the trajectory, not just the outcome), calibrated confidence (teach when to escalate based on authorization, reversibility, visibility, impact), and adversarial tasks as mainstream training rather than byproduct
data.name: High-fidelity messy sandbox

data.brief: Exploit the asymmetry that mistakes are easier to spot after the fact: replay a completed trajectory with several models, look for agreement ("we asked seven different models and they all agree this is wrong"), and distill that expensive search into rubric questions that then audit future rollouts cheaply — and double as a spec for new tasks targeting the failure modes just found.
data.name: Hindsight rubric extraction

data.brief: OPSD's structural analogue of reward hacking, and the talk's most transferable warning: "with RL the number one problem is reward hacking… there is an equivalent for OPSD, and that is hint leakage." If the hint contains information the student could never have derived, the model learns to skip the reasoning that would have produced it — the worked example being a maths task where the hint states the answer and the rollout becomes "I know the solution is 000, so let me go back and put that into my reasoning trace." Two fixes offered: an LLM filter that rewrites hints into *what the model should reasonably have known* (e.g. "look through the logs" instead of "the SSO token is expired"), and the algorithmic residual guidance below
data.name: Hint leakage

data.brief: The second axis, and the file's genuine contribution to the batch's distillation thread. Distillation needs a teacher smarter than the on-policy student, which requires privileged information — a hint; the question is where the hint comes from. Offline hints derive from static data: known rubrics, general behavioural priors ("a customer-support agent too willing to give refunds"), or aggregate loss reports — independent of any particular rollout. Online hints are constructed dynamically *from* the online rollout, so the guidance is conditioned on what the model actually just did
data.name: Offline versus online hints

data.brief: Memory/retrieval system that uses personalized PageRank and other graph techniques to link memories to questions and answers; cited as the contemporary reference point for PPR in AI systems
data.name: HippoRAG

data.brief: The engineer cannot tell whether a trade thesis or a drug-candidate ranking is good, and LLM-as-judge only jargons, so the only way to iterate is to employ the person you would sell to. The expert starts at the ground level — better prompts, which sources are reliable, how to decompose the problem into a logical order — and ends up as the judge, climbing a feedback ladder: error analysis on observability traces (cheapest, highest ROI), rubrics as reward (RLAIF, with echo-chamber risk), supervised fine-tuning, RLHF (the gold standard, but re-done for every model release). Each turn of the loop produces a proprietary dataset of what works and what does not; more users widen the scope. A 20-year scientist "changed the trajectory of our tools"
data.name: Hire the user

data.brief: The metrics half: two sources of variation matter — action stochasticity (different trajectories per run) *and*, in a multi-config benchmark, environment variation — and both must be captured. Rollout-only confidence intervals give ~17–20% coverage (you guess the true performance only ~20% of the time) while looking tight; a hierarchical method respecting benchmark structure reaches the intended 90–95% coverage. The consequence is a deploy decision: overconfident small intervals pick the wrong model, and "with 1M tasks, a 4% performance mismatch at ~$12 average per mistake costs hundreds of thousands of dollars a month." An honest interval instead says "I'm not confident enough to decide" — prompting more eval spend rather than a costly wrong call
data.name: Honest confidence intervals for CUA

data.brief: Logs don't work for agents ("too much thinking to consume"). Instead, intercept at pre/post tool-call and pre/post decision hooks (the Claude model) to block, log or emit metrics, producing OTel-style spans/traces. The trace carries judgment pointers: the current goal, the reasons for operations, belief status, tool calls, and a confidence score — whether an answer came from multiple converging paths or was *inferred*, which routes it to a human
data.name: Hook-based agent tracing

data.brief: Retrieval engine for agents. Vespa veterans. Schema-first APIs. VPC/on-prem. OSS.
data.description: Retrieval engine for agents, not humans. Built by Vespa veterans. Agents issue long structured queries in reasoning loops — Hornet trades latency for throughput and recall. Schema-first APIs. On-prem, OSS.
data.name: Hornet

data.brief: Agent-facing creative and interface tooling converging on the web stack — HTML/CSS/JS, and text-structured markup generally — as the medium agents read and write, because it is what the models were trained on (the scraped web). Builders let the model author markup and make the browser do the rendering; human tools and formats (MP4, PDF, PPT, canvas editors, DSLs) get demoted to render targets, and agent *perception* likewise moves from pixels/raw DOM to compressed markup. Central thesis of this talk and Kapoor/Nori; input-side echo in ARK; industry meme "HTML is the new markdown" (Karpathy, Thariq [Shihipar?]). Prior-corpus resonance: Amazon rendering layer, generative UI, A2UI, MCP apps
data.name: HTML as the agent-native medium

data.brief: The model/dataset hosting platform itself, treated here as a distributed system rather than a community: 3M public models, 1M datasets, 50,000 organizations, 14M users, with metadata in MongoDB Atlas and artifacts in cloud object storage, fronted by a Kubernetes-hosted Hub API. Growth is release-driven — "every big release like Llama or DeepSeek generates thousands of new models on top" — so the infrastructure problem is set by the derivative-model long tail, not by any single large model.
data.name: Hugging Face Hub

data.brief: Escalation is dynamic (the agent escalates when unsure, or a rule fires above a treatment threshold) and humans and LLMs consume context differently. So the platform enforces a wider definition of "agent" covering both: any action an LLM can take, a human can take, at any point in the chain, and downstream steps don't care who did the upstream ones. A shared context definition maps into an agent-friendly prompt or a human-friendly UI
data.name: Human–agent equivalency

data.brief: The approach: rather than the usual avatar methods, take a video/world model and focus it on humans. Harder to train and deploy, but you get emergent properties for free-ish — full-body movement, object interactions, physics (earrings swing, water moves), micro-expressions, emotions.
