Trained with heavy focus on audio (audio drives emotion/expression; standard audiobook-trained audio encoders are too monotone, so they built expressive audio embeddings)
data.name: Human-focused world model

data.brief: Browser-automation shopping (screenshots, DOM parsing, form-filling) was clunky, brittle and tripped merchants' bot defenses; assistant checkout replaces it with an API call to the merchant, and payments stay deliberately human-in-the-loop with a processor carrying liability: ChatGPT only through a shared payment token, Gemini only through Google Pay, no x402 or autonomous rails — "we're just not confident yet." AP2 mandates are the path to autonomy when confidence arrives
data.name: Human-in-the-loop assistant checkout

data.brief: Measurement discipline that sets the ceiling on any human-alignment score. In the field's best-known demonstration (~1,000 people interviewed for ~2.5 hours each, then put through personality tests and surveys; transcripts handed to agents that took the same battery), the headline 83% agent-human alignment is normalized against the humans' own consistency — the same people were brought back two weeks later and were only ~80% self-consistent.
data.description: Where re-testing humans isn't possible, approximate it: split the human ground-truth data in half, treat one half as "synthetic", measure the correlation, and repeat hundreds or thousands of times to estimate the floor. Corollary: because a persona is a forecast, re-running it does not buy certainty — a thousand rain gauges improve an estimate of today's rainfall, a thousand reruns of tomorrow's forecast improve only your estimate of what the model says.
data.name: Human noise floor

data.brief: The talk's closing design rule and its answer to its own title. In a nine-step pipeline (parse requirements → root-cause analysis → implement fix → local end-to-end test → PR → review → merge → build/deploy to dev → deploy to stage), the human is needed at step 1 and step 9 only — to see what the agent is doing and to validate before it reaches QA. "Always have the human as a verifier, but not the throughput ceiling, because human attention is very limited." The finance corollary makes it non-optional: an auditor reviews and a controller signs for SOX compliance, and agent reviewing agent leaves accountability nowhere.
data.name: Human as verifier, not throughput ceiling

data.brief: AI IDE and collaboration platform — "building blocks for your software factory": a Figma-like collaborative workspace for Claude Code / Codex-style agents that walks teams through product review → architecture → program design → vertical-slice workflows; software-quality verifiers announced as upcoming. Free for small teams
data.name: HumanLayer platform

data.brief: Spec-driven development (e.g. with Kiro) with a proof at the end: write what correct means — formally in Lean, or in natural language that AI auto-formalizes — then validate the specification (human review, or test that it holds on some inputs), because the spec is upstream: "a living, breathing artifact the builder interacts with; everything else is downstream." The coding agent implements from the spec; the verification tool proves the implementation satisfies it, for every possible input. Contrast: LLM-as-judge is probabilistic, tests cover some inputs, human review can't match agent throughput
data.name: Humans own the specification; machines own the code and the proof

data.brief: Two-stage review of natural-language capability packages: deterministic pattern checks for the risks that can be expressed as patterns, then LLM review for the behavioural/contextual ones (destructive shell commands, how credentials are actually requested and used, behavioural drift). The hybrid is deliberate rather than incremental — an LLM reviewer's verdict varies run to run with temperature, so the deterministic layer supplies the stable floor and the LLM supplies the coverage regexes cannot.
data.name: Hybrid deterministic + LLM skill scanning

data.brief: Retrieval combining BM25 keyword search (exact matches: SKUs, IDs, medication names, product names) with vector/cosine semantic search, fused via reciprocal-rank-style scoring (in plain PostgreSQL here) and optionally reranked; top-k is a product decision — retrieve more for catalogs, fewer for high-liability domains like medical
data.name: Hybrid search (BM25 + vector + rank fusion)

data.brief: HeyGen's open-source framework (free forever; released ~2 months before the talk) that turns agent-authored HTML/CSS/JS into deterministic MP4 video: it freezes the browser clock and seeks frame-by-frame, waiting for every asset before screenshotting, so the pixels the browser previews are exactly the pixels the video gets; anything a browser can render (three.js, charts, SVG, shaders, WebGL/WebGPU, Lottie) becomes video-able; markup is plain HTML plus a few data attributes for timing metadata; ships skills that teach video taste rather than syntax, plus a studio (incl. keyframes) for human last-mile editing; works with any coding agent that writes HTML
data.name: Hyperframes

data.brief: Shifting the unit of velocity from code shipped to ideas explored: when teams adopt decision-layer work, "people start to plan and then *not* implement their plan — and this is actually a really good sign," because ideas get fleshed out, compared and triaged before any build. The cure for shipping too much code that goes nowhere: escape "prototype gravity" (building the first navigable path and falling in love with it) and explore the whole idea maze to "find the gold around the corner." ⚠ terminology convergence with the b6 Snap talk (see review note 3)
data.name: Idea velocity

data.brief: Google-originated pattern (GCP IAP): identity provider + policy engine + reverse proxy in front of an internal app, so policy — not tokens pasted into UIs — dictates access; implementations include Pomerium (open core) and Caddy+OAuth; now applied to agent control planes
data.name: Identity-aware proxy

data.brief: Policy lives in two places: text (context files explain the why; works ~80% of the time, cheap, but "just advice — no enforcement, and prompt injection can talk it around") and infrastructure — a per-session proxy that doesn't read the prompt, sees a delete or a crossed budget and returns 403. The proxy holds the real credentials and stamps every outbound call with the identity it *knows*, not the one the agent claims; the cluster writes the stamp as a label, child jobs inherit it, and every safeguard (ownership, quotas, rate limits, approvals, tripwires) keys on it. Without this an agent hitting a limit can just change the header and "you don't have a rate limit, you have a suggestion"
data.name: Identity from the infrastructure, not the request

data.brief: Instruction-following benchmark cited on many model cards, used here as the taste antipattern: built by mashing together arbitrary constraint prompts no user has ever asked in earnest ("do not use any commas", "use the letter T at most once"), so its value rests entirely on an unargued generalization claim. Contains fully unsolvable tasks (repeat this verbatim and translate it into Hindi; a riddle with exactly one bullet point and a few bullet points), a sentence splitter that doesn't match how humans split sentences, and unverified prompts — "write a story" is graded only on the count of the ASCII letter i, so every response scores full marks, including one that reward-hacks with the
data.description: Cyrillic homoglyph.
data.name: IFEval

data.brief: For SOC 2 / HITRUST / HIPAA an audit trail is not a developer log: a *complete* record of every action the agent took, every data access, every authorization — "if the agent's decision came up in a court of law, could we show a justifiable chain of evidence?" Architecture choice: decide what you want to be *easy*. An append-only, timestamped, unified transaction log as the single source of truth across all parallel agents makes auditability "fall out of your storage paradigm — it's impossible not to be able to roll back time." Trade-off (event sourcing): writes trivial, reads require replay (mitigated by snapshots/caching); views are ephemeral projections, which healthcare wants anyway when later events change the interpretation of a journey
data.name: The immutable action ledger

data.brief: Field gold-standard for RPLA personality fidelity, evaluating via psychological interviews rather than self-report scales; reports state-of-the-art systems at 80.7% alignment with human-perceived target-character personality — the talk's anchor example of an eval that measures convincingness (fluency, personality consistency) with no mechanism to measure fidelity to the documentary record
data.name: InCharacter benchmark

data.brief: Why temperature 0 ≠ reproducibility on hosted APIs: greedy sampling fixes only the argmax, not the underlying scores; floating-point non-associativity means operation ordering shifts logits and can flip the winning token; the real culprit is batch variance — a request is grouped with whatever traffic co-arrives that millisecond (a lone matmul is bit-stable); MoE expert-capacity limits reroute tokens depending on co-batched traffic. Identical prompts can yield dozens of distinct outputs over 1,000 runs
data.name: LLM inference non-determinism

data.brief: A serving observation specific to diffusion transformers (unlike large LLMs needing multi-node inference): "whatever GPU works — the GPU can be hot, falling out of the bus, exploding, inference still runs." So low-priority production inference can run on the worst, cheapest, most-preemptible capacity while the good GPUs do training, and users feel nothing
data.name: Diffusion inference on any GPU

data.brief: Errors as types inferred and propagated up the call graph without annotation: `divide` throws a division-by-zero error, so `calculate` (which calls it) knows it throws it, and so does everything above. The compiler can then prove whether an error is handled — an API declared never to throw fails to compile while an unhandled error remains, and catching it makes the guarantee provable. Contrast drawn with what agents actually do in existing languages: nest try/catch inside try/catch until they give up and console.log("some error happened").
data.description: Framing: "the type system never lies... the absolute center of truth that prevents invariants from entering your codebase", and "code is a matter of trust — the reason we don't use LLM code blindly is that the systems underneath don't have enough rigidity".
data.name: Inferred, exhaustively-checked error types

data.brief: The observation the company was founded on: models are "proficient at handling the application layer but struggle when it comes to reasoning through infrastructure complexities" — the example given is MVCC in a database engine leading to corruption issues, one of the roots of the DynamoDB failure. Diagnosis: "like with everything in ML, a gap in models is usually a gap in data — models are typically only as good as data is", supported by the claim that model capability has never regressed when you introduce more high-quality data.
data.description: What is missing from the data is named precisely: current benchmarks have the agent produce a couple-thousand-line PR over 50-100 turns, but never do what a PM does (talking to customers, understanding their problems), what an engineer does (trying different approaches and performance-testing them), or what an owner does (owning the underlying infra for the code base over the course of not just months but years).
data.name: The infrastructure capability gap

data.brief: Durable-execution platform for AI agents: durable steps, event triggers, scheduling, agent-to-agent coordination, full session traces, no infra to manage; pluggable context layer (any model/framework/tool) and compute layer (any sandbox/browser); positions the execution layer as the instrumentation point for outcome-based agent scoring
data.name: Inngest

data.brief: The talk's load-bearing distinction. Intelligence = "the capacity to reason through unfamiliar problems from available context" — what frontier models are increasingly good at, where every episode is independent. Expertise = "accumulated and situated competence… the ability to act reliably, efficiently, and with judgment" in a particular domain. They differ on which way context flows (intelligence *consumes* supplied context; expertise *knows what context to bring*) and on search behaviour (intelligence expands the search, brute-forcing 100 parallel attempts; expertise compresses it, having learned the shortcuts). Drawn from cognitive science: experts don't know more facts, they *see differently* — pattern recognition, deep structure, conditional rules with known exceptions, and taste including "when it's good enough"
data.name: Intelligence vs expertise

data.brief: Still bottlenecked on review for architectural changes — "and more subtly, on human ability to even fully conceptualize what we're doing." A 2,000-line PR "looks like code to me," so Claude Code artifacts ship the explanation, intention and trade-offs; code stays verifiable by tooling, humans discuss intent and trade-offs and measure in production. Krieger's own review: "I talk to Claude about the code — these are the questions I'd have, go investigate" — Claude-powered, human-driven; cosmetic changes fix forward. Instagram-era priors: pre-measure everything, first-class flags and dynamic config; MonkeyType's runtime-type capture as a model for production-data-guided conversions
data.name: Intent artifacts over diffs

data.brief: Software that adapts to the user's intent instead of the user adapting to static screens. Pipeline: the user's query → an orchestrator classifies intent → locates and invokes tools (first-party, third-party, agents on MCP servers) → maps the returned entities to eligible components in the catalog → broadcasts a UI spec → the UX agent renders native components; the user reviews and approves ("this is already live"). Placement, information architecture and component choice are made by AI, guided by codified UX knowledge; consistency across turns (the same query must not yield four scopes) is the bar
data.name: Intent-driven UX

data.brief: The core mechanism, and the fix for spec-driven development's waterfall flaw (spec written before everything is known, no feedback loop, "LLMs aren't deterministic — they make decisions themselves"). Intent doesn't only live in the spec — it lives in the Jira ticket, the PRD, and most of all in the prompts, "where the real decisions are being made" in the back-and-forth with the agent. The mistake today: "we create a PR and then throw away the prompts." Capture the user responses from the session as acceptance criteria — and crucially build the test plan from the *session*, not the code, because "if the code is built by the same agent building the test plan, it won't catch issues" (crediting Dex Horthy)
data.name: Intent captured from the session

data.brief: The core flip: "by default the context is on the game engine — we should flip that to game design." Instead of learning meshes, renderers, animators, rigid bodies, colliders and hundreds of sliders, you describe intent in the language players already know ("make this robot move with WASD," "double jump," "when you collect a coin, increase the score"). The LLM otherwise "reinvents the wheel every time" (a camera-follow reimplemented differently each run) because it lacks the right vocabulary layer — so the fix is a domain-intent layer above the engine, not a better prompt
data.name: Intent in player vocabulary, not engine vocabulary

data.brief: The synthesis: session→acceptance-criteria + AI-slop-registry → a test plan, verified by spinning up a live preview and running it end-to-end ("even if the code looks right, does it actually work?"). That verification output *becomes the review surface* — reviewers look at intent, whether the capability was implemented, and whether behaviour met the criteria, plus screenshots and DB snapshots as evidence, rather than reading the diff. "Deterministic where it can be, LLM where you must." Closer to behaviour-driven than test-driven development; the test plan is English, so PMs and designers can participate. Tests are created in real time, so you don't maintain a test suite
data.name: The intent-and-evidence review surface

data.brief: The light-bulb moment from the agent-run repo: agents providing structure and context mean "anyone can participate in translating their intent into implementation" — and the people with the most interesting intents are often domain experts using the software, not the developers building it. Most software is developers building for non-developers; with the structures and guardrails in place, non-developers "can ship serious software"
data.name: Intent-to-implementation for non-developers

data.brief: Treating every human-AI interaction (approve / reject / modify / override / follow-up question) as a label: intentionally structured interactions are a system property that yields high-quality training and eval data — a compounding flywheel. Unstructured rubber-stamp UIs log false positives as truth, making the model more confident and the human more deferent
data.name: Interactions as labels

data.brief: The taxonomy: (1) infinite/interactive Veo-likes — continue forever, changeable mid-stream, real-time (prompt "a cat shows up" and it appears); (2) Genie-3-like controllable worlds — image+text in, control a character/world, beyond games into interactive experiences (Bandersnatch-style), robotics training-data generation, and education ("step into a history lesson"); (3) live interactive avatars — still not cracked, "kind of off," but rising in research preview for customer support, sales, streaming. Combining the three is where new experiences emerge
data.name: Three classes of interactive video models

data.brief: The consistent data substrate every GTM system and agent reads from: CRM, product, enrichment, web and buying signals (internal propensity models — "likely to attach procurement or treasury" — and external ones like funding), plus interaction data (emails, meetings, calls, page views). Real-time events flow over Kafka into Postgres, which keeps transactional guarantees and referential integrity between CRM, product and third-party entities, attributes everything at the right level and records provenance; unstructured sales data is embedded for search; online batch jobs pre-compute enrichment for the entire addressable market; offline dbt/Snowflake compute returns by reverse ETL into the same layer
data.name: The internal customer data platform

data.brief: A single canonical internal marketplace of plugins and skills, deliberately treated as the enforcement boundary rather than merely a discovery surface: publication requires a pull request, which is what gives the scanner somewhere to stand. Extends to third-party material — anything downloaded from outside must be uploaded to the marketplace to be used, so it gets scanned and then becomes safely shareable. Named residual risk: other teams can stand up other marketplaces, so proactive detection of new marketplaces (and installing the scanner into them) is an open work item.
data.name: Internal AI skill marketplace (as a security boundary)

data.brief: The productization, in research-preview beta with customers at the time of the talk. Uses the outcome-grounded LLM to proactively raise opportunities for a business at any given point in time — what to do, why, grounded in "who is like you, who's similar to you, what they did" — with drill-down into the reasoning and the ability to turn a recommendation into an action plan. Design requirement he attaches: grounded science alone is insufficient; the experience must also understand the user's preferences and make them feel part of the decision.
data.name: Intuit AI business advisor

data.brief: Starting evaluation with deliberately non-scalable, intuition-based inspection of agent outputs instead of building the comprehensive eval first. Justified by three properties of the early stage: failure modes are obvious to the naked eye, prompt tweaks and radical architecture changes still produce large swings, and a premature scaled eval both hinders those changes and produces violent up-and-down measurement while you are calibrating the eval and the agent at the same time. The output of the phase is familiarity with the failure patterns — which is the input to building the real eval.
data.name: Intuition-first evals (deliberate early "vibing")

data.brief: The first production lesson, and the most transferable. The naive approach takes all traces and clusters them, which "is useful for one-off analysis but doesn't really scale well." Two structural defects: clusters are hard to track reliably over time (temporal clustering being a research problem in itself), and you do not control the boundaries — "wrong price quoted" and "wrong refund calculated" collapse into a "price issues" cluster despite having extremely different root causes. The analogy given is telemetry: nobody clusters ordinary logs, because what you actually need to know is when something started and how much it has grown
data.name: Clusters are not issues

data.brief: What a production agent issue must carry to be actionable, argued as obvious-but-neglected: when it started and what percentage of users it affects. The first is what turns a report into an investigation — "if I tell you this issue started yesterday, suddenly your mind starts turning: what did I do, what changed, did we change model?" — and the second is the difference between three users and 100,000. Motivated by the claim that "agents will have an infinite number of problems… that's the great and terrible thing about them," so triage, not enumeration, is the job
data.name: Onset and percentage of users

data.brief: Psychometric successor to classical test theory applied to LLM benchmarks: fit each question ("item") a difficulty (B) and discrimination (A) parameter and each model a latent ability (theta), via per-item curves mapping ability → P(correct). Yields calibrated model comparisons with likelihood intervals, item-quality audits (negative-A items are broken), benchmark compression, outlier/residual analysis, and bias detection between model groups
data.name: Item Response Theory for LLM evals

data.brief: The routing-side premise: coding (or any domain) is not one capability — within data-science work, scikit-learn vs matplotlib vs model-building strengths differ per model, driven by each lab's training corpora and post-training teacher/sub-task mixes. A model that wins a coding benchmark is not "plain better at every task"; overlapping strengths create an arbitrage an orchestrator can harvest — "up to 10% higher accuracy" on router benchmarks (⚠ "LM router bench" garble), depending on model pool and task. Routing = "intimately understanding the behavior, strengths and weaknesses of different models, and applying them thusly"
data.name: Jagged model capabilities

data.brief: The agent's security layer. Premise: an agentic system cannot be secured the way an LLM is — an LLM's output can be inspected, but an agentic system acts, so its exposed surface is vastly larger (every web page crawled, every group message and pasted screenshot, every GitHub issue, every promotional email) and larger still in a group. Design consequence: do not gate the input — let the agent read everything and place a deterministic guard at the action boundary (reading bash or secret/config variables, exporting data), fast enough to add no latency, classifying actions into three buckets: allow, require approval, block.
data.name: Jatayu (action-surface guard)

data.brief: TwelveLabs' video agent product (demoed): corpus-level Q&A over 67 World Cup videos (near-misses-that-weren't-goals with explanations, goal build-up sequences naming passers, cross-corpus player tracking), traffic-camera analytics (vehicle counting/classification, red-light and near-collision safety events, rain/crowded scenes), and ad-insertion point detection on commercial footage.
data.name: Jockey

data.brief: Treating an LLM-as-judge as a trained binary classifier rather than a score generator: define pass/fail per metric, hand-label ~100 examples, split train/dev/validation (few-shots from train inform the judge prompt, iterate on dev, hold out test), then report the judge's precision/recall against human ground truth — plus ongoing re-calibration for criteria drift
data.name: LLM judge as classifier

data.brief: Keeping a model judge pinned to human taste as a standing process rather than a one-time alignment: short (10–15 minute) team annotation sessions on randomized axes (never one annotator rating one video on ten axes), annotations fed back into the judge prompt, and the accumulated annotations reused as the training set for the next judge version; agreement between human and model raters tracked over time as the drift alarm. Explicitly accepts that taste is subjective and the alignment never fully converges.
data.name: Human calibration of model judges

data.brief: The judge/critic is an agent, not an LLM call: it is given the same harness and tools the trained agent had, with read-only permissions, so it can verify the final state of the environment (did the PR merge, did the redeploy actually go green in the CI/CD and cloud logs) rather than trusting the agent's self-reported tool calls, which are "usually not very reliable". Safeguard requirement: the judge must not be able to mutate the environment after the rollout — no triggering deployments, no writes.
data.name: Judge with environment access

data.brief: The best rubric judge the speaker had seen — transcript, note and context, a detailed faithfulness rubric with worked pass/fail examples, optimizer-tuned, plus deterministic medical-concept diffing — signed off most production notes, and one in five of its clean passes still held a serious error, usually an omission. It is not blind; it can spot every difference between transcript and note, which is the easy half of verification. The hard half — which differences matter here — was never written down anywhere it could read ("a rubric you pre-specify is only the taste you could write down; the taste that matters is the part you couldn't"), so it nods along with the generator. Verifier's law holds for math and code where the checker comes free; for "is this note safe and complete" the verifier must be built, and its hard part is harder than generation
data.name: A judge without taste is a second silent failure

data.brief: Broad "good taste" is not a moat: taste is preference under feedback, which is exactly what these systems learn — "anything you can demonstrate enough times with a better/worse signal attached, the machine can imitate." What resists: (1) judgement about what hasn't happened yet (no data for events that haven't occurred) and (2) judgement embedded in a relationship the model can't observe — the model "has read everything written about your customer but has never met them"
data.name: The two kinds of judgement that resist training

data.brief: Personally built agent deployed for 8 months in a real group setting — friends, family, and a conference attendee group — across group chat and glasses. Behaviours shown from production: answering a venue question by DM instead of in the group because the answer was privacy-sensitive; syncing multiple calendars to find a shared slot; noticing sleep-deprivation and adjusting; speaking to the wearer through the glasses rather than the car's speakers while driving so passengers wouldn't hear; curating a months-long evolving group conversation down to what stays relevant; and tutoring the speaker's three-year-old while reporting progress to the parents.
data.name: Judith (multi-user always-on agent)

data.brief: For questions with no empirically correct answer: spin up a jury of independent analyst agents that each examine the data separately and return an evidence-cited opinion; a consensus judge treats those opinions as input (not fact), weighs each analyst's reasoning quality, synthesizes the final answer, and escalates by expanding the jury when consensus is insufficient. Modeled explicitly on human trial-by-jury; shipped in Upside's multi-touch attribution product, enabled by Claude Opus-class models.
data.name: Jury-and-judge workflow

data.brief: Context-management strategy paired with semantic routing: wait until the query is known, then inject only the context that request needs — lazy loading / JIT compilation applied to the LLM context window; the fat-agent design does the reverse (load everything, then reason). merge candidate vs el-progressive-disclosure [registry, batch 2]
data.name: Just-in-time context injection

data.brief: Speaker's open-source inference cost-optimization project (input-token compression, context management for agent loops); benchmarked against Netflix's Headroom and claimed superior on many parameters (both names auto-caption-garbled — see Review notes)
data.name: Just Token Max

data.brief: Raw sources → LLM-compiled .md wiki → schema file. Ingest, query, lint. ~400K words without RAG.
data.description: Raw sources → LLM-compiled .md wiki → schema file. Ingest, query, lint. ~400K words without RAG or graph DBs. Obsidian as frontend. 2.4M views. "There is room here for an incredible new product."
data.name: Karpathy LLM Wiki

data.brief: The headline experimental result across 11 presets, two models (Gemini, DeepSeek V4 Flash), and single/multi-turn tasks: not touching the context beat every compaction technique on recall, cost, and latency. Recall: keeping everything answered specific buried facts ~95% of the time vs ~32% after summarizing/compacting (summaries drop the details). Cost: the setup sending the *most* tokens was *cheapest* because ~97% were cached; a 36-turn / 1.78M-token conversation still came out ahead. Latency: compaction forces the agent to re-retrieve information it already had, adding tool calls. Long context held: no context rot on distinctive facts up to ~800k tokens
data.name: Keep-everything wins (with caching)

data.brief: General Reasoning's long-horizon benchmark, built because existing benchmarks do not test open-ended real-world competence. Agents must build machine-learning models to bet on Premier League football matches over a one-year horizon, each starting with $100,000. Chosen deliberately for real-world implication rather than Kaggle-style scoring — "there's real money to be made, and if it was successful you could make billions; there's a whole industry on sports betting". Result: every frontier model tested lost money. Reception: front page of the Financial Times, which "caught us off guard — how much the mainstream have interest in this".
data.name: KellyBench

data.brief: Keycard's security-token-service + policy-governance product; works with off-the-shelf and custom agents, CLIs, third-party/proprietary MCP servers, MCP gateways, A2A, any OAuth IdP
data.name: Keycard platform

data.brief: Moonshot AI. 1T/32B MoE. OSS frontier. Agent Swarm: 100 parallel sub-agents. Modified MIT.
data.description: 1T-param open-source MoE (32B active). Beats Claude + GPT-5.2 on agentic benchmarks (50.2% HLE-Full, 78.4% BrowseComp). Agent Swarm: 100 parallel sub-agents. 76% cheaper than Claude. Modified MIT.
data.name: Kimi K2.5

data.brief: AWS's AI IDE + CLI (kiro.dev) built around vibe mode vs. spec mode: spec mode runs the requirements → design → tasks flow with clarifying questions, a quick-plan variant, steering docs, spec-mode-for-bug-fixes, and generated property-based tests; born from watching customers hand-roll the pattern; launch went viral (tens of thousands of downloads, gated preview that people bypassed)
data.name: Kiro

data.brief: ZenML's newly launched open-source tool implementing the durable-runtime/checkpoint-replay layer: timeline view of checkpoints with config/code/artifacts, replay-from-checkpoint CLI (skips checkpoints whose state is already held), side-by-side diff UI, cohort replay to JSON, and an MCP server so agents can query the runtime and analyze replay cohorts. ⚠ name garbled in captions
data.name: Kitaru

data.brief: Verification instrument for compressed models: compute KL divergence between the BF16 model's and the quantized model's output logits over calibration data — goal: distance → 0 while size shrinks. Positioned as better than accuracy benchmarks for quant QA (benchmarks need sampling, many trials, averaging); reference: the paper "Accuracy is not all you need"
data.name: KL-divergence quant evaluation

data.brief: Every GTM workflow reduces to four questions, which became four layers: Know — a context layer about every customer that can be trusted (modeled, versioned entities with ownership and timestamps, served in milliseconds, plus agent-written artifacts keyed by the same ids); Decide — one next best step per customer; Act — a concrete action (lifecycle email, in-app nudge, a task handed to a rep); Learn — every action is a decision log, every outcome threads back to the decision that caused it, and engagement history drives continue / advance / pivot, so the system self-corrects instead of waiting for an analyst. Sales workflows are durable multi-agent runs on Temporal (research sub-agents → three scored drafts → a review agent → the rep's task; transcript → MEDDPICC extraction → grounded follow-up), every LLM step traced
data.name: The know–decide–act–learn loop

data.brief: Mixedbread's name for the widening gap between exponentially improving LLM reasoning and barely-improving retrieval (~20 years of slow search progress); operationalized as Oracle performance (model score when handed the right documents alongside the question) minus actual performance with real search tools over a noisy corpus — positioning knowledge access, not reasoning, as the binding constraint for agents beyond code (legal, finance)
data.name: The knowledge gap (Oracle gap)

data.brief: Domain knowledge graph (entities: geography, payers, accounts, brands, KPI hierarchies and drive-relationships, built with domain experts) used not as a data-lookup layer but as the control plane/control surface for an investigating agent: the graph dictates what the agent may look at and which paths it may take; every edge is a hypothesis; the agent loop is entity → graph neighborhood → hypothesis → back to raw data → support/contradict → traverse, until root cause or hypothesis exhaustion. Bounds an otherwise combinatorial investigation space
data.name: Knowledge graph as agent control plane

data.brief: Apple's 1987 concept film — foldable tablet, touchscreen, a conversational voice assistant with strong personality, global + personal information access, real-time vision and video generation, seamless calls, delegation of complex tasks for autonomous execution, and what "we might call today continual learning." Kramer's yardstick artifact: it "divides our timeline neatly in half," the web was "a conscious attempt to make that video real," and Tavus's weeks-old remake — one 4-minute take on real, available technology — is the talk's evidence that the target is now buildable
data.name: Knowledge Navigator (1987 concept video)

data.brief: Container-orchestration substrate (declare needs, a scheduler places workloads; compute, secrets, tools abstracted beneath). Invoked here as the layer that already answers an agent fleet's unsolved problems — the plan is to stack it underneath and build only the agent-native orchestration (task routing, review flow, context management) on top.
data.name: Kubernetes

data.brief: At agentic context lengths (concurrent requests of 500K–1M tokens) KV-cache management stops being a serving detail and becomes a distributed-filesystem/large-database problem — where to store the cache, how to know you have seen this prefix before, how to fetch it, how to move it between machines. Framed as rediscovered undergraduate distributed systems: "not that complicated, but you do have to do a good job".
data.name: KV cache as a distributed store

data.brief: The cost physics under multi-model systems: cached tokens are ~10× cheaper, so architecture follows the cache — switching models or compacting takes a cache miss; cache lifetimes (~5 min) are operational choices (GPU memory eviction), not physics, and self-hosters can extend them; a scheduled cache refresh can carry a "free" frontier-model check; providers amortize everyone's workload shape into one price, so self-hosting a known shape (e.g. 32K cache / 1K in / 1K out) "you'll likely pay much less"; futures floated: S3-backed cache offload, dynamic cache durations, switching-tolerance knobs. ⚠ merge-check vs el-prompt-caching / el-prefix-caching — those nodes name the mechanism; this one is the economics-as-design-constraint claim. Fold at seeding if preferred
data.name: KV-cache economics

data.brief: Labs' cadence is a two-week review of every project — persevere, pivot, or shut down — and projects are shut down nearly every cycle; the intention is to prototype quickly, ship internally, maybe early access, and wind down what doesn't work. Aligning the org chart to projects would mean re-orging biweekly, so a pod for each "bet" draws people from product and engineering with a bet lead / DRI who usually manages none of them; engineering managers coach and keep everyone on what excites them. "Loose until it solidifies" — once a product has legs (Claude Design) it gets a dedicated, hired team. "The death of the engineering manager has been greatly exaggerated"
data.name: Labs: bets, persevere-or-pivot, DRIs who manage no one

data.brief: poolside's model line, and the company's first move from enterprise-only releases to public open weights. Laguna M.1 and Laguna XS.2 were released open-weight on Hugging Face with a tech report; XS.2 is 33B parameters and pitched as one of the most competitive models at its size for coding, specifically agentic coding. Laguna S (previewed, not yet public) is 118B total / 8B active parameters, trained on 30 trillion tokens across 4,000 GPUs. XS.2 is called a new generation because it folds in the data and numerics fixes learned on M.1: more diversity, fewer data repetitions, FP32 accumulation at the unembedding, and more observability and checks.
data.name: Laguna (poolside model family)

data.brief: Open-source LLM observability/telemetry platform: per-conversation traces, model + latency + retrieved-chunk visibility, session/user tracking, cost estimation for external models; runs fully locally in this stack (captions garble it as "LangChain Fuse"/"length fuse")
data.name: Langfuse

data.brief: LangChain's agent-orchestration framework; its deep-agent library gives each agent a dedicated prompt + MCP-tool subset plus built-in steering tools (to-do list, virtual file system) — mirroring what Claude Code/Codex do natively; its deterministic workflow mode proved brittle for diagnostics vs ReAct agents
data.name: LangGraph / deep agents

data.brief: Safe clinical models answered in tens of seconds; fast models were not safe. Instead of choosing, Hippocratic built the stack ground-up and made the trade-off compound: every optimization buys back latency, which is not banked but spent packing more intelligence (more specialists, more verification) into the same conversational budget, and then the next optimization is found. Named lossless wins: 4-bit quantization of the model math, speculative decoding with a small draft model, and KV-cache compression that keeps long conversations warm (96% hit rate, prefill 18× faster). "Quality is the constraint, speed is the work"
data.name: The latency–intelligence flywheel

data.brief: The first and most fundamental persona failure mode: when context is missing, the model invents it, so parts of the experiment that should be held fixed silently become random variables. Documented case: asked about willingness to purchase at varying prices, humans slope downward as basic economic theory predicts, while LLMs produce an inverted-U — purchase probability rising with price over part of the range — because the model reads price as a proxy for unstated properties (expiry date, competitors' prices) that human respondents held fixed.
data.description: "If it's a poorly grounded persona, it's a little like the LLM is playing improv with you — gold watch on a table? We must be in a jewelry store." The fix inverts human-subject practice: paint the whole world in the prompt, including the study's own construction, which you would deliberately hide from a human participant.
data.name: Latent-confounder invention

data.brief: Agreeing the gatekeeping rule *before* it is needed: a stated launch criterion (a precision/recall threshold, or a use-case-appropriate metric when precision/recall is the wrong frame), an A/B diff or ablation to localize where a regression comes from, and an explicit classification of each regression as an acceptable trade-off or a critical failure rather than reading one aggregate number.
data.name: Launch-readiness gate

data.brief: Coding agents write memory to the local desktop; enterprise healthcare cannot, so memory lives in-database with logical separation at three levels — partner, organization and user. It pays because people in multidisciplinary practices do the same things daily ("they usually mean eligibility"), but persistent memory across chats and days also biases the agent toward repeating yesterday when the user wants something else, so every user must be able to step outside it
data.name: Layered enterprise memory, with its bias

data.brief: Splits brand voice into four separated jobs assembled in one place, in a fixed, load-bearing order: (1) immutable identity — hard rules and forbidden vocabulary nothing below can override; (2) situational mode — real-time conditions: who the user is (customer vs staff) and what they're going through (soft context notes used for tone, never quoted); (3) example-anchored voice — the tone guide/dials/phrase lists where most teams start and stop, trainable from staff edits; (4) post-generation veto. Replaced 24 ad-hoc system prompts scattered across one codebase with a single composition entry point; layer 1 is identical across tenants, 2–3 load per tenant
data.name: Four-layer voice architecture

data.brief: The demand-side consequence of benchmark quality problems: "I have not met an engineer in the last 6 months that would choose a model based on the leaderboards." Practitioners still read them for hype, then run their own tests and decide from those. Framed as quality gap to trust gap: the benchmarks kept their audience's attention but lost their decision authority.
data.name: Leaderboard trust gap

data.brief: Skill-steering technique: compact, high-prior phrases (e.g. "vertical slice" instead of a paragraph about not coding layer-by-layer) placed in skill text; the agent repeats them in its reasoning traces and output, re-emphasizing the packed-in behavior. Consistent use across the skill is the lever; the phrase surfacing in thinking traces is the observable success check
data.name: Leading words

data.brief: Benchmark instruction that hands over the answer inside the task text — distinct from training-data contamination. Two observed shapes: the instruction points directly at the test file, so the model has everything it needs to implement against the tests rather than solve the problem; and the instruction specifies the complete interface of the intended implementation, locking the model out of any design freedom. Both convert a capability test into an instruction-following test.
data.name: Leaky prompt

data.brief: Interactive theorem prover / dependently-typed language, used in the talk to type LLM signatures (IO marking real-world mutation, propositions-as-types for safety proofs); currently the AI-safety-adjacent formal-methods tool VCs anchor on (peers: Isabelle, Rocq/Coq, PVS, TLA+)
data.name: Lean theorem prover

data.brief: Lean is a programming language and a proof assistant in the same language — no translation layer — implemented in Lean (extensible), with a small trusted kernel and proofs that can be exported and checked by independent kernels (C++, Rust, Lean — you can write your own). Proving is chess: tactics are moves, the theorem is checkmate, you traverse a tree and backtrack from dead branches; an incorrect proof is rejected immediately by the kernel. AI decomposes a theorem into lemma subgoals, proves each with tactics, assembles the theorem, and the kernel checks it
data.name: Lean: one language for code and proof, a small kernel, tactics as chess moves

data.brief: Short-lived, request-scoped execution DAGs — explicitly contrasted with persistent/property graphs (Neo4j-style) you query — that represent how a request actually flows through services (edge layer → gateway/ingress → authn/authz → orchestration → parallel systems → client notification), with each loop/retry modeled as its own entity. Baselines learned per client/endpoint from telemetry; deviations detected against the baseline and localized to the exact node.
data.name: Learned execution graphs

data.brief: "Investing in verification is probably the highest-value thing we can do in our codebase." Every check that moves from a human to an agent is a win (Playwright + MCP letting the agent explore instead of a human). When the agent finds something useful, encode it into a deterministic, repeatable flow — tokens and time saved, and the LLM is used only where reasoning is needed. Ask the agent to write tests first (red → green) so code fits the verification criteria rather than tests fitting the code. Testing pyramid: deterministic analysis (lint, compiler, unit tests) at the bottom, agent review on encoded architectural standards in the middle, humans only at the top for functionality and "is this the right thing to build"
data.name: Left-shift verification to agents

data.brief: Graph clustering algorithm (refinement of Louvain) that labels densely interlinked node clusters; powers the themes shape — surfacing document groupings deterministically from link structure alone (no LLM in the loop), with a conductance metric for tight/loose linkage and a gamma granularity parameter; the same algorithm Microsoft GraphRAG runs before its LLM community summaries.
data.name: Leiden community detection

data.brief: Simon Willison's name for the deadly combination that makes agents exploitable: access to private data + exposure to untrusted content (prompt injection) + tool-call ability; any mitigation must break at least one leg — Meijer's proposal breaks the tools leg by deferring execution behind verified plans
data.name: Lethal trifecta

data.brief: ChatGPT Enterprise launched at $60 per user per month, priced on cost to serve as the first product on the market; competitors arrived lower and organizations bought seats only for subsets of staff. Moving to a base license plus usage dropped the barrier to entry, licenses multiplied and usage grew from there — "seats are out" is now common knowledge learned the hard way; usage pricing now draws pushback as costs climb, answered with spend caps per month and per employee that customers rarely use but want to know exist
data.name: The license-plus-usage pricing lesson

data.brief: Software factory run with no human code reading: code review is dropped entirely, investment shifts to testing/monitoring/rollout, and the human job reduces to queueing work. Term "software factory" dates to a 1968 NATO conference; "lights off" coined by Dan Shapiro (StrongDM built one). Horthy's talk is an argument that this configuration fails
data.name: Lights-off software factory

data.brief: The strategic reading of ontology work: every organization is made of nouns (entities) and verbs (operations), and the same entity is named differently per function — sales says customers, ops says clients, finance says billing entities, engineering says org IDs — which breaks integrations, corrupts data quality and stalls pipelines. Canonicalizing that vocabulary inside the product means users adopt your language along with your software, and "if you become the linguistic foundation, you're locked in". Palantir "tripped into" its ontology this way, not by schematizing everything into search. Live 2026 examples offered of vocabulary capture in progress: skills, and MCPs used to mean function calls with prompts. Diagnostic checklist: which terms are overloaded, where the integration points and translation layers are, which systems of record can never be swapped out, and what words people use when describing failures ("my agent keeps failing" — what is an agent?).
data.name: Linguistic lock-in

data.brief: Python LLM-gateway package, ~3.5M downloads/day, widely embedded in enterprise internal gateways. Compromised for three hours: attackers used a GitHub app to steal PyPI publishing tokens and shipped a version installing a credential harvester (API keys, SSH keys, crypto keys) plus a remote-command-execution backdoor. Detection was luck — the malware had a bug that crashed Cursor when the LiteLLM MCP server ran, and a security researcher noticed. "A single compromise and a massive chain of contributors to get pwned"
data.name: LiteLLM (and the 2026 compromise)

data.brief: Google AI Edge's open-source on-device runtime stack for deploying models to edge devices — the toolchain behind every throughput number in the talk, spanning CPU, GPU and NPU backends across phones, single-board computers and IoT modules. Carries the memory work (mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization, per-layer embeddings) and multi-token prediction. Developed first-party for Google products, then released so the wider world can build the same class of thing.
data.name: LiteRT / LiteRT-LM / MediaPipe

data.brief: Go-to-market reduced to data: the world of what your product does and the world of every potential customer, learned and kept current. Internal data (customers, people, product usage) plus external data (60M+ companies, a billion-plus people, daily news). Exa's two interfaces over it: the ICP dashboard — every company in the addressable market classified into segments with anticipated spend and metadata, built by semantic filtering over embeddings of the internet — and Request Lens, alerts on every significant customer event (signup, heavy use, use stopping, a notable visitor) the team can act on
data.name: A live model of your world that agents act on

data.brief: Balancing liveness (work keeps moving, no blockers) against verification (a human-reviewed task is assured but dead in its tracks); three invariants for an agentic control plane: productive work continues, only real blockers stop work, infinite loops are bounded; full liveness with no approvals = AI slop, full human review = an unreviewable queue
data.name: Liveness model (agent control plane)

data.brief: The de-facto open local-inference engine, now acquired by Hugging Face (team hired/absorbed — ⚠ caption phrasing, see Review note 4); previously cited in-corpus as "the most bug-free path" for self-hosting (batch 3, prose). Active development aimed at running "everywhere," explicitly including phones; the runtime layer under much of the quant ecosystem
data.name: llama.cpp

data.brief: The talk's organizing artifact, credited to a Karpathy gist: take a raw directory of unstructured personal notes and have an agent compile it into a navigable, interconnected knowledge base scoped to a focus area. Four stages — raw capture, enrichment, wiki generation, visualization — with markdown as the substrate throughout so any viewer (Warp, Obsidian, a custom app) works. Framed as the antidote to "an Apple Notes folder that's a complete disorganized mess," and as making forgotten ideas rediscoverable rather than merely stored
data.name: LLM knowledge base

data.brief: The talk's canonical bad-but-dominant benchmark: millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets over its outcomes while industry leaders openly brag about gaming it; Karpathy's observation that teams optimize LMArena models (nested bullets, emojis) rather than better models; no filtering of its voting workforce, so a crowdsourced army can be hired to vote and a watermark in the model's output tells them which response is yours; a published paper on its dynamics documents overfitting and undisclosed multi-model testing. Captioned "Elm Marina" throughout.
data.name: LMArena (crowd-vote model leaderboard)

data.brief: A local search layer between the codebase and AI coding tools, replacing whole-file context: semantic chunking into functions/classes/methods (not random windows); dual retrieval — meaning-based plus exact-word search fused (each alone misses ~1 in 4 relevant results, together ~1 in 10); result compression to signatures + descriptions (50-line function → 5 lines); call-graph links so one hit pulls connected code; sub-millisecond weighted relevance gating that drops low-scoring results (no bad context); runs entirely on-machine, with one shared index and persistent memory serving all coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex)
data.name: Local code index

data.brief: The context-engineering technique, borrowed from game rendering's level-of-detail: just as you render nearby objects in high fidelity and distant ones as a cube, assemble the LLM's context by proximity — feed full tag/setting detail for objects near what the user is editing, minimal info for far ones, ignore filler (grass). As the user moves, update what's fed. A domain-native answer to context bloat: relevance by spatial proximity to the edit
data.name: Level-of-detail context assembly

data.brief: 1.2M questions classified by LLMs into topics, subcategories and example questions — technically fun at 40K a week without breaking the bank — become the product's real-time signal: feature gaps and quality problems (users swearing or repeating themselves), a sales-enablement goldmine (a new product's knowledge gaps visible in minutes, battle cards and enablement docs generated from Confluence, Jira, Slack and PRDs and fed back into the agent), and matchmaking between teams unknowingly working the same accounts. The first features are hard, the next are easy, and the hockey stick starts when the logs are tapped
data.name: Logs as the feedback loop

data.brief: "Long horizon" is a scalar, not a category — useful for ranking tasks, not for a binary label, and the threshold moves every year. Two incommensurable rulers: the human ruler (expert-hours per task) and the model ruler (tokens consumed, steps, tool calls per trajectory). The model ruler is noisy — token counts swing with model family and harness — but it tracks real agent difficulty (context limits, compaction, coherence over steps) and defines the technical frontier. The human ruler breaks down in the opposite place: at the top-10%/1%/0.1% expertise tail, and on tasks that are tedious-but-trivial for a model (a day of Excel reformatting a model solves with a Python script). Use both.
data.name: Human horizon vs model horizon

data.brief: The empirical core: ~200M active websites (~1B total), and infrastructure that "changes very slowly — there are still places faxing each other." The head of the distribution may publish APIs; the long tail never will. Worked exhibits: restaurant menus ranging from plain German text (easy) to a menu-button-opens-PDF (medium) to JPEGs of PDF pages embedded in a gallery (hard); school-district procurement ranging from a portal to scanned PDFs to a district that answers FOIA requests by scanning your emailed request onto a Google Drive. "These are the people you're telling me will give you an MCP server. The amount of delusion here is off the chart"
data.name: The long tail of the web

data.brief: Private capability measurement by re-running an identical, real, already-completed task on each model generation and diffing the outcome. The talk's worked run (a Temporal activities/workflow refactor replicating the legacy pipeline): O3 (2025) — 3 hours of back-and-forth in Cursor, 10 major mistakes, constant manual intervention (guide the model, hand-edit, delete code); Sonnet 4.6 — solved with one additional iteration; Opus 4.8 — "basically able to one-shot" it. Also captures what leaderboards can't: the *interaction shape* changed — O3 made few substantial tool calls; modern harnesses spawn sub-agents, plan calls, shell commands and verification passes, costing more per model-step but far less human attention. Net: same task ≈ 1/5 the time to rebuild today
data.name: Longitudinal same-task re-run

data.brief: A markdown file tracked in version control that is deterministically loaded into the actuator agent's context on every run (after the controller). An /iterate comment on one of the loop's own labelled PRs triggers the workflow to load the PR context — diff, comments, review comments, description — alongside the skill and instruct the agent both to fix the code and to update the feedback file. Turns re-steering from a checkout-edit-commit-push chore into a PR comment, and makes the steering history diffable and revertible.
data.name: Loop feedback file

data.brief: Adaptive throttling that keeps a loop from outrunning human review: every loop labels the PRs it creates, and before doing any work the workflow checks whether any PR carrying its label is still open — if so it shuts down immediately, before checkout and dependency install. Invariant: at most one open PR per loop, no stacking, no duplicated work, few conflicts. The reasoning is explicitly about review capacity, not compute: an open PR means no human has reviewed the loop's last output, so there is no reason to manufacture more.
data.name: Loop flow control

data.brief: The three primitives managed agents is designed around. Agent — model, prompts, tools and skills defining what it does. Environment — the container it runs in, reusable across sessions with isolated instances, and the place network boundaries are set. Session — the combination, persisted as a durable cloud resource recording every interaction, with four states: *idle*, *running*, *rescheduling* on a retryable error, and *terminated* when unrecoverable. Durability is what makes long-horizon reliability possible: the agent can always return to a session and resume
data.name: Agent, environment, session

data.brief: Engineers built skills everywhere — duplication, painful discovery/configuration, "superpar" quality — so Uber built a lifecycle: core and domain skills in a marketplace (2,500 skills), lint checks and automated reviews for a quality baseline, one command to discover/install, persona-based auto-install so agents pick the right skill without installation, and now traces/comments captured as continuous evals fed back to skill authors. 20,000+ skill executions/day
data.name: Managed skills marketplace

data.brief: A feature end to end: idea in Slack → Cortana (assistant on Slack/CLI/web with skills, MCPs and the context graph; 300 personas, 20K sessions/day, personalizable per team channel) researches the opportunity, drafts requirements, Figma mock-ups and A/B variants → Minion (cloud coding agent on a devpod, interactive or autonomous, cross-repo) builds to a *draft* PR and does not push to CI until validated → inner-loop validation shifts left: static analysis, visual validation (simulator screenshot vs Figma spec via a skill), staging integration → outer loop: self-healing CI, tiered review (small fast model inner, powerful reasoning model + skill outer), and a table on the PR listing every check and screenshot so a human trusts the autonomous diff → maintenance skills (e.g. feature-flag cleanup) enrolled on a managed loop surface (runs Sunday for CI capacity, throttled so Monday isn't flooded); landed/not-landed diffs are label data to improve the skill; monthly, incident reviews become new maintenance skills. Bottlenecks now: CI capacity, experiment slots, and "should we build it"
data.name: The managed software factory

data.brief: Pre-agents, a leader's influence ran through communication — roadmaps, docs, meetings — "incepting" context into engineers. With autonomous, long-task coding agents, Paul Graham's manager schedule becomes usable for building: 2–3 hours a day (a morning review block, steering blocks between one-on-ones, the 5 p.m. setup block) yields 2–10 PRs a week. Building is now part of the job: (1) model families change every three months and "it is impossible to tell what a new model is good for unless your hands are in it"; (2) showing a working prototype beats convincing engineers every quarter; (3) leaders hold the most context, so their steering is more impactful per token; (4) delegation — goals, context, check-ins, coaching — transfers to agents; (5) models are "really good at execution, still not unbelievable at judgement," so a leader's "have you tried this?" is worth a lot
data.name: The manager schedule as building time

data.brief: Deliberately fabricating the "bad" half of preference pairs, since good video is abundant online and bad video is cheap to make — by corrupting good footage or generating random slop. Load-bearing failure mode: corrupted-vs-clean pairs teach the model to detect gloss and artifacts rather than the named axes. The fix used here is pairing real footage against AI footage with identical encoding on both sides and the identical annotation method for both, so the model cannot shortcut into being an AI detector.
data.name: Manufactured badness (negative-pair construction)

data.brief: TwelveLabs' multimodal video embedding encoder: turns semantic chunks (meaningful temporal units) into spatio-temporal vector representations of video content — the embedding tier of the video-memory stack.
data.name: Marengo

data.brief: Agent-hosting platform positioned as a cheap cloud default for running OpenClaw and other agents; sleep/wake architecture so idle agents don't burn compute — targets per-agent cost at fleet scale
data.name: Maritime

data.brief: With frameworks he "spent all my time editing the prompt within the code." Instead: an agent is a YAML/markdown file — versioned, diffable, reviewed in a PR — dropped in a folder, picked up by the runtime. "Frameworks just call code; your agents live inside their abstractions." Kernel analogy: the runtime schedules, isolates and journals agent processes; the markdown definition is user land (a front end that doesn't use markdown at all also exists)
data.name: Markdown agents over frameworks

data.brief: Arithmetic's first released benchmark: a black-box, live-environment eval where a low-privileged agent must exploit real, self-found zero-days chained across real applications (Keycloak → Vault → broker) to escalate privilege; the model sees neither the code nor the vuln and has no internet/codebase access, only basic execution tooling; extremely hard (one solve at K1). Name caption-sourced — verify before public-facing use
data.name: Masov (access-control exploitation benchmark)

data.brief: Open-source TypeScript agent framework supplying the primitives of the agent/harness/claw ladder for teams building their own — the response to users wanting OpenClaw/Hermes-agent features but "with power and control", not just "a claw on a box"
data.name: Mastra framework

data.brief: A clinical conversation with no patient in it: PatBot, an LLM patient conditioned on scenarios grounded in real clinical workflows (e.g. asks whether it is talking to a human), validated first for script adherence and then in a patient-and-public-involvement study where real patients could not reliably tell simulated from real (in three of four sets the majority picked the simulation as more realistic) — with the lesson that there is no single realistic patient, so personas are diversified. BevJudge, an LLM judge given expected behaviours and the hazard list, returns a structured pass/fail with reasons; validated against ten clinicians across ten specialties on 240 labelled conversations it matched or beat them (F1 0.96, near-perfect sensitivity — over-calling a hazard is preferable to missing one). Grading thousands of dialogues becomes scalable and expert-level; hired actors would not
data.name: Matrix: simulated patients and a validated hazard judge

data.brief: Popular open-source engineering skills repo (2PRD, grill-with-docs, domain-modeling, grill-me, writing-great-skills…) built around user-invoked skills, minimal skill.md files, and branch-specific reference hidden behind context pointers; the talk's whole checklist ships as the writing-great-skills skill inside it
data.name: Matt Pocock skills

data.brief: Model Context Protocol. Agent-tool communication standard. Agentic AI Foundation governed.
data.description: Model Context Protocol. The consolidating standard for agent-tool communication. Azure MCP Server 2.0: 276 tools across 57 Azure services, self-hosted. 2026 roadmap: audit trails, SSO, gateway patterns.
data.name: MCP

data.brief: First-party MCP directories — ChatGPT apps (chatgpt.com/apps), Claude connectors directory, Cursor directory — with self-serve submission, automated + partly manual vetting (tool-annotation scan, auth declaration checks, test prompts/cases), and one-click install URLs replacing hand-shared JSON config. On Claude, extends to dynamic task-time connector discovery from the MCP registry
data.name: MCP app stores

data.brief: Official MCP extension (January 2026; formerly MCP-UI, started May 2025 by the MCP-UI creator) letting tools return sandboxed-iframe widgets instead of just JSON, with bidirectional host communication: set-state (sync widget state into model context), send-follow-up-message, widget-initiated tool calls, streaming partial tool-args into a live-updating UI, dual UI-vs-model outputs, display modes (inline / fullscreen / picture-in-picture), OS theme sync. Rendered today by Claude (Desktop, Cowork), ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, VS Code
data.name: MCP Apps

data.brief: The spec moved while they built (SSE deprecated weeks in; OAuth in March 2025) and clients implemented subsets at different paces — Claude Desktop early, Claude Code incomplete, OpenAI and VS Code only after the spec update, VS Code GA in July and the eventual golden client; often only tools were supported. Server instructions were in the spec but unimplemented until Anthropic's blog post, so instructions were injected into every tool call; elicitation and sampling (now deprecated) were hacked via tools and prompts. The MCP Inspector is essential. "The spec is only two years old; we're still figuring it out"
data.name: MCP spec vs client drift

data.brief: Thousands of internal APIs were not agent-accessible; SaaS tools each had their own auth. An automated crawler projects internal APIs into MCPs with one config change; SaaS MCPs (Google, Slack, Jira) are hosted with token exchange — one entry point, one install path. Enough MCPs add up to "a massive token tax," so: direct MCP → Omni MCP (one MCP that discovers and invokes any other) → CLI projection (responses don't eat context) → an auto-installed code-mode skill that writes Python on the fly for the top token-consuming uses. 1,000+ tools; 40%+ fleet-wide savings
data.name: MCP gateway and the token tax

data.brief: MCP extension for asynchronous, long-running tools: tools/call returns a handle instead of a response, with a spec-defined lifecycle (working → input_required → working → completed / cancelled / failed) and a hard durability requirement — per the spec, once launched a task must survive client crashes, server crashes, dropped connections and humans-gone-on-vacation. V1 (November 2025, marked experimental) was a stateful protocol: task/list for server-side enumeration (no filter — a million-task scan at scale) and input_required tunneled through a held-open connection with server-driven elicitation. V2 (announced May, spec "coming out in July") rebuilds it as an extension on a stateless core: task/list removed, a client-initiated update endpoint replaces the elicitation session (effectively a *signal* into the running task), clients are told to persist task IDs ("should", though an unpersisted ID is unrecoverable), and the lifecycle model is unchanged. A notifications protocol (one "did anything change?" endpoint replacing per-task polling) is the sketched path to million-task scale
data.name: MCP Tasks (async MCP extension)

data.brief: Manufact's open-source SDK family (8M+ downloads, ~10K GitHub stars) abstracting over the official MCP SDKs to build servers, clients, and agents; for MCP apps: React widget files in a resources folder auto-register as UI resources returnable from tools (compiled to HTML/CSS), plus client-capability detection primitives; npx create-mcp-app template
data.name: mcp-use

data.brief: Three rungs of increasing human-likeness, climbed only as high as the page forces (lowest working rung wins). Rung 1 — don't act human at all: use an exposed in-page API or a synthetic JavaScript click ("easy, free, instant, the right default"). Rung 2 — a real click via CDP's input domain when synthetic clicks are silently dropped, because Chrome stamps every event trusted/untrusted and pages quietly discard untrusted input. Rung 3 — genuine human input and behavior: real mouse paths with dwell and jitter, deliberate overshoot-and-ease-back, and vision, for pages actively hunting bots. Then write down the path that worked as code and/or an agent skill
data.name: The meatbag ladder

data.brief: Where the taste lives: the agent's skills encode editing craft — cut rules (how to select best moments), font pairs, how to generate B-rolls — plus sub-processes for music generation, voiceover, sound, and photo animation. The composition is emitted as Remotion (video-as-React-code), chosen because "agents are really good at writing code," so video generation becomes code generation. Skills as the repository of domain taste, the same shape as coding-agent skills
data.name: Media editing as agent skills

data.brief: The reliability piece: "agents make mistakes, so we developed a verification layer to make sure the composition is clean, well-defined, and will render — and if there are problems the agent reiterates." Deterministic verification that the generated Remotion composition is valid before rendering, with a retry loop. Plus mass-consumer delivery choices: mobile-first, directional templates (speak-to-camera, add-B-rolls) so no prompt is needed, and a building editor for manual tweaks
data.name: Media verification layer

data.brief: "Clinical brain": reads patient notes + policy criteria, queries a per-patient biomarker graph, returns answers with supporting and contradictory facts plus a confidence score; escalates only low-confidence cases to a clinician (has a linked publication)
data.name: Medical necessity agent

data.brief: Turning every external signal — Slack threads, customer/onboarding/sales calls, internal meetings, Sentry, bug reports, emails, feature requests — into prioritized, evaluable work automatically. Flagship: a meeting bot invited to Meet/Zoom/Teams that listens all day, links to existing work instead of duplicating it, files tickets, and starts implementing: at the expo booth a spoken idea (agents should get explicit acceptance criteria before declaring done) became a ticket, a working form change and a screenshot with "none of us doing anything manually." The gap it closes is stated precisely: MCP hookups already let agents *read* email/Notion — "but how does it know what to work on?"
data.name: Ambient signal-to-code ingestion (meeting bot)

data.brief: The talk's organizing distinction between two machines the industry keeps conflating. A demo: one clean document in, one fluent answer out, whose entire job is to make a room say "oh" for five minutes. A memo: the real committee document written before real money moves — hundreds of pages, filings, transcripts, broker notes, someone's rushed notes from a call last Tuesday, half the sources disagreeing with each other — whose job is not to impress but to survive an argument. The claim: almost every AI finance product is built for the first and none for the second. And the closing twist — "there is no safe demo anymore": the moment real money is watching, every sentence becomes a memo sentence.
data.name: Memo versus demo

data.brief: Teams think of agent context "as just context," but context that can influence an action is state — it goes stale, conflicts with authoritative data, and corrupts future actions. Two memories: short-term (the chat thread, tied to one execution) and long-term (project files, system prompts, databases, the cache layer). Decide the source of truth when they conflict, and treat memory as a cache that carries provenance and is invalidated when the source of truth changes
data.name: Memory is state; treat it as a cache with provenance

data.brief: Store agent memory as outcome-tested reasoning about tasks ("if someone asks for a refund, check the settlement first so the customer isn't refunded twice") rather than static facts/preferences ("user prefers dark theme", "call the user by a shorter name"); context is updated per task instead of stuffed; positions memory as the agent's accumulated judgment, distinct from chat personalization
data.name: Memory as reasoning, not facts

data.brief: The economic frame that explains the design differences. A running profile has two costs: maintenance (how often you update it × how much compute per update) and serving (it sits in every context window, so length is a per-conversation tax). The ideal system — update after every conversation, spawn subagents for the update, store 400,000 tokens instead of 4,000 — is unavailable "because we live in a GPU-constrained world." The two vendors take exactly opposite trade-offs: ChatGPT 4,000 tokens updated every few days (high serving, low update), Claude 1,000 tokens updated every 24 hours (low serving, high update)
data.name: Memory as a function of compute

data.brief: The survey's central finding: after three years of independent evolution from opposite starting points — ChatGPT from stored facts toward retrieval, Claude from retrieval toward a stored profile — both now have a running profile that is visible and editable, plus tools to search past conversations. Gemini has a running profile too, but with detailed per-memory timing logs. The general architecture converged; the implementation details did not. Notably, neither uses the RAG-chunk-and-embed approach the industry assumed was the answer: "it wasn't too long ago that everyone, including me, assumed that RAG was the way to go about memory"
data.name: The memory convergence

data.brief: The first serious memory implementation (ChatGPT V1, February 2024): the user asks the model to remember something, it extracts a fact ("the user is vegetarian"), stores it in a visible list, and injects the list into every conversation. Two structural flaws named: the burden of memory management fell on the user, who had to curate memories while trying to have a conversation; and staleness — facts true when written ("Shlok is going to Bengaluru") persist indefinitely. Deprecated by ChatGPT in mid-2026 once the running profile and conversation-search tools superseded it
data.name: The user-editable fact list

data.brief: Languages (Rust, Go — anything not C/C++) whose guarantees make memory-safety vulnerabilities impossible to introduce; ~60-70% of vulns in memory-unsafe products preventable; a control that holds no matter how smart attack models get
data.name: Memory-safe languages

data.brief: The mental model the talk asks the audience to adopt: memory is "not just a database store — it's actually a control loop around the model," with distinct write, manage and read stages. Instantiated as a harness with three blocks: a core of traces always shown to the agent, a recall block where retrieval policy varies, and an archival block tracking information across sessions. Deliberately built over research agents with *zero durable memory* so that all memory behaviour comes from the harness and can be ablated
data.name: Memory as a write-manage-read loop

data.brief: Agents do not browse: a beautiful website is a token-burning HTML blob to them. A merchant becomes agent-ready with (1) a publicly reachable JSON manifest in /.well-known declaring the store's capabilities, supported payment methods and API endpoints; (2) a structured catalog in JSON with only the necessary data — including policies such as shipping and returns, since agents filter, rank and justify recommendations and will hallucinate or refuse when the fact is missing; (3) logs of which structured attributes matched, because in agent commerce the catalog "doesn't just power decisions, it becomes evidence of how those decisions were made." Humans keep the website; the agent sees the manifest and catalog
data.name: The merchant capabilities manifest and agent-ready catalog

data.brief: Speaker's coinage for a self-watching harness of agents around a production agent: a log-monitoring agent (short-window cadence, codebase access, auto-PRs / Slack alerts), a separate fresh-context review agent that adversarially scores and criticizes those PRs, a session analyzer scoring every real conversation for system health, and a computer-use agent simulating the customer in the browser — all wired with human-grade access (trajectories, metrics, database, UI, code) so diagnoses are grounded in the real problem rather than guessed
data.name: Meta harness

data.brief: Meta's internal autonomous agents. Source of first major enterprise agentic breach (Mar 2026).
data.description: Meta's internal autonomous AI agents. Source of first major enterprise agentic breach — agent exposed sensitive data to unauthorized engineers (Mar 2026).
data.name: Meta Internal AI Agents

data.brief: The Hub's foundational split: the database stores everything about the models (users, repositories, model and dataset records, bucket/space information, configuration, billing, access control) and never the models themselves; weights, tokenizer files, model-card assets and config files live in cloud object storage (AWS S3). Consequence: metadata, binary storage and compute scale — and get optimized — independently of each other.
data.name: Metadata / artifact separation

data.brief: Benchmark methodology that expresses model capability as the length of human work it can complete: a threshold pair of success rate and human hours (e.g. "16-hour threshold at 50%" = solves, half the time, tasks that take a human 16 hours), backed by a rigorous protocol for timing the humans. The de-facto industry yardstick for "long horizon" and the reference the talk measures published benchmarks against.
data.name: METR time horizon

data.brief: Young (~3-4 months) YC-funded open-source agent-sandboxing project with batteries included (network access controls etc.); Johner's pick if rebuilding Patch Pilot today
data.name: microsandbox

data.brief: Microsoft's agent platform: hosting, observability, management, a model catalog of thousands of models (now incl. Claude GA), knowledge bases, and the agent optimizer; the demoed hub for grounding and tuning agents (ai.azure.com)
data.name: Microsoft Foundry
