Applied historically: SFT gets parallelism and per-token reward but is off-policy on a curated distribution; DPO/RLHF gains online task distributions but reverts to sequence-level reward and pairwise infrastructure; GRPO is "a Faustian bargain" — maximal on-policy power at the cost of off-policy task distributions, exploded parallelism demanding one-to-one environment replicas, and whole-sequence reward
data.name: The four criteria for post-training

data.brief: Feng's ladder, framed on the human-learning analogy that you master simple tasks first and compound into harder ones. L1 single-turn Q&A: orchestrator holds a task bank of prompt/answer pairs, sends to the model, sends the answer to a grader, feeds graded chats to a training engine, syncs weights to inference engines, repeats — nothing lives outside the training stack, chats are in one controlled format. L2 synthetic environments: environment state moves out (tool specs, initial file system, sandbox), the orchestrator runs many turns, a full task trace goes to the grader — still replayable.
data.description: L3 bring your own harness: almost everything is outside; only the completion endpoint and a request/response recorder remain. L4 agentic citizens: deploy once, adapt to out-of-distribution tasks, learn from interactions. The organizing rule is that each rung buys realism and pays for it in training signal.
data.name: Post-training levels (Q&A to synthetic env to BYO harness to agentic citizen)

data.brief: Guardrail and authorization checks before and after every tool call — the governance layer for sensitive data piped to models. The identity question has changed: an agent acts *on behalf of* a user ("book me a flight whenever it's under $200 — is it me buying, or agent-me?") or under a service account; the line blurs and fine-grained policy decisions are needed at the tool boundary
data.name: Pre/post-tool guardrails and authorization

data.brief: Agents reinforce bad decisions at scale. FDE productization loop's dark twin.
data.description: Agents learn from bad decisions and reinforce them at scale. One flawed template propagates to 100+ clients via FDE productization loop. The moat mechanism is also the risk vector.
data.name: Precedent Poisoning

data.brief: Pay the tokenization cost on write, never on query: a model name (meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B) is split into small tokens at insert time and stored as an array on the document, in a denormalized read-only copy of the main repo collection built purely for reads and listings. Query-side becomes an autocomplete lookup over the token array, sorted by a trending score recomputed every 5 minutes from the last ~7 days of downloads and likes.
data.name: Insert-time search tokenization

data.brief: The mechanism underneath the divide. An RLHF reward model has a GAN-like asymmetry: it is very easy to detect and punish a model that signals uncertainty, so the optimization pressure pushes models to drop modes and answer confidently. Consequences stated as design properties rather than bugs: overpromising is a feature, every RLHF model carries a structural gap between human preference and actual results even when the results are good, and hallucination is intrinsic to optimizing for human preference rather than a pre-training defect.
data.description: Illustrated with a ChatGPT response to an audio file of fart noises — "a very eerie vibe atmosphere piece". The end game of any RLHF model is engagement; automation needs the opposite — a model that "doesn't give a damn about the human and just does the task correctly in a calibrated way".
data.name: Preference reward-model asymmetry

data.brief: Attaching a modelled preference profile to the person a preference datum came from, so pluralism survives aggregation. Premise: "the world is multi-preference" — two people preferring different styles are not evidence that one is wrong, and the best answer is not the average of what they like. Without rater identity, context and reasons, preference collection produces datasets whose internal contradictions read as noise; with it, the same contradictions become a matching problem the model can learn.
data.name: Preference vector (multi-preference data)

data.brief: Inference-platform optimization: when the leading portion of the context is identical across requests it is cached, giving up to ~90% cheaper/faster turns; architectural consequence — keep the first ~90% of the context window stable request-to-request, vary only the tail, and minimize output tokens
data.name: Prefix caching

data.brief: Quantified movement in published data recipes. GPT-3: Common Crawl + WebText-2 + books + Wikipedia, with web text alone (including Wikipedia) ~85% of the mix and no dedicated code dataset at all. Llama 3: web text still a majority, ~50% of tokens as general knowledge. MAI Thinking 1: web text down to ~15%, displaced by code and STEM — and code is now "the dominating data subset" in pre-training recipes. The speaker's read: web text is still important but has taken a backseat, because downstream RL performance depends on code and STEM abilities rather than on breadth of general knowledge.
data.name: The pre-training mix shift (web text to code, STEM, synthetic)

data.brief: The company's environment-anchored training platform: hosted training, evaluation and inference organized around environments, with experiment monitoring, run management, eval iteration and model deployment, starting from open-source base models. Product name taken from captions ("a training platform called Lab").
data.name: Prime Intellect Lab

data.brief: Prime Intellect's async-from-the-ground-up open-source RL training framework on a TorchTitan base: orchestrator decouples inference and trainer as separate servers; FP8, wide expert parallelism, disaggregated prefill, pluggable loss/algorithm registry; also runs as a hosted platform (multi-tenant LoRA today, full fine-tuning rolling out)
data.name: Prime RL

data.brief: Altos flow-matching single-cell model (on arXiv) that matches ground-truth distributions where autoregressive/autoencoder baselines predict the mean; evaluated via MMD
data.name: PrimeFlow

data.brief: The system that lets one cluster run both training and production: researchers "don't think about GPUs" — they submit to a gang-scheduling queue (Kueue) with workload priority over normal Kubernetes priority. Training pods always outrank inference, so a submitted training job evicts inference, which is then flipped to another cluster or external GPU rental via a virtual-kubelet fake node that routes evicted pods to a provider. A taint system adds/removes taints as in-cluster GPUs free up, and a descheduler (not no-execute, to avoid taking production down all at once) slowly migrates pods back — a self-healing system where you "mark the pod failed and let Kubernetes handle it"
data.name: Priority scheduling + GPU spot-arbitrage

data.brief: Guiding principles for robust, trustworthy environments so replay can't win: multiffactorial variation (vary data, appearance, initial state — stochasticity), with a system that verifies every generated combination is valid; sandboxed; verifier-supported (privileged information); and realistic (faithful reproduction so the score means something). No existing benchmark satisfies all of them — "some do some things well, others do other things well, but there's no unified benchmark that matches all these boxes"
data.name: PRISM principles for environment design

data.brief: Pre-registered instrument for measuring anachronistic compositing: figure × documented life-moments × seeding conditions matrix (bare model / primary sources / modern biography), expert-written diagnostic questions on documented fault lines, and a three-axis weighted rubric — anachronism detection 40%, documentary consistency 35%, contextual plausibility 25% — with rhetorical authenticity deliberately excluded as a criterion; predictions locked and timestamped before data collection; expert holds sealed a-priori vignettes. Pilot design: 4 Lincolns (1847/1858/1860/1862–65) × 3 conditions × 5 questions = 60 scored responses
data.name: Prism protocol (pre-registered persona-fidelity instrument)

data.brief: The thesis element: every company needs its own benchmark, mimicking its real tools, API services, policies, and workflows, and continuously repopulated from its production traces rather than frozen. Public benchmarks are domain-narrow (SWE-bench = fixing GitHub issues, Terminal-Bench = terminal agents, a computer-use bench = GUI agents) and report pass rate, which measures the model frontier but not a production deployment — "public benchmark is useful to orient and build your prior, but your private benchmark is useful to ship". Serves three jobs at once: pre-release validation, release gate/regression suite, and training set for optimization.
data.name: Private (company-domain) benchmark

data.brief: The problem stated formally enough to compare methods: given a pre-trained θ and an unstructured private corpus D (every email you have written, every meeting transcript your company has ever had), produce θ\* that *knows* D — where "know" is explicitly flagged as the load-bearing, under-defined term that gives the field its leeway. Requirements are behavioural, not loss-based: answer questions about D, generate new artifacts like those in D, generalize beyond exact matches
data.name: The θ→θ\* problem

data.brief: Distributed systems have always had services coordinating multi-step workflows, but deterministically — a decision tree mapped out in advance. An agent is a probabilistic coordinator: the range of actions it may take varies widely and can have severe consequences unless confined by deterministic controls. Text-in/text-out LLMs could only produce a wrong output; agents that call external services, tools and state have moved the architectural boundary beyond the model and can cause side effects in the world — so recognize which external systems, states, credentials and actions are in scope
data.name: The agent as a probabilistic coordinator

data.brief: The trajectory rather than the artifact: the reasoning trace and the sequence of decisions that carry a professional from a blank page to a finished work output. Contrasted with state-based data — the rows in an ERP, the final output, the saved file — which is what most buyers picture, is the 2023 next-token-prediction era's substrate, and is mostly personal data wrapped in privacy law. The claim is that process data is what is actually newly available and what encodes how the work gets done.
data.name: Process-based data

data.brief: The single source of truth for how a company actually functions, used as the substrate the FD agent reasons over. Claim about shape: enterprise workflows are "remarkably linear, they just have a lot of cycles in them", and process owners want them dependency-driven (person C should not act before A and B have approved) — so a dependency graph fits better than a document store, and the storage choice is deliberately un-opinionated ("five companies downstairs will sell you a graph DB; you can just use Postgres — it doesn't really matter"). What it must capture beyond the documented golden path: the exception routes ("Sarah in AP handles it this way, but when it breaks she sends it to Chris, who takes four days to reconcile a PO against an invoice"), which are unique per company and are the stated reason agents can't yet run end-to-end. Hard part is traversal, not storage.
data.name: Process dependency graph

data.brief: Rewarding each line/step of a reasoning trace separately instead of splattering one outcome reward across the whole trajectory; fixes RL crediting wrong reasoning (trace says 2+2=10 yet earns +10), but doesn't scale by hand — labs substitute LLM-as-judge, which reimports the self-verification problem
data.name: Process supervision

data.brief: Translating production observability into the level coding agents actually reason at: function/file-level context (invocations, callers, timings, outbound calls) connected back to the endpoint/consumer/cron that triggered it, plus forensic evidence captured only for anomalous requests (beyond P99) — instead of service/endpoint-level metrics that "don't speak the agent's language"
data.name: Prod-to-code runtime context

data.brief: The talk's task decomposition: a task = execution (knowing what to do, tool access, loading the dashboard) + production context (the judgment that "that metric smells off… this feels wrong and I don't know if I can even explain why"). Execution is necessary but commodity; production context is what makes a background agent's work worth anything — it decides what is important, not just what is checkable
data.name: Production context vs execution

data.brief: The stated hard part and moat: not model smarts ("models have gotten incredibly capable… especially over the last 6 months") but *truly understanding your environment* — how services interact, where the hotspots are, the current causal chains — captured in an underlying learning/memory system that must grow as the system evolves, because the system now evolves faster than ever. Reflection after each task feeds it; knowledge learned in one task applies to others; "we spend so much time on our knowledge system" is the company's differentiation claim. ⚠ pattern-relevant to the uncoined pat-agent-memory-layer — no pattern edge, Review note 2
data.name: Production learning system

data.brief: Braintrust Topics: cluster analysis over all production data to surface new categories of failure — situations with no guardrail and no eval — so teams expand their eval sets to cover them as they make systemic architectural changes. Turns the flywheel from "more examples of known failures" into "discovery of unknown ones"
data.name: Production topic clustering for unknown failures

data.brief: The talk's founding assumption: every profiler speaks the same language. Whatever the service's language or runtime (Java, Python, Go), a profiler run against a single production instance emits the same well-structured artifact — the call stack plus self CPU and inclusive CPU per method, sampled at high frequency — which is "very well-structured for an LLM agent to use" even though it is poor for humans (raw JSON of call stacks, needing a flame-graph visualizer and a real learning curve). The second half of the assumption is the model side: common inefficiency patterns (O(N^2) loops, loop invariants, repeated object allocation in hot paths, contention fixable by batching) are already in a good coding model's training data, so the agent can identify a bad pattern purely from the call stack, before looking at the code base.
data.name: Profiling output as agent-readable context

data.brief: Three-level loading of packaged capability: front matter (<~100 tokens, always in context, acts like a DB index) → markdown body (loaded on activation, <~5K tokens) → scripts/resources (executed or read on demand, only outputs return to context). The mechanism that makes skills ~10× cheaper in context than equivalent MCP tool definitions; also usable *in front of* an MCP server
data.name: Progressive disclosure

data.brief: The concrete technique behind smart prompt injection, expanded in Q&A. Keep CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md as a thin index that points to the right files, not one big overloaded document, because that is what loads on the agent's first prompt. Cap SKILL.md files at ~100 lines on the reasoning that "your skill is really a folder." Put runbook-style documentation in the code comments, so an agent that greps its way into a file finds the pointer to everything relevant. The measurable test: watch what the first prompt costs — "I think like 20, 25K tokens get taken anyway, but if you're coming to 40K, 50K, something's wrong. That's not really progressive disclosure"
data.name: Progressive disclosure at codebase scale

data.brief: Palantir's rotation and training program, built by the speaker, that converted software engineers into forward deployed engineers — ~350 engineers went through it, and its alumni now staff FDE functions at OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI. Curriculum condensed to a cheat sheet: redefine the problem rather than take requirements, get badged on site, ship the fix before leaving to win goodwill, own the fix end to end inside the product ecosystem, convert fixes into product leverage, and be the person who gets the call when it breaks. Rebuilt afterwards at Citadel and now at Kepler; contrasted with the common failure mode of running the function as product-management plus customer-success process (requirements intake, scheduled user research, insight decks) with no mechanism for steering the product.
data.name: Project Frontline

data.brief: Anthropic's defender-first release of Mythos for securing critical software.
data.description: Anthropic's defender-first release of Mythos Preview. Partnered with Linux Foundation to secure critical OSS before similar capabilities become broadly available.
data.name: Project Glasswing

data.brief: Provider-side caching of repeated prompt segments (system prompt, tool definitions, messages): the first call sends the full prompt, subsequent calls send a much-reduced cached reference — a one-flag cost lever (e.g., cache_prompt="default" in Strands Agents) that works across model providers
data.name: Prompt caching

data.brief: The open-source evaluation tool used for the per-site model matrix: run prompts against multiple models and providers (local models and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), compare accuracy and latency continuously; complemented by a manual in-site model/temperature/token switcher for customer demos
data.name: Promptfoo

data.brief: Air-gap the agentic loop from the agent: instead of executing IO side effects while computing an answer, the model emits a reified program (a free-monad expression representing the plan) plus a machine-checkable proof of its safety; standard compiler machinery (type checking, data-flow and taint analysis, inductive interpreters) verifies the plan before a trusted executor runs it. A revival of 1990s proof-carrying code (Necula) aimed at agents; a reference implementation by academics (incl. Harvard collaborators) is on GitHub
data.name: Proof-carrying agent plans

data.brief: Tests generated from the requirements + design documents and run dozens-to-hundreds of times with randomized values (fast-check in the TypeScript demo) to verify that agent-implemented tasks actually satisfy the spec — machine verification wired to the spec artifacts rather than to hand-written cases
data.name: Property-based testing (against spec docs)

data.brief: "I've been humbled a lot; my code has annoyed engineers and caused sevs." Test everything yourself before the PR (the morning block); small readable PRs — leaders model what good looks like, and three 5,000-line PRs teach the team to do the same; never put reviewers on code you haven't read; rely on the scaffolding — AI reviewers, agents.md hygiene, trustworthy CI, feature flags, a prototype branch to employees — so you don't take prod down
data.name: Prototyping hygiene for leaders

data.brief: Python runtime type-validation library; adds typing to an untyped language so agent tool parameters conform to declared types before execution — the "at the door" half of the talk's validation stack.
data.name: Pydantic

data.brief: DSPy 4 research direction: instead of hand-building evals (lossy "good/bad" labels, proxy hills), models interpret whatever textual feedback the environment produces — production traces, user actions, product analytics, questions back to the developer — and convert it into evals and a hill that is iteratively refined; "use reality to inform our evals automatically"
data.name: Qualitative learning

data.brief: Non-deterministic systems earn trust in the first five questions and lose it overnight, at ten times the cost to win back. So before touching the agent, write the questions the sellers will ask from the sales process (150 of them) and measure (50%); then ship fewer answers at higher accuracy — 50 questions at 95% beats 100 at 70% — because a good first impression turns "this doesn't work" into "can I get more of that." "Quality is P-minus-one"; 60% of the data came after launch, added where demand concentrated
data.name: Quality over coverage

data.brief: Training-side compression: below ~20B parameters PTQ stops sufficing and accuracy must be recovered by quantization-aware distillation. Pain point stated: QAD needs the *original* training data, and modern models are multi-stage RL-trained with multiple teacher distillation (per-domain expert teachers), so assembling correct QAD data is hard — "if we do QAD with wrong data it most commonly breaks the model." Labs increasingly ship QAT variants themselves (Gemma QAT, Q8/MXFP4-style release formats)
data.name: Quantization-aware training / distillation (QAT/QAD)

data.brief: As trajectories lengthen, stuffing the whole trace into a judge's context window stops working. Instead process the trajectory into something searchable: store it (e.g. in a database), enrich it with sub-agents, segment it into phases (log triage, code edit, post-change verification), and tag candidate failure points, so the judge-agent can navigate to the critical steps and adjudicate them.
data.name: Queryable trajectory

data.brief: Huntley's while-true orchestration pattern for coding agents: `cat` a hand-engineered prompt into a fresh agent each iteration, use the file system as state, recycle the context window every pass so work stays in the "smart zone"; deliberately reduced to a bash loop as the simplest teaching primitive; since absorbed by Anthropic into platform-level loop/batch/goal commands
data.name: Ralph loop

data.brief: The operational kit that makes human rating usable: rubrics with explicit pass/fail criteria and worked examples so raters don't return "I'm not sure" or a pile of unknowns; rater templates; explicit training of scale raters and cross-functional teams on what is expected; multi-dimensional ratings when an output has independent quality axes (accuracy vs brand safety vs expectation match) rather than one verdict; and a required written explanation with every rating, single-side or side-by-side, because pass/fail alone says nothing about where the agent should improve — and the explanations themselves become training input.
data.name: Rater rubrics and templates

data.brief: Popular distributed-compute framework for ML workloads; authentication was off by default, which produced the 2023 open-cluster exposure
data.name: Ray

data.brief: Fork a live real-world deployment's full state into simulation: up to the fork the agent history is real, after it everything is sim — dramatically reducing simulation awareness (first turns indistinguishable). Enables reproducible science on N=1 deployments: replay incidents across models (the Nazi-song replay), red-team safely (rm -rf demands), run counterfactuals via a Slack-connected interface
data.name: Real-to-sim forking (digital clones)

data.brief: The most valuable tasks are not on the internet (closing the books with missing receipts, scoping a blueprint, coordinating a roof repair) — they live in heads and 20-year-old software. Agents collaborate with employees on real work → rich traces (tool calls, hiccups, papercuts) → real-world evals with ground truth (did the roof get repaired?) → hill-climbing; every week's benchmark becomes a regression test. Explicit and implicit feedback (the diff between AI output and what was submitted); internal post-training on out-of-distribution business data; customization per company, per user, per client. "The exceptions are the job"
data.name: Real-work traces as evals and training data

data.brief: The core claim: generated video today "is still a recording — a slot machine you can't change," but real-time makes video programmable (addressable, conditionable, changeable like software). The historical argument: real-time has always been the unlock — GPS made maps real-time and enabled Uber; digital viewfinders let you see what you're shooting and enabled Instagram/TikTok. "Instant feedback is the ultimate level of control." Defines world models *as* real-time interactive video, against the Gaussian-splatting or batch-video readings
data.name: Real-time interactive video as a medium

data.brief: The infra the applications need: GPUs worldwide, connection routing, WebRTC/ICE/TURN, and for the interesting use cases multiple models wired into continuous streaming workflows synchronized frame-by-frame with user controls. uRun's answer: a drop-in React component plus a programmable Python runtime to build avatar / video-to-video / magic-mirror pipelines generating asynchronously. "The models are here; the frontier is really in how we serve them"
data.name: Real-time media harness

data.brief: An honest limitation: evaluating real-time interactive video for consistency/fidelity is an open research problem — "the entire research community, including DeepMind, hasn't solved this." Fidelity is easy (pixels); consistency and world-coherence evaluation is "literally just look at it and human judgment" today. A frontier-labs-included admission that the field lacks measurement for its core capability
data.name: Real-time video evals are unsolved

data.brief: The call to action: treat the recall function as something you design, measure and report — "what type of memories do you want to store, how do you rank them, how do you design your recall function, and what survives across multiple sessions and runs?" Backed by the cost heuristic the experiments produced: bad memory is expensive, because it burns tokens *and* sends the agent the wrong way, while a good structural recall policy saves both budget and error
data.name: Recall policy as a first-class metric

data.brief: The experimental design, and the file's most reusable artifact: hold the model fixed and vary only the recall policy across four rungs — (1) no recall baseline, (2) vector RAG, pulling on similarity alone, (3) a decisions ledger recording what was decided each turn, so entries can be ranked and prioritized, and (4) an oracle that is handed the ground-truth memory for each loop. The oracle is the ceiling estimate, and the finding that it does *not* reach maximum performance is itself a result
data.name: The recall-policy ladder

data.brief: The third harness concern for multi-user agents, and explicitly not model routing to save tokens: routing the finished information to the right person, channel and moment — DM rather than the group when the answer is sensitive, glasses rather than the car audio when passengers are present, silence when nobody asked. Includes the observed failure mode (group-deployed agents are "over-articulative when they are not asked questions") and the proposed fix: a small learned classifier for role and speaking permission.
data.name: Recipient routing

data.brief: Once every app, connection and login runs through one center with scoped access, a layer above it logs every action an agent takes across every app — what it touched, skipped, what worked and did not. Two effects: the agent gets memory (look back at how similar tasks were done and replicate success instead of starting blank) and the human gets trust (see exactly what it did rather than believing "done," offload more as the record proves reliable). Logged at volume, the record reveals patterns and distills into skills at three levels — how a tool works in general, how this company does things, how this person prefers — a queryable picture of how the organization operates
data.name: The record of work

data.brief: Applying RLM principles to coding agents: the harness can invoke itself/sub-agents to a settable depth, with the model choosing the decomposition. Rubric for "is it an RLM": executable environment; prompt externalized as a variable (file/files); code is the thing calling the model; the model picks the decomposition into sub-calls; state stays symbolic. Hard-coded map-reduces (e.g., lambda-RLM) fail the rubric — decomposition isn't model-chosen
data.name: Recursive coding agents

data.brief: Context-management pattern from an MIT paper: externalize context into a programmable execution environment — the repo (or corpus) is treated as data, the model writes REPL code to inspect/slice/compute relevant chunks feeding the main context window, and recursion happens via LLM sub-queries (delegating sub-questions to another model) until the loop terminates with a synthesized answer; a pattern to implement, not a product
data.name: Recursive Language Models (RLM)

data.brief: Each released model is distilled into derivative models (judges, reward models, eval graders, data generators) that speed up every part of the next training run's inner and outer loops; raising the smartest model in the system raises the intelligence floor of the whole flywheel, compounding across simultaneous training runs
data.name: Recursive model improvement (RSI loop)

data.brief: Socher's line between two things that get conflated. Auto research = a system that improves some other AI or process (e.g. optimizing a 5-minute NanoChat run) — valuable, an important milestone, but "a weak form". True RSI = an AI with a sense of self-awareness of its own shortcomings, full access over its entire arsenal — pre-training, RL training, harnesses, everything — that then updates that whole system into the next version of itself. Newly feasible for one reason: AI is code and AI can now code over long horizons, an ability that "has really only happened in the last 6 to 8 months".
data.name: Recursive self-improvement (strict definition)

data.brief: The proposed missing ingredient, drawn by analogy to AlphaGo: the reason RL self-play scales is that "AlphaGo makes its own training questions harder by getting better through training." Applied to private corpora, the goal is a technique where the model generates data, improves, and then generates *better* data recursively — converting the flat post-saturation curve into one where compute continues to buy depth. Presented as the company's active research direction and as an honest open problem: their early curves plateaued exactly like everyone else's before "more sophisticated things that make the training gradually harder"
data.name: Training that makes itself harder

data.brief: "A tool built for the decision layer" — doc-centric planning surface that works with existing implementation tools; the productization of the talk's docs-not-chat / stateless-agents model
data.name: Ref (decision-layer tool)

data.brief: The decision the talk audits: treat tech debt like financial debt (it compounds "in mysterious and sometimes unexpected ways" and can outrun the ROI it bought), against the fact that refactoring later gets exponentially easier as models, tools and infrastructure (sandboxes, monitoring frameworks) improve. The counterweight: AI-native development at velocity *recreates legacy conditions* — lots of code, low performance/quality, "people don't actually understand what's happening there" — so waiting without guardrails compounds the debt you'd be deferring. Decide on business value (throughput, cost, feature latency), and partial isolation of codebase layers is a legitimate alternative to a full refactor
data.name: Refactor-now-vs-wait calculus

data.brief: The most concrete budget: a ceiling that refills per caller per time window; spend it freely, no approvals, and past the line the request bounces with a count. Every write is rate-limited, only the size varies (own namespace higher than shared). After the incident an admission webhook caps deletes per hour per resource kind per namespace; the bypass flag exists for on-call, but inside an agent session it refuses and tells the agent to ask the human — the agent gets the limit, the human keeps the override, nobody files a ticket
data.name: Refilling rate limits on every write

data.brief: "The agent loop is not the system. The refining loop around the agent is the system, and it's the most complex part." Three parts: SOP memory, execution runtime, and feedback capture from experts. Quality "comes from replaying real examples with writes disabled, not from vibes or a bigger model." Accuracy "wasn't designed in one diagram up front — it was earned one small correction at a time"
data.name: The refining loop around the agent

data.brief: Identity, authority and boundaries within and between agent organizations are established with plain JWTs carrying claims, scopes and time-to-live, chained up to the organization registered with a public authority — DNS-like resolution where the registrar is a Secretary of State rather than a company consortium ("resolve it to Kaiser Permanente or Disney, not a fentanyl dealer") — and a blockchain audit trail from organization down to the individual action. Anyone can publish a token on a website or Slack; convergence is expected the way SMTP and HTTP converged
data.name: Registry-anchored identity chains

data.brief: RELAI's learning loop as a product: lifts logs/feedback/instructions into replayable learning environments, does root-cause analysis and routes fixes to the right layer (memory/harness/model), runs regression-aware optimization, and outputs a reviewable version-update pull request; added to an existing agent (any major framework, own LLM) with a one-time learning-harness setup plus two commands
data.name: RELAI VCL engine

data.brief: The second technique, with a published write-up on the company's site: use an LLM judge to select which tokens to learn from in the teacher's output, because "the teacher model has preferences of certain connector words that are not really relevant to what we're trying to teach the student." Reported to improve learning of very out-of-distribution behaviour while reducing catastrophic degradation — i.e. it attacks the plasticity and stability sides simultaneously
data.name: Relevance-masked self-distillation

data.brief: Open-source progressive web app (iOS/Android) that attaches to your existing tmux sessions over a private tunnel (Tailscale by default; Cloudflare Tunnel/ngrok possible): agent-agnostic mobile monitoring and steering of Claude Code, Codex, Pi, etc. — pane zoom, touch gestures, plan-mode toggles, and an install skill that turns your tmux config into touch keybindings
data.name: Remobi

data.brief: React-based programmatic video framework; the speaker's vehicle for code-generated product tours, video overlays, and motion graphics — cited as a framework class that couldn't proliferate until AI made code cheap
data.name: Remotion

data.brief: The talk's central economic argument, from a 100-company × 25-field enrichment test (Opus 4.8 loop, budget-guarded). Coverage: AI-search, one major CaaS, and DIY-scraping-plus-Google all converge well; the two pure CaaS providers underperformed counterintuitively because "they know what they have about an entity — ask beyond it and the data is never there," while a searcher can keep exploring. Cost: search solutions need heavy token burn to *structure* results, CaaS charges its service fee; per-record costs spread widely. The killer is frequency — "every repeated query costs the same as the first even if nothing changed" — so renting makes teams cut corners (query weekly not daily, take 10 results not all). Owned context (build the scrapers, merge into entities, store) is upfront cost then near-free retrieval — "owned context compounds while rented decays" — with a computed tipping point (~15,000 entities/queries in the test, use-case-dependent) above which building beats renting
data.name: Rented vs owned context

data.brief: The cheapest and most common synthetic form: regenerate existing seed documents in new phrasings to break repetition. Deployed by poolside against the token-uniqueness problem — a generic scalable multi-model pipeline plus two specialized ones (math to code and text; STEM documents). Because the pipeline is cheap and seed-heavy, quality rides almost entirely on the seed, which is why the STEM variant got extra work. Ablation-supported: replacing repeated tokens with rephrased variants consistently beat seeds-with-repetition. Lineage acknowledged to BeyondWeb-style work.
data.name: Rephrasing (token-uniqueness synthetic data)

data.brief: The exploit that motivates the whole talk: run a good frontier model on a benchmark, record one successful trajectory (taps, types, scrolls) per task, and compile them into a blind script <1MB that replays the recorded action sequence when a task arrives. On deterministic benchmarks (OSWorld, MobileWorld) this replay agent's success rate equals or beats the frontier model it was extracted from — "we shouldn't accept blind scripts beating frontier models." The tell is that most existing benchmarks are static and deterministic, hence gameable by memorized sequences
data.name: The replay agent

data.brief: Simulation + evaluation environment inferred from a single production log + feedback: synthetic users/personas and intents, mock-or-real tools, and inferred evaluators that define success — "inferring a distribution from one observation" so a one-off failure becomes a rerunnable, gradeable test of the pattern, not the instance
data.name: Replayable learning environment

data.brief: Workload placement across a 7-node MongoDB replica set as an explicit engineering discipline rather than a driver default: all writes and only strong-consistency reads on the primary; everything tolerating slight staleness on secondaries; heavy aggregation pipelines (large scans, sorts, groups, transforms) and change streams (cache invalidation, sync to Redshift, event-driven workloads) off the primary; and one hidden analytics node — invisible to the driver, still replicating from the primary, connected to directly for reporting and ad-hoc/experimental queries so they never touch production traffic. Stated rule: "primary should focus on what only primary can do".
data.name: Replica-set read routing

data.brief: Higharc's required handoff artifact for every ML research prototype — a technical design document with ML twists: domain context and novel data representations (what a new hire from outside the field must learn), business goal, type contract between the core product repo and the ML repo, persistence-layer mapping (researchers map it, engineers build it), system anatomy (workflow? chained workflows? external LLM calls?), and a merge/decomposition plan
data.name: Research Prototype Taxonomy (RPT) document

data.brief: Using IRT residuals (observed − expected correctness per item) as a signature: (a) anchor set + per-organization secret "fingerprint sets" of very hard items expose orgs that later train on a leaked benchmark; (b) residual-correlation "DNA" clusters models by lineage — same lab, same base, distillations, effort variants — enabling detection of unconsented distillation
data.name: Residual fingerprinting of models and benchmarks

data.brief: The more principled anti-leakage method. Run a partial hint (e.g. half of it) to get a slightly-smarter teacher alongside the full-hint teacher, then train against a linear combination of the two. The combination measures how strong and how out-of-distribution the hint is, keeping the student from being shifted into territory with no overlap with its own distribution — the failure the talk illustrates as "entirely shifting distributions with almost no overlap between your model and the original solution"
data.name: Residual guidance

data.brief: The productized stack: on-call agent (alert triage + root-cause investigation), incident coordination agents, and background agents over the shared learning system; visibility UI (task inspection, previous runs, per-task work traces) but the first-party surface is Slack/MS Teams, "where you live"; conversational setup (the agent explores your environment, asks clarifying questions, drafts the recurring task, you test then share); behavior tuned by replying in-thread ("this is too verbose — make it shorter" persists into the task definition); exposed via MCP servers so internal harnesses can graft in Resolve's execution and learned production context; bring-your-own skills supported ("don't go duplicate a bunch of stuff")
data.name: Resolve AI platform

data.brief: Durable-execution platform whose protocol was shrunk over ~3 years to two core objects — a durable promise and a durable task ("what can we take away?" as method); reference server plus polyglot SDKs; now recast so the spec is the product and target-native servers are derived from it
data.name: Resonate

data.brief: OpenAI's agentic replacement for chat completions, "released last year as a rethinking of the chat completions API in a more agentic world" — restructured message shape plus built-in agent capabilities (web search, image gen, tool search, server-side compaction, WebSocket transport). Deliberately not proprietary: OpenAI worked with Ollama, LM Studio, NVIDIA and others to codify an open Responses schema with a governance body, so any Responses-compatible provider can be plugged into the Codex harness. The talk's central claim rests on it — the standout Codex features "are actually features that are exposed in the Responses API… you can use those directly regardless of what harness you're using"
data.name: Responses API

data.brief: As outbound, demos, security and paperwork automate, buyers crave in-person time: conferences, booths and dinners work and are cheap, and humans still sell value — what the product does for the champion, which AI does not yet do well. Hire sellers only when buyers say "I need to talk to someone," resist moving up-market early (one large customer consumes legal, security, product and engineering), hire AI-native sellers who authentically use the product, and pay the first two or three builder-type hires on equity before "coin-operated" enterprise sellers require variable comp. Forward-deployed engineers are scarce (~55,000 requisitions for ~5,000 people) and would ideally be unnecessary, but make the product sticky
data.name: The revenge of the steak dinner

data.brief: The forward task is unstructured data + policy → reasoning trace → label. Synthesis runs it backwards: sample a label, derive a reasoning trace consistent with it, then generate data conditioned on that trace. Because the conditioning is sampled rather than prompted, the generated records are diverse where one-shot LLM generation mode-collapses, and the label is known before the data exists — a round-trip check confirms the generated record still produces it, so ground truth comes free
data.name: Reverse the inference workflow to synthesize data

data.brief: AI made PR creation abundant, so pressure moved to review and to CI/merge. Anti-pattern: engineers stop splitting PRs to dodge a one-hour CI run — bigger PRs, thinner human attention, riskier reviews. Responses: AI review as the first line of defense (style, missing coverage) so authors clear it before a human reviewer, who then applies deep judgment on architecture, security design and quality and keeps final accountability; DX/platform investment to remove flaky tests and speed CI; humans or agents "babysitting" PRs through reruns waste time and tokens and hurt morale. Metrics: wall-clock from PR-ready to merged versus CI duration (two to three hours against a one-hour run is a red flag), and PR retry counts
data.name: Review and CI are the new bottlenecks

data.brief: The problem stated in numbers: line-by-line review "has already stopped" (30%+ of changes merge with no review at all); code churn and incident-to-PR ratio rising; median review time up ~4x — "coding is solved, now reviewing is the bottleneck where everything gets stuck." ⚠ figures caption-sourced ("861% code churn"), see review note 3
data.name: The review bottleneck

data.brief: Hundreds of teams each with their own review conventions cannot be centrally managed, so uReview piggybacks on Uber's code-ownership model: customizations (rules, AI linters, custom agents, skills) are co-located next to the code so teams can keep updating them; smart deterministic routing decides which team gets which review kind, model and generators; and the observability — trajectories, address rate, sentiment — is surfaced back to rule authors ("I wrote this rule but my developers don't like it — let me update it") and to platform contributors. Writing a skill was easy (ask Claude to read your past PR reviews and write one); running those skills at scale with consistent quality and low cost took many iterations from the platform team and every contributing team
data.name: Review customization through the ownership model

data.brief: The reframe the talk turns on: review catches bugs and conventions, but its load-bearing function is alignment — knowledge sharing, mentorship, architectural feedback, onboarding, collaboration — the piece missing from the speaker's earlier five-layer model. "For semantic accuracy we can build better tooling, but alignment must survive." The dysfunction to avoid: "when AI reviews and nobody reads, we've configured the wrong thing" — a UI where two or three AI agents review and the human just skims and merges
data.name: Code review is alignment, not just correctness

data.brief: uReview began as one per-file logic-check prompt, a thorough-review agent and a dispatcher, observed only by cost, an NPS survey, Google Forms and Slack support — quality-to-cost "all over the place." Step one: classify the sentiment of developer replies to review comments and categorize them, exposing whole classes of fixable bugs. Step two: track address rate — does the developer act on the comment? Step three: a runtime profile of the agent trajectory (tool calls, thinking) explaining why it did what it did, used to tune runtime and performance. Lessons: "the model doesn't know that it's wrong" (always 100% sure), needs each team's style guide and anti-patterns baked in, and needs guardrails on what not to waste turns on because review has a time budget. Result vs the naive version: cost −60%, accuracy +70%; 25K comments/week, 10% get feedback, only 4% of PRs any negative feedback, 67% address rate, ~¾ of high-severity issues addressed
data.name: The review observability ladder

data.brief: Deterministic (no-LLM-judge) PR scorer: 5 signal families / 10 checks — diff size & coupling, test-evidence gap (test lines ÷ production lines), directory & code-owner spread, AI-authorship indicators (co-authored footer, branch prefixes, body phrases; amplifier-only, "information only, not a penalty"), evidence & rationale gaps (does the PR body say why) — combined into a 0–100 score, four bands (low / normal / needs-evidence / high), plus structured reviewer-focus and author-next-action lists and estimated review minutes
data.name: ReviewDebt scoring framework

data.brief: Healthcare is many specific workflows, so decompose the clinical note into sections and post-train small models per section instead of asking a frontier model for everything — cheaper and faster for problems where quality is already maxed out. Where quality is not maxed, the common objection is "the frontier model will generalize you"; Abridge's counter is that with ~100M conversations a year — a dataset nobody else has — and focus on a problem the labs are not focused on, it can beat the frontier's rate of change. The data flywheel is the license to train
data.name: The right to win in training

data.brief: End-to-end oncology prior-auth automation: intake → eligibility/benefits verification → auth-status determination → medical necessity → submission, with a growing "no-touch" (no human review) share
data.name: Risa prior-authorization pipeline

data.brief: Hallucination cannot be eliminated and eliminating it everywhere is not worth it, so classify failures first: an appointment scheduler failing one in 10,000 is acceptable (the user taps again); a reimbursement claim paying $50 for $200 is not — so several models review the same receipt and the flow proceeds only when they agree, otherwise the customer is offered a human. Release gating: hundreds of integration tests run many times each with a required pass rate (~90%) because outputs vary; after launch an auto-eval scores every conversation against rubrics and a dedicated group manually spot-checks, rising to ~20% of conversations for new features, to tune both the system and the rubrics
data.name: Risk-tiered reliability for generative features

data.brief: Three-layer reference architecture for building environments and post-training on them. Bottom: compute and orchestration — sandboxes, spinning up rollouts, and for long-horizon rollouts checkpointing with snapshot/rollback. Middle: the environment layer — how you build RL environments, how you measure their quality, how you version them. Top: the training methods — SFT, RL, and prompt/harness optimization via reflection (GEPA). Presented as converging with the "algorithms / environments / compute" decomposition from another talk in the same session.
data.name: RL-environment reference stack

data.brief: "RL worked when the world was a game, and IRL starts when the game fights back." The catch after coding agents proved deployable beyond coding (email, chat, receipts, research — all representable as code via MCP/API/Playwright): six ways real life breaks the reward function's assumptions — partial observability (DOM lacks dynamically-generated content; screenshot may need scrolling; model doesn't know which to trust), irreversibility (submit/delete/lock can't be undone), non-determinism (a click may work, hang, or trigger a restart), ephemeral authority (sessions and credentials expire constantly), ambiguous success ("done" ≠ successful — "filed the expense but also sent a resignation letter to the CEO"), and adversarial content (everything is designed to grab attention)
data.name: The RL-to-IRL gap

data.brief: The algorithm behind ChatGPT and, by the speaker's estimate, roughly 100% of LLMs in use today. Reduced to two steps: collect human preferences, optimize for human preferences. The claim the talk builds on is that the objective is the product: the human is in the loop of every deployed LLM because the training loop literally put them there — "the goal of the loop is to optimize for human preference, not to run software autonomously".
data.name: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback)

data.brief: Superagentic AI's open-source reference implementation of the RLM pattern: CLI + experimental coding-agent-style TUI harness, Docker-sandboxed REPL, pluggable local or cloud models (demoed with Gemini), budget/recursion-depth limits, JSONL traces exportable to any observability platform
data.name: RLM-Code

data.brief: The second post-training branch, distinguished by its North Star: it optimizes for log error rates of pure correctness rather than human preference. Used here as a contrast class — a purely-RLVR coding agent "would look very very different" from Claude Code — and as evidence that each post-training branch has its own optimization target and its own API shape.
data.name: RLVR (RL with verifiable rewards)

data.brief: Transcriptomic modality (~20K-gene expression matrix per cell); the most-available/most-used modality for foundation-model training, but a noisy, heterogeneous *snapshot* of a continuous process
data.name: Single-cell RNA-seq

data.brief: A robot's preset functions and programmable policies are exposed to an agent exactly as software tools are, and the agent orchestrates which to call and when from natural language — "give the same AI agent a hardware tool called a robot." Five lines with Strands Agents (import the agent, attach the robot tool, "pick up the red cube") and the robot can be taught new tasks by description rather than reprogramming; the Strands robot package covers 40+ robots in eight categories as simple tool calls
data.name: The robot as a hardware tool

data.brief: Reframed unit of analysis for persona AI, replacing "agent": the whole configured encounter — structured prompt, anchor material from primary documents, a temporal anchor, an off-the-shelf swappable model (the voice, not the mind), and a human curator with interpretive custody. The persona is the configuration, not the checkpoint: versionable, diffable, auditable, reproducible, and legible to domain experts
data.name: Role-playing language system

data.brief: Skill files that carry the business context — the semantics of the business tied to the tables and columns — so technical users write better SQL faster and non-technical sellers ask questions of the data directly; the recurring questions the business asks (closed-date changes on opportunities, amount changes) are embedded through testing so 80%+ of questions are answered without a data person, leaving the 20% of strategic questions for people. The same files let the operations team build applications that would otherwise wait on IT. Curation is deliberate: a central alias, review by GTM and operations to prevent skill proliferation, an expert-level knowledge skill at every level — predictable, near-deterministic execution across the team
data.name: Role-specific skill files over the data

data.brief: The talk's title primitive and the unit of execution underneath every use: start a sandbox from a task, hand it to an agent (running outside and executing commands in, or inside calling its own commands), run to a stopping condition producing a trajectory, hand the sandbox to a verifier, stop the sandbox, emit a reward — then aggregate rewards across a dataset. "Relatively simple… actually extremely universal": the same rollout serves eval scoring, sellable task data, SFT (trajectories), RL (trajectory tokens + rewards), text-feedback optimization (GEPA/evolutionary hill-climbing over a harness or scaffold), and non-eval production batch work
data.name: Rollout (agentic)

data.brief: The unit that turns out to be movable. Training is one tightly coupled job — every step has collectives, all-reduce and model-parallel communication, which genuinely want RDMA — but rollout is a fleet of serving jobs with no global all-reduce between them. So the thing that leaves the cluster is not backpropagation; it is the rollout island: a coherent endpoint or local group of endpoints serving one policy version, free to keep local parallelism and prefill/decode disaggregation inside itself. Across islands the dependency collapses to two directions: policy version in, trajectories and metadata out
data.name: Rollout serving island

data.brief: The synchronization contract that replaces "the current checkpoint." After each optimizer step the trainer publishes an immutable, named version to a shared bulletin board; requests become version-aware, stating which version to serve and which versions are acceptable, and responses carry the version back alongside tokens, logprobs, router-replay information and metadata — "exact same information as if they are in the same cluster as the trainer." Artifacts are materialized in Hugging Face safetensors layout so any standard engine can load and shard them itself, which is what keeps the scheme engine-agnostic across SGLang, vLLM, attention backends, parallelism strategies, serving dtypes and GPU generations
data.name: Immutable rollout weight version

data.brief: First principles: the token is the unit of cost, so value must be seen in tokens too; cost is created at the model-call boundary; without attribution (which agent, which run, which user cohort) you can't control it; policies should fix problems in place (compact the context, cache, trim tool output, detect loops and lack of progress) and only halt at a budget cap as the last resort. Enforcement must be in the call path and cumulative across attributed runs, at the run layer not the request layer
data.name: Run-level token governance

data.brief: Evidence that survives the turn, recording the whole chain — what the model proposed, what policy allowed or denied, what execution attempted (tool/API, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external result), and what the user-visible edge confirmed or failed to confirm — plus the terminal outcome of every external boundary (success / failure / timeout / cancel / max attempts). Explicitly distinguished from a transcript (what the agent said) and from a tool result (what one component claimed): "a transcript is not the proof".
data.name: Run receipt

data.brief: The architecture both leading assistants converged on. Every few days (ChatGPT) or every 24 hours (Claude), a background process reads recent conversations, extracts what matters, and rewrites a persistent profile that is then injected into the context window of every new conversation. ChatGPT's is ~4,000 tokens across 16 sections and written as extremely dense keyword clusters — "almost like clues," relying on frontier models' ability to infer context from limited information. Claude's is ~1,000 tokens of complete sentences. Introduced in ChatGPT V2 (April 2025) and Claude V2 (September 2025)
data.name: The running profile

data.brief: Safety alone isn't enough; the runtime must be omnipresent — laptop, cloud, cross-cloud orchestration, your VPC, the customer's VPC — "connected by a fabric so you can move agents up and down." Docker's portability lineage applied to safety: the same sandbox, policy plane and controls travel with the workload
data.name: The runtime follows the work

data.brief: LLMs running during play as a living entity that modifies and directs the game: unscripted NPC decision-making from assigned personalities, game-master-style per-player adjustment (e.g. difficulty for a coordination-challenged player). Distinct from build-time generation; became feasible ~2025-2026 as inference got fast and cheap enough; every session is unique/non-repeatable
data.name: Runtime-LLM gameplay

data.brief: Containment — a sandbox where the agent runs *inside* the untrusted VM boundary and controls run *outside* it (more than "throw a rock and hit a sandbox company"). Scoped access — beyond network and tool allowlists: just-in-time tools composed over existing MCP tools but restricted to the task (e.g. only the Slack conversations about this incident), run in a scoped sub-sandbox for that task rather than one big sandbox accreting capabilities. Intent-based access — decide what access a request should get from the user's/task's intent and context, deny or escalate to a human what the intent doesn't justify (read Slack for the incident: yes; suddenly wants email: no), at a control layer independent of the model or harness. "A hard problem, not fully solved yet"
data.name: The safety runtime: containment, scoped access, intent-based access

data.brief: The existing saga orchestrator — the layer that already sequenced distributed transactions across bounded contexts — is where the agentic tier is installed, as sub-orchestrators (tier 1 deterministic, tier 2 agentic) rather than as a new service. The agent's verdict re-enters the saga as an ordinary event, the payment context approves, and the flow returns to the transaction context; no consumer of the saga needs to know an agent participated.
data.name: Agentic saga orchestration

data.brief: Incumbent CRM platform. Replaced by Klarna with homegrown AI system.
data.description: Incumbent CRM. Replaced by Klarna with a homegrown AI system — the canonical "SaaS is dispensable" case study.
data.name: Salesforce CRM

data.brief: Incremental, block-level checkpoint/restore of an agent sandbox's disk (copy-on-write base image + changed-extent diffs with lineage, uploaded to object storage): makes sandboxes survivable across node death, migratable across a fleet, and forkable for backtracking search
data.name: Sandbox disk snapshotting

data.brief: Verification and reversibility for a world without tests or undo. Before an agent sends, its drafts are checked against the user's past emails and sense of good; before anything destructive, agents act on sandboxes that mock the real tools, so the blast radius hits the sandbox and a human reviews before the real action — the agent closes its own loop instead of stopping to wait. Where undo exists (a label added can be removed) it is provided; where it does not (hard deletes, sent mail, wires) the action goes sandbox-first with a notification ("1,200 emails will be deleted — do you want it?"); across billions of tool calls the platform learns which actions can be walked back. "In code you catch the mistake after it happens; here you catch it before"
data.name: Sandboxed tools for irreversible actions

data.brief: SAP's AI consumption-based platform. First major incumbent to pivot from per-seat pricing.
data.description: SAP's AI consumption-based platform. First major enterprise incumbent to formally abandon per-seat pricing for AI usage-based model (Mar 2026, Bloomberg).
data.name: SAP AI Platform

data.brief: Access to information doesn't equal understanding. Attaching a wiki doesn't tell an agent where the needed information is; searching it triggers the radiologist's *satisfaction of search* — find one indicator and stop, missing the others. Agents don't distill how dependencies, architecture and future plans fit together without prior legwork. Dumping the whole codebase and docs into a million-token window fails too: it exceeds the window and distracts the agent from task-specific flow, wasting tokens and time
data.name: Satisfaction of search

data.brief: The third war story: scaling Web Unblocker from 10k to 60k req/s in under two months (now "project 150" → ~100k). At that load "even adding 2,000 servers doesn't solve the problem — you need an architecture," reliable central components, observability that still tells the truth (telemetry becomes part of the load), and testing that resembles reality. The real bottleneck showed up in load testing, not outages — organic-traffic testing (behaving like real client usage) is far harder than synthetic; they hit a wall at ~20k req/s where the question became not "does it work" but "do we know it can go further," and uncertainty was the bottleneck. Ends accepting "real testing is with production traffic"
data.name: Scale is never a finish line

data.brief: Ramp's second FDE principle: unless you are scaling with model capabilities you fall behind, so jobs must be reinvented continuously — whatever knowledge work you do today, figure out how models and agents do it for you. Applied to FDE it means taking the whole lifecycle (gather context, scope the request, write the spec, implement the feature) and replacing each stage with agents. Daunting whole, tractable in pieces: the first stage and the last stage are largely solved (intake agents; frontier models one-shot medium-size features), the middle is "gnarly, unformed and difficult" and is where the investment goes.
data.name: Scale with tokens

data.brief: The talk's name for the problem and its proposed fourth scaling axis. The three classical axes — more data, more compute, bigger models — have driven the entire deep-learning revolution but operate only on public data. For a private corpus the data axis is unavailable (you cannot create more of it) and training from scratch is off the table (you want the world knowledge), which leaves compute as the only axis: *how do you spend arbitrarily more compute on a fixed D and keep getting a better model?* Explicitly catalogued as one concept under many names — sleep-time compute, continual learning, neural memory, write-time compute, note taking, dreaming, studying, machine studying, and classically amortized inference — with the naming chaos read as evidence the paradigm is pre-paradigmatic
data.name: Scaling compute on context

data.brief: Using two small curated dense runs to predict a much larger one: two dense Llama-style models trained on 1T tokens of curated data define a line that passes through a 17T-token, 50x-larger hypersparse model's actual result. Requires that you "simulate token scarcity appropriately" at the small scale so the small runs sit on the same curve. Consequence: a hero run can be derisked with 50-100x less compute before you commit to it.
data.name: Small-run scaling prediction (hero-run derisking)

data.brief: Offline agent evaluation built around simulated end-to-end workflows (customer support, code generation, research) rather than single prompts: the agent operates inside the simulated environment and is scored on task completion rate, tool correctness, planning quality, and resource usage — the middle tier of Gupta's eval pyramid between benchmarks and production telemetry
data.name: Scenario-based agent evaluation

data.brief: Figma is a C++ scene graph (like the DOM). Candidates: a sparse JSX/XML-like internal form (abstract, low fidelity); React-Tailwind (from the Sites product — pixel-perfect if pasted into a server); a plain image (early-2025 agents were poor at image → code). Winner: React-Tailwind *plus* an image of the node — code context and image together gave better agentic output. Never inline base64 images in code ("blew up the context window"); hoist images to the top level
data.name: Which serialization an agent converts best

data.brief: BERT-style masked-gene-count prediction over cells-as-sentences (with Geneformer et al.); compresses cells to a latent vector — where information is lost
data.name: scGPT (transformer single-cell models)

data.brief: Extracting graphs from unstructured text by giving the extractor an explicit schema (typed nodes/edges instead of free-form triples) plus an ontology of formatting/standardization instructions, then entity-matching with embeddings before creating nodes; consistent types make relationships queryable
data.name: Schema-guided graph extraction

data.brief: In the absence of canonical ground truth, having a panel of scientists grade each other's work is the best available proxy. Two rounds run against trajectory data from successive model releases (~Jan-Mar 2026) invalidated many of the team's assumptions and exposed defective tasks rather than defective models: a prompt asking to split a gene list, count "inflammatory" genes, normalize, and use "an appropriate radius" leaves a host of undetermined choices; and much of bioinformatics QC rests on arbitrary numerical thresholds nobody had ever justified.
data.name: Scientist cross-grading (human verification)

data.brief: Kepler tenet 2. The model decides what to compute; it never does the computation. Reasoning and planning stay with the model ("intelligence is commoditized"); parsing a PDF or XBRL and running the arithmetic is code, and the deterministic layer persists the result outside anything the model can see. Rationale is both correctness and cost: "why would I run 1 + 1 through a multi-billion-parameter model instead of one CPU cycle?" Described as a contrarian position with VCs a year earlier that has since become mainstream.
data.name: Scope determinism

data.brief: Human approval modelled as an object bound to the action it authorized rather than a vague memory that someone clicked yes: who approved, in which session and run, for which tool, for which arguments, for how long, with what outcome, and a pointer to the receipt. Expiry must terminate, not loop. If those fields fall off during a retry, replay or channel callback, the harness can no longer prove the executed action is the approved action. Governing rule: "capability is not execution — the model can request, the system decides".
data.name: Approval as scoped execution state

data.brief: The operating principles of a decade of web scraping, summed up as "cost matters": use a browser only when you absolutely have to; validate content (HTTP 200 does not mean you're good to go); prefer lighter content (JavaScript/CSS/HTML bytes that deliver no value); expect results on the first try. The talk's thesis is that these transfer unchanged to agents that touch the web
data.name: Scraping-industry principles applied to agents

data.brief: Accumulated personal notes/highlights/meeting recaps/saved links across tools (Obsidian, Readwise, Notion, Apple Notes, Granola, Google Drive), typically organized PARA-style (projects/areas/resources/archive, Tiago Forte); in the talk it is the immutable, human-curated substrate agents read from via research skills — and never write to
data.name: Second brain (personal knowledge base)

data.brief: CISA-originated doctrine (March 2023 paper Cable co-authored): build systems fundamentally resilient to known vulnerability classes rather than patching one-off; in the AI era, the frame for making AI the default code writer without exponential vulnerability growth
data.name: Secure by design

data.brief: A skill instruction of the form "you must ask for confirmation" that the agent satisfies by confirming to itself: from the human's perspective there is a human in the loop, from the agent's perspective a confirmation happened and it proceeds. Named as one of the review programme's most important findings — prompt-level human-in-the-loop is not human-in-the-loop, so the check has to move to whether the executing tool actually passes through an approval gate or hook.
data.name: Self-confirmation loophole

data.brief: MiniMax's M2/M3-series post-training loop: the model builds its own harness, trains inside it, and produces the next checkpoint. Its second face is organizational — the lab actively uses its own models to speed up internal development, and the resulting work becomes a source of internal evals "closely related to our own work" that are unavailable to outsiders.
data.name: Self-evolution (model builds its own harness)

data.brief: Start from a judge prompt and what to measure → baseline scores on traces → an optimization loop (the GEPA prompt-optimization library) against the golden dataset → promote the calibrated prompt as the LLM-as-judge. Packaged as a self-serve UI: a PM or operator sets a few configs and runs the loop with any model (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI); the original and calibrated prompts are shown side by side so partners can see why the judge improved and trust it
data.name: Self-serve LLM-judge calibration

data.brief: Elicitation technique that recovers distributions instead of point estimates. Rather than forcing a persona onto a 1-5 purchase-intent scale (a format LLMs aren't used to producing), let it answer in free text — its native format — e.g. "I'm somewhat interested. If it works well and isn't too expensive, I might give it a try." Then have humans write anchor texts for each scale point ("Hell no, I'll never buy that" ...
data.description: "Absolutely, I'll buy 20"), measure semantic similarity between the model's text and the anchors, and read off a probability distribution over the scale. Result reported: the technique reconstructed not only accurate willingness-to-pay values but the shape of the distribution, which naive rating prompts flatten.
data.name: Semantic-anchor scoring

data.brief: Lightweight alternative to fine-tuning: episodic memory (past similar cases and their decisions, referenced automatically) resolves recurring situations without human intervention; semantic memory (distilled domain rules/policies from human review) sharpens the decision boundary; the two are complementary, not competing
data.name: Semantic + episodic agent memory

data.brief: Curated single layer of KPI definitions, metric calculations, canonical queries, and business definitions that a data agent references first; the cleanest source of truth and the first thing an enterprise should build
data.name: Semantic layer

data.brief: "RAG for tools": embed every tool's description into a vector index offline; at runtime embed the user query, nearest-neighbor search, and inject only the top-K (K≈3–5) matching tool schemas into the model call — the model picks from a focused set instead of the full catalog; the router both adds the right tools and removes the wrong ones from the choice set
data.name: Semantic tool routing

data.brief: The control loop: perceive through one channel, take exactly one action, then verify through a different channel — "if you've clicked something, don't ask the click if it was successful; check the network or check the screen." Repeat until the page gives in; when it won't close despite sense-act-verify, that is the page fighting back, and the signal to climb the ladder
data.name: Sense–act–verify loop

data.brief: Cognition's ROI instrumentation: one agent trace/trajectory is a "session", and metrics derive from sessions how many engineering hours were generated and how many were productive. Rolled up into three customer-facing deltas measured before vs after deploying the agent — headcount equivalent, delivery-timeline compression, and raw merged-PR counts — as the counter to the objection that session counts are just token maxing with extra steps.
data.name: Session-derived engineering hours

data.brief: The counter-recipe to filtering synthetic data out. Nemotron 3 Ultra's published mix labels several of its largest components "SFT-" — the question-and-answer chat data you would normally see only in post-training — pulled back into pre-training so the model learns the shape of the conversations and the tasks it will be expected to do from the very beginning. A second, structural benefit for MoE models: expert load balancing aims for roughly equal expert utilization per batch or sequence, and if the post-training data distribution is very different from the pre-training one it causes massive imbalances — MAI's own report describes overcoming this by cranking up the load-balancing coefficient during the SFT stages, which the speaker calls the thing you do not want to be doing that far into a run.
data.description: The preferred fix is continuity: the model should learn stable representations from early on.
data.name: Pulling post-training data into pre-training

data.brief: The same agent session — same context, same memory — addressable from every relevant interface rather than trapped on one laptop or "trapped in Slack": start a session in Slack, continue in the desktop/mobile app, finish in GitHub. Sessions carry a visible participant trail (who created, interacted, got notified, has seen it — "has this been vetted by an engineer or not?"), and a reviewer can interrogate the session directly ("why did you do it this way?") instead of waiting for the human author, because "the answer is almost certainly in this thread" and you can ask the agent rather than read the thread
data.name: Shared agent sessions across surfaces

data.brief: UCP's checkout primitive: a token representing a raw card or a wallet (Google Pay, Apple Pay) that can also carry fraud signals, customer reputation and anything agents and merchants want to share at the point of purchase. The agent requests a payment method from the provider (Stripe in the demo) and receives the token, not the card; it passes the token to the seller, who unwraps it and forwards it to the provider; the provider enforces every guardrail — expired token, invalid amount or currency — and answers success or failure; the merchant confirms the order. Neither the agent nor the merchant ever holds the card number
data.name: The shared payment token

data.brief: The line between an FDE function and a dev shop: FDEs assemble solutions from a shared set of platform primitives and never write software from scratch. Without it, per-customer bespoke code compounds into unmaintainable sprawl ("55 repos"), maintenance costs "eat your P&L alive", and the engineers quit. Primitive granularity is a function of customer breadth — some platforms ship apps 60% built with 40% customized, others (AWS/DynamoDB) offer extremely granular primitives to serve a broad swath.
data.name: Shared-primitive platform (the FDE precondition)

data.brief: The architectural stance: not an AI layer on top of the business but the agent as another operator in the same system as humans, reading and writing the same context. Agents do the repetitive work at scale — gathering context, researching, drafting, writing artifacts — and humans provide judgement, nuance, the decision and the relationship; a rep starts the day with a prioritized task inbox and pre-researched drafts and adds their taste. Agents never talk to customers directly (humans approve in sales-assist; an inbound form is untrusted input). Be headless by default and design for agents as operators, not copilots; if humans and agents cannot read the same substrate you have two systems that will drift apart. The floor rises for the whole team — new reps learn the signals, playbooks and what good follow-up looks like from the strongest reps' patterns
data.name: One substrate for humans and agents

data.brief: The staged migration of performance work from reactive to proactive, with the catalog as the vehicle. Stage 1 (reactive): production profiling, agent finds and fixes, code review; the right place to start, and how the catalog gets populated. Stage 2 (review time): a reviewer agent looks up the catalog against an incoming diff and leaves an inline comment ("based on the pattern catalog and observed profiling data, this is an anti-pattern — can you rewrite this?"). Stage 3 (authoring time): the catalog is hooked into the coding agent itself so it consults known anti-patterns before emitting tokens and writes the optimal code first. Stated cost of stage 3: slower generation and more tokens consumed — which is exactly why the catalog must be navigable rather than loadable.
data.name: Shift-left performance loop

data.brief: The single high-value shared skill the team invested in, and their adoption lever: it takes over everything "from code done to PR ready for review" — opening the PR, writing the description, handling review comments and merge comments, and working through CI failures in a loop. Often runs over an hour, which initially scared people, "but once they saw the value they get invested, because it's one skill which tells them: this AI thing can actually work for me, I don't need to constantly babysit it, I can trust it." Paired with a code gardener that runs nightly over the repo checking organization against the codebase's own standards
data.name: The "ship it" skill

data.brief: How a human decides when five rational stakeholders see five different risks days before launch. Worst case wins — severity comes from the worst plausible outcome, not the average or the frequency (a bug that lightly annoys everyone is less severe than one that could seriously harm 0.1%). Severity is not capacity — it comes from harm, not from who owns it or whether the fix fits the schedule; the options are fix, delay, or accept with explicit sign-off, never a quiet downgrade. Asymmetric default — when unsure, choose the safer mistake: hold for safety bugs, ship for polish bugs. Revealed risk tolerance — what the org already runs in production without escalation is the floor, not what it says it accepts. Humans are the constraint — judges and dashboards scale, pattern interpretation does not, so design for people in the loop. Fast-follows are committed debt, not a wish list
data.name: The ship-or-hold rules

data.brief: The replacement for the reactive loop: real calls plus manufactured edge cases (rare symptoms, mis-transcriptions) → optimized prompt → simulation safety gate → gated deploy → more calls, a flywheel.
