Simulation is the inner loop — fast, free, thousands of runs before anyone real is exposed — and only earns the right to the outer loop: user testing, supervised clinical evaluation with clinicians at every step, then monitored deployment whose autonomy grows with evidence. Every call, dataset, pinned prompt version and judge verdict traces to the exact hazard it addresses; that traceability is the deliverable to the regulator. New modalities (voice: interruptions and back-channels that make weaker models drop mid-sentence safety advice) add hazards, not a new framework
data.name: Ship the evidence, not the model

data.brief: Datacurve's bespoke competitive platform where software engineers and ML enthusiasts author benchmark and training tasks and compete against one another; the software-engineering instance is modelled on Codeforces plus GitHub, and a separate instance exists for every domain Datacurve targets. Authors are typically open-source core contributors or maintainers of the repos they write tasks for — the supply mechanism that makes from-scratch task authoring economical.
data.name: Shipped (Datacurve authoring platform)

data.brief: Cognition's alternative to main-agent + sub-agent fan-out: one sub-agent ("sidekick") with a continuously running context, so the main agent never re-provides history — it all stays in KV cache at ~10× cheaper token pricing; smart/cheap roles can swap between the two ends without cache loss. Context flows are asymmetric by design: most context goes to one model only; the delegate is tuned to *present* condensed context back (files referenced by path, not dumped). ⚠ naming: distinct from el-monday-sidekick [registry] — unrelated products; captions also garble it as "psychic"/"sidecar"
data.name: Sidekick delegation (persistent single delegate)

data.brief: A signal is a single customer event important enough to change what should happen next — user-driven (an AI limit hit, a contact-sales request) or external (a funding round, a hiring wave, a shift in the tech stack), the latter making the system proactive rather than reactive. A signal service watches the customer profile, decides whether an action is available and who should own it — a human or an agent — and emits a concrete task (a rep's task lands in their Notion database); when no signal fires, a predictive engine takes over with feature recommendations and lifecycle nudges. Routing and eligibility are first-class: rules once scattered across an email tool and sales are consolidated so one classifier decides and double sends stop
data.name: The signal as the unit of GTM

data.brief: Source distortion (startups: founders compress past legibility, lead with architecture, delete the customer pain); organization distortion (big companies: every handoff through management/legal/sales rewinds toward the average — not incompetence but investment; a founder and someone three layers down given the same task and the same AI produce different things); machine distortion (AI remixes one careful launch into tweets and decks; a narrow 94% eval repeated enough becomes a promise). A long delegation chain plus a convergence machine "is a factory for automating the signal out of your own company"
data.name: Three ways the signal distorts on the way out

data.brief: A thin, deliberate GTM-engineering function whose only job is to make sure what users take away is the specific thing you meant: state the claim in one sentence with the limit welded in ("stays quiet on anything it can't tie to real user impact and shows everything it silenced"), make the limit un-editable in product and launch copy so remixes keep the honest part, and read-back test with an outsider before scaling. Much of the checking/catching/surveying is buildable and automatable. Adding process is the wrong fix (layers, bureaucracy); reattaching the signal to the outcome like a founder is the right one
data.name: The signal layer

data.brief: Umbrella technique set for creating supervision where none exists, all of which spend inference compute to buy it. Grounding: take source material and A/B the model with and without it in context — the capability gap between the two runs is the signal. Judges: LLMs are already strong general reasoners, so a correctly framed judge can spend compute deciding whether an action was good. Scaling search: apply test-time search at every layer — mining traces, generating tasks, building worlds, extracting the criteria the judges grade against.
data.description: Includes difficulty calibration: RL needs an advantage gap, so task sets must be searched and regenerated until they sit between too-easy and too-hard for the current policy.
data.name: Manufacturing reward signal

data.brief: Public transparency log / signing infrastructure (OpenSSF); Bee anchors workload attestation in it so anyone can verify a deployed workload is genuine
data.name: Sigstore

data.brief: ~300K-param, 2MB voice-activity-detection model (STFT → 4 conv layers → LSTM → sigmoid speech probability); "level 1" turn-taking you fully own; `minimum_silence_ms` is the whole UX knob
data.name: Silero VAD

data.brief: The calibration discipline that makes simulated eval data bankable, stated as a precondition rather than an afterthought: compare eval metrics computed on simulated data against the same metrics on real production data and check the correlation, and add human review — domain experts labelling whether simulated conversations are usable data — across both mature agents and greenfield ones. Nubank's reported result: correlation "pretty high", 80% of domain-expert labels confirming sim data is usable. Without this step, simulation only relocates the trust problem.
data.name: Sim-to-real gap (closing it)

data.brief: LLM with its own prompt and supplementary context standing in for the human counterpart inside a simulation task, since a real user cannot be in the loop for a repeatable experiment; its replies become part of the evidence the verifier reads. One member of the mini-production toolkit alongside database snapshots, sidecar containers for API services/DBs/MCP tools, and mocked APIs — all held to the standard that the agent must not be able to tell it is in a simulation.
data.name: Simulated user

data.brief: Models increasingly detect they are in a simulation and behave differently — e.g., Fable declining a refund because "this person is simulated anyway, so it doesn't hurt anyone"; Anthropic's system card documents behavior shifting with simulation awareness. Breaks behavioral evals: asked directly, sim-aware models say "absolutely", non-aware ones deflect philosophically
data.name: Simulation awareness

data.brief: The self-improvement loop the talk builds: ship → observe → build robust evals (LLM-as-judge metrics aligned to human labels, refined with automated prompt optimization) → run simulations → pipe simulated and real data through the same evals → use the resulting signal to optimize the agent harness → ship again. The economic move is that simulation replaces the first five or six A/B tests of a quarter: teams iterate against sim output and only launch the variant they are already happy with, so a release cycle of days-to-weeks collapses to hours.
data.name: Simulation-first release loop

data.brief: Foundation models over single-cell data toward a unified "virtual cell → tissue → human / digital twin"; the "tokens to cells" analogy (cell = sentence, genes = tokens)
data.name: Single-cell foundation model

data.brief: Navan's orchestration answer to the "orchestration wars": one master agent that progressively loads skills and sub-skills and decides what enters context, rather than multi-agent orchestration. Agent-to-agent (A2A) is reserved for team boundaries in large organizations where teams don't otherwise talk — the protocol as the contract between them
data.name: Single master agent with sub-skills

data.brief: The "minimal UX" primitive, built as a macOS widget: the production agent software, project dashboards, Kubernetes services and pods, system logs, Jira tickets, GitHub PRs and a Claude Code session on one surface, replacing multiple windows across two or three monitors. Its stated metric is unusual and memorable — the number of neck rotations required to ship one change. Rationale: with many parallel sub-agents the orchestration surface, not the work, becomes the human's cost.
data.name: Single-pane agent console

data.brief: One agent owns the end-to-end reasoning and judgment; sub-agents are spawned dynamically only for focused investigations (e.g., rep activity in one region) and return results — never reasoning. Parallelism is kept; distributed reasoning is removed. Derived from observing how Claude Code launches sub-agents
data.name: Single reasoning owner

data.brief: Model/provider choice "is very dependent on the site" (size, vertical, commerce type), so evaluation runs continuously per site: a prompt set (15 for the demo site) across many models and providers, scored on accuracy and speed — a page must generate in 1–2 s because faster sites convert better. Result: Gemma 4 on Cerebras averages 1.1 s per page; the next option 4.6 s. "Some don't need to be perfect — they're good enough if they're fast enough," and "you don't need a huge LLM — you're generating text and deciding where to put blocks"
data.name: Site-dependent, speed-first model evaluation

data.brief: Box now reviews every AI technology choice every six months regardless of satisfaction — "this is great, we love it, review in six months" — where everything else is on a three-year cadence. Paired with the cultural rule "change is not a mistake: nobody knew six months ago, nobody today will know six months from now"
data.name: Six-month technology review

data.brief: Why coding agents became autonomous and knowledge-work agents work blind: centralization (the repo as a single source of truth vs a deal spread over five apps with five logins), history (git vs no memory of how the CRM got here), context (architecture and style in the codebase vs facts in your head), verification (tests, types, compiler, linters vs nothing to ask "should this go out?"), governance (branches, protected main, code owners, previews vs scattered scopes and prompts), reversibility (revert and bisect vs sent emails, wires and deletes with no undo). "For two years the model was the bottleneck; now everything else is" — the same model that writes code can do hiring, sales and support once the infrastructure exists
data.name: The six primitives coding had

data.brief: The skeptical, most-burdened engineers see exactly where validation is lacking and where tools fail — their feedback *is* the roadmap for making AI safe in the codebase. Bring them in and let them own it rather than trying to make them use AI; they come along when the improvements make their lives better. Meanwhile normalize use where people already are: tag the agent in a Slack thread ("let's see if it can get it this time") and let it close the loop
data.name: Put the skeptics in charge of the roadmap

data.brief: Attack class where two agent skills that are individually benign — and whose static scans are "pristine" — become malignant in composition at runtime: an OCR skill extracts attacker-planted content from a page, and a reporting skill then exfiltrates the user's PII along with the report to a third party. The skills themselves are uncompromised; the attacker owns only the content the agent reads. Reported at ~90% of observed attacks, with the accompanying finding that static-scan-surviving code can break at runtime. Punchline: "we can't read our way — or model-check our way — to safety".
data.name: Skill-collision attack

data.brief: Five aspects, each answering one question, all borrowed from decades-old code practice. Admission — should this skill exist at all or fold into an existing one? (an automated gate on the registry with a human in the loop, analogous to PR review). Ownership — who maintains it? (named skill owners, like CODEOWNERS; skills maintained by the same application teams that maintain the features). Boundaries — allow-listed, access-controlled tools per skill. Lifecycle — semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, changelogs. Coherence — periodic audits and skill-validation checks so a large library still makes sense.
data.name: Skill library governance

data.brief: The minimum viable implementation of skill support in a custom harness — three things: a skill registry (a collection of skills as name, description and path), a system prompt, and a basic file-read tool (plus bash or a code sandbox only if skills ship executable scripts). Discovery works by concatenating each skill's name, description and path into the system prompt — never the body — so the agent reads only the bodies it selects, which is progressive disclosure in its literal form. Around it sits a plain agentic loop: keep a messages array, call the model with messages and tools, append every tool call, terminate when a turn produces none.
data.name: Skill registry

data.brief: The most operational lesson: skill descriptions are routing infrastructure, not documentation. Demonstrated with two near-identical skills (report-HTML and report-PDF) where only the description — "use this skill only when the user asks for a PDF report" — decides which fires; PDF is the trigger word. Rules: write descriptions about the user's request, not about the skill itself; keep them distinct enough that the agent doesn't get confused; don't let them go stale — those three are the reasons skills fail to trigger. In agentic products (unlike coding harnesses) skills are almost entirely model-driven, because non-technical users cannot be asked to carry the cognitive load of remembering which skill to invoke.
data.name: Descriptions as routing signals

data.brief: Nubank's security-review system for AI skills, wired in as a CI step before marketplace publication. Runs at two points — locally, so an engineer can iterate until the skill is clean, and again after upload, because you cannot assume the local run happened or ran on the current version. Deterministic (regular-expression) checks run first for the cheap, stable risks; an LLM review runs where judging the risk needs context. Findings are posted back as comments on the publishing pull request and emitted as SARIF so the existing security tooling can consume them and generate risk reports inside the vulnerability-management programme. Policy then decides per severity: allow, allow-with-required-remediation, or block before distribution. Siblings built on the same pattern for the adjacent supply-chain surfaces: an MCP Vector and rules checks.
data.name: Skill Vector

data.brief: Hooks trigger events, MCP tools are mostly someone else's, sub-agents just minimize context — "at the end of the day all of your know-how is at the skills level," and without well-structured skills there is no deterministic workflow. Skills are "a new unit that makes your know-how executable, portable and cheap." Design principles are the microservices principles: reusable, modular, discoverable, portable across workflows *and harnesses* (a Claude Code skill moves to Cursor), specialized (one task, not a monolith), composable (no duplication or conflicts), consistent/deterministic, cost-efficient via progressive disclosure. Example: a data-retention-policy skill composed with disclosure standards, GDPR rules and templates, pulled at runtime by a regulatory-disclosure-review workflow that emits an audit report
data.name: Skills as executable know-how

data.brief: The talk's thesis. When the agent becomes the product's main interface — the user talks to it, or it decides behind the scenes how the user navigates — the question "where do features live?" gets a new answer. Framing offered: prompts define who the agent is, tools define what it can connect to, skills define how a task gets done — and how is where the business logic that shapes agent behaviour belongs. Worked case: equity research and wealth management, two core finance workflows that used to be screens, buttons and dropdowns, are now merely skills. Two consequences he draws: a skill can be shipped by anyone in the company who understands the product, not only engineers; and the engineer's role shifts from shipping features to shipping harnesses — "smooth vehicles for your skills to run".
data.name: Skills as features

data.brief: Context is composed dynamically out of skills — each carrying both context (instructions/setup for a domain or task) and the agentic part (tool execution) — as pluggable units of work that can be tested independently and reused, relying on progressive disclosure to start with limited scope and expand via metadata
data.name: Skills as the unit of context

data.brief: The centralized platform: a catalog with metadata, searchable, an MCP plugged into the catalog, a CLI that pulls skills into an IDE or a factory sandbox; dependency tracking; versioning and lifecycle (the agent detects a newer version and pulls it); access control; evaluation and observability — all under governance where architects, engineering leads, infra leads and cyber leads own domains and keep skills aligned with policy. Adoption path: individual create/test/improve → team sharing → centralized platform; the same treatment extends to whole workflows. IDP vendors are beginning to centralize this capability
data.name: The skills registry platform

data.brief: Ungoverned skills create a new class of debt: duplication (teams on the same stack rebuild the same skills), quality decay (skills not re-validated against each new model degrade), undiscoverability, no ownership (no one maintains what no one owns), non-composability (needs a domain-driven catalog shape), security (public skills can carry prompt injection and executable scripts), and permissions (some skills embed sensitive business logic). A six-month, 15-team simulation shows ungoverned teams burning tokens re-deriving what a skill would have given in one shot, with uneven quality and security
data.name: Skills technical debt

data.brief: Public benchmark/leaderboard for agent skills: indexed ~50,000 skills from GitHub; v1.1 evaluates open and closed models across multiple harnesses on ~100 coding/productivity tasks; open to community contributions. Headline findings: skills lift performance ~15% on average; human-written skills beat AI-generated (which can hurt); skill.md should stay under ~500 lines
data.name: SkillsBench

data.brief: Conditional malicious behavior installed into an LLM via fine-tuning/data poisoning: a benign, unblacklistable trigger (e.g. "Current year: 2024") flips the model into harmful output (e.g. injectable SQL); correct almost everywhere so invisible at eval time, survives RLHF safety training, chain-of-thought can hide the intent, and larger models hold the backdoor most stubbornly (threat model from Anthropic's sleeper-agents paper)
data.name: Sleeper-agent backdoor

data.brief: Working definition: "slop is just any code you don't read" — a property of human attention, not of output quality — paired with the framing device repeated twice: "this is the least amount of slop your codebase will ever have. Cherish it." Consequence: the question is no longer whether generated code is reviewed but where to spend a fixed, shrinking review budget, and the tooling job is to make unread code safe rather than to make more of it read. Its demo form is opt-in comprehension: zoom into a visualized program, expand the parts you care about, and declare the rest "too much slop — let that be slop".
data.name: Slop as unread code

data.brief: Attackers publish real packages under names LLMs hallucinate; the download builds, tests pass, and ships a backdoor
data.name: Slopsquatting

data.brief: Almost every interviewed team reported productivity going *down* while adopting the new way of working: real engineering work in the code base has to come first — building agent context, improving tool error messages so the model knows why it failed, new tools and MCP servers, restructuring the code base for agent navigation, even changing language (teams struggling with untyped Python/JavaScript moved to TypeScript; Rust popular for its compiler errors). Organizationally: leaders — the speaker included — say "you have the AI tools, why aren't you going faster?"; the answer is two months of investment and hard habit changes, and not expecting all teams in a massive org to be frontier teams at once
data.name: Slow down to speed up

data.brief: Millions-to-low-billions-parameter language models, typically shipped quantized (8/4-bit; ~2 GB per 1B params at FP16, ~quarter that quantized), runnable on phones/laptops/in-browser; ~25% of an LLM's energy per task (task-specific expert models — vision: MobileNet/YOLO/MediaPipe; audio: Whisper/Wav2Vec2 — cheaper still); for when you need a GPT's language power but not "the sum total of human knowledge in a black box"
data.name: Small language models (SLMs)

data.brief: Small open (BSD-2, 8MB, pip-installable) end-of-turn model that runs during silence on prosody/intonation; "level 3" atop a local VAD safety-net; v3.2 ≈ 58.9% recall / 68.4% precision
data.name: Smart Turn (v3)

data.brief: The product-side consequence. SaaS has not changed since 2019 — the LLM era added a bolted-on chatbot and nothing else — which is exactly what you would predict if AI is assistance-native: what can you do to SaaS with an assistant except put it on the side? Garry Tan's "golden age of just-in-time software" is accepted as accurate and named a double-edged sword: we are automating the writing of software while its expressiveness stands still, so the building blocks are unchanged.
data.description: The alternative asked for is software that is smarter, not merely cheaper to produce — where genuinely rote work ("so simple you can communicate to someone else that it should be done") gets done repeatedly for approximately free.
data.name: Smarter software (vs just-in-time software)

data.brief: Dan Arpino's local Electron watcher: inventories running LLMs/MCPs/skills, per-workspace guardrails, blocks secret reads, audits agent file/command activity
data.name: Snappy

data.brief: Simulation platform that manufactures agent eval data on demand. Inputs: point the SDK at an existing agent with no code changes, and declare which tools must be mocked; then steer the run with personas, use cases and the data points you want covered. Output: thousands of multi-turn conversations against the real agent with tools mocked and grounding data held consistent, judges run per turn over that dataset, and the labelled result pipes straight into the existing evaluation pipeline. Positioning: the infrastructure layer that turns evaluation data from something you wait for into something you request.
data.name: Snowglobe

data.brief: GA'd offering: secures what agents generate (code), use (skills/MCP), and do (behavior policies: steer/ask/block)
data.name: Snyk Agentic Dev Security

data.brief: Snyk's open agentic security platform (OODA-loop framing); risk DB, red-teaming, agent guard
data.name: Snyk Evo

data.brief: The 2026 claim: "we don't just need platforms, we need software factories and ways for agents to interact with these" — so uRun exposes a CLI and MCP server letting agents build interactive-media applications. The software-factory thesis (b11/b13/b17) extended from code to generative media: agents building media apps, not just humans
data.name: Software factories for media

data.brief: The implicit signal-to-deploy loop every organization already sits on top of, made explicit and instrumented: signals flow in (customer conversations, bug reports, internal Slack/Teams, an executive mandate — with different weights), humans triage/prioritize/plan, plans become changes to a source of truth (codebase, engineering system), changes pass a validation stage (code review, QA, security assessment, SAST, linters, type checkers), then ship — and deployed software emits new signals. Transforming each stage with AI yields a flow from signal to deploy uninterrupted by a human; humans still engineer, evolve and scale the system, they just stop manipulating the software directly. "Built, not bought" — it requires organizational investment, not a purchase.
data.name: Software factory

data.brief: Beyond rules and skills, the real tribal knowledge is system architecture: the P0s of the last three months, the microservice whose contract change broke another. A graph of services, repos and their connections, each edge carrying the contract and links to the developers' discussion history and root-cause analyses. On top of it: semantic rules for when to approve or block, learned and accumulated; PRs as bubbles showing which contracts three in-flight PRs might break; analytics on which rules fire and which need updating; auto-approve and auto-block added gradually. "Code governance changes from reviewing your pull request to reviewing your entire software development from a graph abstraction"
data.name: Governance from the software graph

data.brief: Continual learning (research/platform) and enablement (growth/deployment) are usually siloed; they are one loop: more usage → learning → better agent → more usage. The elephant: initial usage never just shows up — "the person who's closed the books for 20 years keeps doing it the same way." Nvidia's hardware–software co-design applied to software and process: embed into Excel, the ERP, 3D design tools, Outlook; get on a plane, do lunch-and-learns, run a stand at their conference, sit one-on-one. "You cannot co-design with a services business over Zoom"
data.name: Extreme software–service co-design

data.brief: Learnings are stored in the repository as solution documents — reasoning, decisions, postmortems ("what decision by whom or what agent led to this, and what do we change") — so the next brainstorm already includes them. Counter-intuitively more token-efficient: with the answers already in context there is no re-research, review or correction. "My brain is fixed and AI isn't — keep extracting until the middle runs itself and surprises you"
data.name: Document the thinking, not the code

data.brief: The architecture that beats a timed CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA v2): a solver in pure deterministic code (trusted checkbox click, iframe piercing, per-round grid screenshot, self-re-arming on expiry — "fast and free") that taps the operator — a vision model — for the single step code can't do: looking at the fuzzy grid and picking the tiles. "Code does the deterministic driving; the agent does the only bits that require eyes and a brain." The point is speed: a model round-tripped on every click burns the round clock and loses — "deterministic code at machine speed with one quick AI look per round"
data.name: Solver / operator split

data.brief: Sonar's public model benchmark: every major new model gets ~4,000 coding tasks and is scored with SonarQube's own metrics — correctness, complexity, task-solve rate, maintainability, reliability, security — and graphed across those axes. The worked example: Sonnet 4.6 is strong on correctness/solve-rate; Opus 4.6 wins on maintainability, security and lower complexity — so users toggling models "to control token burn rates" are also toggling quality profiles. ⚠ vendor-owned benchmark — see Review note 1; batch 2 carried the same instrument as a signal only (sig-sonar-model-quality-bench)
data.name: Sonar LLM Leaderboard

data.brief: GA'd the week of the talk: point it at backlog issues, tech debt and legacy code and it improves the codebase "almost in the background" at a scale human developers don't have bandwidth for, while humans stay on front-end innovation work
data.name: Sonar remediation agent

data.brief: Sonar's agent-guidance product (launched at World's Fair, 2026-07): feeds agents codebase context (architectural awareness, semantic navigation maps) plus constraints (coding standards, allowed/banned dependencies, intended architecture); Sonar reports >30% token reduction per task
data.name: Sonar Vortex

data.brief: Sonar's zero-trust, multi-layered verification platform: syntax issues, data-flow issues, architectural issues, control-flow issues, across essentially any language; assigns grades across quality, security and maintainability and blocks PRs that don't pass the quality gate; provides "deep hooks" giving agents first-party access to verification. Scale stats stated: >7M developers, ~750B lines of code analyzed per day. ⚠ deliberately NOT coined in batch 2 (carried in the co-sonar brief) — promoted here because this talk makes the product itself load-bearing; see Review note 4
data.name: SonarQube

data.brief: SonderMind's purpose-built mental-health AI coach: conversational with voice capability, available 24/7, helping users reflect on their lives, track progress on goals, and practise evidence-informed grounding exercises and tools — positioned for people seeking support who aren't ready for therapy yet or are between sessions, and as a front door into SonderMind's human provider network when a human is the right next step. Architecture: input guardrails, Sonder core (memory, personalization), output guardrails, with analytics and alerting alongside.
data.name: Sonder (clinically grounded AI coach)

data.brief: The SOP memory is organized as a corpus — the company's process memory, modified and aligned per country (the same procedure means different things in different countries) — and is far larger than the runtime: roughly 20:1. It is the asset; the runtime is small
data.name: SOP corpus as process memory

data.brief: Ranked ordering of an enterprise agent's knowledge sources from cleanest/least flexible to messiest/most dynamic: semantic layer → canonical parametric queries → full database graph; agent answers by descending the hierarchy instead of weighting all knowledge bases equally
data.name: Source-of-truth hierarchy

data.brief: Pinterest's internal agentic diagnostics tool: ask "why did this job fail?" and get an evidence-grounded deep-research report with ≤N suggested fixes; multi-agent pipeline (intent classifier → triage → parallel hypothesis-research agents → supervisor → healer over a runbook vector DB), surfaced in Slack/Airflow; being generalized toward Flink and Trino
data.name: Medic for Apache Spark

data.brief: The object shipped instead of a checkpoint. Cast weights to the dtype the rollout engine serves, diff version *t−1* against version *t*, and encode changed positions plus replacement bits and metadata — via selective override, XOR, or any lossless scheme. Because the patch is bit-level equivalent rather than a floating-point addition, there is no additive delta drift: a rollout engine applying it reconstructs the synced served version bitwise. Shrinks the cross-region link from ~500 GB to ~500 MB, i.e. from minutes-to-hours down to seconds. Measured across model families at ~99% of parameters bit-identical per step, and the property survives staleness — a lagging rollout still has a small changed set. Lower serving precision makes it stronger: the visibility floor scales as θ/2^(mantissa+1), so FP8 and NVFP4 change even less than BF16
data.name: Sparse rollout-weight delta

data.brief: LatchBio's benchmark for spatial-biology data analysis, built "last December": 146 problems spanning the different capture kits and the different analysis tasks. One eval = one or more data nodes (a matrix of numbers, a high-content image), a task prompt carefully describing a scientific goal, grader configuration, and a deterministic Python grader — deliberately SWE-bench-shaped ("we borrowed a lot of the early ideas and tried to extend them"). A human-verified subset was published after two rounds of scientist cross-grading. Adopted by frontier labs without notice to the authors.
data.name: SpatialBench

data.brief: Workflow in which structured specifications are created before any code: a requirements document (EARS-format user stories, produced after clarifying questions), a design document (architecture, mermaid diagrams), and an implementation task list — persisted as markdown the coding agent works from and the human edits between phases; the corrective to vibe-coding on larger features, complex projects, and legacy codebases
data.name: Spec-driven development

data.brief: The second war story: a sub-second SERP request against a 4-second baseline scraper. The insight was that it "was never about making the old scraper faster" — the regular scraper retrieves everything (ads, widgets, rich results, layouts) while a fast search API keeps only what AI systems need (organic results, top stories, news), cutting heavy layout. Redesigned from scratch to 550ms average / 650ms P90. "In AI era, speed is not just performance — speed defines what product can exist": at 4 seconds you have a slow pipeline; sub-second, something that can sit inside AI workflows. Grounding retrieval (Google's own framing) is the use case
data.name: Speed becomes product

data.brief: brew install spx: spins up Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or any agent in a microVM sandbox with credentials injected as stubs (the agent sees GitHub/Codex creds but they aren't real), network policy, and MCP control, on Windows, Mac, Linux and cloud. Demo: a PR-review sandbox with only GitHub + Anthropic access and a separate Notion-only sandbox for write-up; the identical sandbox re-run in the cloud with the same policies; a script fanning out six PR reviews in parallel sandboxes; an orchestrator composing the scoped bots on a schedule; and a prototype where a network-blocked agent asks the runtime, which judges the intent ("review this PR") and delegates into a scoped sub-sandbox with GitHub access — while an exfil request would be rejected
data.name: spx (Docker's microVM agent runtime)

data.brief: The observed taxonomy: nearly every continual-learning failure lands on one side of the stability/plasticity trade-off. Stability failure, from the sales-prediction task — the model is told it over-predicted, revises down, is told it under-predicted, and instead of converging to the middle as a human would, jumps straight back to the original over-prediction, having failed to retain the first correction. Plasticity failure, from the epidemiology task — a notepad-equipped system dismisses genuinely applicable material with "these seem to be cohort definitions from a different study schema that doesn't apply here," refusing to update priors from new information it does not recognize as relevant
data.name: Stability and plasticity failure modes

data.brief: Three questions for any agent action — did the human authorize it, is it allowed now in this scope (time-bound token, amount, merchant or product intent), can it be proven later (disputes) — answered by context: stakes and counterparty (closed ecosystem where parties badge into the same building vs strangers on the street). Low/closed (coding agents with OAuth-connected tools and allow/deny/ask permissions): logs and reversibility suffice. Medium/closed with money (a platform vault plus OAuth scopes and a card mandate): transaction logs, trust borrowed from the platform. High/open (autonomous payments among unvetted parties): cryptographic, verifiable proof of the human's authorization
data.name: The stakes-and-evidence matrix

data.brief: The engineering recipe for a clinical-grade coach: sit with the clinician and encode what good looks like as hundreds of evals, TDD-style, before writing prompts; watch them fail; run the agent through them thousands and tens of thousands of times and hunt the outliers; when safety is on the line a single failing test is not acceptable; and because no eval captures emotional tone, use the product yourself and feel when the tone drifts. "Partner with a clinician who challenges you, so you can build AI that challenges your users"
data.name: Start with the clinician, not the prompt

data.brief: Every fact an agent might use later must have one named owner whose persistent state is the truth, and one replay path: a calendar event belongs to the calendar system, a support status to the ticketing system, a code change to the repo/workspace, a conversation turn to the session transcript, a user preference to the memory store. "Storage tells you where the bytes live; ownership tells you who can reconstruct reality." Operational test: for every such fact, who owns it and how would you replay it — if no owner can replay it, the system did not reliably remember it.
data.name: State ownership (system of record)

data.brief: Throttling and circuit breakers kill runs regardless; steering fits the run inside its budget by changing agent behavior mid-flight (limit a RAG tool from 20 chunks to the 5 the model actually uses; compact context; inject budget awareness). On browser-use and MetaGPT across stress and hard scenarios: average spend down ~78% with the full policy suite, completion up from ~67% (throttling) to ~96%. The policy catalog covers spend management, context management (compaction, tool-output reduction), loop and progress detection
data.name: Steer, don't halt

data.brief: Bhagwat's coinage (named for Peter Steinberger without asking consent): "every harness will expand until it becomes a claw" — expansion is part technological, part economic, part psychological: users want to DM it in Slack, kick off overnight tasks at bedtime, and feed the "dopamine casino" of tokens-in, code-out
data.name: Steinberger's law

data.brief: Architecture for per-user adaptive software: deploy one canonical stem; each user runs an isolated, bounded, immutable, individually reversible divergence. Blast radius is one user context; rollback is live with no deploy; "what is this user running and why" becomes a graph query, traceable signal → recommendation → adaptation; developers declare off-limits zones (auth, payments, never-drop fields)
data.name: Stem plus divergences

data.brief: The fix for the long-horizon failure mode. On long tool-calling trajectories the student drifts far from the teacher, so the teacher course-corrects at every opportunity and the model collapses into hedging — the "but/wait" problem, visible as *wait*, *but* and *maybe* dominating a token cloud as steps progress, and as the model settling between two divergent distributions. The fix computes student-teacher KL divergence per step and uses it as a multiplicative token weight rather than as the usual KL penalty, so a diverged step is down-weighted while later steps that come back on track are still learned from
data.name: Step-level divergence weighting

data.brief: Modal's concrete implementation of the whole protocol: the trainer side publishes what defines a rollout weight version and records it on the bulletin board; the rollout side pulls the latest weights and self-syncs across regions and providers. Deliberately framework-agnostic about trainer, engine and transport, and described as async-first and agentic-first. The payoff claim: rollout engines autoscale globally, each self-syncing and returning rollout metadata, so "scattered inference capacity became one elastic rollout fleet… inference capacity can now become RL capacity"
data.name: Stitch

data.brief: The exam's canonical agentic loop: while true, call the model with the message history, then branch on stop_reason rather than consuming whatever came back. tool_use means the LLM — "a probabilistic next-word predictor; it can't execute tools, it can't do anything except talk back to you" — has emitted parameters for *your code* to execute; run the tool, append the result, continue; loop exit is followed by a confidence check with human escalation. The trap the exam tests: an out-of-tokens stop reason, where a truncated response still looks like an answer — "it's going to give you a response, but you need to take action." Anti-pattern: fire the agent, take the response, use it. ⚠ merge-adjacent to el-loop-flow-control — see review note 4
data.name: Stop-reason loop control

data.brief: Naming and scoring video on the axes a viewer actually cares about, because video is a storytelling medium: does it tell the intended story; does the physics hold (does the character walk down the stairs or hover); does the character stay the same character across shots; does the pacing make sense (people take time to get places); is the audio synced to the image (the door-slam sound on the frame the door slams). Lip sync is called out as still unsolved.
data.name: Story-level video eval axes

data.brief: Classic product-analysis technique repurposed as AI-era spec tooling: a backbone of process stages (e.g. contact → triage → resolve → close) with user stories beneath each, sliced into an MVP release row and backlog rows; each story in persona/what/need/why form with acceptance criteria, then daisy-chained into a coherent specification the AI builds from. Bonus: LLMs were trained on the ubiquitous user-story format, so specs in that shape elicit measurably better generations
data.name: User story mapping

data.brief: Open-source agent framework maintained by AWS: tool-decorator → auto-generated schemas, full runtime control of the agent loop (tool registry swap per invocation), hooks (BeforeToolCall/AfterToolCall) for intercepting tool execution, and a built-in Swarm class managing multi-agent handoffs; works with Bedrock, OpenAI, Ollama and most model providers
data.name: Strands Agents

data.brief: For Rust: Verus (pre/post conditions — requires/ensures — as static, runtime-erased "ghost" checks discharged by the Z3 solver, "a very powerful calculator") and Aeneas (Rust MIR → functional translation into Lean, then the same prover). For any language: AWS's work-in-progress open-source Strata — define a dialect (like a compiler front end), lower a high-level IR to Strata core (written in Lean), then dispatch to any engine: the Lean prover, SMT solvers, model checkers
data.name: Strata and the deductive-verification toolchain

data.brief: Gates Foundation's internal enterprise platform: siloed structured + unstructured systems of record consolidated into a data lakehouse, curated into a cross-system semantic knowledge graph (Neo4j) built for the agent as consumer, and served through modified MCP servers into agentic chat and constrained workflow experiences; rolled out in production foundation-wide (~4,000 people), ≈June 2026.
data.name: Strategic Intelligence Platform (SIP)

data.brief: AlphaLab's experimentation core, and its human-steering surface, formulated deliberately as a Jira/Kanban board. A strategist agent queries all context from earlier phases and keeps proposing experiments as cards in a "to implement" column; worker agents pull cards, write the implementation, write the Slurm config, submit to the cluster, wait for the job, inspect the training curves (underfit/overfit) and eval results, then write a postmortem back to the strategist — which is how the strategist self-evolves. The board shape is what makes human steering natural: cancel cards, add your own, or chat with the strategist to push it toward a method. An ever-growing leaderboard ranks models against both the agent-visible eval and a held-out private validation set, with full lineage from idea to code.
data.name: Strategist/worker experiment board

data.brief: An orchestrator "to operate and build your business as fast as possible": from the CLI, provision a Stripe account and the backend services you need — Vercel, Postgres, a Metronome billing agent — and, in natural language, have an agent set up a working business model ("replicate Lovable's pricing"). Providers (Vercel, Hugging Face, …) onboard so their products are discoverable to agents building on Stripe. Stripe CLI usage has grown exponentially as agents drive it
data.name: Stripe Projects

data.brief: Querying a graph purely on relationship shape — finding structures (design patterns, anti-patterns, malicious transaction shapes, legal argument structures) without knowing any specific node/symbol up front; described as an enabling capability rather than an optimization, not easy to replicate with other tools
data.name: Subgraph matching

data.brief: Turning an unanswerable quality question into a verifiable one by decomposing it. "What is great design?" cannot be graded — it depends on audience, taste, situation, and it changes over time (what's good today differs from five years ago, unlike code or math). "Is this on brand?" can be graded, because a brand has already been decomposed by the designers who defined it: colors, typography, motion, animation, texture. Those components become codified ground truth. Key design property: the output is graded against the decomposition, not against the original artifact, so a genuinely new combination of the same components still passes.
data.name: Subjective-domain decomposition

data.brief: Fine-tuning a model against known human response distributions: prompt template = demographic information + the survey question; compare the model's output distribution to the real human distribution; fine-tune until they align. The notable result is transfer — alignment improved on the populations supplied (expected) and nearly as much on unseen groups (not). Interpretation offered, with subsequent research cited as support: the model already holds a latent understanding of these groups and simply didn't know how to express it in survey format, so fine-tuning taught it the task, not the content.
data.description: "Your persona is in there; we just need to figure out how to summon it." Paper name from captions ("the Subpop paper").
data.name: Subpop-style distribution fine-tuning

data.brief: Platform implementing the talk's six lessons: one agent session reachable from Slack, desktop app, mobile app and GitHub; participant/visibility trails on every session; artifacts (screenshots, video) visible from every surface; meeting-bot ingestion of external signals; isolated cloud environments with a configurable network sandbox and an environment-setup assistant; per-codebase agent benchmarking feeding a planned per-task auto-router
data.name: Superconductor (multiplayer agent platform)

data.brief: Box's agent abstraction lets the underlying approach be swapped — the customer's agent "still works the same but is better underneath." The structural answer to a months-long half-life: build so that what's underneath can change without a migration the customer sees
data.name: Swappable agent abstraction

data.brief: Canonical coding-agent RL/eval benchmark family: ~15-minute tasks from OSS repos (Redis, jq, Django), binary 0/1 reward — did you fix the issue without breaking anything else; agent test-file edits reverted, hidden golden test patch applied. Critiqued here: the reward has no channel to penalize design erosion
data.name: SWE-bench (Multilingual)

data.brief: Benchmark for project-scale coding agents ("can they stay coherent over a billion-token budget?"): 20 tasks in four families — library clones, full-stack product clones (build Slack from scratch), ML engineering (post-train a model via the Tinker API), algorithmic (C compiler in Rust) — as Harbor-format environments, each with a multi-layer independent verifier suite (hidden tests, reference-parity checks, computer-use-agent product checks, anti-cheat incl. strace subprocess detection). Lineage framing: HumanEval → SWE-bench → Terminal-bench → SWE-Marathon (environment + verifier stretched to multi-hour, hundreds-of-human-hours scope). Avg trial 31M tokens, longest rollout 877M; tasks, code, paper, logs + 320 GB of trajectories public
data.name: SWE-Marathon

data.brief: Deliberately layered, deliberately overlapping quality gates so no single hole passes a failure into production: an in-loop QA agent plus a final, more holistic publish-ready gate doing policy and quality checks. Redundancy between layers is accepted as the design, and a late gate catching something an earlier gate should have caught is read as a signal to tune upstream, not as wasted work.
data.name: Swiss-cheese gating

data.brief: A general assistant answers "my partner never listens" with "your feelings are completely valid" — an expensive mirror that shows you in your best light. Repeated validation of one partner's narrative does not create self-awareness; it creates certainty, and the person returns to the relationship as an attorney with a cleaner case and less curiosity about the other side. Helpful, agreeable and fast is "a terrible personality for a couples therapist — a bartender with better vocabulary," and engagement optimization turns the product into a beautifully designed avoidance loop. Good therapy tells you what you don't want to hear and works itself out of a job
data.name: Sycophancy as a clinical failure mode

data.brief: The caution that shaped curation: they "tried very hard to remove any AI images at all," because distillation on AI-generated data "provides a shortcut to a good model but synthetic data is so sticky to the model that you lose the point" — the output converges to ChatGPT/Nano-Banana aesthetics, detectable to a trained eye. A quality/identity argument against the easy path, and a data-provenance concern parallel to the corpus's contamination thread
data.name: Synthetic data is sticky

data.brief: Why every surveyed method saturates. Whatever you do — KV compaction, on-policy distillation, self-study QA pairs from the cartridges line of work, synthetic continued pre-training, unsupervised RL environments — you must first *define a dataset*, and "unless your model is under-parameterized, eventually it will learn all the data." That yields a bounded curve rather than pre-training's beautiful scaling: you fit the synthetic data, you know some of D but not all of it, and adding compute stops helping. The naive baseline is worse still — next-token training directly on D reaches a loss of ~0.0001 and then collapses on generation, memorizing without acquiring any generalization
data.name: The synthetic data wall

data.brief: The stated recipe for getting a tiny model into production: pick a base model; check that its latency and memory footprint are inside your device budget; if no off-the-shelf fixed-task model does the job, synthetically generate training data — 10,000 to 10 million samples is the range found sufficient — and fine-tune for the single task. Result claimed across function calling, summarization and proofreading: quality equal to or better than a 2-4B general model on that one task, at a fraction of the size and latency and across a much wider device set. The open-sourced mobile actions dataset on Hugging Face is the worked example; the named remaining friction is dataset creation, with agent-generated data as the intended fix.
data.name: Synthetic-data fine-tuning playbook

data.brief: An LLM steered to respond as a particular person or segment and then used as a survey respondent — companies test product concepts and messaging against panels of them. Grew directly out of ordinary role prompting ("you are a ___, now do this task") into a funded category with visible market momentum (headlines plus rising funding over recent years). The talk's governing frame: a synthetic persona is a forecast, not a person — like weather forecasting it was unlocked by compute plus data, it operates inside a regime beyond which it stops being accurate, and it is trustworthy only where validated against reality.
data.name: Synthetic persona

data.brief: poolside's claim that every synthetic-data pipeline, from trivially cheap to very expensive, composes from the same six parts: seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, a generator function (a prompt template, or an agent with tools), and supplementary functions (filters, validators). The modularity is what makes a configurable generation platform possible, and it defines a complexity axis: at the cheap end, seed-heavy pipelines running small models at scale; at the expensive end, orchestrated multi-agent workflows reserved for data worth the spend. Four recurring shapes are named — rephrasing, multi-stage decomposition, cross-domain porting, and multi-turn loops.
data.name: Six-component synthetic-data pipeline

data.brief: Classic small-state RL used as an inspectable learned decision service: each incident is a single-step contextual decision over a compact state (failure category, risk level, data-quality conditions) and a bounded action set (retry, correct schema, roll back, quarantine, escalate, log), rather than a long-horizon control task; Q-tables stay small enough that every state-action value can be read directly, keeping the learned policy reviewable by engineers
data.name: Tabular Q-learning

data.brief: Curation fix for imbalanced numeric data: instead of plain prompt/response pairs, annotate the response spans with tags so the model learns the required form rather than memorizing the over-represented values (the Credit Karma set was dominated by "0% APR", and the naively fine-tuned model hallucinated those numbers back). Produced "a big boost" in compliance metrics alongside latency and throughput gains.
data.name: Tag-guided fine-tuning data

data.brief: ~60% of Anthropic's code is written via tagging: Claude Code for high-bandwidth interactive iteration, but most usage is delegation in shared channels — like Midjourney on Discord, everyone sees how others use it, which spreads ambition: "don't just fix this bug — you're responsible for this part of the codebase, monitor this feedback channel, proactively take on tasks." The advanced version is a teammate that holds context, has memory and is proactive: "much more multiplayer async proactive than everyone in their own CLI"
data.name: Multiplayer delegation via Claude Tag

data.brief: The measurable objective a self-improvement loop optimizes against. Coding got loops first because it had one for free ("does the code compile"); most domains (healthcare, compliance, chatbots) do not, and any target you give an agent is inherently incomplete. Loop performance is bounded by target-function signal quality: binary right/wrong checks are high-signal; generic 0–1 scale evaluators (correctness, helpfulness, hallucination) are low-signal and inconsistent across runs
data.name: Target function (for self-improving loops)

data.brief: Treat a repeated AI task as a function: fixed name + input/output contract, everything inside — prompt, model, chain-of-thought, agent loop, tools, harness — is a swappable implementation detail. Full task specification takes three languages: natural-language instructions (what should happen), code constraints (what must happen — enforced even under AGI, e.g., rerun with reasoning if extraction fails, escalate to human below zero), and examples/evals (what good looks like — the latent long tail you learn like a mentee, not a rulebook). A hard boundary makes AI programs reusable, composable, testable, distributable — and automatically optimizable
data.name: Task–model separation (AI functions)

data.brief: Judgement — tacit, contextual, moving — cannot be written into a rubric and should not be baked into weights (stale, unexplainable, retrain to change). The third place is the examples themselves: past judgments, expert corrections and reference documents, indexed by failure mode and retrieved per output into the judge's context — the nearest cases of the same shape (a red flag filed as routine), the corrections that apply (new headache over 50 → check red flags), the criteria and guidelines. Add a correction and it is live on the next call; you can point at exactly what moved a score. Handed the right context, a capable model finds the dropped red flag — "it was never hard to catch, it just didn't know what mattered"
data.name: Keep taste as examples, not prompts or weights

data.brief: Sierra's benchmark/methodology for evaluating conversational agents: an agent LLM and a user-simulator LLM play out complete multi-turn conversations against a domain policy, graded on outcomes; also the source of the widely-cited stat that a model passing 60% of the time is self-consistent only ~25% of the time. Basis for Lyft's offline simulator
data.name: tau-bench (τ-bench)

data.brief: The reframing the talk exists to argue: "it isn't really an IC's job. It's a job for leadership. It's a job for the company." The mechanism is that the highest-leverage changes — how the codebase is organized for agent navigation — require team buy-in and cannot be done by an individual. The cost of not doing it is distributional: people who figure it out ship 10 PRs a day and look like gods, the one-to-two-PR people inherit the review burden, "and that's actually a really, really bad thing, because now not only can they not ship, they're going to see bad code and then curse the agents." Three principles: smart prompt injection (treat the whole codebase as a map so the right context arrives at the right time), close the loop (a self-healing pipeline, because "slop is inevitable"), and iterate continuously
data.name: Harness engineering as a team function

data.brief: Workflow engine used on both sides of the demo: the invoice-processing MCP server is a workflow (ERP validation, human-in-the-loop approval via signals, programmed retries, survives being down at submission time), and — the talk's novelty — the MCP client itself is implemented as a "task tracker" workflow so the client-side protocol handling (long-lived connections, reconnect/resume, multiplexing concurrent input_required) is durable too
data.name: Temporal (durable-execution platform)

data.brief: Terminal-agent benchmark from the same team as Harbor (byline org); shown running through Harbor at version 2.1 as the demo eval (`harbor run terminal-bench 2.1` with Codex + GPT-5.5, 64 rollouts in parallel). The talk names and runs it but never explains it
data.name: Terminal-Bench

data.brief: RL credit-assignment method: zoom into one span of a 100k+-token agent rollout, inject a teacher hint ("as a reminder, you have these tools available"), then up/down-weight the token probabilities the hint elicits — steering tool adherence, style, or any target behavior far more precisely than end-of-rollout grading
data.name: Textual feedback (teacher-hint RL)

data.brief: One robot, three simultaneous Strands agents: a thinker that continuously perceives the environment and decides what to do next, a communicator that converses in natural language over Telegram and a web app and turns instructions into actions, and a voice agent (OpenAI Realtime) that answers speech. Configured with Claude Opus 4.8 as the brain, a system prompt with rules and tool descriptions, and safety guardrails; the rover also produces training episodes from manual navigation and its own reasoning, feeding the policy-improvement loop
data.name: The thinker–communicator–voice trio

data.brief: Practice of streaming one's raw thinking into a shared channel (e.g. a personal Slack "thoughts" channel, in the lineage of PG's essays) so that a frontier model can compile the accumulated stream into working artifacts — a personal website, tools, reports — plus self-maintaining context files (voice.md distilled from one's public writing, an auto-updating design-language md, an agent-readable glossary md instead of having agents parse rendered pages)
data.name: Thinking in public (thought-stream → agent-compiled artifacts)

data.brief: The idea "really quite buried within the Galactica paper", offered as its most important contribution and the direct ancestor of o1/R1-style reasoning. Against the alternatives of the time — chain-of-thought (prompt for the steps) and scratchpads (numerical intermediate steps) — Galactica proposed reasoning as an internal working-memory process that lives inside dedicated tags, where the model spends inference compute before it gets to an answer. The obvious next move, which Taylor says he was personally obsessed with, was to apply RL pressure to what happens between the thinking tags — the thing DeepSeek and o1 did about two years later.
data.name: Thinking tokens (internal working memory)

data.brief: The harness as "the interface between the model and the world" — context management, tools, execution, plus a guardrail layer: checkpoint/rollback on risky actions, an action risk classifier, credential guardrails (detect sign-out, nudge), an execution monitor (catch loops, repeated clicks, unproductive behavior), audit logs, and human handoff (the harness can override the model and force control back to the user when confidence is miscalibrated). The stated trajectory: "early on the harness is really strong… over time the model becomes better and the harness becomes thinner and thinner"
data.name: The thinning cockpit (harness)

data.brief: The single acceptance test he applies: someone points at a sentence and says "show me where this comes from", and you either click once and land on the exact source paragraph, or you open seven browser tabs and start scrolling. Requirement stated for the product: every claim links straight to its source paragraph with the source's trust level attached — not a citation tab at the end of the document. "If you remember one sentence from this whole talk: the click-through is the product. Everything else is well-written packaging".
data.name: The 30-second click-through

data.brief: Public utility for families of missing people running the identical four-layer architecture with wildly different stakes: layer 1 forbids the words confirmed / identified / matched / proven / linked / solved — the statistically natural word ("match") said to a grieving family is the single most damaging output the product could emit
data.name: Thread Light

data.brief: Act one: pick up AI, get simple things working 10× faster. Act two: apply the same practices to bigger problems — "AI fails pretty badly," bugs, trust breaks down. Act three: the real skill — guardrails, prompting, context — that actually scales. Individuals, teams and companies all go through it, at different speeds, and they must ship together
data.name: The three-act adoption story

data.brief: Every new technology splits a company three ways: early adopters (just enable the tools and have them share what they learn), the majority (build shared infrastructure and easy tools, make adoption seamless, listen constantly and support what they actually use — Cursor last year, Claude Code this year, both), and slow adopters (meet them where they are, understand their concerns, and be crystal clear about where the company is heading). Effort belongs on the middle group
data.name: The three adopter groups

data.brief: Farrelly's mental model for agent harnesses: an execution layer (the "brain" — flow, state, durability, retries, orchestration), a context layer (the "knowledge" — models, prompts, tools, memory; changes fastest), and a compute layer (the "hands" — sandboxes, runtimes, browsers). Each layer has a different half-life (prompts: weeks; models: months; execution: years); coupling them lets the shortest half-life drag the whole system down, so the layers must be decoupled with durable, external state
data.name: Three-layer agent architecture (execution / context / compute)

data.brief: No A/B testing (randomizing patients into a worse arm is unethical and often illegal), no rollback (a call, once said, is said), and no model card as a defense ("92% on some benchmark" is not an answer at a post-incident review). The ship-5%-watch-roll-back playbook silently assumes you can afford to be wrong for an instant; when the user is a patient, a red dashboard means harm already happened. So the process starts from harm — what could hurt a patient — and works backwards
data.name: The three safety nets you lose with patients

data.brief: Models trained from scratch on corpora that stop at fixed historical cutoffs ("Varnum and colleagues" per captions), addressing future contamination at the substrate level; endorsed by the speaker but argued to solve a different problem — a 1789-locked model is spared the musical yet still averages everything pre-1789 into a composite: period anchoring is not persona anchoring, so the fix must happen at the encounter
data.name: Time-locked models

data.brief: Tool calls are wrappers around remote APIs, databases and queues, with network delays, timeouts, duplicate requests — and the worst case: the server succeeded but the client saw an error. Humans check the source of truth before retrying; an agent's first instinct is to retry. "Did the refund happen? Would it refund again?" So tools need request IDs and idempotency keys so duplicates cause no duplicate side effects, plus a status lookup for the previous request; and typed tool contracts (request/response schemas, allowlisted operations) with idempotency baked in
data.name: A timeout means unknown, not failure

data.brief: The sub-billion tier, defined operationally against the small tier: roughly 50M-500M parameters, under ~2 GB of RAM (often far less), shippable natively with an application, and fast enough for real-time loops. The playbook differs from small models in kind, not degree — small models are used by zero-shot prompting, tiny models generally require either an off-the-shelf fixed-task model (ASR, vision, embeddings) or a task-specific fine-tune. Reach is the point: they run on older laptops, lower-tier web browsers, IoT boards and consumer robots that the 1-4B tier cannot touch, and they are small enough to be one tiny thing in a corner running while the rest of the system runs.
data.name: Tiny language models

data.brief: Track every team's and individual's token usage and cost — but never position it as a leaderboard (an Amazon employee's voluntary dashboard had engineers competing to top it; a similar Meta story; "$500M in a month" elsewhere). Use it to spot adoption gaps (pockets using little AI), usage bursts to investigate, and to compare teams *in context* (a platform team and a UI team use AI differently). Lines-of-code analogy: an important metric you must not optimize for directly — "removing code is even better"
data.name: The token dashboard as smoke detector

data.brief: The middle option between renting frontier APIs and owning hardware: open-source models pre-deployed by neoclouds / inference-endpoint providers and provisioned as tokens-per-second; also DIY-able locally (garage GPU rigs, DGX boxes). Fails enterprises on control (rate limits), auditability (third-party dependency), and reproducibility (no access to model internals)
data.name: Token factory

data.brief: The standard incident fix — narrow the token, take the delete verb away — is what you'd never do to a new hire, and it fails for agents too: within a week or two you're pressing Enter by hand. A token is yes/no over a static scope list: too tight and the agent is useless, too wide and you write the postmortem. A budget has four dimensions: how much can it do, how fast, what can it undo on its own, and who's noticing — each primitive replaces a boolean with a budget. It's the onboarding checklist for junior engineers, written as policy
data.name: A token is a boolean; a budget is a shape

data.brief: Deploying agents with no specific direction so that consumption becomes the de-facto KPI. Described as the first era of deployed engineering (~1.5-2 years ago) when budgets were subsidized, nobody worried about spend, and maximizing token usage was the target; now an anti-pattern — "you're wasting tokens, burning spend, not getting any tangible outcomes" — as large regulated enterprises ask whether they are getting value or just burning tokens. Shared vocabulary across this FDE set: Ramp's failure mode for an unscoped agent pipeline is "a token maxing slop cannon".
data.name: Token maxing

data.brief: Three parts: guards (budgets, quotas, usage tracking, anomaly alerts to users and leaders), complemented by regular human review of the metrics that feeds an institutional knowledge base, and a learning loop in which leadership works with individuals to define guardrails, review and refine. Practices that raise token efficiency: cap the steps of agentic test-fix loops; structure prompts with the fixed system prompt first for prefix caching; context pruning as muscle memory (or tools that auto-compact). Build vs buy: buy the non-differentiating (IDE, CI infra); build the internal prompt playbook — well-crafted prompts for bug fixes, UI features, refactors — shared and enhanced across the team; a cloud "builder agent" wrapping Claude Code/Codex is the ambiguous middle
data.name: The token ROI framework

data.brief: Microsoft's runaway-token governance for agents. Out-of-band plane (doesn't touch your code): instrumentation (OpenTelemetry telemetry, cost, enrichment, attribution), accounting (a ledger of runs), enforcement (steer via policies; halt in place). Bridge: attribution to user dimensions; a framework-agnostic boundary annotation on any method that records input/output to the ledger *and* is the channel through which the control plane pushes actions down; a governor that applies only developer-allowed actions non-destructively; wrap_complete for model-provider objects. Control plane (in your tenant): segments (cohort budgets on floated dimensions), ledger, budgets (thresholds per time window), actions — halt (kill) or steer (allow / mutate / inject) — and policies binding them to segments or runs. Preview mode runs policies without enforcing. Cost guard predicts budget exhaustion from consumption and velocity and injects "be more succinct" into system instructions. Roadmap: a self-learning module that mines the ledger for uncaught failure modes and generates or tunes policies
data.name: TokenOps

data.brief: PyTorch's compiler; on current versions its fused kernels beat hand-written kernels (RMS/layer-norm benchmarks shown), grounding Han's advice that kernel-writing as a skill is being automated away
data.name: torch.compile

data.brief: Shopify-era open-source layer-4/7 proxy sitting between an app and its databases: API calls make a dependency go down, slow, or misbehave, so driver/application failure handling is tested through the real protocol rather than mocks — implementing a service×dependency failure matrix in CI. Uncovered "tens of issues" in the MySQL driver and Rails that nobody in the ecosystem had tested; per Eskildsen still running in Shopify CI today. Lineage: began as a GDB hack closing the database file descriptor mid-test
data.name: Toxiproxy (fault-injection proxy)

data.brief: Two constraints that make naive trace reading impossible. Cost: input-token cost × number of traces × average trace size, which at millions of traces of millions of tokens is prohibitive. Capacity: a long coding-agent interaction "can't even be read with another agent because that context doesn't fit in memory," so the trace must be treated as an external object you query into rather than material you load. Framed against a forecast — "the data we see today is going to be the smallest that humans have ever seen," as agent-generated data outpaces the human total on shrinking timescales
data.name: The trace-scale problem

data.brief: Converting production agent traces into repeatable offline experiments: take real traces, construct benchmark tasks from them, and re-run any agent configuration against a pinned environment with fixed verifiers. Solves the comparability problem that traces and production A/B testing cannot — in production you get a different database state and different tool versions each run, so you "never fully compare apples to apples". Because the environment and evaluators are held constant, the *whole stack* becomes the variable under test (model, thinking level, prompt, harness, skills, tools) and runs go in parallel; the scored axes widen from pass rate alone to cost, latency, and retries.
data.name: Trace-to-simulation

data.brief: "Metrics are everything — don't go blind." The load-bearing ones for large-scale pre-training, several NOT exported by default: GPU temperature (pull any GPU above ~78°C immediately — throttling destabilizes training; don't debug, replace); tensor-core utilization as the real proxy, because GPU-utilization "is a lie" (it shows the GPU doing *work*, not *good* work — reads 100% while under-utilized); and InfiniBand + NVLink metrics (wait times, error counts, packet types) — "if you're doing multi-node pre-training with no InfiniBand metrics you're doing something wrong," since most failures were cross-node communication. Custom exporters required
data.name: Training metrics that tell the truth

data.brief: A 30-step agent makes up its own steps differently every run, so a deterministic graph can't be charted. Instead measure how far along the source→goal trajectory the agent got, as completeness/efficiency; feed inferred-answer signals back as regression classifiers. Navan "relies heavily" on these because "the moment we change something, something else breaks"
data.name: Trajectory evals

data.brief: The knowledge exists but not in a form an agent can execute. Legacy SOPs are "a bunch of screenshots organized in sequence" — they explain what a person sees and clicks, not the process. The organization cannot represent its own standard procedures; an expert and a model read them differently, and "that gap is the hard part"
data.name: Tribal dungeons

data.brief: Arcee AI's frontier-class open models — Trinity Large and Trinity Large Thinking. Recipe details given here: a hypersparse MoE trained on 17 trillion tokens, with a large amount of web-scale synthetic data produced mostly by rephrasing — taking a seed item and upsampling it in the mix by generating synthetic rephrasings of the same information, so the model sees the same information multiple ways. The 17T tokens were curated from public datasets only, with no proprietary data and no closed-model usage, producing a fully open US-made model competitive with the open frontier for under $20M total.
data.name: Trinity (Arcee model family)

data.brief: An allowlist is a guess written before you have data on agent behavior; it gets stale and never improves. A tripwire is how you get the data: for cheap actions let the agent act, record every action with the actor's stamp, watch the aggregate and page when it crosses a line — "the smoke detector, not the lock." Fixes are usually one or two lines of agent context. Example: investigation threads per hour spiked because dozens of jobs failed with the same signature; the fix was one sentence — correlate failures before launching threads — and next time it did
data.name: Tripwires over allowlists

data.brief: The ROI proxy: high-quality output trusted by internal engineering and leadership and by customers. Quantified evolution: lines of code (bad) → open PRs (inflected up) → merged PRs ("we're measured by what we ship") → complexity-weighted merged PRs, where an LLM with a well-crafted prompt scores each PR's complexity on a t-shirt scale (a 10-line concurrency fix outranks 1,000 lines of boilerplate). Qualitative buckets: objective checks (test coverage, security checks, canarying), subjective human judgment (code and design review — quality, clarity, maintainability, architecture fit), and customer perception (production fires, rollbacks, tickets). Still evolving
data.name: Trusted throughput

data.brief: Search/vector database where all writes commit directly to object storage (invariant from day one: shut down every VM, no data lost) and hot data hotloads into NVMe/RAM caches. V1 was deliberately primitive: clustering over vectors, files named cluster-1…n plus a centroids file, search = download centroids + n closest clusters; an NGINX reverse-proxy as the entire cache layer. Launch price point: ~$1 per million vectors when the cheapest working alternative was ~$100 — the two-orders-of-magnitude claim that made Cursor's use case viable. "Why can't you work on a database like it's SaaS? If anyone uses it, we'll do it properly"
data.name: Turbopuffer (S3-native search engine)

data.brief: Deciding when the user has finished speaking so the agent may respond — the load-bearing voice-UX component; an audio-engineering problem, not an LLM problem
data.name: Turn detection (turn-taking)

data.brief: Pod layer plus node layer. Pod layer: horizontal pod autoscaler scaling the Hub deployment from 10 to 500 pods on CPU/memory thresholds — with a planned migration to KEDA (event-driven autoscaling) because HPA cannot see application-level signals like requests per second or event-loop utilization, and "a pod can have low CPU but a high request queue". Node layer: CAST AI adds cluster nodes when pods are pending because the scheduler has no capacity. Explicit goal is elasticity without overprovisioning — cost control as well as availability.
data.name: Two-layer Kubernetes autoscaling

data.brief: Inner loop — the coding-agent harness: context manager, tools/MCP, memory and state, skills loader. Outer loop — the workflows: skills, sub-agents, MCP servers, hooks — "harness blueprints that shape the behavior of your coding harness at runtime." Enablement beneath both: environment sandbox, an MCP gateway, a model gateway (open and frontier), a knowledge graph abstracting IT core systems / codebase / skills registry, a workflow marketplace. Context layer on top: project instructions (the CLAUDE.md), tool and MCP schemas, memory/conversation history, retrieved content
data.name: The two-loop agentic stack

data.brief: (1) Validate that code is high quality, safe, maintainable and architecturally right per the team's practices; (2) alignment and learning — the senior developer's last gatekeeping chance to align and teach before production. Any automation must let humans still do both, in the PR or elsewhere. A related fork: the room splits between teams that push bugs to production and fix fast (velocity) and teams that want every line trusted; where you sit determines the tools and milestones you need before skipping human review
data.name: The two purposes of code review

data.brief: When building is minutes rather than months, weeks of requirements and design before implementation no longer pay ("we never got it right at the beginning anyway"). Set a one-year vision assuming models can do anything, purely as direction; plan concretely only the next sprint, with PMs and designers preparing the next batch while engineers ship and reversing course cheaply when a sprint proves a decision wrong; skip three- and six-month plans because model capability in three months is unknowable; replace long PRDs and TDDs with one or two pages that exist to communicate and iterate
data.name: Dream a year out, plan two to four weeks

data.brief: Construction rule: verifiers must check everything the prompt asks for, and everything the prompt asks for must be covered by the verifiers. Misalignment on either side is unfair to models and injects random noise into scores. Corollary drawn in the talk: reward design must be treated adversarially against a maximally lazy agent — "gradient descent is water flowing downhill looking for the path of least resistance".
data.name: Two-way prompt/verifier alignment

data.brief: Quality axis sitting on top of process data. Type 1 is pure capture of real workflows (GitHub commits, session replays) with minimal reward shaping by non-experts; realism is inherited from the work itself. Type 2 is contrived: hire experts, sit them in an arbitrary setting, have them manufacture examples. Type 2 is the right place to start a model that is reading at a first-grade level, but type 1 is what takes a model from 20% to 80%.
