Structural consequence: a dataset is only valuable as far as the frontier has moved, so the only durable supply is a live business you partner with, not a dead startup's codebase. The dirty secret of the industry is that everybody sells type 2 and bills it as type 1.
data.name: Type-1 vs type-2 data (non-contrived vs contrived)

data.brief: "The job of the kernel is to make bad actions impossible, not just unlikely." Two boundaries between an agent and the world: typed tool calls (no calling tools that don't exist) and typed events between agents — "non-negotiable, you get a lot of errors just from this." Structured outputs are the enforcement; ~20% of events were rejected before typing
data.name: Typed boundaries: the kernel makes bad actions impossible

data.brief: Typed superset of JavaScript; per the talk, the default output language of coding agents and the emerging language of the agentic application layer — one language and one type system (e.g. Zod schemas) from UI through backend to agent loop, on top of NPM
data.name: TypeScript

data.brief: Execution traces showed agents burning time and tokens finding basic context in the monorepo — where a service lives, its dependencies, owners, patterns — scattered across 20–30 systems each needing its own skill or MCP. One context graph of "how Uber runs": 150 unique node and edge types, 40 million entries, from mobile app builds to backend to the data lake, design docs, Jira, incidents and bugs. Plugged into skills for on-call RCAs, planning, data analysis, security scans; example (cash trips in India → SQL) shows "massive improvement in tokens, turns and latency" with the graph
data.name: Uber's context graph

data.brief: One OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint for every internal use case, coding harness and external use case: SPIRE identity/auth, a data anonymizer redacting 20+ PII types (no PII leaves the perimeter by default), an AI guard of five specialized safety/policy models — all under 100 ms — plus caching and token optimization. Every request is attributed to a catalog project, caller, user and team, in real time and in the data lake, enabling spend guardrails across the portfolio; audit logs and session traces feed benchmarking and self-improvement loops. 800+ projects, 100M+ model requests/day, frontier and self-hosted open models
data.name: Uber's model gateway

data.brief: Shopify's (with Google) protocol for agent-driven checkout: an agent can locate shops, list candidate products, place and pay for an order and receive a receipt and tracking without a human filling forms — demonstrated as a terminal purchase of a sub-$10 Father's Day gift with the agent's memory supplying preferences and address
data.name: UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol)

data.brief: The thesis under the spec: websites stop being destinations and decompose into branded, interactive UI atoms that a personal assistant composes with the user's own context — the calendar chunk, the storefront chunk, the map chunk — so the user never leaves the assistant. The three-way payoff as the speakers state it: the user keeps a brand they recognize and trust, the brand keeps its identity instead of being reduced to text, and the host gains capabilities it didn't build. The structural consequence: no application controls the user journey anymore — every interaction routes through the chat, which is also what makes the journey auditable
data.name: UI atomization (the agentic web)

data.brief: The platform's evolution: UIs so non-engineers can contribute; then stable table APIs (scores, datasets) so engineers build without being blocked on the central team; then, with coding agents, workflow-first — S&O and PMs navigate the platform and run operations themselves. "As self-served as possible so people aren't blocked by our team"
data.name: UI-first → API-first → workflow-first

data.brief: He doesn't disclose it's a bot ("if people know it's a bot they might close the issue"; it posts exactly what he posted manually). Out of thousands of issues, two negative replies ("please close this slop"); researchers from Apple and Google DeepMind replied to "him"; a Chinese OCR company migrated all its models; a trending paper's issue got 60+ upvotes; agents completing Margaret Mitchell's model-card template even credited "Niels, community science team." Increasingly "people use an agent to reply to my agents." Guard against slop with evals (Hamel Husain's LLM-evals FAQ)
data.name: Undisclosed agent outreach and its reception

data.brief: The lens for sizing the other primitives: *can the agent put it back by itself?* and *how bad if it's wrong?* Verbs ask whether you'd notice the failure; undo asks whether you can recover. If both answers are fine, log it and let it go; if either is no, a second key held by someone other than the agent plus an audit record. Feature flags: the agent's key has the full dial on canary (ramp 0→100, toggle on bug reports) but only *proposes* production promotion — the second key is a scoped production key, not a new auth system
data.name: The undo test

data.brief: AI-forward teams coexist with teams still experimenting or who lost confidence. Reduced developer agency: engineers who took pride in flow-state coding sit in a prompt cycle waiting on output — less fun, burnout. The best engineers become the bottleneck: the ones holding all the context in their heads are "mental duct tape" for every place agents fail, so they carry the burden, see the problems first, and are slowest to adopt. Communication inflation: docs, Slack and email are 3–4× longer and 2–3× more numerous while saying the same, and quality markers are harder to read
data.name: The frictions of uneven adoption

data.brief: The talk's diagnosis of who gets to work at the frontier, credited to Rosanne Liu. Science's professionalization moved discovery from independent "gentleman scientists" to institutions, and in AI it compressed into one route: the right PhD programme, the right industry lab, sufficiently interesting work, and only then a contribution to the frontier — "a very aggressively filtered system" where being uncurious about the right problem at the right time excluded you entirely. Double-compounded in AI by compute, producing the GPU-poor/GPU-rich split and a handful of labs building the technology everyone uses. Illustrated with a Stanford map of significant breakthroughs showing whole regions of the world absent
data.name: The unreasonably narrow path

data.brief: A "project unship" channel asks what should leave the product: styles (small usage, prescriptive) were unshipped because skills do it better — "take the primitives of one generation of AI and unship or supplant them with the next." The biggest deletion candidate is product complexity itself: the code / cowork / chat distinctions don't interoperate, can't delegate to each other, and "the average person could not explain why those are different" — pasting a Cowork plan into Claude Code "is a 2020 workflow that shouldn't exist." Claude Design's next steps: surfaces that talk to each other, and the blur from design to persistent, shareable app
data.name: Unship the previous generation's primitives

data.brief: The agentic security shift: in the old world the risk was a program misusing a credential; now a ticket, email, document, web page or Slack message is not just data — it can be an instruction with downstream actions, and the attacker "doesn't need code execution, just the text the agent will read." Willison's lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted input, external communication) plus a fourth element — the action layer. Useful enterprise agents want all of it: a help-desk agent needs private data, reads untrusted tickets, and acts across identity, device and SaaS systems. "That's not a bug — that's the product spec," so the architecture must assume the content is adversarial
data.name: Untrusted text causes trusted action

data.brief: Just-in-time context service inside Upside's product: before touching data, an agent consults the librarian — company documentation, a curated library of knowledge items (e.g., fiscal year runs Feb–Apr; "pipeline" means stage ≥ 2), and the schema of prior failed queries — then answers with citations. Prevents the confident-wrong default (assuming quarter = Jan–Mar on created-date).
data.name: Upside Librarian

data.brief: Uber's in-house multi-agent code review engine. Surfaces — GitHub, Phabricator, and the agent loop — feed one uReview service that takes review requests, ingests user feedback and routes; multiple generators tuned for different cost/performance points (a single-file "find the logic bugs" reviewer; a multi-file deep reviewer per monorepo with its style guides and anti-patterns baked in; few-shot AI linters that fetch deterministic context and apply rules; custom team agents linked to a knowledge base, past PRs and a review skill), plus pluggable third-party review systems for benchmarking; then post-processing that rates, categorizes, filters and deduplicates so engineers get only high-confidence actionable comments. Built in-house for Phabricator support, inner-loop parity for agents, distributed ownership, risk/complexity-aware routing, and guaranteed security/compliance review on everything
data.name: uReview

data.brief: Retrieval scoring = semantic similarity to the current task weighted by whether each memory historically helped or hurt task outcomes; outcome becomes a first-class signal in retrieval re-ranking rather than similarity alone; components include a credit/re-ranking hyperparameter (lambda); known failure modes: cold start (pure semantic search until reviews accumulate), utility drift, and noisy review labels making utility noisy
data.name: Utility score (outcome-weighted retrieval)

data.brief: The nature of the work shifted: the team no longer designs entire flows and pixels; it designs the schema, curates the catalog, writes rules, generates synthetic queries that map to components, and specifies interaction patterns. A hit for non-technical PMs and designers; the leader's framing is people, product and a lightweight process, with the people element the hardest
data.name: The UX team designs schemas, not pixels

data.brief: The chosen high-value target: V8 executes JavaScript for Chrome, and also runs Edge, Node.js and Cloudflare Edge Workers (where each tenant is a separate thread), so JavaScript — attacker-controlled by design, via any malicious website — is the input surface. V8 has an internal sandbox in which vulnerabilities are expected: crashing an in-sandbox object means nothing, so value comes only from an out-of-sandbox escape, which typically requires chaining multiple vulnerabilities. Bounties start at $10,000 and reach $100,000, "or millions on the black market".
data.name: V8 (Chrome JavaScript/Wasm engine)

data.brief: VisualLabs' elicitation sequence: start from how value is created (whose problem, what winning looks like), then the process and underlying architecture that support that value, and only then system design — never "build us an agent that handles support" first; paired with four screening questions (whose problem is this? what does winning look like? what would make them refuse to use it? would it change a decision?) whose answers live in a markdown file in the repo so the AI has the context
data.name: VAD (Value → Architecture → Design)

data.brief: The token-waste finding: teams check only content size and HTTP status, then feed all pages to the model; when 10 pages open and only 3 are valid, "we waste 70% of the tokens" letting the model tell e-shop content from a CAPTCHA. The first instinct — compress — is wrong: "the problem is not compression, the content is not valid." A scraper API that fails loudly with an explicit error on blocks means invalid pages never reach the model; markdown output means no raw HTML does either. "No cure, no pay": failed fetches cost nothing
data.name: Validate content before the LLM sees it

data.brief: Reintroducing a learned critic to fix what GRPO cannot handle at long horizons. Benefits stated: reduces gradient variance (which otherwise scales with trajectory length); operates at the trajectory level, which "fits compaction very well"; encourages batch diversity; and enables bootstrapping — generating an expectation of the return before the episode ends, described as "like dopamine in the human brain", so the trainer can update without waiting for a rollout that may run for weeks. Costs: it is more complicated than GRPO, you must train a second model alongside the policy, and bootstrapping introduces value-model bias — a straight trade against GPU idle time.
data.name: Value model / critic for long-horizon RL

data.brief: The delivery platform: spin up and monitor agents with governance and evals built in, deliberately layered on top of the customer's existing systems of record (NetSuite, Dynamics, SAP, Salesforce) rather than requiring migration off them — the stated wedge for enterprises "too large to move". Hosts the workflows FDEs build and, increasingly, the FD agent that helps build them.
data.name: Varick OS

data.brief: Deterministic post-completion verification harness for coding agents: a Claude hook fires when the session ends, runs config-defined test cases against the agent's claimed-done output, and on failure feeds "this is failing — try again" back to the agent until checks pass; positioned as an enforcement contract (given task → fulfill these checks; the middle is developer-defined), runnable at every level (conversation end, pre-commit, multi-agent steps, async agents, optional LLM-as-judge); public
data.name: Vector Harness

data.brief: Named team pathology: "the stress caused by sudden output increases thanks to AI… the result is output without impact." Four presenting symptoms, each individual-level and magnified at team scale: (1) too many PRs to merge (merge queue breaks down); (2) moving in many directions at once (engineers sprinting apart, colliding); (3) declaring agent bankruptcy — 12 terminals cranking all day, next morning "a room of strangers," so you discard the agents and redo the work, "spending tokens twice"; (4) the most important: critical decisions being made by agents — "you are ceding control of your code… if engineers across your team give up ownership of the code, you no longer own the product"
data.name: Velocity sickness

data.brief: Simulated long-horizon eval (created 2024, before long-horizon benchmarks existed) where a model runs a vending-machine business end to end — find suppliers, negotiate prices, read demand, set prices — via general-purpose tools (email, web search) in an agent loop; an arena mode pits agents with rival machines against each other (undercutting, deals). Still one-to-two orders of magnitude longer-running than most long-horizon evals two years on; latterly used to test whether long-horizon coding training generalizes off-distribution
data.name: Vending-Bench

data.brief: Real examples: vaporware the platform team could rebuild in six weeks; upside-down pricing (a wrapper asking the buyer to report its own gateway telemetry so the vendor can margin on it); demo promises with no ETA after two months; re-pitching declined features; data sent to the vendor's cloud against instructions; read-write-all default scopes; beta features on by default each release; "we'll get you the security architecture diagram next week"; "we haven't had a breach yet" as the breach plan; auto-updating clients across 3,000 people with no version control; support-page terms not in the contract; core APIs down for hours on a trading day; features shipped only as "beta" with a permissive data-retention clause; claimed ZDR that quietly retained data
data.name: The vendor anti-pattern catalog

data.brief: Nobody can keep up with everything (Karpathy included), so you rely on platforms and vendors. Beyond current capability and roadmap, look at how they handled the last transitions — "many vendors I like have reinvented themselves three times in the last year; I now trust that if something else comes along they're very good at this." The evaluation shifts from *what they do now* to *how they change*
data.name: Vendor selection by change track record

data.brief: Metronome is "a very complicated and deep product with a lot of foot-guns," so the vendor ships an extensible, portable set of skills files that give the implementing agent context for its API, plus much more verbose, clearer error messages so the agent can self-correct; the DX team hunts failure cases, especially in initialization. The skills direct the agent to flow test usage into the sandbox so a "live customer" can be inspected. Deliberately not production without a human — "business-critical, deep business logic" — the coding agent accelerates into a test environment
data.name: Vendor-shipped skills files and self-correcting errors

data.brief: TypeScript SDK for building AI/agent features in web applications; cited as the marker of the TS AI-ecosystem surge (1.6M → 15.1M weekly downloads in one year)
data.name: Vercel AI SDK

data.brief: Vercel's agent framework, released days before the talk — pitched as "build a company brain, personal assistant, or domain-specific agent"; cited by the speaker as the closest thing yet to a defined way to build an agent, and the first mainstream product copy to use the term "domain-specific agent"
data.name: Vercel Eve

data.brief: Cai's decomposition of Verifier's Law into a classifier you can apply to any profession's tasks: asymmetry of verification (how hard is it to decompose the task into checkable steps), veracity of verification (how much consensus exists about what correct even means), and proliferation of verification (how often does the real world hand you fresh examples of verified work). Coding matured first because GitHub scored high on all three at once. Biology, security, taste, finance, healthcare and law score low on veracity and decomposition with examples locked inside enterprise workflows web 2.0 never captured.
data.name: Three axes of verifiability

data.brief: The talk's stated single takeaway: treat a fuzzy capability as a routing problem. Decompose the domain into components arranged on an objective-to-subjective spectrum (vision alignment and typography near the objective end; style fit and creativity far from it), then route each component to the method that fits it — an RL environment where it can be made programmatically verifiable, post-training data where it can't, context and user-intent work at the application layer, and human judgment where it must stay human.
data.description: Codification is the lever that moves a component leftward: brand adherence starts as human-judgment territory and gets pulled "into the realm of verification" by identifying which pieces matter and making them observable.
data.name: Verifiability routing

data.brief: RELAI's coinage: continual learning where every fix is proven to help and proven to break nothing that already worked — executable test (replay the failure), measured delta (score before/after), regression tests (prior tests still pass); four principles: replayability, holisticness, lifelongness, efficiency
data.name: Verifiable continual learning (VCL)

data.brief: The industry standard PayPal wants convergence on for open, high-stakes agent payments: a multi-layered, selectively disclosed JWT — layer one from a trustworthy credential provider, layer two the user's instructions to the agent signed with the user's private key, layer three (autonomous payments) signed by the agent — so merchants verify the checkout, processors verify the payment mandate, and nobody needs a prior relationship. Not yet seen in production; the same construction fits any hard-to-reverse action (medical orders, e-signatures, securities trades)
data.name: FIDO verifiable intents and AP2 mandates

data.brief: The gap between the quality AI tools produce by default and the quality the application actually needs — a gap that scales with criticality. For experiments, solo projects and short-lived internal tools the gap is small enough to live with; for large codebases with many users (some adversarial), many concurrent changes and regulatory exposure, the needed quality is far above the default, and humans are pulled in to close the gap before shipping. Causes named: models are error-prone by construction; they are missing context (the wider codebase, the business, "the meeting you had 2 weeks ago"); and they don't know your objectives. ⚠ merge-check vs el-reviewdebt and el-cognitive-debt — see Review note 5
data.name: Verification debt

data.brief: The talk's core distinction. A citation shows where information came from and is "effectively an after-the-fact audit"; it got the industry "50% of the way there" and is undermined by uncurated sources (a random Substack, Seeking Alpha, Reddit are data points, not vetted sources). A verification is a deterministic, repeatable, numerically checkable mechanism proving a specific number is the correct one from a specific source. Corollary stated hard: "evals are not verifiable — you cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic", and fine-tuning to 94% extraction accuracy is not a fix because "a wrong number is still wrong if you're in that unfortunate 6%".
data.name: Verification over citation

data.brief: Prime Intellect's open-source library for RL environments and evals; V1 overhaul decomposes an environment into composable task set (agent-agnostic data + rules), harness (default tool-loop, or real CLI agents like Codex / Claude Code / OpenCode / mini-SWE-agent / RLMs), and runtime (local, Docker, or sandbox layer); repo: PrimeIntellect-ai/verifiers
data.name: Verifiers (V1)

data.brief: The ease of training a model to do a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. Used here as the organizing law of the whole data market: it explains which application-layer domains mature first and therefore where data demand goes next.
data.name: Verifier's Law (Jason Wei)

data.brief: The small piece of machinery that makes an ordinary, unmodified rollout engine participate. Three cases: if the engine is already at an acceptable committed version, the sidecar proxies the request; if it is behind but can catch up, it applies the missing transitions; if it cannot, it returns not ready. That last case is what makes the fleet genuinely elastic — any idle GPU anywhere can be enrolled, and a straggler degrades to unavailable rather than to silently-wrong
data.name: Version-aware rollout sidecar

data.brief: The data that would let a model reason about niche industries is structurally hidden: institutional managers over $100M must file 13F long positions quarterly and their returns fall measurably once others reverse-engineer them; ~30% of pharma sponsors never disclose failed trials despite the law, and the FDA publicly reminded 2,000+ of them in 2026 — the failures are the golden goose. Labs cannot buy it or annotate it (NDAs; the experts earn more than $100/hour). The moat is therefore expertise plus data that is not on the internet; model, infrastructure and ecosystem are commodities
data.name: Why the vertical data was never there

data.brief: The safety architecture that gives the talk its title: assume the AI-written code is buggy and make the bugs non-events. Client UI runs in a null-origin iframe sandbox with CSP — no network, no cookies, nothing but postMessage to the parent; over that channel a Cap'n Web RPC session forwards to the gadget's server code, a Durable Object running in a dynamic-worker sandbox equally cut off from the world. A vibe-coded client and vibe-coded server can talk only to each other, so "there is no security bug you can have in this code that matters" — demonstrated with an agent-added paste-SVG feature where potential XSS simply has nowhere to go. External-service access exists but only through a platform-mediated system
data.name: Double-ended vibe-code confinement

data.brief: Use cases vary (session-level quality judgments, image annotation, manual testing, trajectory evals for multi-agent systems) and a platform team can't build a UI per case — but the underlying patterns are the same, so with stable APIs the operators use Codex or Claude Code to vibe-code their own annotation UIs. Result: reduced per-annotation spend at DoorDash scale, faster loops, higher velocity
data.name: Vibe-coded annotation UIs on stable APIs

data.brief: Representing a video collection as a context graph — a durable, queryable structure: time-bounded moments (evidence units) → appearances (where/when each entity shows) → entities (people, brands, places, concepts) → relationships, co-occurrences, timelines → corpus-level context (themes, patterns, gaps, coverage). Different question classes traverse different levels (search hits moments; entity workflows expand from a person into appearances; narrative questions follow relationships across time). Memory = a navigable structure over the entire video volume.
data.name: Video context graph

data.brief: Harness-engineered agent for video, contrasted with a static stateless model call: operates inside a deterministic system, knows what memory is available, plans tasks, retrieves evidence, inspects moments, synthesizes, validates, and returns output under an operating envelope (explicit time/cost/depth/scope/autonomy limits) and an output contract, with the whole workflow evaluable.
data.name: Video worker

data.brief: The reverse direction of MCP Apps interactivity, in the spec now and "released very soon": until this, the flow was app→host (user clicks, app raises an event, host decides); view tools ("app tools" — both names used in-talk) let the chat drive the app — "fill out this form for me" and the host operates the embedded UI on the user's behalf. Explicitly framed as MCP Apps standardizing what WebMCP (Google's standard for agent↔web-view interaction) addresses
data.name: View tools (host→app channel)

data.brief: The data goal of GTM engineering: a perfect model of the accounts and contacts you target, kept current although accounts change constantly (acquisitions, new offices and products, your own marketing changing their status, hiring and firing as signals). Populate current contacts, then hierarchy, firmographics, technographics and signals; since no single vendor gives the whole picture, enrich by waterfall across many providers and cross-check them; refresh selectively because data is expensive (headcount moves daily, headquarters rarely); ingest signal programs continuously; and reconcile the same entity across sources. Without this layer automated GTM is very hard; with it the interesting work begins
data.name: A virtual copy of the market

data.brief: The bootstrapping step: ~6–7k assets couldn't be hand-tagged, so a vision model screenshots and describes each (astronaut, knight, castle) to seed the tag/description index the assistant searches. Vision models as the mechanism for making a large asset library agent-navigable
data.name: Vision-model asset tagging

data.brief: The market thesis: because humans understand best with a visual component, most AI-human interaction will carry a visual layer, and LemonSlice builds that layer as an API over any voice agent — "anything that's a voice agent today becomes a video agent." A claim about the default modality of future AI interfaces, not just an avatar product
data.name: The visual layer on every AI interaction

data.brief: Open-source verification piece: the agent turns a design.md of design rules into checks (inferring them if unwritten) and runs two kinds — a visual on-brand/layout check and an automated user-flow walkthrough (adds/deletes tasks like a real user) — then writes a pass/fail report a human reviews
data.name: Perception-agent verification

data.brief: The input stage, argued as the load-bearing one: dictation runs ~200 words per minute and "will be faster than any other method unless you're an absolute Olympic typist," so it is how you generate the volume of raw material the later stages need. Explicitly permissive about quality — scrappy, rambly, unformatted is fine, because the agent does the structuring. Local, on-device options named (Handy, open source; VoiceInk, one-off fee) as removing the subscription barrier
data.name: Voice-first raw capture

data.brief: Interaction paradigm pairing spoken input (highest-bandwidth human output: more words/minute, more meaning per word) with generated visual output (rich HTML, interactive controls, images); trades the ~200ms conversational-voice latency budget for the ~1s visual attention envelope, so real-time AI feels seamless without waiting for novel model architectures
data.name: Voice in, visuals out

data.brief: The interaction pattern the team calls the key capability for IoT and edge devices: a small ASR model in front of a fine-tuned tiny action model that maps arbitrary free-text input to one of a fixed set of device functions. Demonstrated with a mobile actions model covering ~10 output functions at over 86% reliability on arbitrary text — schedule a calendar event, turn Wi-Fi on or off — entirely on device. The motivation is interface, not novelty: small devices push their capabilities into settings menus, which are a genuine accessibility barrier, and speaking the desired outcome replaces the menu.
data.name: Voice-to-function-calling

data.brief: Bugcrowd/CMU pipeline built on a decade of DARPA-funded work on novel vulnerability discovery: mine unique, previously unknown proofs of vulnerability out of open-source software and package them as reinforcement-learning environments. Zero-days are used deliberately so that success cannot be memorization of public exploits. Operated at commercial scale — "up to 10,000 reinforcement learning environments per month" delivered to model companies to accelerate their cybersecurity training, positioned as continuing where benchmarks show frontier models stop.
data.name: Zero-day mining machine (RL-environment supply)

data.brief: Seller-side edge monetization: AWS WAF detects 650+ bot types (PerplexityBot, GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google's), classifies intent (fetching to train vs answering a RAG search), verifies bots by signature so partners get their own pricing, and — with CloudFront — charges for content over x402 by path (/blog vs /research vs an API), bot identity (verified vs unverified vs human) and intent, through WAF rules that can be combined. No SDK or origin change, no transaction or subscription fees, publishers keep 100% of revenue; dashboards show revenue by bot and path; internal APIs MCPified through the gateway can be monetized the same way
data.name: WAF AI traffic monetization

data.brief: Agents make one-, five- and ten-cent calls constantly, so a human approving each is impossible; instead the wallet enforces policy — maximum per call (15 cents in the demo), per session, per day — and the agent stays autonomous inside it. The authorization decision moves from the moment of purchase to the budget policy
data.name: Guardrails in the wallet, not per-transaction approval

data.brief: The missing infrastructural layer that lets an agent "operate freely on the open web": search (fan-out queries over indexed engines), fetch (validated, lightweight, geolocated content without a browser), and — only for execution — a stealthy browser with residential proxy and geolocation. Structured as the shopping agent's stages: discovery → decision → user confirmation → purchase, with the browser confined to the last
data.name: The web-access layer

data.brief: The reframing under the category: historically the web was the world's greatest *data* source; with knowledge-work agents it becomes a *context* source — "the data itself is only a step for something bigger: the actions I take, the conclusions I draw, every downstream application." And search only tells part of the story — you can search a sneaker's price this morning but not how it changed over six months, or a company's open roles but not its headcount over time. There is far more context in the web than search extracts
data.name: Web as context, not just data

data.brief: The discipline the talk proposes: optimizing *how* an agent sources web context per task and per team, mixing AI-search (ad hoc, always-changing needs) and CaaS/owned pipelines (persistent, consistent, escalating needs) rather than throwing AI-search at everything. "As an AI engineer I need to serve different teams with different needs — it's tempting to throw AI search at all of them, but maybe that's not optimal." Frequency is "the cost killer," and the tipping point "is much lower than you think"
data.name: Web context engineering

data.brief: The first war story's lesson: a client's "video API for AI training" ask (5PB/month, two-week deadline) "stops sounding like a product feature and sounds like infrastructure" — collection, transfer, storage, delivery, at AI-training reliability. It grew by iteration (downloader → transcripts → *actually* subtitles → search → metadata → channel info) into a full multimodal suite in ~3 months. "Clients don't buy the first product iteration, they buy your ability to adapt." AI infrastructure is increasingly multimodal — video, metadata, transcripts, subtitles, structural context around content
data.name: Web data as pipeline, not feature

data.brief: Google's standard for how agents interact with web views; named in the talk only as the thing MCP Apps absorbs into view/app tools — the two standardization efforts converging on one host-mediated channel
data.name: WebMCP

data.brief: Replaces server-sent events over HTTP with a persistent WebSocket carrying stateful context, so each turn sends only what changed — a tool call returns just its result rather than replaying every item (demoed as 1 item versus 9). Built because at ~1,000 tok/s "inference was no longer the bottleneck, it was actually the network"; the win compounds across the many tool calls an agent makes
data.name: WebSocket mode (stateful Responses transport)

data.brief: Proposed success metric for delegation-era products: a task completed by a human or an agent, counted whether or not the user is on the platform; replaces weekly active users — the target is WAU down while WAS up
data.name: Weekly active sessions (WAS)

data.brief: The boundary conditions where keep-everything fails and you must compact/retrieve: local models (hardware caps context — a 32k MacBook window can't hold lessons that individually exceed it; raising model *size* doesn't raise the *window*), and any context exceeding the window. Their decision rule: "do not compact by default — name the constraint, then choose." Final production choice: DeepSeek V4 Flash (cheapest given cache discount) + hybrid retrieval + keep-everything up to a 30k-token compaction threshold
data.name: When compaction still wins

data.brief: The open-source, self-hostable Cloudflare Workers runtime. The entire demo ran locally on Varda's laptop on workerd (which is why the venue's dead internet didn't matter), and his stated intent is basement self-hosting for home automation via Home Assistant and Spotify connectors
data.name: workerd

data.brief: Anthropic's *Building Effective Agents* (2024): workflows are predictable and controllable, agents flexible but less predictable — start simple, avoid frameworks. So the outreach was a workflow. By late 2025 Anthropic's own workshop said models are good enough that agents may beat workflows; Cursor replaced 12,000 lines of custom workflow with a 200-line skill. His follow-up automation therefore became an autonomous agent — "I can replace thousands of lines of custom code with a simple agent with a CLI as a tool and a skill"
data.name: Workflow first, agent when the models allow

data.brief: Build tasks from a known-reachable end state and then throw the solution away. Documents: sample a corpus, have models generate grounded question/answer pairs, verify with other grounded models that the questions are answerable, then discard the source so the real task is upstream of the answer. Code: take real PRs — diffs, descriptions, test cases — and remove pieces of files, so a completed artifact becomes a target you know is reachable. General principle: "verify the easy problem and learn on the hard problem"; supervision for free wherever you can move backwards from a solution.
data.name: Working-backwards task synthesis

data.brief: Pushback on "software factory" ("where's the people in this?") via a potter who sells hundreds of handcrafted mugs a day: the craft is in the *workshop* — stations, sourcing, verification steps ("if the dimple isn't right, what part of the process restarts?"), observation of how people work, refinement over time. Workshops are heavy-duty, malleable, signal-reactive systems for doing work, in a close loop with the humans in them. Software's version: event-reactive automations, observability, a system that modifies itself toward its goals, and cost-effectiveness (fewer broken mugs, fewer wasted tokens)
data.name: The workshop, not the factory

data.brief: Reactor's infra thesis: serving real-time interactive video is fundamentally different from batch video generation. Batch = a request runs a cloud job returning a file; real-time needs streaming pixels server→client, treats everything as a live session with memory (the hard problem: models like Genie 3 forget when a character looks away, so maintaining the context window is core), and needs global scale — sub-100ms latency means routing a user in India/Japan to a nearby GPU, or "the medium breaks." Integratable in ~10 lines of code behind an API key
data.name: The world behind an API

data.brief: Learned, high-fidelity simulation of the systems you cannot program against — MCP or CLI tools, websites, applications whose back-end state you don't control. Built from universal back-end infrastructure plus test-time scaling and search, iterating between the simulator and the real system and grounding in production traces, with agents refining the implementation. Two payoffs: production data makes the simulator monotonically better, and full back-end controllability lets you plant the answer — verifiability baked into the simulator even where the real deployment has none and you can't know in advance whether a task was solvable.
data.name: World simulator

data.brief: LLMs work best within clear, limited, predictable boundaries, and X12 — the public EDI standard for eligibility (270), attachments (275), acknowledgments (999), remittance (835) and the rest — is exactly that: a structured contract between what the agent means and what the insurer accepts. Every payer interaction, including phone calls and browser portals that are not X12, reduces to an X12-like internal transaction, so the whole 50-step claim journey becomes a sequence of typed transactions the agent executes and the system can check. Because the schemas are public, an agent asked to generate one produces something grounded rather than invented, and a new engineer can read it
data.name: X12 as the agent harness

data.brief: Coinbase's agent-payment protocol (May 2025) built on HTTP's long-reserved 402 Payment Required: the client calls, the server must answer 402 with payment requirements, the client signs a payment from its wallet, the server verifies it with a facilitator (e.g. Coinbase), does the work, then asks the facilitator to settle on-chain (Base; stablecoins). Payment schemes: exact (fixed price per call), upto (a ceiling the server charges against; promised December 2025, shipped mid-2026), and the new batch settlement (escrowed deposit, vouchers, off-chain micro-signatures, batched on-chain settlement). No protocol fees, nominal gas, ~200 ms settlement; under Linux Foundation open governance with Coinbase, AWS, Google, Stripe, Anthropic, Cloudflare and Circle behind it; ~20× the transactions and volume of Stripe's MPP
data.name: x402

data.brief: (1) Between signature and on-chain settlement the buyer can reuse the same funds — sign 1,000 requests, get 1,000 results — so servers with non-zero marginal cost must settle *before* doing the work; (2) x402 mandates a 402 first response while MCP auth mandates 401, so vendors duplicate hosts per payment protocol (x402.example.com, mcp.example.com, mpp.example.com) — "20 different Amazons for 20 credit cards"; headers alone should be allowed; (3) exact is for fixed-price calls, not jobs that run seconds to hours with metered resources — upto arrived late and still double-spends — so Apify charges a fixed amount and refunds the remainder (two transactions, settlement delay, fees, trust). Batch settlement is the promising fix, not yet implemented
data.name: x402's rough edges: double spend, 402 vs 401, metering

data.brief: Yutori's computer-use model. V1 (Nov 2025) acted purely human — screenshot in, clicks/scrolls out. The next version writes JavaScript on demand (a Chrome extension filling multiple form fields via a generated function): "click buttons when you have to, write code when you have to, and look at the result through pixels, because that is the source of truth" — the screenshot acting as a built-in verification system. N1.5 reported at 97% human eval on Online-Mind2Web (8/300 trajectories incorrect — "retire the benchmark, build something harder"), competitive with Opus 4.7/GPT-5.5 on browser-use benchmarks but at far lower latency (smaller footprint) and ~$0.80 per 20–30-step task versus ~$2.30 (⚠ figures caption-sourced, see review note 3). Orchestratable: one orchestrator launching parallel Navigators in cloud sandboxes, "superhuman because no human can parallelize that many instances"
data.name: Navigator (Yutori)

data.brief: Enterprise agent-memory infrastructure built on Graphiti; derives context/agent memory from many user touchpoints (chat, voice transcripts, email, business data) for multi-agent, multi-user, multi-source scenarios.
data.name: Zep

data.brief: Language-level premise that in a world where nobody reads all the code, the execution trace is the comprehension surface — including where time was spent in which part of the program. Argued to be impossible to retrofit ("think about how slow your program would be if you had to trace everything in Python or TypeScript — it's untenable") and effectively free if designed in from first principles. Built for two consumers at once: humans, and agents — every file carries a tracing system Claude can navigate to find bugs, errors and inefficiencies and optimize the code itself.
data.name: Zero-cost execution tracing

data.brief: Volkov's framework (coined ~82 days before the talk): a spectrum from Zechner ("read every effing line of critical code") to Lopopolo ("code is free; inspect the system, not every line"), with a capability-drift arrow — model improvements keep pushing the industry toward the YOLO pole. His own correction: the continuum sorts *tasks*, not people — the same engineer should sit at both ends for different changes; the operative question is "what proof does this specific change need?"
data.name: The Z/L continuum (route-to-proof framework)

data.brief: Automated statistical pipeline (methods + guardrails + thresholds + prioritization) that scans commercial-pharma data for KPI anomalies/trends and puts confirmed signals on a queue; the agent wakes only when a signal arrives — "the agent's job is to investigate, not to identify"
data.name: Deterministic signal-detection pipeline

data.brief: On-prem AI platform for regulated industries. PrivateGPT (57k stars). Air-gapped, fixed-cost.
data.description: Full-stack on-prem AI platform from the PrivateGPT creators (57k stars). Air-gapped, fixed-cost, production-ready in days. Three tiers: cloud VPC, managed on-prem (via certified partners), or "Zylon in a Box" pre-configured server.
data.name: Zylon
